By explicitly modeling the resolution gap through statistical learning, sAMY enables generation of continuous 90-year stochastic ensembles (2011–2100), facilitating multi-year extreme event assessment using publicly available data. The framework provides a reproducible pathway for climate-informed weather files that preserve observational realism and climate signal fidelity.

title: Towards zero emission building by refurbishment: A multi-criteria decision-making approach
abstract: With each revision of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD), the requirements for both new and refurbished buildings have become increasingly demanding, driven by the need to reduce CO2 emissions, lower energy dependency, and enhance user comfort. Fortunately, the market now offers a wide range of solutions to meet these goals both through the use of passive (different envelopes) and active (HVAC systems) measures. In this context, optimization algorithms play a key role in identifying optimal design strategies. However, there is no single solution that satisfies the regulatory requirements, and additional factors such as initial investment, operational costs, and user comfort, among others, can lead to significantly different results. This research proposes a hybrid approach that combines multi-attribute decision-making algorithms with multi-objective optimization algorithms in the search for optimal solutions that take into account both regulatory requirements and user-specific criteria. Through the analysis of a real case study, a four-dwelling building in the south of France, the research shows the different configurations and objectives of the optimization algorithm used, the Non-Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), as well as the key performance indicators (initial investment, operational cost, CO2 emissions, comfort, etc.) used by the multi-attribute decision making algorithm, TAMARIN, that help to select the most suitable solution for the user.

title: Automated urban archetypes: Integrating urban morphology and topology for scalable urban building energy modeling
abstract: Climate change and urban densification have escalated energy demand in urban environments, highlighting the need for sustainable energy strategies. Existing urban-scale energy models are structured with aggregated building archetypes to represent energy consumption at the urban scale, often overlooking intra-building relationships within urban settings, limiting the scalability of energy applications. This paper introduces urban archetype, a graph-based representation enriched with metadata that maps cities to representative urban archetypes. This model captures both the morphological characteristics of buildings and their topological relationships within urban fabrics. Applied to San Francisco, the framework identifies four urban archetypes that reproduce city-scale annual energy consumption with 2.77% error compared to a full-resolution baseline with 4170 blocks, and preserves spatial structure (Δ Moran’s I = 0.6%). This approach supports city-scale energy simulation, community-level energy strategies, and downstream urban analytics while substantially reducing computational cost, offering a scalable, data-driven foundation for energy-resilient urban design.

title: Short-term probabilistic forecasting of residential electricity consumption via the Hungarian algorithm
abstract: Accurate residential load forecasting is essential for effective energy management and demand response. At the household level, high variability in consumption patterns makes short-term forecasting particularly challenging. Many forecasting approaches are built on point-wise error metrics that treat each time step independently and do not explicitly account for temporal misalignment of shifted demand peaks; in probabilistic forecasting, this can lead to overly sharp yet miscalibrated predictive distributions and temporal spreading of peaks across adjacent time steps. To address this limitation, this paper presents the novel application of the Hungarian Algorithm (HA) in a probabilistic forecasting framework for individual household electricity consumption, formulating forecasting using the solution of an optimal temporal assignment problem that explicitly resolves peak misalignment. Recognizing the HA’s high computational demands, the paper also introduces a clustering-based data-reduction method to substantially enhance computational efficiency, enabling practical deployment on large-scale datasets. The proposed method is evaluated on three real-world residential datasets and consistently improves over benchmark models, reducing CRPS by about 5.3–7.0% and MAE by about 3.6–6.7% relative to the kNN baseline. The clustering technique reduces runtime by about an order of magnitude, from 1 s to about 0.1 s per task, while maintaining comparable accuracy, making the approach computationally practical at scale.

title: Thermoelectric performance of ultra-high-performance concrete incorporating nano carbon black and its interaction with mechanical properties
A cross-sectional survey of effect of physical and perceived environmental qualities on occupants’ mental wellbeing and satisfaction in Chinese offices
abstract: The indoor environment in an office is a complex psycho-physical system comprising not only physical space (the nature and arrangement of all the objects) but also perceived environment (occupants’ perceptions and evaluations for objects). However, how physical and perceived environmental qualities of offices can affect occupants’ mental health and satisfaction have not been fully identified due to the inconsistent findings across studies, especially in Chinese office buildings. This study presented a cross-sectional survey conducted in 108 office buildings in China’s four main urban agglomerations, collecting physical environmental factors (24 variables) and subjective feedback from 1131 occupants. The occupants’ subjective responses were evaluated in terms of perceived environment (nine variables), psychosocial factors (job demand & social capital), mental wellbeing and satisfaction. The structural equation modelling (SEM) was adopted to test the relationships between physical/perceived environmental factors and mental wellbeing, and between physical/perceived environmental factors and satisfaction, and the mediating effects of psychosocial factor on these relationships. Key findings were achieved as follows. Occupants’ mental wellbeing was associated with four physical factors (interior finish material, finish colour, workstation area, HVAC system) and three perceived factors (privacy, indoor climate, cleanliness and maintenance). Significant relationships were identified between satisfaction and eight physical factors (business events centre, amenity space, finish material, finish colour, finish pattern, window to wall ratio, workstation area, and HVAC system) and between satisfaction and four perceived factors (decoration, privacy, indoor climate, cleanliness and maintenance). These associations can be fully or partially mediated by psychosocial factors (job demand and social capital).

title: Hygrothermal performance of bio-based building materials in urban street canyons
A novel electric energy router for enhancing the resilience of building distribution networks under extreme cold wave conditions
Photovoltaic yield gains from green roof retrofitting: A multi-year field study accounting for structural bias
abstract: • Small structural asymmetries between PV areas can substantially bias PVGR yield data, highlighting the need for pre-retrofit data analysis or shading simulations in future studies. • Correction methods reduce the apparent yield gain during the vegetation period from ∼ 3 % to a net range of 0.95–1.14 %, reflecting the combined effect of increased module mounting height and vegetation cooling. • Lack of maintenance and vegetation overgrowth can temporarily negate or reverse yield gains. The integration of photovoltaics (PV) with green roofs is widely promoted as a synergistic building technology, yet reported impacts on PV electricity generation remain inconsistent. A major factor is the limited comparability bewteen PV systems in field studies, where structural differences are often confounded with vegetation effects. This study presents a long-term, large-scale assessment of PV yield changes following the retrofit of an extensive green roof, while explicitly accounting for such structural biases. Two adjacent PV systems on an operational office building in Austria were monitored, one remaining gravel-covered and the other retrofitted with an extensive green roof. Despite identical modules and layouts, pre-retrofit measurements revealed inherent performance differences between the two arrays, primarily caused by asymmetric shading. To account for this bias, different empirical normalization approaches based on pre-retrofit data and a simulation-based correction were applied. Performance in 2023 was variable, with temporary negative deviations caused by vegetation overgrowth and operational anomalies. For March–August 2024, when the green roof was well-maintained, the raw comparison indicates a yield advantage of 2.99 % for the greened system. After applying the correction methods, the net system-level increase ranges between 0.95 % and 1.14 %, depending on the method. This increase reflects both the effect of the green roof itself and the additional mounting height required for the retrofit. While the study indicates a small benefit for the specific configuration, it also underscores the importance of identifying and correcting structural biases when assessing PVGRs.

title: Dynamic thermal comfort in part-time-local-space heating mode: Interplay effects of localized space heating terminal forms and zonal temperature transitions
Heat pipe integration in vapor compression systems for building energy efficiency: A critical review
Penguin-inspired Antarctic research station design strategies: Integrating proximal policy optimization with bio-inspiredheat-conservation strategies
Modeling policies for the EU building stock decarbonization at sub-national resolution
abstract: Understanding how the energy needs of the different sectors will evolve in the future is key to informing climate policy design. For the buildings sector, this involves considering heterogeneity in technological, socioeconomic and climatic conditions. In this paper, we develop a building energy sectoral model for Europe that considers technology adoption dynamics at the subnational scale, with high (0.5° x 0.5°) resolution. The model focuses on energy efficiency by considering building renovation, space heating, space cooling, and their interplay. We simulate wide-scale renovation waves in Europe, understanding where we may expect more household renovation efforts, and where policy support will be most needed in the following decades. Space cooling energy demand increase is expected, along with a substantial reduction of space heating energy demand and a general electrification of end-uses. This study implies that energy renovation investments in EU27 need to increase by roughly 18%, in respect with historical data, to significantly reduce energy demand and emissions. Spatial clustering of renovation activities, which this work uncovers with unprecedented detail across the EU both between and within countries, should be anticipated and explicitly accounted for in the design of European-level policy instruments. To increase renovation rates through subsidies, we find that public government support should roughly match private investments, especially in those regions where the conditions of the building stock, construction costs and energy expenditures might not motivate households to renovate. This is a significant departure from the current situation where private investments are about 20 times higher than public ones.

title: Exploring the impact of urban morphology on land surface temperature in urban functional zones: A case study of Xi’an, China
Multi-dimensional analysis of indoor temperature in Chinese district heating systems: Across different heating periods and building energy efficiency levels
A coordinated scheduling approach with electricity peak shaving capability for integrated office Building-EV system
Informative yet compact monitoring for building retrofits: Joint information entropy–based measurement system design applied to a real office building
abstract: Building energy retrofits are essential for enhancing the sustainability of the built environment. However, their effectiveness is impacted by the performance gap, the difference between expected and actual building energy performance, particularly when pre-retrofit building knowledge is inaccurate. Advances in monitoring technologies have improved the ability to measure energy performance and indoor environmental quality, helping to reduce this gap. Nevertheless, the systematic design of measurement systems remains insufficiently explored. Measurement-system design in building energy contexts, carried out prior to sensor installation, requires the simultaneous consideration of measurement type, location, and time interval. The integrated treatment of these design parameters has received little attention, especially in full-scale applications. This study addresses these gaps by implementing an approach that identifies the most informative measurements through the maximization of joint information entropy, demonstrated in a full-scale case study of an office building in Germany. Using building management system data from 2017, measurements were ranked with a hierarchical greedy algorithm that maximized joint entropy. The resulting ranking was validated through system identification. The findings indicate a trend between increased joint entropy and improved model parameter identification performance, suggesting that joint entropy is a meaningful proxy for information gain in building energy retrofit scenarios. Comparable system-identification performance was achieved using only 45% of the available measurement devices, demonstrating the potential for compact yet informative measurement systems. While the findings are specific to this study and future research is recommended to generalize the observations, this study provides empirical evidence that maximum-entropy-based measurement system design supports rational and efficient monitoring strategies for assessing building energy performance and guiding retrofit decision-making.

title: Load separation method for Enhancing performance of central heat pump water heater system with hot water recirculation
Experimental study of thermo-mechanical properties of binary PCM-fiber composite energy piles
Revisiting the potential of geothermal heat pump systems in cold climates with thermal energy storage
Risk-informed multi-objective techno-economic assessment of air-to-liquid retrofits with heat recovery in legacy air-cooling data centers
Temporal resolution matters: a comparative life cycle assessment with energy balancing using real, annual, and disaggregated data
abstract: Life Cycle Assessment of buildings is used to support renovation and decarbonization decisions, yet it usually relies on annually aggregated operational energy data that neglect temporal variability in consumption, generation, and grid interactions. This study quantifies the influence of temporal resolution on LCA outcomes by comparing three operational data representations: (i) real monitored hourly electricity consumption and photovoltaic production, (ii) synthetic disaggregated hourly data reconstructed from annual values, and (iii) annual aggregated values. The analysis is applied to an office building in the Netherlands, assessed using a dynamic LCA framework developed within POCITYF project. Results demonstrate that, for the examined case study, the disaggregated hourly approach closely approximates the benchmark assessment based on monitored data, with deviations of 1.5% for primary energy consumption and 3.4% for global warming potential. In contrast, reliance on annual aggregated data leads to substantial underestimation, for the examined case study, of operational impacts, reaching 18.6% for primary energy consumption and 42.8% for global warming potential, due to the inability to capture intra-day and seasonal mismatches between electricity demand and on-site renewable generation. Increasing battery storage capacity reduces these discrepancies, but complete convergence is only achieved under near-isolated system conditions. The findings demonstrate that temporal resolution is shown to be a decision-relevant modelling choice in the context of buildings with dynamic operational profiles, rather than a secondary methodological detail. Annual aggregation can produce structurally biased results for grid-connected buildings with dynamic operational profiles, while disaggregated hourly data offer a promising alternative under conditions similar to those examined when high-resolution monitoring is unavailable. This work provides empirical evidence and practical guidance for improving the reliability of building LCA in renovation and positive energy district contexts.

title: The effect of climate change, building retrofit and cooling system adoption on future thermal energy demand in the Swiss building stock
abstract: Analysing the evolution of thermal energy demand of buildings based on different scenarios is essential for assessing the effectiveness of national energy policies. This study applies a bottom-up archetype model in combination with a dynamic building simulation model to calculate the heating and cooling demand of Swiss residential and non-residential buildings based on different climate and retrofit scenarios. The results show a substantial reduction in space heat demand in 2050 (MFH: 32-48%, SFH: 44-56%, Offices: 23-32%, Schools: 21-31%). Assuming climate scenario RCP 2.6 and an advanced retrofit scenario (annual deep retrofit rate = 1.5%, assumed to be fully effective, predominantly with renewable heating), final energy consumption for residential space heating is expected to reach 21.7 TWh/year in 2050, compared to 39.9 TWh/year in 2023. This demonstrates that retrofit policies and the adoption of more efficient heating systems will substantially reduce heat consumption, but will not be sufficient to achieve the reduction targets according to the national energy plan (18 TWh/year by 2050). Among the various factors influencing these savings, the switch to more efficient heating systems is most effective (-36.8%), followed by building envelope retrofit (-23.7%) and the effects of climate change (-6.0%). Assuming different adoption levels for cooling (10%-45%), the related electricity demand will increase substantially, considering population growth and rising average temperatures (MFH: 234-350%, SFH: 235-394%, Offices: 7-35%, Schools: 200-300%). Building envelope retrofit leads to a substantial reduction in specific heat demand for all types of buildings, with an average of 57% for residential buildings, but at the same time leads to an increase in specific cooling needs (average 5.8 kWh/m²/year).

title: Generalizable annual daylighting performance prediction: Unified-field encoding for partitioned interiors
Digitalization of buildings for energy Efficiency: Life cycle assessment of two building monitoring systems
abstract: The digitalization trend in buildings is accelerated with advancements in information and communication technologies (ICT). These technologies enable many opportunities in buildings to achieve resource and energy efficiency based on either monitoring or advanced control of buildings. The ICT solutions’ overall impacts on the environment are often presumed positive without an assessment based on life cycle thinking. The research on ICT solutions in buildings is mainly related to occupancy, energy, and indoor environmental monitoring with the focus on technical performance and potential benefits while the environmental impacts are often overlooked. This paper analyses two case study buildings in Sweden with building monitoring systems (BMS) based on life cycle assessment (LCA) methodology. The two cases were chosen to represent a range between simple and more sophisticated. The results show that sensors and wires contribute significantly to several impact categories and the impacts of electronics used for data acquisition are also important. The climate impact of the production phase is significantly higher than the use and waste management. Depending on the energy mix, the minimum required energy saving to offset the climate impacts of the BMSs are 5% (standard BMS) and 24% (extensive BMS). This is comparable to the energy savings that often are assumed when building monitoring systems are introduced. Thus, the direct impacts of the enabling technologies for digitalization might be significant and it is crucial to employ a life cycle perspective when assessing the environmental benefits of digital solutions in buildings.

title: Self-assembled thermoresponsive colloidal particles for smart windows and structural color ink displays
Occupant-aware co-optimization strategy for shading and lighting in open-plan offices
Machine-learning assisted optimization of residential building envelopes across contrasting Italian climates: energy, thermal comfort, and carbon footprint
abstract: Energy efficiency, thermal comfort, and life-cycle carbon are central to residential design, yet practical automated workflows that scale across climates remain rare. This study aims to optimize residential envelopes in two contrasting Italian climates, identify cross-climate solutions that remain competitive in both contexts, and then re-rank the shortlist with life-cycle carbon (A1–A3, B6) to reveal energy–carbon interactions. This study develops and validates an automation pipeline around EnergyPlus that explores 14,400 envelope options and simulates 2,880 space-filling cases (Latin Hypercube with corner-point coverage) to model EUI, heating/cooling loads, and comfort (PMV/PPD). Eight algorithms are benchmarked as surrogates under a uniform tuning budget. CatBoost delivers the best fidelity for EUI and heating, while a tuned artificial neural network performs best for cooling and PMV; both achieve R 2 > 0.96 with low errors across targets. Re-simulation and Pareto-front identification yield five top-performing envelopes per city and reveal a robust overlapping subset that remains competitive in both climates. Although the most energy-efficient design (Wall 12) achieved top simulation scores, its high embodied carbon reversed its overall ranking; the Wall 14 configuration emerged as the most balanced low-carbon solution across climates, as confirmed by a component-level sensitivity analysis identifying walls as the dominant carbon contributors. The workflow demonstrates cross-climate portability by accurately predicting building performance in an unseen climate (Rome) using local weather descriptors and envelope U-values, incorporates boundary-aware sampling, identifies high-accuracy surrogate models for each key performance indicator (EUI, heating, cooling, PMV), and compares carbon-informed re-rankings with energy and comfort-based rankings of building envelopes.

title: Smart, data-driven decision support for neighborhood-scale energy retrofit planning
abstract: The transition toward low-carbon and resilient built environments requires scalable decision-support frameworks that extend beyond individual buildings to the neighborhood level. However, existing retrofit planning approaches often rely on fragmented datasets and tightly coupled simulation workflows that limit interoperability and transparency in decision-making processes. This study proposes an ontology-driven Knowledge Graph (KG) architecture to support data-driven, stakeholder-oriented decision making for neighborhood-scale retrofit planning. The framework semantically structures neighborhood assets, operational datasets, retrofit scenarios, and performance indicators within a unified KG that acts as an interoperability layer connecting heterogeneous data sources and analytical tools. Within this framework, retrofit intervention scenarios can be evaluated through any combination of external assessment methods such as energy simulations, life cycle cost (LCC), and life cycle assessment (LCA). The multi-domain indicators are semantically integrated into the KG and retrieved through SPARQL queries, enabling multi-criteria assessment of retrofit alternatives and transparent traceability between scenario assumptions, performance metrics, and stakeholder preferences. A multi-criteria decision analysis using PROMETHEE II is explored to perform preference-driven scenario ranking for different stakeholder profiles. The methodology is demonstrated through a real-world campus-scale case study at the Technical University of Crete, where photovoltaic and photovoltaic-battery retrofit scenarios are assessed using measured operational data. The results illustrate how the proposed KG-based architecture enables interoperable integration of datasets, simulation outputs, and decision-support analytics, supporting transparent and scalable stakeholder-oriented retrofit planning at the neighborhood scale.

title: Comparative analysis of the energetic performance of wood-fiber insulated panels in North American climates
abstract: Improving the energy efficiency of buildings is one of the most influential actions that can be taken to reduce life cycle energy costs and mitigate building and construction related environmental impacts. This can be done through the use of off-site panelized construction methods, which offer greater safety, efficiency, and speed than conventional building practices. Wood-fiber insulated panels (WIPs) are a family of prefabricated wall and roof panels for modular (new construction) and retrofit applications. These multi-component assemblies utilize wood fiber insulation as a core material adhesively bonded to engineered wood composite faces. A series of whole building energy models have been developed and simulated using EnergyPlus to assess the thermal performance and energy efficiency of buildings constructed with WIPs. Models were developed for single- and multi-family benchmark buildings representing minimum code requirements for residential applications in eight U.S. climate zones, ranging from hot and humid to subarctic conditions, and seven International Energy Conservation Code iterations. Although prior studies have examined the energy performance of residential buildings across multiple climate zones and energy code iterations, there has not been a systematic evaluation of wood fiber insulation (WFI) and WIPs using a consistent whole-building modeling framework. By simulating eight climate zones and seven successive code iterations, this work provides a holistic assessment of the relative energy performance improvements achievable with WFI-based enclosure systems in residential construction. Findings demonstrate that the use of WIPs led to an increase in efficiency in all cases considered within this study. However, modeled building performance was influenced by local climate conditions, code vintage, and building type, leading to energy use intensity improvements ranging from 3.92 to 56.5 percent. This work indicates that the deployment of these panelized systems can reduce energy consumption in multiple building types and underscores the importance of tailoring thermal performance to local climate conditions.

title: Advanced framework for evaluating energy saving potential across multiple building types via implementing multi-hybrid methods
Thermal performance of foamcrete composite blocks in hot–humid climates based on real-time monitoring
Editorial Board
Dematerializing the city in the digital era: A Structural–Internalization Transition Model (SITM)
abstract: Classical real estate models often assume specialized property types—industrial floors, office towers, and retail storefronts—remain essential for on‐site tasks. Yet occupant knowledge and technology increasingly unbind tasks from physical footprints, pushing collaboration, production, and commerce into virtual or home‐based settings. We present the Structural–Internalization Transition Model (SITM), which quantifies occupant meltdown: usage in a given category dissolves once digital readiness exceeds structural anchoring. SITM integrates occupant knowledge, building “smartness,” structural constraints, and correlation‐based reallocation, showing how meltdown from one category can reappear as intangible synergy in another—or vanish into virtual space. Using long‐horizon data (1900–2025) from Industrial, Office, Retail, and Housing, SITM reproduces (i) steep industrial contraction, (ii) partial office erosion via telework, (iii) moderate retail downsizing, and (iv) housing’s resilience. As occupant cognition—rather than cyclical rent—drives specialized usage, SITM bridges classical land‐use theory with a dematerialized digital reality, guiding policymakers facing chronic vacancy, adaptive reuse, and the post‐physical cityscape.

title: Global carbon viability of glass retrofits: Life-cycle assessment of standard, advanced and water-filled glass (WFG) building retrofit solutions
Decarbonisation potential of Switzerland’s building sector through thermal Nanogrids utilising surplus heat from neighbouring heat pumps
abstract: Space heating contributed around one third to Switzerland’s total heat consumption in 2023. Despite widespread integration of renewable energy systems, fossil systems are still dominant and contribute therefore strongly to the emissions. A fast implementable concept helping to reduce the activity of fossil systems is the thermal Nanogrid concept: small-scale local heating networks that interconnect heat-pump-heated and fossil-fuel-heated buildings to share surplus renewable heat. Using data from the federal register of buildings and dwellings combined with weather data and heating-demand modelling, potential thermal Nanogrid clusters were identified through a distance-based algorithm and evaluated under varying temperature thresholds. The results show that, in terms of fossil heat coverage relative to the required pipeline length, an optimal thermal Nanogrid configuration is achieved when the building selection criterion requires that all included buildings can be completely heated by the heat pump at outdoor temperatures of 4 °C and above. Under this condition, 85’223 potential thermal Nanogrids were identified across Switzerland, comprising 207’159 buildings. In this configuration, the existing heat-pump infrastructure could replace approximately 1.2 TWh of fossil-based heat demand, corresponding to an estimated 281 Mt of CO₂ emission reductions and 5.7 % of the total residential fossil heating demand, under the assumption that all heat pumps operate entirely on renewable electricity. The analysis further reveals significant regional variation, with the highest potential concentrated in cantons with dense residential areas such as Zurich, Bern, and Aargau. These findings demonstrate that thermal Nanogrids could serve as an effective and complementary measure to accelerate building-sector decarbonisation.

title: A methodology for evaluating the effects of personalized environmental control systems (PECS) on building whole-life CO2 emissions
abstract: Through localized control of the thermal environment, personalized environmental control systems (PECS) have demonstrated energy savings potential by effectively offsetting the conventional ambient heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) loads. A dynamic simulation-based methodology was introduced and combined with the life cycle assessment (LCA) framework to evaluate the effects of various standalone PECS on whole-life CO 2 emissions of an energy-efficient Danish office building, considering both new building and retrofit scenarios. The ambient system was a variable air volume (VAV) system. In retrofit scenarios, extending the setpoints of the ambient system with PECS reduced HVAC primary energy use by up to 6.6 kWh/m 2 /yr (50%) and whole-life CO 2 emissions by 0.9–5.1%, depending on PECS capacity and building thermal mass. In design scenarios, HVAC downsizing enabled by PECS led to 4.9–48.5% energy savings and 6.9–26.5% reductions in whole-life CO 2 emissions. Embodied CO 2 emissions were reduced by 10.4–27.9%, primarily from air handling unit and duct system downsizing. PECS with moderate capacity to offset ambient comfort limits and low maximum power use achieved the greatest operational and environmental benefits. The developed methodology supports quantifying optimal heating and cooling capacity, energy and environmental performance of PECS, and identifying building-HVAC configurations which may benefit from utilizing PECS.

title: A cross-building few-shot energy load forecasting framework via transferable temporal learning and residual correction
Operationally oriented Multi-Horizon electricity demand forecasting for industrial building zones using deep learning ensembles
A review of fly ash-based insulation materials: mechanism, application, and evaluation
Transparent radiative cooling: Review of fundamentals, materials, applications and future pathways
Comprehensive performance prediction of a semi-transparent PV-PCM ventilated curtain wall system coupled with an air handling unit
Scalable dynamic radiation-regulation fabric for improving body comfort under varying ambient temperatures
Household willingness to pay for CCS-based low-carbon cement
abstract: This study assesses the willingness to pay for low-carbon cement among Danish households, with a specific focus on cement produced in a plant implementing Carbon Capture and Storage to decarbonise its production process. The research employs the Contingent Valuation Method to estimate the premium Danish households are willing to pay for low-carbon cement used to build a hypothetical new house or terrace. Data was collected from 2,520 respondents through a national survey in Denmark during the autumn of 2023. The results indicate sample- and national-weighted mean WTPs of € 1,274 and € 1,164 for low-carbon cement for a new house, and 132 for new terrace tiles, respectively. For low-carbon cement in a new house, the WTPs translate into sample means of € 119/ton CO2 , and a national weighted WTP mean of € € 137 and € 109/ton CO2. For low-carbon cement for new terrace tiles, the WTP per ton of CO2 is € 205/ton CO 2 and € 197/ton CO 2 , respectively. The study finds that socio- demographic factors, such as gender, education level, income level, housing type and electric vehicle ownership, significantly influence WTP. Additionally, CCS awareness and positive perceptions of CCS technology are correlated with higher WTP. Only respondents with a positive perception of CCS have significant and positive WTPs for low-carbon cement products. The results suggest that market acceptance of low-carbon cement can be enhanced through targeted information campaigns, but also that higher WTPs and larger market shares potentially can be obtained if the low-carbon cement is produced with other and more accepted technologies such as photovoltaic and offshore/nearshore wind energy.

title: Energy responsive ventilation control strategies to improve sleep health for wildfire smoke resilience
abstract: Sleep health is a critical yet often overlooked dimension of pediatric patient recovery in hospitals. Conventional ventilation design primarily targets infection control and energy efficiency, with limited consideration of sleep-promoting environmental factors. Meanwhile, the growing prevalence of wildfire smoke exposure, now a major contributor to PM 2.5 exposure in the United States, further challenges hospital indoor air quality (IAQ) and patient well-being. This study develops a sleep health–driven ventilation control framework to enhance hospital resilience to wildfire smoke while maintaining energy efficiency. The proposed approach integrates a pediatric sleep health model into Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) operation strategies and is assessed using EnergyPlus simulations of a prototype hospital across 16 climate representative cities in the United States. Baseline and health-driven strategies were compared under varying air-side economizer and filtration configurations, assessed by obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) exceedance hours, energy consumption, and utility costs. Results show that the sleep health-driven strategy consistently improved IAQ, reducing OSA exceedance hours by up to 201 h (13.4%) and lowering energy use by up to 13.1 kWh/m 2 . Compared with the sleep health-driven only strategy, the strategy combined with economizer control achieved additional energy savings of up to 6.2%, with OSA exceedance hours increased slightly by 41 h. Higher filter efficiencies significantly reduced OSA exceedance hours but sometimes increased energy demand. Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value (MERV) 16 achieved the greatest energy reduction (6.9%), while High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filters increased energy use in 10 cities (0.7–6.3%) due to higher pressure drops. On average, utility cost savings reached USD 552 and USD 1,514 for MERV 14 and MERV 16, respectively. These findings demonstrate the potential of health-driven HVAC control to reduce operating costs and enhance hospital resilience to wildfire smoke across diverse climates.

title: Isolating adobe thermal performance in vernacular dwelling under cold desert climate: a case study of Ksar Zgag El-Hadjadj, Laghouat, Algeria
Integrating generative AI and BIM for sustainable construction and built Environment: An AHP–DEMATEL-based strategic framework
Hybrid SSA-GA-NARX modelling of HVAC energy consumption in buildings: a comparative study in the frame of a real case
abstract: This study addresses a key challenge in real building environments by demonstrating efficient data usage under practical constraints. The study compares advanced modelling strategies for building HVAC consumption to improve energy management systems (EMS). Two singular spectrum analysis (SSA) strategies were explored: a denoising approach that filters noise while preserving dynamics, and a component-wise approach that decomposes the signal for individual modelling. A nonlinear autoregressive with exogenous inputs (NARX) model, optimised with genetic algorithms (GAs) using small datasets, has been benchmarked against a traditional linear Box–Jenkins (BJ) model. Both models have been validated with two independent datasets. While the BJ model reproduced system behaviour accurately in specific scenarios, its performance deteriorated when generalising across broader operating conditions. The component-wise approach failed to improve NARX and significantly reduced BJ accuracy. The proposed hybrid SSA–GA–NARX approach, novel for its efficacy with limited data, has reduced errors by 4.77% and 4.48% compared to the BJ model.

title: Milp-based optimum operation of heating and cooling plants considering bidirectional heat interchange among multiple buildings in cooling season
Performance evaluation of a PCM-integrated task air conditioning system for mitigating heat stress
Evaluation of urban heat island effects based on a three-tier ecological integration network of heating and cooling sources
Multi-point indoor illuminance prediction using hybrid LSTM-XGBoost for daylight-responsive lighting control
Field-based AFDD for refrigerant undercharge in residential HVAC systems: enhancing reliability through false alarm mitigation
Enhancing thermal comfort in district heating systems through machine learning based estimation and operational control optimisation
abstract: This study investigates operational optimisation strategy of a district-heating (DH) substation supplying a DH-connected building, with the goal of reducing delivered heat while preserving an indoor-temperature-based comfort requirement. Optimisation is carried out in discrete time and only during the heating ON regime and is structured in two layers: a prediction layer, which relies on one-step-ahead surrogate models, and a decision layer, in which the optimisation selects control commands under prescribed constraints. The prediction layer comprises two one-step surrogate models: the first predicts the indoor apartment temperature at the next time step, while the second predicts the secondary-side return-water temperature at the next step. Based on these predictions, the decision layer evaluates multiple candidate secondary commands u(t)=[u1(t),u2(t)] at each step and selects the one that best meets the objective subject to the constraints. Candidate commands are bound by data-derived limits and by rate-of-change constraints between successive steps, and feasibility is further enforced through a primary-side available-power balance constraint. Within this constraint framework, an additional penalty weight βᵤ is introduced to penalize deviations from the measured (reference) commands; βᵤ is tuned via an outer bisection loop so that the resulting strategy operates at a predefined savings level (≈30% reduction in surrogate-estimated energy relative to the existing control), thereby enabling a fair comparison of comfort-signal variants. The methodology is validated using real supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) measurements and meteorological data for substation L17 (Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, University of Niš) during the 2024/2025 heating season. Performance is assessed using energy and comfort key performance indicators (KPIs), including achieved savings, the share of strictly feasible steps, fallback share, and the distribution of infeasibility causes. The results show that the proxy comfort signal significantly improves operational feasibility at the same savings level.

title: ConsenNet–based fully decentralized MARL for residential flexibility coordination in resilient community microgrids
Integrating urban morphology and thermal environment characteristics for urban form classification: A case study of Nanjing, China
A review of challenges and opportunities in occupant modeling for future residential energy demand
abstract: Electrified heating and electric mobility are increasing residential electricity demand and, together with distributed energy resources, reshaping load profiles, necessitating substantial investment in distribution grids and flexibility measures. Yet key behavioral factors that drive present and future residential demand remain poorly captured in many demand models. Activity-based, bottom-up models make dependencies explicit, better informing flexible operation and investment in low-carbon technologies. We review 45 activity-based, bottom-up models and assess coverage of appliances, domestic hot water, space heating and cooling, and electric vehicle charging, which are rarely considered jointly in one integrated model. To our knowledge, this is the first review to include activity-based mobility modeling, thereby identifying methodological gaps in consistent behavior modeling across residential energy services: First, most studies simulate single occupants and overlook interdependencies among household members. Second, predominant approaches are structurally limited in producing temporally consistent activity schedules. Together, these shortcomings hinder a consistent, cross-service representation of household demand and can bias estimates of coincident peaks and residential flexibility. We provide guidelines to overcome these shortcomings and to support high-quality behavioral foundations for future bottom-up demand modeling. Future studies should combine complementary behavioral datasets with sophisticated models (e.g., deep neural networks). Such models can capture complex dependencies to generate high-quality synthetic behavioral data as a basis for future bottom-up residential energy demand modeling. In order to ensure consistent progress in this field, reproducible validation frameworks based on open datasets are needed to enable the benchmarking and comparison of activity-based models.

title: Day-ahead net load forecasting in ZEBs: A comparative ML study with novel feature engineering and simulation-based evaluation
abstract: The growing deployment of zero-energy buildings supports the transition toward a more sustainable building stock. In practice, many of these buildings operate under behind-the-meter configurations to reduce infrastructure costs and simplify data management. However, this monitoring approach constrains the effective exploitation of their flexibility potential, as forecasting shifts from load to net load and must account for the combined uncertainty of demand and photovoltaic generation. To address this challenge, we systematically benchmark a broad range of classical machine-learning and state-of-the-art deep-learning models within a forecasting pipeline that directly predicts the net load profile of a zero-energy building. We further propose a joint hyperparameter and feature selection optimisation framework that integrates model-based feature importance with greedy forward feature addition inside a Bayesian optimisation procedure. Model performance is evaluated using conventional forecasting metrics as well as newly introduced domain-informed measures designed to assess peak and valley prediction accuracy. To reflect the ultimate objective of flexibility provision, we also embed the forecasts in a simulation-based battery dispatch framework that enhances photovoltaic self-consumption and provides peak-shaving support to a distribution transformer. Results show that although several models achieve strong statistical accuracy, XGBoost delivers superior operational performance in the simulation-based evaluation, an advantage not fully reflected by statistical error metrics. The proposed domain-informed metrics, however, successfully identify LightGBM as a consistently strong alternative in capturing operationally relevant dynamics. A sensitivity analysis across different battery capacities further reveals that the selection of forecasting model has a limited impact at low storage levels, where outcomes remain comparable, but becomes increasingly critical as storage capacity grows, significantly influencing planning and flexibility provision.

title: A probabilistic assessment of hail hazard impact on the life cycle of BMPV systems
abstract: Building-mounted photovoltaics (BMPV) are increasingly used for sustainable and autonomous energy generation in the built environment. Furthermore, policies are pushing BMPVs as enablers of a decarbonized energy grid. Their lifecycle performance is a critical factor influenced by environmental hazards. Among others, hail hazard poses a significant threat. This study presents a probabilistic risk assessment of hail hazard for BMPV systems. By leveraging the performance-based engineering approach, it incorporates hail hazard, physical vulnerabilities, and consequence modelling. The analysis employs hazard models to predict hail frequency and specific intensity measures linked to damage scenarios for BMPV. Hail size is found to be well correlated with expected damage to the front glass, making it a viable intensity measure. Hail risk can reduce the operational lifespan of BMPV by up to 10.87 years and the Energy Return on Energy Invested (EROI) by 46.52% when the glass thickness is 3.2 mm, and 2.22 years and 15.07% for a 4 mm thickness. Repair costs are significant compared to both the BMPV initial costs and the hail-related expected losses of whole buildings. This study underscores the importance of hail risk assessment for BMPV lifecycle analyses and of setting minimum impact resistance based on hail hazard levels.

title: A self-contained model-based predictive control framework for HVAC systems using sequential proactive system identification
abstract: • Proactive system identification enables automated inverse model training. • Disturbances representing solar and casual heat gains are estimated as time-variant parameters. • SARIMA models forecast disturbances for MPC. • MPC shifts HVAC loads away from on-peak electricity periods. • Heating and cooling costs reduced by 12% and 15%, respectively. This paper presents a self-contained model predictive control (MPC) framework for small commercial HVAC systems that integrates proactive system identification, short-term disturbance forecasting, and receding-horizon optimization. A proactive system identification sequence is designed to create operating conditions suitable for inverse model training and to enable systematic estimation of zone thermal parameters. Unmeasured disturbances arising from solar and casual heat gains and ventilation loads are forecast using seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA) models, which are incorporated directly into the MPC formulation. The proposed approach is demonstrated using EnergyPlus as an emulation environment on a three-zone small commercial building equipped with rooftop units. Results show that the MPC maintains indoor temperatures within comfort bounds during occupied hours while strategically exploiting thermal mass through preheating and precooling to shift loads away from on-peak electricity periods. This yields annual electricity cost reductions of 12% for heating and 15% for cooling, alongside reductions in total heating and cooling energy use of 3% and 12%, respectively. Practical considerations related to model retraining frequency, interzonal heat transfer, and system configuration are discussed, and pathways for extending the approach to larger multi-zone systems and field deployment are identified.

title: When interior thermal mass helps—and when it hurts: a dynamic parametric analysis across climate, insulation, and passive use
abstract: The effect of thermal mass on building energy demand remains a debated issue, with studies reporting both significant benefits and potentially adverse effects depending on climatic and constructive factors. This paper addresses this gap by systematically evaluating the conditions under which interior thermal mass is beneficial, neutral, or counterproductive. Using dynamic energy simulations, the study analyzes a residential building model where thermal mass is located in interior partitions and intermediate floor slabs, ensuring that all of this capacity contributes to the conditioning of the indoor spaces. In a first phase, 36 scenarios are simulated, combining three climate zones, three insulation levels, and the presence or absence of passive strategies (solar gains and night-time cross ventilation). A second phase explores eight representative cases with varying thermal mass quantities (25% to 150%) to identify optimal values. Results show that interior thermal mass consistently reduces cooling demand (typically 10–40%, corresponding to approximately 0.5–8 kWh/m 2 ·yr depending on climate, insulation level, and night-time ventilation), but may increase heating demand by up to 13 kWh/m 2 ·yr (approximately 5–7%) in cold climates (e.g., E1) with low insulation and no solar gains. In contrast, under favourable conditions—when sufficient insulation and solar gains are available—thermal mass can lead to moderate reductions in heating demand, even in cold climates. These findings indicate that the energy impact of interior thermal mass is highly context-dependent, with no universal optimum, and governed by the combined effects of climate, insulation level, and passive activation strategies. The study provides practical design guidance for energy-efficient buildings and energy retrofits and calls for its explicit consideration in performance-based regulations, especially in Southern European climates.

title: Performance analysis and optimization of the MHPA-BIPVT air-cooled curtain wall fresh air system
Computational performance assessment of very shallow energy geo-structures for multi-storey buildings in moderate climates
abstract: Energy geo-structures have been studied mainly for shallow foundation elements and predominantly in heating-oriented applications, whereas the performance of very shallow foundation-integrated heat exchangers under cooling-dominated building operation remains insufficiently quantified. This study presents a coupled thermo-hydraulic numerical assessment of two very shallow energy geo-structure configurations, namely a foundation slab and a retaining wall, integrated into a single-building closed-loop ground source heat pump (GSHP) system for a multi-storey nearly Zero Energy Building (nZEB) residential case in Cyprus. Hourly heating and cooling loads derived from a building energy model were coupled to COMSOL simulations and used together with preliminary ground-loop sizing to evaluate both short-term and yearly thermal behaviour. The investigated dwelling was strongly cooling-dominated, (August cooling demand was 4.4 times higher than February heating demand). For the foundation-slab configuration, the average outlet fluid temperature was 29.5 °C in August and 16.6 °C in February, with average HP coefficient of performance, COP HP , 5.4 and 6.5 respectively. Compared with the Air Source Heat Pump (ASHP) benchmark, the GSHP configurations showed higher COP HP (4.6 vs 6.5 in February, and 4.3 vs 5.6 in August), corresponding to an improvement of approximately 41%. Preliminary sizing also showed that full-load coverage would require approximately ∼1800 m of horizontal ground-loop pipe, whereas only ∼300 m pipe could be integrated into the foundation elements investigated. Both very shallow foundation-based GSHP configurations outperformed ASHP, but their thermal response remains strongly influenced by ambient conditions due to their very shallow depth. The retaining-wall configuration exhibits more stable thermal behaviour than the foundation slab, while the overall analysis shows that such systems are better interpreted as hybrid or partial-load geothermal solutions rather than stand-alone full-load replacements for the entire building demand. The study therefore clarifies both the performance potential and the operational limitations of very shallow foundation-integrated geothermal systems for cooling-dominated residential applications.

title: Quantifying provincial contributions to carbon intensity reduction in China’s construction industry: ML-assisted analysis via an integrated LMDI-ANCOVA framework
abstract: A clear understanding of the drivers of carbon intensity in China’s construction industry is essential for tracking progress toward emission reduction targets. We first use the traditional logarithmic mean Divisia index (LMDI) method to quantify the contributions of 30 mainland provinces and their related economic variables to the decline in construction carbon intensity from 2006 to 2020. We then adopt machine learning-assisted analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with K-means clustering as the specific machine learning technique, to quantify the effect size of driving variables. This two-step framework integrates LMDI decomposition results with statistical validation, avoiding bias from single-method analysis. Results show that provincial changes in carbon intensity, energy intensity, energy structure, output value share, and emission share jointly shape the national trend, with the eastern and northeastern regions as the main contributors. Three paradoxical phenomena are identified: (1) large provincial declines may have limited national impact when economic weight is small (Xinjiang), (2) local emission reductions may be offset by rapid economic expansion (Fujian, Shaanxi), and (3) industrial contraction may mask efficiency improvements (Liaoning). Full-chain energy intensity and provincial carbon intensity management are the dominant drivers of reduction, while the carbon reduction potential of the energy structure is relatively large. Zhejiang and Jilin made outstanding contributions, whereas several provinces restrained national progress. This study integrates provincial and national carbon intensity indicators into a unified framework, providing robust evidence for differentiated, region-specific policies to achieve China’s construction industry carbon reduction goals.

title: Redesigning a commercial kitchen grease trap for wastewater heat recovery: experimental and numerical investigation
abstract: Wastewater contains residual heat that can be exploited through technological innovation and is another source of renewable energy that can be used to heat water in buildings. This study focused on the development of novel wastewater heat recovery (WWHR) technology through a redesign of a commercial kitchen grease trap (GT). The GT acts as a heat reservoir where the primary function is to remove fats, oils and grease (FOG) from the wastewater before it is discharged into the sewer system. To exploit this heat resource, heat exchanger (HX) panels were integrated into the walls and baffle of a stainless-steel GT in order to optimally transfer heat from the hot wastewater to a clean cold-water supply. Experiments and numerical simulations were conducted to assess the thermal power available with varying wastewater and HX flow rates and temperatures. The thermal power available ranged from 1.81-4.54 kW with a heat transfer effectiveness of 54.1–89.7%. This would result in an annual energy recovery rate of 6.61–16.46 MWh/a, with a whole life carbon reduction of up to 83.9 tonnes of CO 2 e. The study also found that for every kg of FOG introduced, a deterioration of 0.3% in effectiveness was observed. Economically, the novel GT with integrated WWHR had payback periods ranging from 1-6 years depending on the fuel type and wastewater resources available. This redesigned GT-WWHR system has led to a reduction in energy use, costs and emissions and is a viable form of green technology for the hospitality industry

title: Multilayer thermochromic radiative cooling smart window for building thermal regulation
A cluster-aware shared-personalized TCN with self-attention for residential community load forecasting
Assessing the suitability of PMV and adaptive comfort model for tropical mixed-mode ventilation
Integrated TABS-hygroscopic-material envelope for enhanced indoor temperature and humidity control: Optimal design and climate adaption
Event-based performance modelling and multi-scale adoption pathways for climate-resilient buildings in high-density urban environments
abstract: High–density cities are increasingly exposed to extreme climate events whose intensifying heatwaves, humidity episodes, typhoon–driven moisture loads, and rapid temperature drops (RTDs) exceed the assumptions embedded in typical–year design practice. This study develops a multi–scale adoption framework that integrates climate science, governance structures, neighbourhood morphology, and building–performance dynamics to support event–responsive, climate–resilient buildings in dense urban environments. The framework is constructed through a structured methodology and is illustrated using a scenario–based building–performance simulation (BPS) of a representative low–income flat in Hong Kong, a globally relevant case of high–rise, high–density subtropical housing. A previously validated model is used to simulate a typical summer week featuring an extreme heat event and a typical winter week containing the most significant RTD event, under both historical (2010–2019) and late–century SSP5–8.5 climates. The simulations show that passive and envelope–level summer interventions reduce peak indoor temperatures but cannot fully prevent overheating under late–century conditions, while winter interventions mitigate sub–18 °C exposure during Rapid Temperature Drops (RTDs) but do not eliminate cold–surge risks as RTD magnitudes intensify. These results highlight the limitations of typical–year design practice and demonstrate the value of event–based performance metrics such as exceedances of 28.2 °C and sub–18 °C thresholds for triggering assessment, design, and monitoring actions across scales. The framework clarifies how regional climate warnings cascade through neighbourhood microclimates to shape building–level exposure, and how workflow–aligned adoption pathways can support coordinated, multi–hazard resilience. While the framework spans the building, neighbourhood, and regional scales, the present study validates only the building–scale component; validation of upper–scale elements is identified as future work extending this study. Although the study emphasizes the building-scale component, its findings establish a structured basis for future work in multi-scale modelling, and the advancement of event-based design guidance in dense urban contexts.

title: Synergizing pollution control and carbon reduction in China’s construction industry
abstract: • We study SPCCR in construction industry in China. • 289 cities from 2012 to 2022 are analyzed using CSSM. • The pollution control and carbon reduction subsystems both improved. • Four optimized configuration pathways for efficient SPCCR are identified. • SPCCR strategies are heterogeneous by regions. Using panel data for 289 Chinese cities from 2012 to 2022, this study assesses synergistic pollution control and carbon reduction (SPCCR) in the construction sector through the Composite System Synergy Model (CSSM). To identify the conditions associated with higher synergy levels, we further apply dynamic Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) and Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA). The main results show that: (1) The pollution control (PC) and carbon reduction (CR) subsystems both improved steadily over the study period. Even so, synergy between the two remains limited, pointing to considerable room for strengthening synergy through more integrated governance. (2) Four optimized configuration pathways for efficient SPCCR are identified, including the structural transformation − information disclosure co-driven pathway, industrial transformation − economic agglomeration-led pathway, balanced economic − energy − information pathway, and cleaner production − information disclosure pathway. (3) SPCCR strategies are heterogeneous by regions, specifically developed urban agglomerations leverage differentiated positioning under national policy frameworks to optimize SPCCR, while developing regions actively enhanced inter-regional collaboration to accelerate sustainable transitions in the construction sector.

title: A Performance-Driven framework for building form generation based on 3D shape Grammar: A case study in BIPV performance
The evolution and future of advanced control strategies for chiller plant sequence and optimal loading in buildings: a review of modern control theory and artificial intelligence algorithms
Investigating the impact of two-dimensional and three-dimensional urban structures on seasonal net surface shortwave radiation
From buildings to regions: a cross-scale review of spatial morphology and its dynamic relationship with carbon emissions
Development of occupant behavior models for thermal comfort in office buildings of Nepal
Editorial Board
Climate change reshapes the relationship between urban morphology and energy performance: Building energy consumption and photovoltaic potential in severe cold regions
Numerical and experimental validation of an indirect solar water-heating system with TRNSYS-based parametric analysis under Moroccan Mediterranean climate
In-situ identification of axial borehole thermal conductivity from measured transient heat extraction
abstract: This study presents a novel segment-wise inversion method for determining the depth-dependent thermal conductivity profile λ ( z ) of the subsurface using operational temperature measurements from a functioning ground source heat pump system. The method couples a fluid-side energy balance with a time-dependent 1D radial heat-conduction model and, in the present implementation, uses the borehole thermal resistance R b obtained independently from a standard Thermal Response Test (TRT). This framework enables the reconstruction of high-resolution (10 m) thermal conductivity profiles from operational data without a dedicated depth-resolved TRT campaign. Results show that the reconstructed thermal conductivity profile clearly identifies major lithological transitions, including low-conductivity silty-clayey units and higher-conductivity sandy-gravel layers. The energy-weighted effective thermal conductivity deviates by less than ±2% from the TRT reference value, confirming that the method reproduces bulk thermal behaviour with TRT-level accuracy. A Monte Carlo noise analysis revealed that inversion stability strongly depends on the hydraulic loading: low mass flow rates reduce the signal-to-noise ratio and limit the interpretability of the segment-wise inversion, whereas higher flow rates yield stable, reproducible, and geologically meaningful profiles. The present field validation is limited to one 100 m borehole under conduction-dominated conditions; extension to groundwater-affected and multi-borehole settings requires further study.

title: Integrated renewable energy and demand-side management for low-carbon commercial buildings in tropical climates: A matched-configuration benchmark with predictive control and a multi-agent DRL architecture
Fine-tuned large language models as surrogate schedulers for smart building energy management
abstract: • A fine-tuned LLM is proposed as a decision surrogate for MILP-based energy management in Net-Zero Energy Buildings (NZEBs); novel to this application domain. • MILP-generated optimal schedules are used to supervise LLM prediction of DG dispatch, ESS charging/discharging, grid trading, and heating/cooling device set-points. • The proposed framework is evaluated in terms of prediction accuracy, feasibility of predicted schedules, and resulting building energy system operational performance. • The results demonstrate the potential of fine-tuned LLMs to reduce the computational burden of repeated online MILP scheduling for deployment-oriented NZEB operation. Buildings account for a substantial share of global energy consumption and associated carbon emissions, which has increased interest in net-zero energy buildings (NZEBs) and their efficient operation. In NZEB energy management, operational scheduling must coordinate distributed generation (DG), energy storage systems (ESSs), utility-grid power exchange, and thermal devices while minimizing operating cost under variable renewable generation and demand. Although mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) can provide optimal schedules, repeated online optimization may impose a considerable computational burden in real-time applications. This paper proposes a fine-tuned large language model (LLM) framework as a surrogate for MILP-based NZEB scheduling, with the aim of providing computationally efficient decision support and a flexible architecture for future smart-building energy management. The MILP model is first used to generate optimal set-points for DG dispatch, ESS charging/discharging power, grid buy/sell power, and heating/cooling device operation. These optimization-derived input-output pairs are then used to fine-tune the LLM so that it can directly predict near-optimal operational decisions without repeatedly solving the MILP problem. The proposed framework is evaluated against benchmark learning models using the same prediction-error metrics reported in the Results section. The results show that the fine-tuned LLM achieves the best overall performance, with a test MAE of 0.0853 and RMSE of 0.286, outperforming both ANN and XGBoost under the same evaluation setting. Compared with ANN, the fine-tuned LLM reduces MAE and RMSE by 88.2% and 33.3%, respectively, while also improving over XGBoost by 79.7% in MAE and 24.7% in RMSE. In addition, the predicted schedules are assessed in terms of operational feasibility and system-level performance. These findings indicate that fine-tuned LLMs can serve as computationally efficient surrogates for near-optimal NZEB control.

title: A design framework for smart home energy management systems interfaces to promote energy-saving behaviors
abstract: Smart Home Energy Management Systems (SHEMS) are widely promoted as tools for improving residential energy efficiency, yet their impact is often limited by interfaces that insufficiently account for human cognition and behavior. This study addresses this gap by proposing a design framework that combines design-oriented approaches from Cognitive Systems Engineering (CSE) and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) with behavior-oriented approaches from Human Information Processing (HIP) and Human-Building Interaction (HBI). Through abstraction hierarchy-based decomposition of prior HEMS and HBI studies, five core interface functions are derived, such as Information Delivery, Real-Time Feedback, Personal Motivation, Control Flexibility, and Social Comparison, each representing a distinct functional goal for energy engagement. These functions are systematically cross-mapped with Norman’s Design Principles to construct a function-usability matrix of 30 actionable guidelines. The framework is then embedded within a HIP-HBI-SHEMS loop, forming a layered model that specifies how interface elements should align with cognitive stages, occupant behavior, and system responses. The framework is demonstrated through a structured mapping of representative SHEMS interface types, which reveals functional, usability, and cognitive limitations in current designs. The resulting framework offers a structured, theory-informed, and practically applicable basis for designing SHEMS interfaces that can better support sustained energy-saving behavior in residential buildings.

title: Effects of light color on emotion and cognition in a confined cabin under normal and simulated microgravity: An EEG study
Comparison of methods for generating ex-ante distribution coefficients for collective self-consumption
abstract: Allocation of locally generated electricity is a relevant topic in energy sharing projects. Specifically for PV collective-self consumption, it may require defining distribution coefficients which determine how the generated electricity is distributed among the participants. According to Spanish regulation, these coefficients are determined beforehand and may be fixed or variable with an hourly resolution. In both cases, many strategies can be applied to determine these coefficients according to the project’s criteria and goals being pursued. A Renewable Energy Community analysis tool developed as part of the syn.ikia project is used to calculate energy matching performance indicators and bills of a community. It generates distribution coefficients sets for energy sharing based on the load and production data of community participants. This study examines 16 methods, using different time slicing and value generation criteria, including numerical optimization. The different impacts on self-consumption and cost savings are analysed in two distinct participation schemas within a local renewable energy community in Santa Coloma de Gramenet, Spain. The results provide insights into the most effective criteria for maximizing the impact of collective self-consumption.

title: Multiscale coupled hygrothermal performance of PCM-integrated timber building envelope
A rural load forecasting method for decomposing village-level load into individual building loads using non-intrusive measurements based on hidden Markov model
Assessing seasonal thermal performance of a Mid-Continental USA green roof system under real-world conditions: Moisture-driven thermodynamic implications for building energy performance
A field study of thermal comfort for primary school children in naturally ventilated classrooms in the hot summer and cold winter zone of China
A model and metric for daytime cooling performance of precast concrete insulated exterior walls with passive radiative cooling coatings
Corrigendum to “An integrated approach for evaluation, optimization and prediction of energy flexibility potential in the commercial building sector” [Energy Build. 360 (2026) 117344]
Assessing energy, thermal and visual performance of photochromic glazing: From spectrophotometric characterization to building simulations
abstract: Photochromic (PC) glazing is a promising smart glazing solution for enhancing buildinǵs energy efficiency and indoor comfort through its ability to dynamically adjust its optical properties in response to solar radiation. However, studies assessing the global (energy, thermal and visual) performance of this technology are scarce. This work evaluates the performance of a clear double glazing incorporating a PC film. Spectrophotometric tests were first conducted to determine the thermal and optical properties of the PC film, revealing a dynamic visible transmittance and a low UV and near-infrared transmittance. Subsequently, a previously calibrated dynamic simulation model of an office room was used to assess the impact of the PC film on energy consumption (climatization energy needs and energy use considering an ideal air-conditioning system) and indoor comfort (in accordance with useful daylight illuminance, daylight glare index, predicted mean vote, adaptive thermal comfort model and Portuguese legislation) during working hours (9am-6 pm of weekdays) across the climates of three European cities (Lisbon, Berlin and London). The results show that PC glazing can reduce cooling demand in all studied climates. Total energy use decreased by up to 10% in the warmest of the studied climates, while slight increases were observed in the colder climates. Visual comfort improved significantly, with up to 24% and 74% more working hours with useful illuminance and imperceptible glare levels, respectively. Thermal comfort analysis revealed a negligible change in free-float conditions during working hours, and an improvement of up to 20% when the HVAC system was operating.

title: Fourier-based periodicity analysis and lightweight RC calibration for heating load modeling under limited sensing
Thermal resilience in shrinking cities: Effects of gray–green spatial form on seasonal and diurnal land surface temperature
Disaggregation of Space-Heating load in buildings from hourly Smart-Meter data using a hybrid ICA–PLR approach
abstract: Space-heating dominates electricity consumption in Norwegian public buildings, yet hourly space-heating load (SHL) is rarely sub-metered, limiting monitoring and demand response (DR). The objective of this study is to develop and evaluate a physics-guided, scalable method to disaggregate hourly SHL from whole-building hourly electric load using only weather and calendar information, without SHL sub-metering. Specifically, this study evaluates the performance of a hybrid ICA-PLR estimator for hourly SHL disaggregation against PLR, RFR, and FastICA benchmarks. This study presents a hybrid disaggregation framework that couples Independent Component Analysis (ICA) with a heating-degree-hour piecewise linear regression (HDH-PLR) under a temperature- and schedule-aware cold-hour mask. ICA extracts a heating-like latent component from cold-hour residuals across multiple buildings; HDH-PLR re-anchors scale and slope to a physics-consistent temperature signature; and mask gating with lag, seasonal, and weekend factors suppresses warm-weather false activation. The proposed framework requires only hourly smart-meter, weather, and calendar data. The method is applied to a portfolio of 22 public buildings (schools, kindergartens, offices, and institutions). All quantitative validation is performed on a sub-metered validation subset of 5 buildings using hourly SHL as ground truth. Across the validation subset, results indicate that hourly accuracy reaches R 2 ≈ 0.91 with nMAE ≈ 13 % to 14 %, while estimated hourly SHL remains near zero during summer periods. At the building level in the validation subset, the method tracks morning recovery, night setbacks, and cold-spell amplitudes with fewer mild-weather false positives than the benchmark techniques. The approach yields interpretable parameters (balance temperature, lag, seasonal/weekend factors) that support weather-normalized monitoring and flexibility operations in public building portfolios. This work demonstrates that physics-guided disaggregation can extend operational visibility of public-building heating systems using only utility-grade data and support weather-normalized monitoring and flexibility planning across public-building portfolios.

title: RETRACTED: A Subject-Independent thermal comfort prediction framework using Full-Body thermographic imaging and Transformer-CNN architecture
Towards sustainable educational infrastructure: modelling barriers and drivers of retrofitting in South Africa
Locally interactive bilinear flow modeling for window passive ventilation in multi-zone buildings
abstract: Passive ventilation, enabled by operable elements such as windows, can reduce HVAC energy use and strengthen building resilience, yet it remains difficult to incorporate into scalable, control-oriented thermal models. A central challenge is that changes in window opening configurations can produce strong, configuration-dependent variations in both interzone and zone-to-ambient heat exchange, which undermines the predictive and control utility of conventional reduced-order models that assume fixed coupling coefficients.This paper introduces a Locally Interactive Bilinear Flow (LiBF) model for multi-zone buildings that represents these exchange pathways as explicit functions of passive opening factors, yielding a compact bilinear structure that is well suited for identification and optimization. To estimate model parameters efficiently, we propose a two-step identification procedure: (i) non-negative least squares (NNLS) is used to estimate zone capacitances and conductances from zonal temperature measurements and HVAC input data collected under a limited set of opening configurations, and (ii) monotone conductance–opening relationships are learned via constrained linear fitting to enable prediction under unseen opening combinations without exhaustive re-identification. Using a prototype DOE EnergyPlus office model with operable windows, we show that LiBF reproduces zone temperature trajectories with RMSE below $2^{\circ}$C, including cases with solar exposure. Across representative U.S.\ climate regions and across seasons (winter, spring, summer, and fall), the identified seasonal models maintain an average RMSE below $1.5^{\circ}$C. These results indicate that LiBF provides an interpretable and scalable modeling framework for analyzing, and ultimately controlling, passive ventilation in multi-zone buildings.

title: Non-intrusive load monitoring for smart residential buildings: An AI-based framework with cross-country generalization
abstract: Accurate appliance-level electricity monitoring is essential for smart home energy management, demand response, occupant feedback, and building-level efficiency optimization. However, many existing non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) approaches are evaluated within single datasets and controlled environments, limiting their demonstrated generalizability across different households, countries, and measurement conditions.
