This study evaluates the suitability of publicly available electronic datasets for characterising Ireland’s non-residential building stock and supporting bottom-up energy modelling in the context of the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD 2024/1275/EU). A systematic scoping review of national government and institutional datasets was conducted using an adapted PRISMA-ScR approach. The analysis identified the national Energy Performance Certificate database and GeoDirectory as the only datasets with sufficient scale and detail to support national non-residential stock analysis. However, substantial limitations were identified, including incompatibilities between economic activity classifications (NACE) and building energy typologies (NEAP), incomplete stock representation, and EPC-triggered sampling bias. Frequently transacted building categories such as retail and warehouses are over-represented, while public-sector, healthcare, recreational, and small service buildings remain under-represented. The findings demonstrate that the principal barrier to effective non-residential stock modelling in Ireland is not data availability, but deficiencies in data governance, interoperability, standardised building identifiers, and energy-relevant classification systems. Addressing these structural limitations will be critical for effective implementation of the EPBD and for developing reliable national building stock models. While focused on Ireland, the methodological approach and identified challenges are transferable to other EU member states.

title: Toward net-zero energy buildings in hot-arid climates: a systematic review of energy efficiency and renewable energy integration in the Iraqi residential sector
abstract: Residential building energy efficiency plays a crucial role in curbing electricity demand in hot-arid climates where cooling represents a major share of household electricity consumption. Residential buildings are a fast-growing electricity demand sector in Iraq, but the potential of energy efficiency measures (EEMs) and renewable energy technologies (RETs) has not been comprehensively assessed. This study presents a PRISMA-based systematic review of 55 selected studies published between 2014 and mid-2025 to highlight strategies, performance indicators, and challenges in implementing EEMs and RETs in Iraqi residential buildings. The findings reveal that building-envelope measures are the most significant factor on the demand side, with integrated envelope measures delivering energy reductions that vary depending on the intervention context, reaching around 50% under more comprehensive retrofit-oriented scenarios. On the supply side, renewable energy technologies (RETs) − especially rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems − demonstrate promising potential, with appropriately configured and sized systems able to meet a significant fraction of household electricity loads under Iraqi climate conditions. While EEMs-RETs integrated approaches are limited, optimized NZEB-oriented scenarios combining comprehensive energy-efficiency improvements with on-site renewable energy technologies demonstrated substantial reductions in reliance on grid electricity. Despite such opportunities, the literature is primarily simulation-focused with limited field validation and integrated techno-economic and policy analyses. As such, this study presents a NZEB-oriented integrated framework coupled with an implementation-oriented approach combining retrofit depth, demand reduction, renewable integration, economic considerations, and implementation challenges to support the transition toward energy-efficient residential buildings in Iraq and other hot-arid climates.

title: Assessing the applicability of 5th-generation district heating and cooling for energy-efficient retrofits in a net zero energy campus
Energy, environmental and economic experimental assessment of a typical air-handling unit operating under single faults on valves, fans and sensors in south of Italy
abstract: Data-driven automated fault detection and diagnosis (AFDD) offers a significant advantage in optimizing AHU efficiency by enabling real-time fault detection. This study evaluates the field performance of a single-duct, dual-fan constant air volume AHU in a Mediterranean climate (southern Italy). The analysis considers both normal and faulty scenarios, including eleven commonly encountered faults (1) positive offset of the return air relative humidity sensor (+15%); 2) negative offset of the return air relative humidity sensor ( – 15%); 3) negative offset of the return air temperature sensor ( – 3 °C); 4) humidifier valve stuck at 0% (always closed); 5) positive offset of the return air temperature sensor (+3 °C); 6) cooling coil valve stuck at 100% (always open); 7) post-heating coil valve stuck at 0% (always closed); 8) post-heating coil valve stuck at 100% (always open); 9) cooling coil valve stuck at 0% (always closed); 10) complete failure of the return air fan; 11) complete failure of the supply air fan. The impact of these faults on AHU performance is assessed in terms of electrical power consumption, energy demand, operational costs, global equivalent CO 2 emissions as well as operation time. Among the investigated faults, experimental results highlight that the post-heating coil valve stuck at 100% significantly affects system performance; specifically, this fault decreases daily indoor air temperature met ratio by about 69% during summer and winter tests, while increases total daily electrical energy consumption, operational costs, and global equivalent CO 2 emissions by over than 60% during cooling period and by more than 80% during heating period. Through a comparative analysis between observed faulty data and normal performance under identical conditions, this study provides valuable insights for developing AFDD tools and assists building personnel in identifying symptoms of common AHU faults, thereby contributing to more efficient building management.

title: Target-based risk assessment in building retrofits under climate change: Nonlinear effects of weather data selection
Adaptive control and explainable decision-making in residential energy management using a SHAP-guided multi-objective framework
abstract: This paper proposes a novel SHAP-guided (SHapley Additive exPlanations) multi-objective energy management framework that explicitly transforms SHAP-derived feature attributions into dynamic control-rule weights for real-time battery dispatch. The increasing deployment of residential photovoltaic (PV) generation and battery energy storage systems necessitates intelligent strategies that balance multiple, often conflicting, objectives while remaining transparent and interpretable. The proposed architecture integrates an adaptive PV forecasting module with a rule-based controller whose priorities are continuously updated using SHAP values, enabling context-aware and explainable decision-making. Unlike conventional black-box optimization approaches, the framework quantifies the contribution of key variables, such as time-of-use tariffs, state of charge, PV generation, and household demand, to each control action. The method simultaneously minimizes electricity cost, mitigates peak demand, limits battery degradation, and enhances energy autonomy. Comprehensive simulations under deficit, balanced, and surplus PV conditions, using real residential load data and Irish time-of-use tariffs, demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), Model Predictive Control (MPC), and a heuristic baseline. It achieves the lowest weekly operating cost and highest savings, eliminates peak-period grid imports, and maintains high self-consumption and self-sufficiency with reduced battery cycling. These results show that SHAP-driven control not only improves holistic system performance but also provides transparent, interpretable, and actionable energy management decisions.

title: Development and validation of a hybrid geothermal underground rainwater tank model for passive cooling of buildings
abstract: This paper explores the viability and performance of geothermal rainwater tanks, which represent a promising passive cooling approach to reduce summer overheating in buildings while ensuring on-site water management. This paper focuses on the so-called "Rainergy" concept, which combines a buried rainwater storage tank with integrated water-to-water and air-to-water heat exchangers to supply cooling energy to a double-flow ventilation system. A dedicated one-dimensional multi-layer transient model was developed to accurately reproduce internal heat transfer mechanisms, evaporative and convective processes at the free surface, i.e at atmospheric pressure. The ground conduction was modelled through a 2D axisymmetric model. The model incorporates a variable water level and was implemented in Python to allow future interoperability with building simulation tools.The model was validated using a full-scale experimental prototype located in Alsace (France). Good agreement was obtained between simulated and measured temperatures, with RMSE values within (<1°C), and peak power production predicted with a deviation below 5%. Seasonal cooling energy was reproduced with an error of 7.6% for summer 2022, confirming robust representation of the system’s operating limits.The validated model was used to evaluate Rainergy performance under eight representative French climates. Current conditions lead to annual cooling deliveries between 400 and 600 kWh, depending on location. Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario for 2100, production increases by +25 to +43%, demonstrating enhanced efficiency under aggravated heat stress. The average coefficient of performance exceeds 30 with production peaks of more than 1 kW.

title: Corrigendum to “Environmental impacts of standard building renovations: City-level extrapolation from a real case study in Spain” [Energy Build. 354 (2026) 116938]
Construction defects, envelope degradation and lifecycle carbon implications for building energy performance: evidence from Lagos, Nigeria
Adaptable cooling coil performance under broad load diversity: enabling low-lift chiller operation and resilient performance under climate and pandemic stresses
From vision to physics: Generative occupant modeling and 3D spatial data architecture in indoor environments
Flexibility framework for production-related waste heat and internal gains valorization in building energy supply at facility and district scales
abstract: The recovery of waste heat from the manufacturing industry for building heating and cooling has a high decarbonization potential. Flexibility measures such as demand response can further enhance energy savings. However, there is a lack of case studies on the utilization of production-related excess heat for building energy supply. Both waste heat availability and production-related internal gains as demand response signals remain unexplored. We present an analysis framework for three scenario types for on-site and off-site industrial excess heat utilization: (I) on-site waste heat demand response for building heating, (II) on-site production-related internal gains demand response, and (III) waste heat utilization for district heating. For (I) and (II), load shifting and peak shaving are compared using EnergyPlus Ideal Loads-based simulations. At the district scale (III), the demand of buildings surrounding the production facility is determined through archetype-based energy simulations. The framework was applied to two industrial use cases - one in Spain and one in Norway. Results show that on-site thermal energy storage provides the highest reduction potential under the idealized modeling assumptions: auxiliary heating demand reductions reach up to 98.65 % in the Spanish case and up to 9.02 % in the Norwegian case. At the district scale, targeting building subgroups enables technically feasible waste heat utilization, with adjacent educational buildings in Spain achieving 15.13 % demand coverage and residential buildings in Norway reaching 3.84 %. The proposed framework demonstrates the potential of waste heat utilization across facility and district scales, offering industrial plants a systematic approach to assess the potential reduction in building energy demand.

title: Publicly accessible data and computer vision for retrofit planning: Evidence from London social housing
abstract: Buildings account for approximately 34% of global CO₂ emissions, placing the built environment at the centre of climate action. Aging social housing represents a particularly under-studied challenge: in the United Kingdom, around 78% of the building stock predates 1980, and nearly 60% of buildings carry poor energy performance ratings. Systematic retrofit planning is further hampered by building data that is incomplete and fragmented across disparate sources. This paper presents a pilot study investigating data-driven approaches to support social housing retrofit planning across several London boroughs. Using publicly accessible property datasets, computer vision training data, and street-level imagery, we fine-tuned convolutional neural networks to predict two retrofit-relevant building characteristics: wall construction type and architectural style. In-distribution accuracy reached up to 94%; however, performance declined substantially when models were evaluated against property samples provided by local councils. This highlights the generalisation challenges inherent in applying models trained on publicly accessible data to real-world contexts, and underscores the need for broader, purpose-built labelled datasets. A stakeholder workshop with representatives from local government, retrofit organisations, and industry consultancies complemented the technical findings. Discussions surfaced practical barriers to data use in the retrofit sector, including inconsistent data formats, limited inter-organisational data sharing, and a lack of coordination across the supply chain. The findings suggest that publicly accessible housing data and machine learning hold genuine promise for large-scale urban retrofit characterisation, but that realising this potential will require greater data standardisation, coordinated investment in labelled datasets, and closer collaboration across the sector.

title: Editorial Board
Optimal decarbonization strategies for existing buildings: Comparative analysis of retrofitting, repurposing and replacement
abstract: Decarbonizing existing buildings is a critical priority for addressing climate change mitigation, but decision-making is complicated by the range of available competing intervention strategies: retrofitting, repurposing, or replacement through new construction. Each option has distinct implications for operational and embodied carbon, as well as overall costs. However, stakeholders currently lack a harmonized framework to compare these alternatives on a consistent carbon and cost basis—particularly when demolition is involved. Demolishing a building not only releases the embodied carbon stored in its materials but also requires new materials for reconstruction, compounding the overall carbon impact. Accurately accounting for these effects is essential, yet often overlooked or inconsistently treated in current approaches. Existing studies rarely offer side-by-side analyses or use compatible accounting methods, often leading to conflicting recommendations.This study develops an optimization framework that integrates building energy simulation with novel carbon accounting approaches. The framework explicitly includes the embodied emissions of both demolished structures and new interventions and introduces the concepts of “residual” and “salvage” carbon to account for building components and technologies with remaining useful life before and after the planning horizon. By doing so, the model enables a direct comparison of the optimal intervention measures selected across retrofitting, repurposing, and replacement strategies over a long-term investment horizon.Results show that retrofitting is typically the most carbon- and cost-effective strategy, outper forming repurposing and replacement in most scenarios. Incorporating salvage carbon encourages major retrofits to be phased over time, reducing the need for large upfront investments. Accounting for the remaining useful carbon of existing assets allows stakeholders to fully capture the impacts of demolition and replacement.

title: Field evaluation of MPC and online RL within a policy ensemble framework for chilled water pump frequency control
Thermal-mass-driven energy flexibility in office buildings: a simulation-based assessment of building design parameters and setpoint control strategies
abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources has heightened the need for demand-side energy flexibility in buildings, particularly in heating and cooling systems, which account for a substantial share of building energy use. This study investigates the potential of utilising building thermal mass in combination with flexible temperature setpoint control to enhance energy flexibility in office buildings. A comprehensive simulation-based methodology was developed using EnergyPlus and a Python automation framework to systematically assess the influence of building design characteristics on flexibility performance. The analysis considered variations in envelope performance, HVAC system type, construction thermal mass, building geometry, window-to-wall ratio, and internal gains. For each building configuration, 810 predictive rule-based control strategies were evaluated using half-hourly electricity price and grid carbon intensity data for London in 2024, and the optimal strategy was identified by minimising annual HVAC energy cost. The results demonstrate that energy flexibility potential is highly dependent on building characteristics. In particular, the interaction between HVAC system type and construction thermal mass was found to be a dominant factor, with VRF, fan coil, and radiant systems consistently outperforming all-air VAV systems. Flexible setpoint control achieved reductions in annual HVAC energy costs of up to 15% and decreased average peak power demand by approximately 43%, alongside associated reductions in carbon emissions. These findings highlight the importance of considering multiple building characteristics simultaneously when assessing energy flexibility and underscore the need to integrate thermal-mass-based flexibility strategies into early-stage building design and future smart building performance frameworks.

title: Thermo-economic performance of a heat pump with condenser-integrated latent thermal storage for residential heating
Towards low-carbon grain storage buildings: a systematic review of assessment methods and mitigation strategies
Working from home: Post-pandemic trends, influential factors, and impacts on occupancy patterns in residential buildings
Performance evaluation of air cycle refrigeration systems as a household air conditioner under different configurations
abstract: With growing concerns over refrigerant pollution, air has emerged as a promising alternative for refrigeration systems. This study investigates the evaluation of coefficient of performance (COP) in air cycle refrigeration systems, focusing on various configurations. This paper takes a household air conditioner as an example to compare different system configurations, including single-shaft, parallel-flow and two-stage compression configurations, and the optimal performance conditions under varying pressure ratios and indoor temperature limits are studied. Suitable turbochargers and heat exchangers are used in different configurations. One-dimensional loss model and number of transfer units (NTU) method are used for mathematical simulation to simulate the efficiency under actual operating conditions. The model has been verified by experiments. The research shows that the inclusion of heat exchangers, intermediate cooling, and different configurations significantly impacts system efficiency. The optimal cycle of the single-shaft configuration is the low-pressure open cycle, with a COP of 0.610. The optimal COP configuration is the two-stage compression configuration in the semi-open cycle with heat recovery, with a value of 0.700. Results provide valuable insights into the design and evaluation of air cycle refrigeration systems, highlighting the importance of system layout, pressure ratio, and cooling strategies in maximizing efficiency.

title: Are code-compliant buildings ready for future climate? A case study of thermal autonomy in Australian apartments
abstract: Global climate change and rapid urbanization are intensifying urban overheating, posing challenges for cooling energy demand, thermal comfort, and human health. Apartment buildings are particularly heat-vulnerable and, as a common urban residential typology, expose many occupants to elevated indoor overheating risk. While building regulations mandate minimum performance standards, their adequacy under future climates remains uncertain. This study assesses the thermal autonomy of naturally ventilated apartment buildings in Australia under a range of climate-change scenarios. National Construction Code (NCC)-compliant buildings were compared with a reference building representing existing low-performance apartments. Future typical meteorological year (TMY) files were developed using the 4-km-resolution NARCliM2.0 regional climate modeling ensemble and compared with current TMY and extreme meteorological year (EMY) conditions for representative Sydney locations: coastal Redfern and inland Penrith. Results indicate substantial future warming across the NARCliM2.0 scenarios, with median temperatures increasing by up to 5 °C under high-emissions conditions. Despite the spread across ensemble projections, building simulations consistently show increased indoor overheating risk in both frequency and severity, especially in top-floor units. Although the NCC-compliant design improved envelope performance and reduced inter-floor variability, overheating frequency still increased from 1% to 12% in Redfern and from 10% to 23% in Penrith under the upper-bound EC-Earth3-Veg–WRF412R5 SSP3–7.0 scenario. Adaptation strategies combining envelope improvements, advanced ventilation, and external shading substantially mitigated overheating, reducing weighted exceedance hours for overly warm conditions by up to 94%. These findings highlight the need for regulatory reform to account for climate-model uncertainty and support climate-resilient apartment living under future warming.

title: Valorisation of wood fibre waste in gypsum composites for green building applications
abstract: The construction sector significantly contributes to environmental degradation due to its high consumption of non-renewable resources and carbon emissions. This study presents the development of a gypsum-wood waste biocomposite, as innovative and sustainable material for construction applications. The research investigates the incorporation of this abundant yet underutilized industrial by-product into a gypsum-based matrix, aiming to reduce environmental impact. The wood fibre waste was reused without pre-treatment, ensuring a simple and scalable production process. Experimental results indicate that increasing wood waste content progressively reduces thermal conductivity, from 0.35 W/mK to 0.24 W/mK, significantly improving insulation properties. Simultaneously, density decreases from 950 kg/m 3 to 720 kg/m 3 , making the material lighter and easier to handle. However, a trade-off is observed in mechanical performance, as compressive strength decreases from 8.5 MPa to 3.0 MPa at the highest wood waste content of 10 wt%. Despite this, mixtures containing 2–4 wt% wood waste maintain mechanical strengths between 4.8 and 6.2 MPa, making them suitable for non-structural applications such as insulating panels and eco-friendly plasters. Additionally, preliminary virtual modelling and energy simulation were implemented to isolate the energy contribution of the produced mixes in a building model under Mediterranean-Continental climatic conditions (represented by the city of Rome). Also, a multi-criteria analysis was implemented to rank the produced mixes and identify the optimal compromise between material's functional performance, environmental impact, and economic feasibility. Obtained results highlight that the optimal formulation balances insulation efficiency and mechanical properties while minimizing environmental and economic drawbacks. The direct reuse of untreated wood fibre waste enabled the development of lightweight gypsum bio-composites with improved insulation performance suitable for non-structural building applications. Finally, the best performing formulation was benchmarked against commercial product to investigate the possible positioning of the proposed biocomposite. This bio-composite represents a viable alternative to conventional materials, aligning with circular economy principles and European sustainability policies such as the Green Deal and Renovation Wave.

title: Cooling-load prediction under data scarcity for data centers: Cycle decomposition and conditional data generation with LSTM
Uncovering the structural relationships among transaction costs in nearly zero energy building projects
abstract: Transaction costs are widely recognized as a hidden constraint on scaling Nearly Zero Energy Buildings (NZEBs), yet existing studies largely treat them as isolated items and overlook how they interact across stages and stakeholders. This study adopts a structural perspective to examine transaction cost interactions in Chinese NZEB projects. Based on 36 transaction cost elements identified in prior empirical work, we conducted a two-round Delphi survey with 23 experienced practitioners to elicit perceived directional relationships and construct a consensus-based structural self-interaction matrix. An integrated ISM–MICMAC–SNA approach was then applied to identify the hierarchical structure, driving–dependence categories, and key nodes in the network of transaction cost elements, complemented by Louvain community detection. The analysis reveals a ten-level structure that can be grouped into three functional zones and yields four main findings. First, transaction costs in the bottom driving zone are mainly borne by developers, especially those related to consultant selection and contract negotiation. Second, transaction cost determinants show a hierarchical pattern, with asset specificity dominating the lower levels and uncertainty becoming more prominent in the upper levels. Third, construction-stage transaction costs are not structurally isolated. In the expert-consensus model, they are linked to perceived dependencies from the concept and design stages through consensus-based directional relationships. Fourth, the study identifies twelve key transaction cost elements and groups them into five categories: partner selection, contract negotiation, technical solution development, certification document preparation, and construction change and dispute management. These findings clarify perceived dependencies and reachability patterns among transaction cost elements and provide a basis for proposing prioritized mitigation strategies in NZEB delivery.

title: Performance evaluation of a constructal-based tree-branched underfloor air distribution systems: Influence of outlet number on thermal comfort and indoor air quality
Model predictive control for air to water heat pump in context of explicit flexibility: From design to hardware in the loop experiment
abstract: Building electrification through heat pumps and renewable energies deployment have pushed for a growing interest in leveraging building flexibility to support the grid. To do so, advanced control strategies for heat pumps specifically designed to address flexibility are required. In that context, this study presents the development of a flexibility-focused controller for heat pumps to meet explicit demand response schemes especially relying on shutdown orders. The primary objective is to enhance the response of heat pumps to the grid orders while maintaining safe and efficient HP operations and suitable user comfort. To achieve this goal, a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework is developed and combined with additional expert Rule-Based Control (RBC) rules. The controller is then tested on a Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) test bench. The tests demonstrate significant improvements in energy management by reducing consumption by 16% as well as reducing discomfort degree-hours by 75% compared to baseline control over the course of 4 winter days. Finally, this study highlights that in order not to degrade HP performance after a shutdown order, it is preferable to maintain standby electricity consumption for immediate compressor availability. This enables a significant mitigation of rebound effects after the shutdown period.

title: Impact of thermal retrofitting and reduced ventilation on moisture accumulation and durability in large-panel residential buildings
Experimental investigation of a residential multi-split air-conditioning system with partial heat recovery for domestic hot water
abstract: In residential buildings, the efficient integration of two-pipe VRF systems with heat-pump-based domestic hot water (DHW) production is considered a promising approach to improving overall building energy efficiency and energy utilization. However, system-level experimental investigations of such integrated systems remain limited, and their performance characteristics under different operating modes are not yet fully revealed, introducing considerable uncertainty in the development and optimization of practical operating strategies. To address these issues, this study experimentally investigates a residential VRF with partial heat recovery for domestic hot water. Without introducing complex system configurations, the system enables coordinated operation of space conditioning and DHW production by five modes. A prototype system was developed and tested under standard laboratory conditions. The performance of the system under representative operating conditions for each mode was experimentally evaluated and comparatively analyzed, with particular emphasis on the performance characteristics of the partial heat recovery operating modes.

title: Comprehensive benefit evaluation of photovoltaic-green roof retrofit for low-carbon renewal of old residential communities
Investigation of ventilation strategies for decoupled radiant cooling systems
Winter thermal comfort in Sui-Tang dynasty heritage open spaces: a case study of Lijing Gate, Luoyang, China
Balancing thermal comfort and energy efficiency through comparative HVAC setpoint strategies: Evidence from a field experiment in an SME office building
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between HVAC operational strategies, thermal comfort, and energy performance through a field experiment conducted in a small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) office building in Tokyo during summer. Four HVAC operational patterns were implemented on two office floors with fixed-desk and free-address layouts. Indoor environmental conditions and mean HVAC power demand were monitored. Thermal comfort was evaluated using the Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) model, and thermal dissatisfaction was defined as the proportion of measurements where |PMV| exceeded 0.5. The results showed that the existing uniform 24 °C baseline operation, which represented the prevailing HVAC operation prior to the experiment, produced overcooling conditions characterised by negative PMV values and elevated thermal discomfort rates. Modified operational patterns shifted PMV values closer to the thermal comfort range and generally reduced thermal discomfort compared with the baseline condition. Statistical analyses identified significant differences in PMV across operational patterns. Variations in mean HVAC power demand were also observed; however, these differences were not statistically significant. The fixed-desk office environment exhibited more stable thermal comfort improvements, whereas the free-address workspace showed greater spatial variability associated with occupancy distribution. These findings suggest that practical HVAC operational adjustments, including temperature setpoint revision and spatial zoning, can improve thermal comfort while maintaining comparable mean HVAC power demand under the monitored conditions.

title: Synergistic optimization and performance prediction of a ground source heat pump horizontal manifold in winter
A calibrated white-box digital twin for predictive blind control: A passive strategy to balance solar-driven thermal loads mitigation and daylight availability
abstract: The intensification of heatwaves is increasing the vulnerability of buildings lacking dedicated cooling systems, particularly in educational environments where daylight must also be considered. This study presents a proof-of-concept evaluation of a digital twin (DT) under controlled conditions for predictive blind control as a passive strategy to modulate solar-driven thermal loads while incorporating an indicative daylighting screening constraint. Building on a previously validated winter-oriented framework, the DT integrates a calibrated white-box Building Energy Model (BEM), real-time indoor monitoring, weather forecasts, and a rule-based multi-criteria selection routine capable of evaluating hundreds of hourly shading configurations per room. A novel modelling approach represents each blind as modular shading elements, enabling partial coverage and individualised actuation beyond the capabilities of standard EnergyPlus shading objects. The BEM was calibrated using an envelope-dominant approach based on free-oscillation periods and NSGA-II, achieving CIBSE-compliant accuracy across the analysed thermal zones. During 14 valid implementation periods, the DT generated hourly schedules by evaluating up to 256 configurations per room and selecting those that minimise net window heat transfer subject to an indicative daylighting screening constraint. Given the discrete structure of the problem, the hierarchical decision process relies on exhaustive enumeration of the feasible configurations combined with rule-based multi-criteria decision logic, identifying the best-performing configuration within the adopted reduced discrete set without the computational burden of classical optimisation solvers. Results show that the best-performing strategy within the discrete set reduced net window heat transfer by 49-68% relative to an always-open configuration, indicating a lower ideal loads cooling demand potential. Performance was strongly influenced by façade orientation and solar conditions, resulting in distinct control responses across the analysed rooms. As the case-study building was not actively cooled, the results reflect thermal demand reduction potential rather than measured energy savings. Validation against measured indoor temperatures confirms the predictive consistency of the calibrated model during operation. Limitations include uncertainty in simulated illuminance due to EnergyPlus sky model assumptions and the absence of active cooling, which restricts the assessment to thermal demand rather than cooling energy use. Nevertheless, the findings demonstrate the methodological feasibility of lightweight, simulation-assisted DT control for passive cooling management under controlled conditions.

title: Meta-learning–driven adaptive optimisation of building-integrated photovoltaic envelopes
abstract: Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) offer strong potential for net-zero energy buildings; however, envelope-level optimisation is computationally intensive due to conflicting objectives, high-dimensional variables, and costly simulations. Conventional surrogate models are typically problem-specific and lack transferability, requiring retraining for new design contexts. This study proposes a meta-learning–enhanced surrogate modelling framework for multi-objective optimisation of BIPV envelope design. A multi-output artificial neural network trained with a gradient-based meta-learning strategy learns transferable representations across diverse design tasks, enabling rapid adaptation to new building configurations with limited data. The surrogate model is integrated within a many-objective evolutionary optimisation framework and evaluated across multiple scenarios. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach maintains good predictive accuracy while significantly reducing computational time compared to simulation-based methods. It produces stable, well-distributed Pareto-optimal solutions that capture trade-offs among energy performance, life-cycle impact, daylight, glare, and thermal comfort. The findings highlight the potential of meta-learning surrogates for efficient and scalable building design optimisation. Future work will focus on improving data coverage and generalisation under more complex conditions.

title: Synergistic optimization of bio-PCM and radiative roof coatings for adaptive thermal comfort and carbon mitigation in tropical concrete buildings
Experimental study on the heat storage and release characteristics of phase change radiator with hot water circulation under intermittent heating
Evaluation of the energy flexibility potential associated with reversible heat pumps in Italian residential building archetypes
abstract: This study investigates the thermal flexibility potential of residential buildings in the Italian context, focusing on two archetypal typologies: single-family houses (SFH) and apartment blocks (AB). Simulations were performed using detailed building energy models under two seasonal control strategies: one based on solar irradiance (as a proxy for photovoltaic generation on an aggregate of various buildings, as e.g. an energy community) and one based on the Italian day-ahead electricity market price. Three energy efficiency levels (existing, renovated/NZEB and new/Passive) and three climatic zones (Milan, Rome, Palermo) were considered. Flexibility performance was assessed using the Flexibility Index (FI) and the Peak Load Reduction Factor (PLRF), evaluated separately for the heating and cooling seasons. Results show that solar-based control enables higher flexibility than price-based control, particularly during the heating season and in retrofitted buildings. While Passive buildings offer limited active flexibility due to their very low energy needs for heating and cooling , they lower baseline consumption and indirectly enable greater system-level flexibility. The analysis highlights the importance of building characteristics, control signal selection, and technical building systems design in maximizing residential demand-side flexibility.

title: Representative period selection for flexible control strategies on a reversible heat pump in cooling mode: A comparative case study
abstract: Rising space-cooling demand is intensifying peak electricity loads. Although reversible heat pumps are widely recognised as a key technology for building decarbonisation, it remains essential to avoid peak loads on the electrical grid and shift demand towards periods characterised by higher renewable energy availability and more favourable electricity prices. It is therefore crucial to investigate flexible control strategies that can manage peak electricity demand and overall energy use, while promoting the self-consumption of energy from renewable sources and ensuring indoor comfort. In this context, identifying week cycles representative of a full year or season allows to assess heat pump behaviour and infer the impact of flexible control strategies on its annual energy performance, especially when annual analyses are not feasible or practical, as in lab or field experiments. This study analyses four representative day selection procedures under three day-ahead price-based control strategies applied to a reversible heat pump operating in cooling mode. A comparative analysis is conducted for three southern Europe locations. The dynamic simulations include the building, the GSHP coupled with radiant panels, and a dehumidifier. The results indicate that the clustering method is the most effective method at representing key performance indicators across the climates, whereas the proposed consecutive day selection method provides the most accurate absolute values for extrapolated electricity cost and energy consumption.

title: Unraveling the long-term causal impact of winter indoor cold exposure on blood pressure: a quasi-experimental study across China's district heating boundary
Explainable machine learning for predicting building energy performance and sustainability certification in construction megaprojects
A deep-learning framework for predicting building heat load with hyperparameter optimisation and physics-constrained post-processing
abstract: Driven by global energy transition and carbon neutrality goals, accurate building heat load prediction is of great significance for intelligent heating control, demand-side energy management, and fault detection. This study focuses on a single-apartment located in Bologna and predicts the heat load for the next hour based on the previous 24 h of data. A dataset of 18 typical operating scenarios was constructed, encompassing variations in outdoor meteorological conditions, occupancy, thermostat settings, and equipment heat gains. Subsequently, the Optuna framework was employed to systematically optimize the hyperparameters of five models—LSTM, TCN, MLP, XGBoost, and LR—and their prediction performance was comparatively analyzed. Results show that that the deep learning models LSTM and TCN perform best, with LSTM slightly outperforming (LSTM: MAE = 0.082 kW, RMSE = 0.118 kW, R 2 = 0.863; TCN: MAE = 0.0864 kW, RMSE = 0.1196 kW, R 2 = 0.8606). Whereas the LR model exhibits the poorest performance, achieving only 0.1202 kW, 0.1504 kW, and 0.7793 on the respective metrics. After applying a post-processing (PC) correction mechanism, the MAE and RMSE of LSTM decreased to 0.058 kW and 0.100 kW, corresponding to reductions of 28.2% and 15.3%, respectively. This framework effectively integrates data-driven methods with physical constraints while maintaining low computational cost, providing a scalable and practical solution for intelligent building energy management and low-carbon operation.

title: Optimization of ground source heat pump systems in dense urban environments with limited plot sizes
abstract: In ground source heat pump (GSHP) projects, space limitations for placing boreholes can lead to ground thermal imbalance and suboptimal performance, making the systems unattractive for buildings with limited plot space. This issue is particularly severe in dense urban areas within Nordic climates, where small building plots cannot accommodate adequately sized bore fields to meet high heating demands. This paper addresses the problems caused by spatial limitations by utilizing an ambient air-assisted ground source heat pump (AAA-GSHP) system. This system maintains the thermal balance of boreholes through heat regeneration, allowing highly flexible design and placement of boreholes on building plots. Novel results are presented by optimizing system configurations — including the number, spacing, and depth of boreholes, as well as heat collector unit sizing — based on the available land area across various plot sizes. Optimization is implemented for both AAA-GSHP and conventional GSHP systems using detailed numerical simulations over a 50-year period. The results demonstrate that an optimized AAA-GSHP system achieves substantially higher performance and profitability on constrained plots compared to conventional systems. Depending on plot area, the ambient air-assisted system achieved a 3–26% lower levelized cost of energy, 0–42% lower life cycle emissions, and 0–80% higher heat pump energy production compared to traditional systems. The AAA-GSHP system met targeted energy production and emission goals with significantly lower investment costs. This study enhances the applicability of GSHP-based systems in areas where the conventional solution would often prove suboptimal.

title: Comparative study of conventional and emerging façade systems: Pathways to reducing embodied carbon and enhancing circularity in buildings
abstract: Façade systems play a critical role in building environmental performance, contributing substantially to embodied carbon due to their material intensity, exposure-driven replacement cycles, and complex assemblies. As operational energy demand decreases under increasingly stringent energy regulations, embodied impacts associated with facades are becoming a dominant component of whole-life building emissions. Conventional façade systems typically follow linear end-of-life pathways, resulting in limited material recovery and significant waste generation. Circular economy (CE) principles offer a pathway to address these challenges through durability, design for disassembly, reuse, and high-value recycling; however, comparative assessments integrating environmental performance and circularity across façade typologies remain limited. This study evaluates the whole-life environmental and circularity performance of six façade systems—three conventional and three emerging—using a combined Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), with global warming potential (GWP) as the primary environmental indicator, and a circularity assessment. The analysis covers all life-cycle stages, enabling consistent comparison across contrasting material compositions and assembly strategies. The results reveal clear trade-offs between embodied carbon and circularity potential. Conventional mineral-based systems exhibit higher embodied carbon and rely predominantly on downcycling, whereas façade systems incorporating bio-based materials and mechanically fixed assemblies demonstrate improved circularity potential. Construction technique, connection strategy, and end-of-life pathways emerge as critical drivers influencing both environmental and circularity outcomes. Overall, the findings highlight that façade circularity is shaped by system-level design decisions rather than material choice alone, underscoring the importance of integrating environmental and circularity considerations during early façade design stages.

title: Optimal coupling of shower drain water heat recovery systems with domestic electrical and heat pump storage water heaters
abstract: With the overall increase in the energy performance of buildings, domestic hot water (DHW) will become a major source of consumption. In addition, around 80% of shower water is drained away, representing a significant source of waste heat in buildings. This publication explores the potential for coupling common DHW production solutions (electric and heat pump storage water heaters) with drain water heat recovery units (DWHR). The aim is to identify the optimal combination of systems and settings mainly based on heat recovery from drain water and exhaust air (heat pump), in order to maximize the DHW production efficiency. A theoretical model taking into account biofouling, dynamic effects, seasonality, and static losses was developed and validated using in situ measurements over a year ( cv ( RMSE ) < 6%) and TRNSYS simulations ( cv ( RMSE < 7%). These tools have shown that coefficients of performance can reach values ranging from 6.3 (experimentation) to 8 (simulation) while using commercially available systems that are already widely used. This study also shows that the DWHR increases static heat loss and decreases heat pump COP of about 15–20%. The study also showed that the best energy performance of the overall system [tank + heat pump + heat recovery unit] was achieved with an unbalanced DWHR connected only to the shower mixer, which does not offer the best recovery efficiency but limits heat loss and maximizes heat pump performance. The balanced configuration also offers good performance, though slightly lower, while the unbalanced configuration with a DWHR connected to the storage tank offers significantly lower performance.

title: Achieving high-precision automated urban block units modeling through domain enhancement and instruction fine-tuning of large language models
A two-stage privacy-preserving framework for occupancy and internal heat gain estimation in buildings using deep learning
Cascaded generative design framework for modular prefabricated buildings involving multi-performance response
Enhancing residential building retrofit landscape in Canada: perspectives from public policy professionals
abstract: Despite the nationwide implementation of residential building retrofit programs in Canada, they have exhibited limited effectiveness in achieving strategic objectives. Enhancing the effectiveness of these programs requires insights from public policy professionals who are directly involved in it; however, such perspectives remain underrepresented in the existing literature. This research explores public policy professionals' perspectives on strategic policy objectives in implementing residential building retrofits, their involvement in program development and delivery, and the perceived barriers, effectiveness, and lessons learned from existing retrofit policies. The data were gathered from a cross-sectional survey, which was distributed to public policy professionals who are involved in residential building retrofitting in Canada. The findings revealed that extending the lifespan and functionality of aging housing stock (mean (M) = 4.50) and reducing household energy consumption and operation costs (M = 4.46) are strategic objectives that work well for promoting residential building retrofit decisions, closely followed by climate mitigation (M = 4.33) and adaptation (M = 4.33). Results further showcased that public policy professionals have low involvement in retrofit policy design (M = 2.28) and moderate engagement in implementation (M = 2.94). It was further revealed that the perceived effectiveness of current residential retrofit policies is moderate, indicating the need for a more integrated and coordinated policy framework. The path to transformative impact lies in designing retrofit programs that focus on long-term continuity, introducing financing mechanisms that reduce the upfront cost burden of the homeowners, developing awareness-building initiatives, establishing simple and clear administrative procedures, promoting multi-stakeholder collaboration from an early stage, and training the construction workforce for implementation readiness.

title: Full-scale dual-source dew-point evaporative cooler: experimental validation of sub-wet-bulb cooling without process air loss
Semantic error debugging of building energy models: a multi-agent approach based on retrieval-augmented generation
Thermal-environment optimization towards lower HVAC energy and childhood respiratory incidence in Shanghai
Research on the natural compensation mechanism of reservoir temperature after geothermal extraction stops in open-loop geothermal systems based on heterogeneous reservoirs
Thermal behaviour and energy performance of driven precast energy piles in Norwegian quick clay: a full-scale field study
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive long-term field investigation of the thermal performance of two full-scale end-bearing driven energy piles (DEPs) installed in sensitive Norwegian quick-clay deposits under realistic ground source heat pump (GSHP) operation. This study provides one of the few detailed long-term field investigations of driven energy piles installed in Norwegian quick-clay deposits under cold-climate conditions, while previous studies have predominantly focused on cast-in-place piles and different soil environments. The experimental program was designed to capture pile and ground thermal responses over a six-month period, incorporating both heat extraction and heat storage within a coupled system, where DEP2 operated as the heat source and DEP1 as the heat storage pile. System operation was carried out such that the pile-soil interface remained above the freezing point, as the undisturbed ground temperature at the test site was 6.8 °C. Both piles and the surrounding soil were extensively instrumented using a combination of conventional point sensors and distributed fibre optic sensing (DFOS), enabling high-resolution monitoring of temperature evolution along the pile shafts and in the adjacent ground. The results demonstrate a largely uniform temperature distribution (variation within ±0.8 °C) along the pile depth, indicating conduction-dominated heat transfer, with minor deviations near the ground surface due to ambient effects. The storage pile (DEP1) exhibited a progressive temperature increase, reaching 16–18 °C, while the extraction pile (DEP2) maintained stable temperatures within 4–5.5 °C despite a minimum temperature constraint of 2 °C, confirming safe operation without the risk of freezing. Ground temperature measurements revealed localized cooling near the extraction pile and sustained heating near the storage pile, with clear evidence of thermal interaction between adjacent piles at later stages of operation. The agreement between DFOS and conventional sensors validates the reliability of distributed sensing for long-term monitoring of energy geostructures. Energy performance analysis indicated average heat exchange rates of 210 W m −1 (extraction) and 300 W m −1 (storage), with a stable heat pump coefficient of performance (COP), calculated based on compressor electricity consumption, of approximately 3.8 under intermittent operation. The comparatively high heat exchange rates observed in this study may be partly associated with improved pile-soil thermal contact resulting from the driven installation process; however, direct quantification of local thermal property changes was beyond the scope of the present investigation. Overall, the findings provide rare full-scale evidence of stable and efficient thermal behaviour of driven energy piles in saturated clay under cold-climate conditions with low ground temperatures, supporting their application as sustainable geothermal foundation systems in urban environments.

title: Primarily cooling performance characterization of a solar and sky radiative cooling assisted air source heat pump
Multi-objective optimization of high-density urban block morphology using machine learning: a synergistic approach for thermal comfort and building energy performance
Parametric optimization of high-rise buildings' energy efficiency through volumetric distribution patterns: A case study of Tehran

An integrated framework for enhancing energy efficiency and environmental sustainability in historic buildings and sites: A comprehensive overview of policy, certification protocols and research perspectives
abstract: Historic buildings embody the cultural identity of cities and societies, making their preservation a fundamental component of sustainable urban development. At the same time, current energy transition targets and greenhouse gas reduction goals require substantial improvements in the performance of the existing building stock, including heritage assets. This dual imperative generates a persistent tension between sustainability objectives and conservation requirements. This paper explores this challenge, through a comprehensive analysis of policies, environmental certification protocols, scientific research trends and real-world case studies, with a particular focus on the Italian territory, which is a relevant and significant context with respect to built cultural heritage. The results reveal a fragmented regulatory framework where the integration of energy efficiency into heritage conservation has gained structured attention only in recent years, particularly since 2015, mainly through non-binding guidelines. Among the 32 analyzed papers and case studies, 44% are 19th–20th century buildings mainly located in Central Italy, though they often lack in-depth historical and environmental analysis. The study proposes a replicable and integrated framework aimed at aligning heritage conservation principles with energy performance, environmental sustainability, and comfort objectives, advocating for experimental and numerical methods to design innovative and compatible retrofit strategies. By bridging policy analysis, sustainability assessment tools, and applied research, this study contributes to advancing a holistic approach to the energy and environmental retrofit of historic buildings and sites.

title: Development of an energy monitoring and regulating system to reduce building energy consumption
Numerical and experimental study of non-uniform thermal behaviors in BIPV double-skin façade cavities
Optimal water network management for maximizing energy recovery in building with experimental validation
Experimental–simulation framework for assessing novel insulation performance: A case study on bio-PUR combining measurements with IDA ICE and EnergyPlus modelling
abstract: Reducing energy use and associated CO₂ emissions in existing buildings is a key challenge in the transition towards a low-carbon built environment. Renovation using low-carbon, high-performance envelope insulation materials offers significant potential, but reliable methods are needed to assess their performance under real-world operating conditions. This study presents an integrated experimental and modelling framework to evaluate the thermal and energy performance of novel insulation materials under real outdoor conditions. Two parallel full-scale test cells were used to represent pre- and post-renovation configurations, enabling a direct comparison between baseline and renovated test wall assemblies. High-resolution experimental measurements were combined with transient simulations in IDA ICE and EnergyPlus to investigate a newly developed bio-based polyurethane (bio-PUR) insulation, which was integrated into one external wall and the window frame of the renovated test cell. Model validation was carried out by comparing simulated and measured operative temperatures, internal surface temperatures, heat fluxes, and heating energy demand. Across multiple operating scenarios, the calibrated models reproduced temperature measurements with deviations between measured and simulated values generally below 5% in the heated cases, while heat-flux and heating-energy predictions showed deviations below approximately 16% and 12%, respectively; larger discrepancies were observed under free-floating conditions. Sensitivity and parametric analyses identified insulation thermal conductivity as the dominant material property influencing heat flux and heating energy demand, while air-infiltration modelling primarily affected the latter; operative and surface temperatures showed low sensitivity to material properties and infiltration modelling. The renovated test cell exhibited a 26% reduction in space-heating demand compared with the reference configuration. Overall, the results indicate that combining full-scale experimentation with numerical modelling provides a robust framework for assessing low-carbon envelope solutions and supports their application in energy-efficient building renovation.

title: Prediction and multi-objective optimization of daylighting and energy performance in the university library atrium using explainable ensemble model and NSGA-II
Conceptualizing, practicing and assessing sufficiency in housing: a systematic literature review
Experimental assessment of steel slag asphalt solar collectors for urban heat island mitigation and thermal energy harvesting
abstract: This study experimentally evaluates the combined use of steel slag (SS) aggregates and asphalt solar collectors (ASC) in hot mix asphalt (HMA) pavements for urban heat island (UHI) mitigation and solar thermal energy harvesting. The novelty of the research lies in evaluating the thermo-functional behaviour of dense and gap-graded asphalt mixtures incorporating recycled steel slag under active cooling conditions. Different asphalt mixture combinations were analysed, including conventional configurations and configurations incorporating SS aggregates, resulting in four pavement structures: dense mixtures with an AC22D base layer and AC16D wearing course, and gap-graded BBTM11B wearing course mixtures with an AC22D base layer. Tests were conducted under controlled laboratory conditions using infrared thermal radiation. The ASC system consisted of a serpentine coil embedded at a depth of 50 mm, used to simulate active cooling through water flow rates of 30, 60, and 120 L/h. The thermal evolution of the system was monitored using embedded thermocouples and infrared thermography. The incorporation of SS reduced thermal conductivity (λ), with conventional mixtures exhibiting higher λ values (1.56–1.76 W/m∙K) compared to their SS counterparts (0.92–1.09 W/m∙K). This reduction resulted in slower heat dissipation and higher surface temperatures in mixtures incorporating SS. Nevertheless, dense mixtures containing SS, due to their higher λ values compared to gap-graded mixtures produced with the same recycled material, achieved a more balanced thermal response between heat retention and heat transfer. Under a flow rate of 120 L/h, dense pavements incorporating SS reduced surface temperature by up to 16.3 °C, while conventional mixtures achieved reductions of up to 21.2 °C. These results demonstrate that dense configurations exhibit more efficient thermo-functional behaviour for ASC applications, particularly when incorporating steel slag, promoting a more suitable balance between thermal dissipation and solar energy recovery. In addition, thermal efficiency increased with increasing flow rate; however, this increase caused a reduction in ΔT due to the lower fluid residence time within the system. Finally, infrared thermography confirmed and validated the thermal trends recorded by the embedded thermocouples. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of steel slag asphalt solar collectors in dense mixtures as sustainable thermo-functional pavements capable of simultaneously improving UHI mitigation and thermal energy recovery.

title: Predicting after-renovation value to support investment decisions: A data-driven approach
abstract: The European building stock is highly energy inefficient, highlighting the need for effective incentives to accelerate energy efficiency renovations. Beyond reducing energy consumption, such refurbishments can generate additional benefits, including increases in property value, which are particularly relevant for homeowners and investors. Thus, quantifying the relationship between energy performance and after-renovation property value is essential for supporting investment decisions and capturing the broader economic impact of renovation. This study proposes a data-driven decision-support framework to estimate residential property prices and predict the market value effects of energy efficiency upgrades. Using a large dataset of approximately 270,000 residential listings from Greece, a gradient boosting model is developed, incorporating structural, spatial, and energy performance features. The model achieves strong predictive performance, with an R 2 score of 0.86 on the test set. It is subsequently employed to perform counterfactual simulations of energy performance certificate improvements, enabling the estimation of expected price changes following a renovation. The results indicate a positive relationship between energy performance and property value, with substantial improvements in energy performance certificate ratings associated with price increases of up to 30%. A replication study using Austrian residential market data yields comparable accuracy, demonstrating the robustness of the approach across different European markets. Overall, the proposed approach provides a transparent and scalable data-driven framework for quantifying the economic benefits of energy efficiency renovations, supporting decision-making for homeowners, investors and policy makers.

title: A novel data-analytics based process for load profiling and meter-level anomaly detection in building energy consumption time series
abstract: The ongoing digitalization of building operations, combined with growing demands for energy efficiency and sustainability, has intensified the need for advanced methodologies to monitor building energy performance and promptly detect infrequent and unexpected consumption patterns. However, many existing anomaly detection approaches either depend on rigid threshold rules lacking adaptability or employ complex black-box models that offer limited interpretability and require high-resolution monitoring infrastructures, which are often unavailable in many existing buildings. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel data analytics-based methodology for detecting anomalies in building energy consumption time series, addressing the critical need for precise and scalable tools for energy performance monitoring. Tested on a university campus energy consumption time series, the proposed approach explicitly separates and models the shape and magnitude components of daily electrical load profiles, enabling a detailed characterization of typical consumption behaviors. Historical daily electricity data are clustered to identify recurring load shapes, serving as the groundwork for predictive models that estimate both the expected profile shape and total daily energy use based solely on readily available contextual variables, such as weather conditions and calendar information. By integrating classification and regression techniques with unsupervised learning, the framework generates synthetic daily load profile benchmarks, enabling continuous or recurrent comparisons with actual energy consumption. This supports timely, sub-daily anomaly detection while maintaining low computational cost. Through validation over a 24-week testing period, the framework successfully identified 17 days exhibiting anomalous consumption patterns, corresponding to a total overconsumption of approximately 1400 kWh. These results confirm the robustness and reliability of the approach in defining statistically informed operational baselines and detecting deviations. The method also provides practical diagnostic insight and supports scalable implementation, particularly in contexts where sensor infrastructure is limited.

title: Towards net-zero energy buildings: scenario-based review of passive and active energy approaches
Implications of geometry simplification in dynamic building energy modeling: Comparative analysis of detailed and simplified geometries
Prediction of HVAC operational carbon emissions for schematic design: data-driven method based on functional spaces combinations
Experimental investigation of the thermo-mechanical response of small-scale energy pile groups under inclined loads and short-term thermal cycling
Standardization of urban heat island effects and how different building types reflect solar radiation to form thermal inertia
An improved two-layer co-optimization method embedding divide-and-conquer strategy for accuracy-efficiency balancing design of distributed multi-energy system
Mitigating particulate matter through building-integrated greenery with active airflow: experimental validation and CFD modeling
abstract: Urban or building-integrated greenery systems represent a promising Nature-based Solution for mitigating local particulate matter concentrations. However, field investigations concerning real-world PM filtration by hedges at building air intakes remain rare due to environmental complexities and the highly specific nature of each application. This study evaluates the PM mitigation performance of an active, hedge-based filtration system integrated into a building's HVAC intake through a hybrid approach combining an in-situ monitoring campaign and computational fluid dynamics modeling. The empirical results demonstrate localized filtration potential, with median reductions of 23.2% for PM 2.5 and 24.4% for PM 10 directly behind the vegetation. Considering air stream bypass, reductions at the air intake were observed for 10.6% and 13.1% for PM 2.5 and PM 10 , respectively. The computational fluid dynamics model exhibited discrepancies of 6.48% for PM 2.5 and 8.98% for PM 10 compared to empirical data. Parametric simulations varying leaf area density and geometric configurations indicated that aerodynamic resistance limits structural flow when leaf area density exceeds 3.0 m 2 /m 3 . By optimizing the geometric interface to achieve less bypass, simulated system efficiency was maximized to 17.1%. While building-integrated active greenery cannot replace mechanical HVAC filters, it could possibly serve as a pre-filtration stage under the of requirements of strategic geometric configuration, optimized leaf area density and appropriate choice of plant species.

title: Multi-domain residual learning framework for improving generalization in chiller Modeling

Heterogeneous driving mechanisms of urban-rural residential carbon emissions in severe cold agro-pastoral ecotones and differentiated low-carbon development pathways: a case study of inner Mongolia, China
abstract: Severe cold agro-pastoral ecotones face critical challenges in residential decarbonization, yet the heterogeneous driving mechanisms underlying urban and rural residential carbon emission disparities remain largely unknown, leading to uniform low-carbon pathways with limited effectiveness. Here we address this gap by establishing the first high-resolution urban-rural integrated residential energy database for central and western Inner Mongolia through large-sample field surveys and year-round in-situ measurements, and developing an integrated analytical framework combining multi-model cross-validation, SHAP-based interpretable machine learning, Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition, and ASHRAE-calibrated building energy simulation. Our results reveal a fundamental heterogeneity in driving mechanisms: for rural buildings, envelope thermal performance dominates carbon emissions (47.2% contribution), whereas for urban buildings, heating system efficiency is the primary driver (38.5%). This heterogeneity explains why the endowment effect—differences in envelope thermal performance and heating system efficiency—accounts for 78.6% of the total urban and rural residential carbon gap. The annual operational carbon intensity of rural residential buildings is 1.66 times that of urban buildings. A differentiated pathway combining envelope energy efficiency improvement with clean heating replacement achieves optimal cost-effectiveness, enabling residential building carbon peaking before 2027 and an 87.2% emission reduction by 2060. This study provides a theoretically grounded, empirically validated, and replicable paradigm for residential decarbonization in severe cold agro-pastoral ecotones worldwide.

title: DCMSAC: Device-level collaborative multi-agent soft actor-critic HVAC control for comfort and energy efficiency
Variable carbon benchmarks in low-carbon design of concrete buildings: A stochastic modeling approach with time-dependent analysis
Surrogate-assisted co-optimization of smart thermostat control and building envelope properties for residential peak shaving and rebound mitigation
A framework for assessing smart thermostat fault detection and diagnosis under unmeasurable building load disturbances
A hybrid deep learning–ensemble model for accurate and explainable electricity demand forecasting in renewable energy communities
abstract: Accurate, interpretable, and scalable short-term electricity demand forecasting is a crucial requirement for transitioning towards decentralized, citizen-driven energy systems, particularly within renewable energy communities (RECs). The proposed framework utilizes long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) to capture both the sequential dynamics of consumption and the nonlinear interactions between household and community-level characteristics. A stratified household selection strategy based on contribution-level binning is employed to ensure coverage across distinct demand regimes while maintaining computational efficiency. Based on 15-minute smart meter data from a renewable energy community in Loureiro, Portugal, the hybrid model achieved the lowest prediction errors at both scales, with a best-case household-level mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 1.25% and a community-level average MAPE of 3.14%, corresponding to explained variance ( R 2 ) values of 0.9420 and 0.9558, respectively. Although XGBoost performed slightly better for specific low-variability households, the hybrid approach consistently outperformed the standalone models in terms of accuracy and robustness. The model’s interpretation is enhanced by SHAP, which reveals distinct demand drivers for consumers, including memory-based characteristics and climatic variables like temperature and solar radiation. The Interpretive, multi-level Prediction framework provides a reliable basis for practical REC applications, such as battery planning, peer-to-peer trading, and real-time demand response.

title: Automating BREEAM certification in a BIM environment: analysis of credit achievability using two workflows
Virtual-reality-assisted evaluation of elderly-oriented lighting layouts in indoor communal spaces in geracomia
Quantification of predictability, model accuracy, and uncertainty of cooling loads in real-life buildings
Disaggregation of heating energy into domestic hot water and space heating for apartment buildings: A Norwegian case study.
abstract: Reliable knowledge of domestic hot water (DHW) and space heating (SH) energy use in buildings is essential for dimensioning heating systems, evaluating building performance, and modelling energy demand and flexibility. However, sub-metering that distinguishes between SH and DHW is rare, particularly in older buildings. This article presents a case study comparing five methods for disaggregating DHW and SH energy use and generating average daily load profiles for DHW from total heating measurements. The case study covers 19 Norwegian apartment buildings spanning three locations with both district heating and electric heating systems. A key limitation is that 17 of the 19 buildings belong to the same condominium. All methods are evaluated against measured DHW demand. The results show that DHW energy use has clear seasonal patterns in the case study buildings that may be beneficial to consider when developing average load profiles for building energy simulations. The current standard load profiles for Norwegian buildings do not capture the general shape of the average daily DHW load profiles seen in the case study buildings. A categorical boosting regression model (Method 5) and a seasonally corrected Building-Profet method (Method 3 diss,corr ) performed at a statistically comparable level for both DHW disaggregation and daily load profile generation and were the best performing methods overall. However, Method 5 performed noticeably weaker on the two buildings outside the main condominium while achieving higher performance within it. A broader and more diverse dataset would be needed to validate the generalisability of the results.

title: A novel hybrid cooling strategy for residential buildings integrating PV-powered AC and PCM thermal energy storage with intermittent operation
Autonomy is not enough: why agentic AI in the built environment demands governance
Closing the selection gap in passive retrofit optimization: a pathway-based framework for resident-informed selection in old residential buildings in cold-region China
A parametric workflow for multi-objective optimization of solar-access trade-offs in neighborhood-scale infill design: a case study of Gorgan, Iran
abstract: Solar access in dense infill neighborhoods is shaped by building morphology and surrounding context, making climate-responsive housing design difficult under real planning constraints. This study developed a parametric multi-objective optimization workflow for neighborhood-scale infill design in Gorgan, Iran, under explicit morphological and development-capacity constraints. Solar performance was defined through two annual indicators evaluated during 06:00–16:00: incident solar radiation (ISR) on building envelopes, treated as a maximization objective, and mean direct sun hours (DSH) in ground-level open spaces, treated as a minimization objective. The workflow integrated parametric massing generation in Rhino/Grasshopper, solar simulation in Ladybug Tools, and evolutionary optimization in Wallacei using NSGA-II. The optimization used a population of 50 over 100 generations, producing 5000 solutions. Stable convergence was observed in final generations, with 12 Pareto-optimal solutions identified. Results revealed an ISR–DSH trade-off rather than a single universally optimal solution or uniform improvement across both indicators. Relative to the baseline reference scenario, used only for post-optimization comparison, selected Pareto-optimal solutions reduced annual mean ground-level DSH by about 22.2%, while annual envelope ISR decreased by 17.2–17.6%, quantifying the trade-off between improved ground-level solar control and reduced envelope-level solar access. Across the selected solutions, ISR ranged from 669.344 to 672.043 kWh/m 2 and DSH from 1168.81 to 1169.88 h/point. Building height emerged as the primary driver of the ISR–DSH trade-off, while typology and footprint acted mainly as secondary tuning variables. Overall, the workflow supports early-stage infill design by identifying Pareto-efficient alternatives that clarify how feasible configurations negotiate envelope-level solar access and ground-level solar control.

title: Energy and whole life economic performance of semitransparent photovoltaic glazing in hot arid climate
The evolution of inverse optimization: A cross-disciplinary review of algorithmic approaches and application framework in building life cycle assessment
abstract: Optimization techniques have become fundamental tools for addressing complex decision making challenges across diverse domains, yet traditional forward optimization approaches often struggle with incomplete information, unknown preferences, and dynamic constraints. This literature review examines the emerging field of inverse optimization as a complementary paradigm that works backward from observed solutions to infer underlying objectives and constraints. While forward optimization has been extensively applied in building design and life cycle assessment, it faces limitations in early design stages where 20% of decisions determine 80% of future performance outcomes. This review synthesizes 95 studies across seven disciplines and 69 within the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction industry to analyze how inverse optimization enhances sustainable building design. Results show rapid growth of applications after 2020, led by China, the U.S., and the U.K., with 58% of studies targeting environmental performance, 43% economic, and 10% social factors.
