Hybrid and machine-learning-based inverse methods, particularly genetic algorithms, neural networks, and Gaussian processes dominate recent research, enabling improved model calibration, faster convergence, and robustness under uncertainty. Inverse optimization is found effective in extracting decision logic from empirical data, calibrating energy models, and managing multi-objective trade-offs between energy, comfort, and cost. Despite these advances, methodological gaps remain such as the lack of standardized inverse Life Cycle Assessment workflows, limited coupling between inverse models and Building Information Modeling platforms, and insufficient methods for handling uncertainty and multi-objective trade-offs in early-stage design. Building on this synthesis and on prior methodological reviews in operations research, the review proposes a framework integrating Inverse Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), multi-objective decision-making, and LCA to guide data driven, adaptive approaches for optimizing environmental performance in buildings.

title: Modular modeling and optimal sizing of electrified heating systems in renewable-powered communities considering system complexity and heterogeneity
Bridging the heating equity gap in income-based energy burden metrics: A feature-based framework for identifying thermally vulnerable households
abstract: Traditional income-based energy poverty metrics often fail to identify vulnerable households that deliberately limit their energy use to reduce financial strain, potentially falling under energy poverty thresholds at the cost of unsafe thermal conditions. Failure to detect these thermally vulnerable households creates a heating equity gap —defined as the shortfall between medically-grounded World Health Organization thresholds recommended for healthy adults and indoor temperatures—causes vulnerable households to remain unidentified as energy poor, thus rendering them ineligible for support programs while exposing them to serious health risks. To address this gap, we introduce an explainable AI-driven dual vulnerability assessment framework that integrates indoor temperature-based thermal vulnerability with heating activation behavior to improve cross-context comparability and minimize misclassifications caused by biased thresholds. Analysis employing a synthetically generated dataset of N=6,000 households, created through statistical augmentation of population-level energy consumption and housing characteristic distributions calibrated to Montana’s climate region during winter months, has identified 713 thermally vulnerable households (11.9%), of which 91.2% and 50.4% were overlooked by the standard 10% and 2M energy burden thresholds, respectively. Feature importance analysis shows that the strongest vulnerability predictors are energy consumption patterns, income level, and behavioral inflection temperatures. Interaction effects further reveal that building characteristics and economic constraints impact vulnerability in ways not captured by single factors: 18% of households maintain adequate indoor temperatures despite delayed heating activation, whereas 10% experience thermal vulnerability despite normal heating activation patterns. By distinguishing households that require structural improvements from those that need immediate financial assistance, this explainable framework provides actionable guidance to policymakers. It fundamentally shifts energy poverty assessment toward a multidimensional perspective—one that integrates socioeconomic factors, actual thermal conditions, structural housing characteristics, and behavioral adaptations to capture hidden forms of energy insecurity.

title: A novel demand response control method of heat pump coupled phase change thermal storage heating system based on reinforcement learning and real-time pricing
Robust ZrO2/Na2SiO3 aqueous coatings enabling scalable and low-VOC radiative cooling with enhanced durability
Two-level stacking-RFR architecture for day-ahead photovoltaic energy forecasting: Multi-site validation
Coverage-aware multi-head TabNet with sparsity regularization for unified AHU AFDD: A three-building case study using real operational data from South Korea
Enhancing passive ventilation using a solar chimney with a louvre-shaped vortex promoter
abstract: Existing performance enhancement strategies for solar chimneys often require large installation space or complex structures and offer limited flexibility in ventilation control. To address these limitations, this study proposes a simple and practical louvre-shaped vortex generator for improving heat transfer and the performance of buoyancy-driven passive ventilation. A two-dimensional numerical model is adopted to examine the effects of louvre attack angle and location under different Rayleigh numbers ( Ra ). A baseline analysis shows that a louvre-integrated solar chimney with a louvre attack angle of 60 ° yields substantially higher ventilation rates than the conventional configuration, with 110–180% improvements of Air Change per Hour ( ACH ) over the Ra range of 7 × 10 10 to 2.8 × 10 12 . The performance improvement is due to vortex-induced unsteadiness in the wake of the louvre, which redistributes turbulent energy and enhances thermal homogenization across the chimney width. A parametric analysis has identified an optimal configuration with a 45 ° inclined louvre placed at the horizontal centreline and one quarter of the chimney-height from the inlet, achieving a maximum ACH improvement of 227% relative to the conventional design without the louvre. The ventilation performance gain resulting from the louvre is shown to be highly sensitive to local flow conditions, diminishing if the louvre is positioned too close to the absorber or too far from the inlet.

title: Solar photovoltaic systems adoption for passive houses in New Zealand: A mixed-methods analysis of trends and influencing factors
abstract: Solar photovoltaic systems (SPVS) can complement Passive Houses (PHs) by reducing grid dependence, emissions, and household energy costs. However, existing SPVS–PH research has emphasised technical performance and modelling, with limited attention to stakeholder, financial, policy, and market factors shaping adoption. This gap is evident in New Zealand, where SPVS uptake is increasing in conventional housing but remains limited in PHs. This study investigates the trends, drivers, barriers, and strategies influencing SPVS adoption in New Zealand PHs. A sequential mixed-methods approach was used, comprising document analysis, 34 interviews, and a survey of 96 building and energy professionals. Qualitative data were analysed thematically, while survey responses were examined using mean ranking (M), one-sample t -tests, and reliability testing in SPSS. Findings show that New Zealand's SPVS capacity reached 573 MW in [1] , while PH Plus and Premium certifications remain limited but are gradually increasing. Interviews identified 13 drivers, 18 barriers, and 18 strategies. Survey results ranked the strongest drivers as low-carbon transition support (M = 4.57), and declining SPVS costs (M = 4.55). The strongest barriers were budget constraints (M = 4.09) and low solar buy-back rates (M = 3.87); the strongest strategies were optimised design and installation (M = 4.54) and battery integration (M = 4.53). Although limited to stakeholder perceptions in New Zealand, the study shows adoption is shaped by financial viability, policy support, and early-stage design integration, thereby contributing to Sustainable Development Goals 7 (Affordable & Clean Energy) and 13 (Climate Action).

title: Does the setup of rooftop PV systems unavoidably affect indoor thermal comfort and energy performance?
Experimental investigation into the interactions between rooftop photovoltaics and the surrounding built environment
A review of fuel cell-based combined cooling, heating, and power systems for building applications
Thermal pleasure–based spacing of mist–shade umbrellas in hot–humid outdoor walkways using an extended JOS-3 model
Double-skin roof as a passive cooling system: Modelling and smart control performance assessment through a field experiment
abstract: Improving passive cooling performance in naturally conditioned buildings requires not only effective design solutions but also control frameworks that adapt to dynamic environmental and indoor conditions. This study develops and experimentally validates a model-based predictive control strategy for a novel double-skin roof system integrating night ventilation and evaporative cooling. The key novelty lies in coupling a lightweight physically based model with a predictive control algorithm designed for real-world implementation. A comprehensive monitoring campaign during summer 2024 captured the thermal behaviour of the roof and indoor environment across multiple operating modes for calibration and validation of the passive-cooling roof model. The smart control was implemented and assessed during the summer of 2025. This new control architecture was embedded into the existing KNX communication framework of the double-skin roof system, with the control optimiser deployed in a server service. Unlike conventional rule-based approaches, the proposed controller anticipates future conditions to optimise operation, enabling proactive night-time heat dissipation and improved cooling storage. Indoor conditions remained within the restrictive ASHRAE adaptive comfort limits for 96.6% of the time, with a maximum daily discomfort of 13%. Compared to rule-based control, overheating was reduced by an average of 11.5 percentage points, exceeding 20 points during peak summer periods. The results indicated that this new smart passive cooling roof solution can mitigate energy poverty in vulnerable contexts without requiring additional subsidies for the public administration or imposing an economic burden on householders, as its operating costs are equivalent to less than 3% of household monthly income.

title: Coupled mechanical and thermal performance of fly ash blended mortars reinforced with carbonized bamboo fibers for building envelope applications
Corrigendum to “Semantic error debugging of building energy models: a multi-agent approach based on retrieval-augmented generation” [Energy Build. 368 (2026) 117786]
From optimization to decision-making: A dynamic simulation-based framework for residential building Design in Mediterranean Climates
abstract: The present study develops and applies a validated dynamic simulation-based multi-objective optimization and decision-support framework for residential buildings in Mediterranean climates. A high-fidelity EnergyPlus model is coupled with a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to simultaneously minimize annual space-conditioning energy demand and construction material cost. The optimization process generates a well-defined Pareto front comprising 59 non-dominated solutions, revealing a clear trade-off between energy performance and construction cost. The results indicate that configurations with improved envelope performance—particularly glazing and wall insulation—significantly reduce energy demand at the expense of increased construction cost. A representative global compromise solution is identified using a utopia-based distance criterion, corresponding to an energy reduction of approximately 14% compared to the baseline configuration. The analysis further reveals a redistribution of seasonal loads, with reduced heating demand accompanied by a moderate increase in cooling demand, highlighting the importance of dynamic simulation in capturing climate-dependent trade-offs. To facilitate the interpretation of optimization outcomes and support practical decision-making, a pruning strategy based on knee-point identification is applied to the Pareto set, enabling the extraction of a reduced subset of representative solutions. The results demonstrate that a limited number of configurations can effectively capture the most significant energy–cost trade-offs while preserving solution diversity. By combining Pareto-front analysis with solution-pruning techniques, the proposed framework provides a systematic decision-support approach for identifying representative and practically applicable design alternatives. The proposed framework extends conventional simulation-based optimization by systematically integrating validated dynamic simulation, multi-objective optimization, and decision-support procedures within a unified workflow for residential building design.

title: Thermal performance and microclimate modulation: A year-long, multi-site study of operational green roofs in Barcelona under severe water scarcity
abstract: This study provides a novel, high-resolution assessment of green roof hygrothermal performance in a Western Mediterranean city during a severe, year-long drought. While previous research has broadly demonstrated cooling effects, this work advances the field by offering a uniquely detailed, minute-scale comparison of air temperature, surface temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed across four diverse, long-term operational green and grey roof pairs in Barcelona. Measurements covering an exceptional drought, an extreme summer, and a mild winter allow a direct evaluation of system resilience under water-limited conditions. The resulting dataset, with a 1-minute temporal resolution sustained over a full year, represents one of the most comprehensive empirical resources for Mediterranean climates to date. A rigorous statistical framework correcting for autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity ensures the robustness of the results. Green roofs exhibited up to 18 °C lower surface temperatures in summer and maintained 1–2 °C cooler near-roof air than conventional roofs, while showing enhanced nocturnal thermal inertia in winter. Reduced daytime temperature dispersion under strong solar radiation further indicates that vegetation moderates local air turbulence, a rarely quantified mechanism relevant to urban microclimate modelling. Overall, these results confirm that even under prolonged drought, extensive green roofs can meaningfully buffer temperature extremes, offering solid empirical support for climate-resilient urban design and green infrastructure planning.

title: Thermo-electrical modeling and experimental validation of photovoltaic panels with back-surface capillary material for passive evaporative cooling
Experimental validation of an energy balance model for multi-pane radiant glazing systems using a full-scale outdoor test cell
abstract: This study develops and validates a comprehensive energy-balance model for predicting the thermal behaviour of multi-pane glazing systems, with a specific focus on Radiant Glass (RG) and conventional Double-Glazed Units (DGU). A nonlinear mathematical framework integrating conduction, convection, and long-wave radiation is formulated using established heat-transfer correlations and glazing standards. The model is implemented through iterative numerical methods and evaluated against long-term full-scale experimental data collected from two identical test cells equipped with DGU and RG systems under real winter boundary conditions. Seven representative days were analysed to compare measured surface temperatures with model predictions. Results show excellent agreement for both glazing types, with RG, despite larger gradients induced by active heating, demonstrates high predictive accuracy, minimal deviations and very strong statistical correlation. Discrepancies are mainly attributed to environmental uncertainties and convection-model simplifications. This work fills a gap in the literature by validating the model and providing a robust framework for predicting RG performance under real boundary conditions, supporting future integration into building-energy simulation tools, predictive control strategies, and whole-building energy assessments, thereby enabling advanced assessment of adaptive radiant façade technologies. • Validated nonlinear energy-balance model for multi-pane radiant glazing systems. • Strong agreement between predicted and measured glass surface temperatures. • Model accurately reproduces Radiant Glass behaviour under active heating. • Full-scale winter experiments confirm high correlations for Radiant Glass system. • Framework enables integration of Radiant Glass into building simulation tools.

title: Data-driven discovery of sensor relationships for virtual sensing in predictive building operations
Scheduling operation coordination of multi energy virtual power plant integrating thermal comfort and demand response flexibility approaches
Investigation of the influence of surface coatings on heat transfer in multilayer walls with air gaps
abstract: Air cavities that occur at interfaces in ETICS (External Thermal Insulation Composite System) assemblies (e.g., between concrete structural layers and thermal insulation due to adhesive mortar) can strongly affect heat transfer in walls, because radiative exchange across the gap may dominate under typical design temperatures. The present study investigates the potential of reflective–smoothing surface coatings applied to concrete to reduce surface emissivity in the far-infrared band and thereby increase the effective thermal resistance of wall air gaps. Seven commercially available coatings were applied to precast-like concrete specimens measuring 30×30×3 cm. Surface emissivity was determined using thermography under controlled laboratory conditions, while coating-induced changes in surface morphology were quantified via 3D optical scanning and areal topography parameters. The measured emissivity of uncoated concrete was found to be approximately 0.95. The most significant reductions in emissivity were observed with acrylic enamel (approximately 0.29) and aluminum spray (approximately 0.59). Several coatings produced only marginal changes in emissivity. The scanned surface meshes were incorporated into a validated computational model to quantify heat transfer across a 20 mm vertical air gap. A reduction in emissivity from 0.95 to 0.29 led to an increase in the air-gap thermal resistance from 0.189 to 0.311 m²K/W, and decrease in the overall U-value. The findings underscore the efficacy of emissivity control, which is associated with surface leveling and micro-facet geometry, in enhancing the thermal performance of multilayer wall assemblies with air gaps.

title: Machine learning for district heating and cooling: A review of open problems and deployment barriers
Design of modular temporary emergency spaces for dual-use public infrastructure: enhancing climate resilience and sustainability in post disaster response and recovery
Integrated evaluation of thermal, hygrothermal, and energy performance of aged building retrofits using ply-lam cross-laminated timber wall assemblies in humid continental climates
Full-year monitoring of the real-life performance of a thermochromic smart window in a tailored test building
abstract: Thermochromic smart windows switch between transmitting and blocking solar infrared radiation (IR) based on temperature. These properties enable passive modulation of solar heat gain, which significantly lowers energy consumption in buildings and increases comfort levels for occupants via a balanced indoor climate. In this study, we set up a tailored test building in Eindhoven (The Netherlands) to monitor the real-life performance of a thermochromic smart window. We produced full sized double-glazed windows comprising a laminated outboard made from thermochromic interlayers, installed them in the test building and monitored their light transmission, solar heat gain and glass surface temperature over a full year. This enabled us to study the thermochromic phase transition of a smart window under real-life conditions for the first time. We demonstrated that the temperature of the smart window's outer glass pane regulated the phase transition and that the overall performance matched well with lab data. A glass surface temperature of 30 °C, influenced by the outdoor temperature and solar irradiance (photothermal heating), led to phase transition to the IR blocking state. During summer the smart window transitioned to its IR blocking state around 13:00, whereas in winter glass surface temperatures remained below 30 °C, retaining an IR transparent state of the smart window. In spring and autumn photothermal heating on cold, but sunny days led to undesired transitions to the IR blocking state, where glass surface temperatures exceeded outdoor temperatures by up to 20 °C. We studied the effect of photothermal heating in detail to conclude that optimized behavior of the smart window can be achieved with a phase transition temperature around 35–40 °C.

title: Analysis of heat transfer characteristics and correction of heat transfer coefficients of envelope structures containing multiphase moisture in low-temperature environments
Designing cost–robustness tradeoffs in urban building cluster networks for distributed energy coordination
BMC-FedStack: Secure and robust federated stacking for residential short-term load forecasting
Optimizing machine-learning-based NILM: A comparative analysis of wavelet feature extraction for high-accuracy appliance classification
abstract: There is a pressing need to enhance energy efficiency as the global population and energy demand increase exponentially. One means to achieve this is through Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) aimed at improving energy management and identifying opportunities to reduce or shift energy consumption. While frequently cited as one of the key enablers, current NILM approaches rely on large datasets and high sampling frequencies resulting in a significant computational overhead which all but prevents the approaches from being deployed on today’s smart metering devices. A potential means to overcome this barrier is the use of Wavelets which have shown promise in reducing the sampling frequencies and data sizes necessary to train Machine Learning (ML) models offering vital advantages in systems constrained by legacy infrastructure and limited data capabilities, including smart metering devices. In addition, Wavelets can be considered to be well suited for NILM due to their proven capability to sparsely represent and amplify unique characteristics of signals featuring short periods of transient behaviour generated by electrical appliances. Given the affordances of Wavelets and the requirements of NILM, this paper presents an exhaustive comparative study of two different types of wavelet transform and four wavelet families to identify the most promising combination for a data pre-processing step within an ML-based NILM workflow. More specifically, the study examines the impact of wavelet pre-processing steps applied to the workflow proposed by Young et al. [1] for two large publicly available datasets. The study demonstrates that wavelets can reduce the required sampling frequency by up to 95% with minimal loss ( 0.0022 ) in F1-Score. With the most significant improvements observed for the XGBoost ML technique which required 5647% less computational resources to train and operate. Critically, the high thresholds of >0.99 F1-Score required for accurate appliance detection were consistently achieved at reduced computational loads utilising the Sym2 and Sym4 wavelets. In addition, this realised the ability to maintain high levels of classification at greatly reduced sampling rates - from 1 kHz to only 50 Hz - offering a pathway to efficient, scalable and accessible NILM that is compatible with existing infrastructure including the current generation of smart meters.

title: Energy efficiency in hospital buildings: a socio-technical framework of drivers, barriers, and performance outcomes
abstract: Hospitals are among the most energy-intensive building types due to continuous operation, complex technical systems, and stringent indoor environmental requirements. Enhancing energy efficiency in these facilities is therefore critical for reducing operational costs, lowering emissions, and improving system resilience. This paper presents a systematic literature review of 107 peer-reviewed studies published between 2012 and 2022, conducted following PRISMA guidelines. The review synthesises evidence on energy performance outcomes, implementation strategies, and barriers to energy efficiency in hospital buildings. The analysis identifies a growing emphasis on digitalisation, including Internet of Things (IoT), machine learning, smart monitoring, and renewable energy integration. Despite these advances, implementation remains constrained by financial limitations, aging infrastructure, regulatory complexity, and organisational capacity gaps. Drawing on these findings, the paper organises key drivers and barriers into five interdependent dimensions: Financing, Organisational Structures, Building Infrastructure, Energy Systems, and Digital Technologies. The paper contributes a socio-technical framework that conceptualises hospital energy performance as being shaped by interactions between technical building systems and institutional conditions. The framework provides a structured analytical lens for researchers, designers, and facility managers and supports the development of energy-efficient and resilient hospital buildings across diverse contexts.

title: Quantum fourier transform for unsupervised fault detection in building end-use electricity loads
abstract: Building operational faults can increase commercial energy consumption by 15–30%, yet most remain undetected due to the absence of labeled data in building management systems. Unsupervised detection methods commonly rely on Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) magnitude spectra, which discard phase information and are insensitive to fault modes that alter the temporal alignment of periodic loads without changing spectral energy. This paper proposes a Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT)-based feature representation that captures amplitude–phase relationships through quantum interference. Hourly consumption windows are angle-encoded into parameterized quantum circuits, and measurement probability distributions are fused with compact time-domain descriptors of variability collapse, persistence, and impulsivity. The approach is evaluated against an FFT magnitude baseline using three unsupervised detectors on eight disaggregated end-use streams from the Harvard HouseZero dataset spanning two years. The QFT representation achieves a mean ROC-AUC of 0.856 versus 0.612 for FFT, improving performance in 21 of 24 stream detector combinations. QFT feature extraction runs in statevector simulation on conventional hardware (∼7 ms per window), enabling immediate deployment within existing building monitoring infrastructure without quantum processors.

title: Modelling the individual in the aggregate: A quantitative analysis of user behaviour impact on urban energy consumption
abstract: Achieving net-zero carbon emissions requires enhanced energy planning, driven by the growing penetration of renewable sources, the electrification of heating and transport, and evolving consumer behaviour. Therefore, accurate urban-scale energy analysis is essential for effective planning and policy design. However, existing literature largely overlooks user behaviour as an active and structural component of energy demand, often treating it as a secondary source of uncertainty rather than as a defining feature of the system, whereas technical specifications are modelled with great precision. As a result, models tend to capture the physical performance of systems accurately yet fail to represent the stochastic and socially driven dynamics that shape real-world demand. This study introduces a hybrid, bottom-up framework that integrates user behaviour and building performance within a unified modelling structure. Occupancy dynamics are simulated through a Markov Chain Model capturing transitions between active and inactive states, while appliance-operation schedules are derived using logistic regression, both based on Time Use Survey (TUS) data, thereby enriching behavioural representation. Indoor thermal dynamics are modelled via an RC model, ensuring physical accuracy alongside computational efficiency and scalability. A key innovation is the creation of Agent Energy Consumption Units (AECUs), in which occupant behaviour, appliance usage and building characteristics are tightly coupled, supporting a granular representation of household heterogeneity. The framework is simulated at district scale and includes a sensitivity analysis of the individual user on the aggregate. Results highlight that household-type distribution is as critical as traditional technical parameters, particularly when assessing its impact on energy demand.

title: Policy transfer for HVAC control via implicit diffusion Q-learning
Homes under heat stress: A survey on building performance and occupant behavior in a central European context
abstract: With the increasing frequency and intensity of summer heatwaves due to climate change, understanding how people experience and respond to indoor heat stress is critical – particularly in regions lacking empirical data. In Central and Eastern Europe, especially in Hungary, there is a notable lack of large-scale, country-specific research on how building characteristics and occupant behavior affect summer thermal comfort. This study addresses this gap by analyzing heat perception, adaptive strategies, and satisfaction with indoor conditions across residential buildings. A nationwide Hungarian survey ( n = 1496), representative by age and sex, collected data on demographics, building features, summer heat stress, adaptation behaviors, and awareness of heatwave warnings. The questionnaire focused on thermal satisfaction as the main outcome, aiming to identify its key drivers, while also capturing adaptation behaviors and other related aspects for which limited empirical data are available. Homes were classified using the national building typology system, enabling analysis across 24 archetypes. The analysis combined descriptive statistics, group comparisons, bivariate tests, and regression modeling to identify key influencing factors. Nearly half of respondents reported dissatisfaction with indoor summer temperatures, with the highest dissatisfaction observed in older multi-apartment buildings. The most common personal adaptations include wearing light clothing (95.9%), drinking cold beverages (60.4%), and avoiding direct sunlight (56.8%). Chi-square tests and Cramer's V indicated moderate associations between thermal satisfaction and building typology, insulation, cross-ventilation ability, and adaptation behaviors. To further explore these relationships, regression models were developed with thermal satisfaction as the outcome variable using two approaches: an occupant-based model including demographic and behavioral variables, and a combined model that additionally incorporated building-related characteristics. While the occupant-based model showed limited explanatory power (R 2 = 0.055), the inclusion of building-related variables increased the explained variance (R 2 = 0.291), representing an approximately fivefold increase. Despite high awareness of heatwaves, many relied on only one or two information sources and did not substantially modify their behavior during alerts. Combined with the regression results, this suggests that improving indoor thermal conditions cannot rely on occupant-based responses alone and requires greater emphasis on building-related interventions. The findings also highlight the need for targeted, age-specific communication and building-specific interventions to improve indoor thermal comfort and support effective heat adaptation. This study provides empirical evidence to inform climate-responsive housing and heat adaptation strategies in Central Europe.

title: Numerical investigation of melting and heat transfer in plate-type PCM units with multi-mode gradient-porosity metal foam
CFD investigation of ventilation effectiveness and thermo-hydraulic performance in mixed, displacement, and reversed ventilation systems
AI-enabled pre-design programming for low-carbon buildings: toward spatial form following carbon flow
Reducing electricity use in shared residences through information-based behavioral interventions: Evidence from a randomized field experiment
abstract: Shared residences offer substantial opportunities for demand reduction because many end-use decisions can be adjusted without major retrofits. This study evaluates low-cost, information-based behavioral interventions through a naturalistic randomized field experiment in a large shared-residential setting. Using room-level smart-meter data with end-use separation, we compare weekly-delivered intervention components and estimate effects for base electricity use, driven mainly by lighting and plug loads, and for air-conditioning (AC) electricity use. Difference-in-differences results show that information interventions reduce electricity use by 7.34% for base loads and 9.47% for AC loads, whereas a conventional energy-education campaign yields no statistically detectable effect. A bundled intervention achieves the largest reductions, indicating complementarities across feedback and message components. Among single components, social ranking feedback and narrative information framing deliver the most consistent savings across both end uses. Dynamic estimates further suggest short-run persistence after withdrawal, with faster and larger responses for AC than for base loads. Overall, the findings demonstrate that scalable, feedback-based information interventions can complement technical energy management and provide actionable, low-disruption pathways for reducing electricity demand in shared residences.

title: A new adaptive base temperature method for high-resolution estimation of heating and cooling demand in Algeria
Simulation and design of heat pumps in a neighbourhood context with a focus on buffer tank optimization and performance adjustment to increase PV-self-consumption
abstract: While heat pumps are widely recognized as a key technology for decarbonizing the heating sector, their growing penetration and the ongoing transformation of the energy system introduce new challenges for electricity grids. Consequently, a holistic assessment of grid impacts at the neighbourhood scale is becoming increasingly important. To address this need, we developed a simulation workflow for analysing heat pump and buffer storage operation for a whole neighbourhood. The workflow combines a COP-based heat pump model with a thermodynamic buffer storage model and is applied to a representative district of predominantly unrenovated single- and two-family houses in Stuttgart. Using this workflow, the present paper investigates the extent to which standard-compliant heat pump sizing is compatible with efficient PV self-consumption and examines how optimizing the sizing and control parameters of heat pumps and buffer tanks influence load development within the district. Therefore, four heat pump and storage configurations and two control strategies are evaluated, one with a particular focus on PV self-consumption optimization. The results show that increasing buffer storage capacity without optimized control reduces the self-consumption rate (SCR), self-sufficiency rate (SSR), and seasonal performance factor (SPF). In contrast, a PV-self-consumption-optimized control strategy improves the average SCR and SSR by 5.4 to 25.3 percent points, though at the cost of reduced heat pump efficiency. With this PV-optimized control and large buffer storages, SCR values of up to 52.9 % and SSR values of up to 39.7 % can be achieved, decreasing the overall electricity drawn from the grid by around 8.2 to 8.6 %. For most buildings, a moderate reduction in heat pump capacity results in only marginal changes to SCR, SSR, and SPF, while substantially reducing the peak power demand at the neighbourhood level by up to 9.4 %. When combined with a staggering of start times at the district level, the peak power demand can be further reduced by more than 13 %, reducing grid strain and morning peaks. The findings demonstrate that a combination of reduced heating capacity, larger buffer storage, and intelligent control can enhance PV self-consumption while simultaneously reducing cumulative peak power demand within the district.

title: Accuracy of crowdsourced air temperature observations from multiple networks
abstract: Accurate, high-resolution, and easily accessible atmospheric urban climate data are becoming essential for the design, optimisation, and performance monitoring of sustainable cooling interventions at both building and urban scales. Crowdsourced data from Citizen Weather Stations (CWS) offer a promising opportunity to complement traditional monitoring networks. This study evaluates the accuracy and uncertainty of air temperature observations from two major CWS platforms — Netatmo and Wunderground — for urban climate monitoring, using London as a case study. Meteorological time series from 1502 CWS (1053 Netatmo and 449 Wunderground) were compared against 11 Official Weather Stations (OWS) from the UK Met Office MIDAS database. A comprehensive pre-processing and QC (QC) workflow based on demonstrated techniques was implemented. The results show that, overall, 36.68% of the initial dataset was flagged and removed, with group-based QC procedures accounting for the majority of detected outliers. After filtering, 1327 stations were retained. The platform comparison showed a persistent positive bias relative to OWS, with Netatmo stations exhibiting a higher mean deviation (0.66 °C) than Wunderground (0.40 °C) after pre-processing and QC. Uncertainty was greater in-built environments and during daytime conditions. The findings demonstrate that, when supported by robust QC procedures, crowdsourced temperature data can provide adequate, spatially dense observations to inform urban climate adaptation strategies, particularly at night. However, further improvements are needed to reduce uncertainty and enhance the applicability of CWS observations, particularly under daytime and high-temperature conditions.

title: Development and real-time energy management of a phase change material thermal energy storage system for space heating applications
abstract: Phase change materials (PCMs) provide significant potential for peak shaving and cost saving in space heating applications, yet their practical application with intelligent control strategies remains underexplored. This study presents a comprehensive experimental investigation of a PCM-based heating system, including system characterization, flow rate optimization, and the development of a real-time energy management system (EMS) platform for implementing different control strategies. The impact of flow rates on charging and discharging performance was systematically investigated and optimal flow rates of 1100 L/h for charging and 500 L/h for discharging were identified. A real-time energy management system (EMS) platform was developed and the economic and energy performance of two control strategies were compared for the PCM heating system. The results showed that the cost-driven EMS mode reduces grid electricity consumption by 11\% and achieves 18.9\% cost savings compared to the conventional rule-based control (RBC). The room temperature fell below the comfort threshold for only 10\% of the operating time, with a maximum deviation of 2.6\%. This confirms that both control strategies can be implemented without compromising occupant comfort. These findings show the practical feasibility and economic viability of PCM heating systems. Furthermore, this study delivers a real-time EMS platform capable of implementing various control strategies for practical deployment.

title: Continuous monitoring of personal exposures indoors and outdoors to assess human environmental resilience through sleep quality
abstract: Understanding how environmental conditions influence human resilience is critical for designing climate-responsive buildings. Sleep quality represents a key human-centric indicator of environmental resilience, impacting cumulative exposure to different stimuli. This study presents an exploratory analysis of longitudinal monitoring data which examines how environmental exposures, physiological responses, and personal characteristics interact to shape human resilience through sleep quality in real-life settings. Sixteen participants were continuously monitored for ten days using wearable devices to collect physiological data and characterize environmental exposure patterns associated with sleep quality. A composite Predicted Sleep Score (PSS) was developed by regressing sleep stages and efficiency (R 2 = 0.713) and, together with resting heart rate (RHR), was used as complementary indicator s of physiological dimensions of sleep quality. With PSS and RHR, three distinct sleeper profiles were defined using k-means clustering: poor, resilient, and good sleepers. Six parameters differed significantly across clusters: nocturnal levels of temperature, illuminance, total volatile organic compounds and formaldehyde, and the daily mean level of exhaled CO 2 and temperature. The cluster with resilient sleepers was characterized by slightly lower bedroom temperatures (−1.7 ± 0.7 °C), along with 11.6 ± 1.3 more minutes of deep sleep and 2.0 ± 0.3% higher sleep efficiency. A mixed-effects model showed that female participants had 50% probability of being classified in the poor sleepers' cluster, whereas males and participants with PSQI<5 (indicating undisturbed sleep in the last month) had 59% and 45% probability of being classified in the resilient sleepers' cluster. Nocturnal bedroom environmental quality at night was identified as a key factor in shaping sleep quality, while continuous monitoring using wearable sensors provided valuable insights to draw useful conclusions to support well-being and comfort. Present outcomes demonstrate how integrating environmental and physiological monitoring can uncover sleeper profiles and support the design and operation of resilient, human-centric environments.

title: Editorial Board
Effects of localized heating body segments on the effectiveness of personal comfort systems in cold environments: A meta-analysis
Development of lightweight hydrated salt phase change aggregate concrete for improved thermal energy storage and building thermal resilience
Inorganic calcium carbonate-based ethyl palmitate microcapsules for thermal energy storage with potential building applications
DataNet: linking multi-faceted building energy datasets for effective performance analysis at scale
abstract: Recently, several administrative registration datasets in the Republic of Korea have become public or partially accessible. These include building registries, monthly energy billing data, building footprint polygons, business registration records, datasets on facilities maintained by ministries, and weather information. However, from the perspective of building energy analysis, these datasets remain fragmented because they are by-products of administrative processes not originally intended for integration. To achieve carbon neutrality in the building sector, comprehensive understanding of energy consumption patterns is essential—requiring integration of diverse contextual factors from climate and building characteristics to operational patterns and socioeconomic conditions. This paper introduces the DataNet project, which aims to collect and link these multifaceted building energy datasets at a national scale to enable evidence-based identification of inefficient buildings and support targeted interventions across Korea's stock of 7.3 million buildings. In this project, the building registry serves as the reference dataset, and other datasets are linked via addresses and associated attributes, such as building or business names. This paper outlines the overall data framework used to identify, categorize, and integrate multiple datasets with a macro-level temporal resolution at a national scale. A summary and overview of 13 out of the 17 currently available datasets are presented. The overall matching rate of these 13 datasets, based on the building registry, is 95%. Finally, the paper discusses potential applications of this integrated data framework for evidence-based performance analysis to accelerate the decarbonization of the building stock.

title: Application of a progressive heat stress protocol to cooling clothing: The cooling effect of a liquid cooling vest
abstract: Cooling clothing is a personal cooling system that only cools the microclimate around an individual, alleviating heat stress. This study used a progressive heat stress protocol (PHSP) to evaluate the cooling effectiveness of a liquid cooling vest (LCV), a type of cooling clothing. Through the PHSP, the upper-limit thermal environment for the physiological prescriptive zone was determined for both normal work clothes and the LCV. The clothing effect was evaluated based on this difference. The PHSP gradually increased the operative temperature until the body's thermal equilibrium collapsed, thus evaluating the upper operative temperature limit ( T up ). The experiments were conducted at relative humidities of 40% (R4) and 80% (R8), comparing the LCV condition (LCVC) with the normal work clothes condition (NWCC). The results indicated that LCVC significantly increased T up from 37.9 ± 1.6 °C to 41.0 ± 2.5 °C in R4 and from 31.5 ± 1.0 °C to 34.9 ± 2.5 °C in R8. Using body heat balance equations, the cooling flux was calculated to be 475 W/m 2 , with sensible and evaporative heat transfer coefficients of 11.0 W/(°C·m 2 ) and 58.8 W/(kPa·m 2 ), respectively. Considerable variability was observed in the T up of the LCVC compared with that of the NWCC. The variability was attributed to the decreased reproducibility of the minute spatial presence and a large temperature gradient within the LCV, worn in close contact with a small body area. These findings suggest that the PHSP is an effective method for comparing the cooling effects and evaluating the characteristics of cooling clothing.

title: The impact of cool building materials on the trade-offs between summer and winter thermal resilience and energy use
abstract: The increasing frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, including heatwaves and cold snaps, pose growing challenges to building energy performance and occupant thermal well-being. These impacts are expected to intensify under future climate change, underscoring the need for holistic evaluation of design and retrofit strategies that reduce energy demand while enhancing thermal resilience. This study quantifies the trade-off between cooling energy savings and overheating reduction against increased heating energy use and underheating risk associated with higher solar reflectance applied to outermost building envelope materials. A novel method is also introduced for identifying critical thermal zones in energy models based on elevated exposure to overheating risk. Six U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) commercial building archetypes are assessed for sensitivity to envelope solar reflectance under historical and projected future climate conditions in Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal. Whole-building simulations using EnergyPlus are conducted to evaluate energy use intensity (EUI) and thermal resilience metrics. Results indicate consistent reductions in cooling EUI and operative temperatures across all cities and building types, demonstrating enhanced summer thermal resilience. These benefits are accompanied by winter penalties in the form of increased heating EUI and reduced cold-season resilience. Overall, benefit-to-penalty ratios range from 0.58, where heating penalties outweigh cooling benefits, to 4.68, where cooling benefits dominate, with four of the six archetypes exhibiting ratios greater than unity. The findings highlight the climate- and building-specific effectiveness of high-solar-reflectance envelope strategies and support their targeted application in climate-resilient building design.

title: HABITAS: Home agent-based individualized time and activity simulator for household energy dynamics in smart homes
abstract: The rise of IoT devices and smart technologies has transformed homes into complex interconnected environments, creating new challenges for energy management. Understanding how people actually use energy is now a key requirement for designing smarter, more efficient systems, and simulation provides a controlled way to test decisions before deploying them in real homes. However, traditional simulation tools rely on static occupancy profiles and deterministic models that overlook the variability of real household behavior. This paper introduces Home Agent-Based Individualized Time and Activity Simulator (HABITAS), a flexible agent-based framework capable of emulating diverse household scenarios and testing energy optimization strategies. HABITAS represents occupants as autonomous agents with unique routines, preferences, and needs, enabling realistic modeling of energy and resource use. The simulator integrates solar generation, battery storage, appliance use, water consumption, and environmental monitoring through a modular architecture that supports both real-time and fast-forward simulation. Through detailed simulations, HABITAS generated plausible residential load shapes and variability patterns consistent with behavioral expectations, illustrating its practical applicability. Its detailed, individualized outputs support research in demand response, energy policy, smart home design, and decentralized energy systems.

title: A parametric model for generating dynamic lighting electricity profiles in shopping malls using large-scale longitudinal data
Understanding and improving building energy prediction via data characteristic analysis and adaptive training data reconstruction
abstract: Accurate and reliable prediction of building energy consumption remains challenging due to the variability of operational conditions and the limited interpretability of data-driven models. Existing approaches often focus on algorithm optimization while overlooking the role of training data characteristics and their impact on model performance. This study proposes a data characteristic-aware modeling approach that integrates multi-dimensional data analysis with similarity-based training sample selection to enhance both prediction accuracy and interpretability. The method systematically characterizes energy data using pattern recognition, dispersion metrics, and periodicity analysis, and reconstructs task-specific training datasets through similarity evaluation. An adaptive modeling process is further implemented to automatically select features and algorithms while providing post-hoc interpretability using SHAP analysis. The proposed approach is validated using datasets from four types of public buildings under different operational conditions. Results show that the method significantly improves prediction performance, particularly during transitional periods, with R 2 increasing by up to 22% compared with conventional approaches. The analysis also reveals that reduced data dispersion and improved similarity between training and target conditions are key factors driving performance gains. Overall, this work highlights the importance of training data characteristics in building energy prediction and provides a practical solution for developing accurate and interpretable models in real-world energy management applications.

title: Semi-supervised generative adversarial network with a dynamic discriminator for chiller fault diagnosis under extreme label scarcity
Comparative analysis of BTES, ATES, and power-to-hydrogen systems for seasonal storage in public building clusters
abstract: This study compares three seasonal storage pathways for 44 public buildings with shared rooftop PV in Drammen, Norway. The buildings face a strong mismatch between summer PV surplus and winter heating demand. The three pathways are borehole thermal energy storage (BTES), aquifer thermal energy storage (ATES), and a power-to‑hydrogen-to-power chain. We use measured hourly data from March 2020 to February 2021. Each pathway absorbs the summer PV surplus, stores it across the season, and returns it during the heating period. BTES injects 10,208 MWh of thermal energy into the ground and recovers 5339 MWh in winter. The seasonal recovery efficiency is close to 52%. ATES at a baseline groundwater velocity of 0.15 m per day recovers 6229 MWh from the same input and reaches 61%, the highest of the three. The hydrogen chain recovers 1452 MWh of electricity from 4455 MWh of summer surplus, giving a round-trip efficiency near 33%. ATES recovery depends strongly on local hydrogeology. Across a sweep of groundwater velocities from 0.02 to 0.30 m per day, recovery ranges from 71% down to 50%. At velocities above 0.25 m per day ATES drops below BTES. Under high‑carbon grid conditions, annual avoided emissions reach up to about 85 t CO₂ per building for BTES and 110 t per building for ATES. The hydrogen chain has the highest annualised cost. Per kWh of electricity delivered it is roughly fifteen times that of BTES. BTES remains the robust thermal option when aquifer conditions are unfavourable, while ATES is preferable where hydrogeology permits.

title: Thermal response analysis of permeable energy piles with different backfill materials under seepage conditions based on equivalent permeability characterization
Innovative solar collector on rooftop: Asymmetrical non-imaging optical design to reconcile seasonal energy mismatch
abstract: In the context of global energy decarbonization and increasing natural gas price, utilizing solar energy on rooftop to provide useful heat for buildings is a beneficial approach. However, owing to the instability of solar energy resource, there is a severe seasonal imbalance between the source and demand side of the solar thermal system. Unlike large-scale centralized systems with seasonal storage, decentralized solar thermal systems still lack an efficient method for addressing both winter and summer issues. In this study, we propose a novel rooftop integrated micro concentrating collector to reconcile the seasonal imbalance between the source and demand side. Different from the traditional collector types, the proposed solar collector with asymmetric micro-concentrator has seasonal adjustable performance depending on the seasonal solar altitude, thereby elevating winter performance to meet the heat demand in winter while suppressing summer performance to prevent system overheating in summer. The photo-thermal performance of the proposed micro concentrating collector has been investigated by experimental and numerical approaches. The analysis of 371 Chines cities reveal that the proposed collector type has winter performance enhancement of 100-125% and summer performance reduction of 4-26%, compared with roof integrated flat plate collectors. This study provides new insights into collector design and explored the capability of flexible seasonal performance adjustment for solar collectors.

Barriers to whole-life carbon implementation in construction: A systematic literature review with Baltic regional contextualisation
abstract: The increasing significance of embodied emissions has shifted the focus of the construction sector from operational energy towards Whole-Life Carbon (WLC) assessment, which evaluates greenhouse gas emissions across the entire building life cycle. This transition is reinforced by recent European policy developments, including the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD), the Level(s) framework, and the EN 15978 standard. Despite methodological advancements and the growing integration of Building Information Modelling and Life Cycle Assessment (BIM-LCA), the practical implementation of WLC assessment remains inconsistent, particularly in smaller construction markets. This study investigates barriers to WLC implementation in the Baltic construction sector through a qualitative systematic literature review following the PRISMA 2020 framework. The review synthesises evidence from 58 peer-reviewed studies and 16 policy and institutional documents addressing WLC assessment, BIM-LCA integration, and regulatory frameworks. The findings identify three interrelated groups of barriers. Digital barriers include limited interoperability between BIM and LCA tools, fragmented data structures, and low levels of workflow automation. Policy barriers arise from inconsistencies in the interpretation and operationalisation of EPBD, Level(s), and EN 15978 requirements across national contexts, as well as limited availability of empirical data for benchmarking. Socio-cultural barriers, including skills gaps, institutional inertia, and cost-driven decision-making, further constrain the integration of WLC approaches into routine construction practice. The results indicate that WLC implementation is constrained not by isolated factors but by misalignment between digital capabilities, regulatory frameworks, and sectoral competencies. The study contributes by providing an integrated socio-technical perspective on WLC barriers in smaller construction markets and highlights the need for coordinated development of data infrastructures, methodological standards, and professional capacities to enable effective adoption.

Beyond the dashboard: Architecture, maturity, and performance outcomes in operational building digital twins — A scoping review
abstract: The concept of a digital twin has been widely promoted as a means of achieving smarter building operations in recent years. However, much of the published literature bearing this label merely involves static BIM geometries, isolated energy simulations, or hypothetical building designs that are not linked to a real operating building. This review was inspired by a simple question: how many studies that purport to apply digital twins in practice actually do so in an operational sense? To answer this question, 2301 records were extracted from Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore, and subsequently filtered using a three-stage screening protocol based on document type, abstract content, and evidence of real-time data connectivity, physical sensor deployment, and confirmed operational phase application. Only 37 studies passed all three stages of the review process. These were examined across four dimensions (architecture, functionality, maturity, and validation), yielding the Operational Digital Twin Maturity Matrix. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first empirically derived framework cross-tabulating architectural configurations and functional capabilities against operational maturity levels across live building deployments. All 37 studies feature real-time data exchange, IoT connectivity, and live instrumentation (100%), and 97.3% integrate BIM. Functionally, IEQ monitoring dominates (73.0%), followed by energy optimisation (40.5%) and asset management (35.1%). Nearly half of all implementations (48.6%) remain at the descriptive level, providing real-time monitoring and visualisation dashboards, whereas only 24.3% reach the prescriptive level, where the twin actively drives control decisions. More significantly, only 27% of the included studies report quantified performance outcomes, although prescriptive studies are four times as likely to do so, with reported outcomes including a 34% electricity cost reduction and a 14.52% reduction in HVAC power consumption. Grounded in 37 verified operational deployments rather than conceptual frameworks, the matrix offers a realistic and empirically justified reference point for researchers, developers, and facility managers navigating digital twin investment decisions.

title: Building portfolio retrofit pathways: A generic process development and case study application
abstract: Building portfolio managers face increasing pressure to develop robust decarbonization pathways. Because planning such pathways across heterogeneous portfolios is too complex to handle on a case-by-case basis, managers rely on structured frameworks. Yet existing frameworks remain fragmented, insufficiently transferable, and limited in stakeholder integration. This study introduces a building portfolio retrofit pathway process organized into three parallel layers. A Stakeholder integration layer runs continuously throughout. A technical workflow covers problem scoping, method selection, baseline creation, potential analysis, and pathway design. An evaluation layer handles validation, uncertainty analysis, and goal checking. Together, these elements produce reproducible, transferable retrofit pathways resolved into a building-by-building schedule. The process is applied to a heterogeneous portfolio of 199 state-owned buildings in Bavaria, Germany. It couples machine-learning heating-demand, photovoltaic potential, and life-cycle models to quantify retrofit impacts. Nine decision criteria are weighted by stakeholder priority and combined into a single score to select one retrofit option per building. The measures are then scheduled from 2026 to 2040 to meet the required annual renovation quota. The resulting roadmap prioritizes and schedules retrofits transparently at the portfolio level, achieving 65% of the total annual CO 2 reduction within the first six years. Cumulative emission and cost outcomes stay stable under alternative stakeholder weightings, even though most individual building rankings change. A goal check shows that nearly zero-energy and 2040 climate-neutrality targets are missed with grid electricity but largely met with renewable electricity, underlining the need for iterative goal refinement.

title: A high-resolution carbon emission quantification framework for prefabricated concrete components driven by process functional units

Effect of occupant age and activity level on the performance of a displacement ventilation system
abstract: Displacement ventilation (DV) systems rely on occupant-generated thermal plumes to drive upward airflow and maintain vertical thermal stratification. As heat output strongly influences DV performance, we investigate system behavior with pre-pubertal child occupants producing substantially less heat than adults and at lower elevations. We use a child-specific heat balance model to tabulate sensible and latent heat generation values for pre-pubertal children, pertinent for HVAC design of elementary classroom environments, currently unavailable in literature. A computational fluid dynamics model of a DV-conditioned room with two heated cylinders representing 8-year-old occupants is developed and experimentally validated. Using the validated model, we compare system performance for 8-year-old children and adult females under low, medium, and high metabolic rates, while maintaining identical DV design parameters intended for adult occupancy. Results show child occupants substantially weaken vertical thermal stratification by 1.9 °C and modify airflow patterns, particularly at lower activity levels. This shift modified the diffuser flow, producing a largely isothermal supply-air trajectory in the low-activity child case. With child occupants, indoor air quality indicators showed reduced performance compared to adults; age of air increased by 11% and ventilation efficiency within the occupied zone decreased by 10%. Overall, results demonstrate that DV system behavior changes notably when children occupy spaces designed for adults, particularly at low-activity conditions, affecting airflow, stratification, and air quality. These findings emphasize the need to reassess DV performance in child-dominated environments such as classrooms. The presented sensible and latent heat tables also provide practical reference for future HVAC simulations and thermal comfort evaluations with child-occupants.

title: Field-scale experimental characterization of a solar-assisted ground source heat pump system coupled with single and double U-loop vertical ground heat exchangers in a cold climate
abstract: Several studies have experimentally characterized the performance of conventional ground source heat pump systems. However, there are limited studies on the field-scale experimental characterization of solar-assisted ground source heat pump (SAGSHP) systems. In this work, the performance of SAGSHPs integrated with 150 m single and double U-loop ground heat exchangers is investigated using instrumented field-scale experiments on two different test sites in southern Calgary, Canada. The soil formation of the two test sites is quite distinct, both showing the presence of groundwater. The results indicate that when useful solar heat is available, the outlet temperatures of the ground heat exchanger loop connected to the heat pump increased by up to 1.8 °C, providing higher fluid temperatures to the heat pump. For the double U-loop system, the monthly average heating coefficient of performance (COP) from November 2024 to January 2026 was in the range of 4.5 to 5.05. February 2025 showed the lowest COP corresponding to the lowest average outdoor temperature of −11.4 °C. Moreover, for the double U-loop system, the average monthly heat pump loop outlet temperature is consistently higher than the initial ground temperature, indicating solar thermal storage. Likewise, the single U-loop system shows an hourly heat pump average heating COP between 2.53 and 6.76 for January and February 2026. The highest COP corresponds to the time when useful solar thermal energy was available, and, on the contrary, a lower COP corresponds to the time when higher electricity consumption was required to meet the heating demand.

title: Insights for optimizing campus tree species from children's thermal and physiological responses during transitional seasons
Occupancy-dependent performance of PCM: A comparative review of cooling strategies in different climates
Climate implications of using bio-based materials in tropical buildings: a case study in Thai detached houses
abstract: AbstractThe buildings and construction sector significantly contributes to global emissions, necessitating reduction efforts to comply with the goal of containing global warming under 2°C. Southeast Asia, especially Thailand, with its high urbanization rate, faces substantial emission challenges in its construction practices. Thailand aims to become carbon neutral by 2065. The country predominantly uses concrete frame construction for small-scale residential buildings, with detached houses making up 49% of the total construction area in 2023. This study examines method of reducing emissions from detached houses in Thailand by replacing concrete and steel construction with bio-based construction. Two bio-based designs were created to explore this mitigation strategy. Since Thailand's regulatory energy standards do not cover small-scale residential buildings, three energy scenarios were created and used in the study to address future uncertainties. Among the findings, the extended bio-based design under the photovoltaic integration scenario achieved the highest reduction, compared to conventional designs, bringing emissions down to 64% and 56% for single-story and two-story houses respectively. Under the original insulation scenario, emissions from the extended bio-based design were reduced to 73% for single-story and 68% for two-story houses. By utilizing the extended bio-based design for future houses in Thailand until 2065, up to 473 MtCO2e emissions can be avoided.

title: Rooftop solar photovoltaic Systems for Urban Heat Island Mitigation: A comparative multi-climate review across five Köppen climate zones
abstract: The urban heat island (UHI) effect poses escalating threats to thermal comfort, energy consumption, and public health in cities worldwide. Rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) systems have emerged as a dual-benefit strategy that simultaneously generates renewable electricity and modifies urban surface energy balances. The primary objective of this study is to systematically quantify how rooftop PV arrays simultaneously alter building cooling demands and urban UHI intensities across diverse climates. This comparative multi-climate review cross-evaluates published experimental, numerical, and satellite-derived evidence on the bidirectional coupling between rooftop PV deployment and urban microclimate across five cities representing distinct Köppen climate zones: Singapore (Af, tropical rainforest), Riyadh (BWh, hot desert), Athens (Csa, Mediterranean), Rotterdam (Cfb, oceanic), and Beijing (Dwa, monsoon-influenced continental). Drawing on field measurements from peer-reviewed studies and satellite-derived solar resource data from the PVGIS (SARAH-2 and ERA5) database (European Commission Joint Research Centre), this study evaluates published evidence from WRF mesoscale models integrated with Building Effect Parameterization and Building Energy Model (BEP-BEM) frameworks. Published field data confirm that rooftop PV reduces daytime roof surface temperatures by 5–20 K and ceiling heat flux by up to 63%, while large-scale deployment cools near-surface air by 0.2–1.0 K depending on climate zone and coverage fraction. PV cell temperatures in urban settings reach 52–78 °C, imposing efficiency penalties of 5–18% relative to standard test conditions. Building cooling load reductions of 4.4–16% are documented across climates, with baseline PV generation of 194–395 kWh/m 2 /year based on PVGIS-validated solar resource data. A primary limitation of this synthesis is the reliance on a single representative city per Köppen zone, which may confound city-specific morphological characteristics with broader climate-zone effects, alongside the exclusion of polar and subarctic climates. These findings, grounded in publicly available experimental datasets and satellite observations, provide climate-zone-specific guidance for integrating solar energy deployment with urban heat mitigation strategies.

title: Human response to the thermal environment under a localized desk push-pull system
abstract: The desk push-pull system (Desk-PPS) is a human-centered device that targets individual occupants' microenvironments by supplying clean air at the breathing level and extracting it nearby, reducing cross-contamination and energy use compared to whole-room conditioning. Despite these advantages, evaluating its effectiveness numerically remains challenging, as current thermal comfort models assume uniform conditions around the human body and cannot accurately predict comfort under the asymmetrical environment the Desk-PPS creates. Therefore, involving human participants provides a concrete approach that enables an accurate understanding of how human-centered devices affect occupants' perceived thermal comfort. This work presents human subject experiments performed in a controlled climate chamber to evaluate whether the operation of the Desk-PPS under thermally neutral winter-like conditions (~22 °C, ~1 clo) introduces unacceptable thermal or air movement discomfort, and to characterize its effect on subjective thermal and air speed (global and local) sensation, physiological reactions, and cognitive responses under three different operating flowrates: 30 L/s, 40 L/s, and 50 L/s, corresponding to mean local air velocities of 0.12, 0.15, and 0.20 m/s at the seated occupant's breathing zone level. The results reveal that, under the neutral winter-like tested conditions, the Desk-PPS induced convective cooling and elevated air speed sensation at the upper body without impairing overall thermal comfort across all tested operating flowrates. Of the three conditions examined, 40 L/s (0.15 m/s at 1.1 m) emerged as the most acceptable operating point, providing perceptible convective cooling while maintaining acceptable air movement; at 50 L/s (0.20 m/s at 1.1 m), occupants reported reduced satisfaction with the air movement intensity. Segmental subjective responses show that upper-body thermal sensation approaches neutrality with increasing airflow, while lower-body thermal sensation remains near neutral regardless of flowrate. The operation of the device has no impairment on occupants' cognitive performance; however, attention skill is found to be highly correlated with occupants' thermal comfort.

title: An observation-based quantile delta mapping method for generating future weather data in building performance simulations

Drivers and barriers to the energy renovation of residential buildings in the EU: a systematic literature review
abstract: Accelerating residential Energy Renovation (ER) is critical to reducing energy poverty, addressing changing household needs, and achieving the European Union's (EU) 2050 climate-neutrality targets. Despite substantial policy ambition and investment, ER rates across the EU remain below targets, with limited integration of process-, people- and project-centred perspectives in existing research and policy approaches. This systematic literature review (SLR) adopts a novel, systems-oriented approach to examine the interrelationships between ER barriers and drivers within EU research and policy contexts. It analyses 29 studies and identifies 62 drivers and barriers, conceptually organised across process-, people-, and project-related dimensions —providing a structured analytical framework aligned with EU policy documents. Unlike previous SLRs focused on isolated barriers or single thematic issues, this framework captures the dynamic interactions shaping ER uptake and implementation, providing a more actionable evidence base for policymakers and stakeholders. The findings reveal persistent fragmentation in the literature and EU policy frameworks. Process-related factors are strongly connected to people-related influences, while project-related factors remain comparatively disconnected, highlighting gaps in integrated retrofit governance and implementation strategies. The evidence base is also dominated by case-specific studies, with limited cross-country comparative analysis to support broader EU policy learning. The study further evaluates the 2024 recast of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) against the SLR findings, identifying strengths and areas where the recast could better integrate people-, process-, and project-related approaches to accelerate residential ER outcomes. Overall, the review highlights a misalignment between policy ambitions and the empirical understanding of ER decision-making. It underscores the need for more integrated, multi-dimensional, and context-sensitive policy and research approaches to accelerate ER and enable large-scale transformation of the EU's inefficient housing stock.

title: Thermal performance of a coupled thermal curtain and earth-air heat exchanger system for Chinese solar greenhouses in cold climates
Development of a novel multi-objective energy management methodology through a building management system structure
