Skin temperature as input to behavioral thermal adaptation for energy-efficient HVAC control
abstract: Insufficient understanding of occupant adaptive behaviors may limit the potential to reduce building energy use. This study examines the relationship between skin temperature and thermal adaptive behaviors to develop a physiology-based prediction model and HVAC control strategy. Semi-controlled experiments were conducted with 12 participants exposed to temperatures ranging from 18 to 33 °C. Four voluntary adaptive behaviors (window operation, clothing adjustment, fan use, and posture change) were recorded along with environmental parameters, skin temperature, and subjective thermal sensation to explore associations with behavior initiation. The results show that: (1) changes in skin temperature before and after behavior activation effectively quantify effectiveness of behavioral regulation and are associated with environmental conditions and behavior type. Clothing and fan adjustments were medium- and high-effectiveness, while posture change and window operation under hot conditions were low-effectiveness; (2) behavioral activation exhibited sequence and state dependence. Participants tended to follow a progressive response pattern, influenced by environmental conditions; (3) no significant difference in mean skin temperature was found at thermal comfort between participants with and without behavioral adjustments. Based on these findings, a skin-temperature-based behavioral adjustment model was developed, integrating behavioral effectiveness and HVAC compensation demand in a layered control strategy of “behavior first, energy compensation later.” The study highlights the role of physiological feedback in leveraging occupant behavior for adaptive and energy-efficient control, providing a theoretical basis for human–environment-integrated building operation.

title: Defining system-level sustainability thresholds: a life cycle emergy assessment for vertical greening in the built environment
Towards a data-driven profiles of household energy consumption in collective housing: Machine learning clustering with insights from Bab Ezzouar (Algiers)
Occupants' adaptive behaviour and thermal perception in social housing buildings in Brazil
abstract: Social housing is often not well designed nor fit-for-purpose, delivering poor indoor environmental quality conditions, especially thermally, to occupants. This situation is often worsened by occupants' limited capacity to adapt their surroundings and to cope with heat exposure. Considering the increasing number of extreme heat events and the likely vulnerability of social housing occupants, further research is needed. This study addresses this knowledge gap by examining occupants' adaptive behavioural strategies, thermal perceptions, and the key factors shaping subjective thermal responses in four social housing developments in hot and humid regions of Brazil. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, combining indoor environmental monitoring, interviews, and a thermal comfort survey, with 103 participants. The analysis revealed sustained exposure to high indoor temperatures (>25.24 °C), particularly during summer, when mean operative temperature is 31.22 °C. During this period, most occupants reported warm and hot thermal sensations (69.35%) and a preference for cooler conditions (85.48%), suggesting difficulties in cooling indoor spaces under prevailing conditions. To analyse whether variables beyond the physical environment — including socioeconomic conditions, residential experience, and behavioural aspects — were associated with occupants' thermal responses, logistic regression models were developed. The results revealed that thermal sensation was significantly associated with operative temperature, relative humidity, age and patterns of fan use, while thermal comfort was associated with a broader range of predictors, including residential experience variables such as perceived safety and length of residence. While acknowledging the limitations associated with the sample size, these findings contribute to the development of more integrative approaches to thermal comfort assessment that incorporate social, psychological, and behavioural dimensions.

title: Optimized 3D hierarchical canopy Modeling of urban street trees for enhanced microclimate regulation
A climate-sensitive multi-objective optimisation framework for building envelope retrofit decision support: Methodology and proof-of-concept
abstract: Building envelope retrofit optimisation studies overwhelmingly rely on a single historical weather file, yet retrofitted buildings will operate for 25–50 years under changing climate conditions — raising the question of whether optimal retrofit strategies identified today remain valid under future climate projections and local microclimate variation. A systematic analysis of 157 genetic algorithm-based building retrofit studies confirms this gap: 75.2% optimise under a single Typical Meteorological Year file, only 12.7% consider future climate scenarios, and no existing framework provides cross-scenario Pareto front composition analysis, integrated multi-criteria decision support, or across-job experiment orchestration. This paper presents a modular, climate-sensitive multi-objective optimisation framework that composes established tools — EnergyPlus for simulation, NSGA-II via Pymoo for optimisation, the Future Weather Generator for CMIP6/SSP weather morphing with LCZ-based urban heat island adjustment, and six MCDM methods via PyMCDM — into a unified pipeline implemented as a web-based platform with two-level parallel processing. The framework is demonstrated on a DOE Small Office reference building (pre-1980, Atlanta, ASHRAE 3 A), optimising energy consumption, thermal discomfort, and retrofit cost across seven weather scenarios through an orthogonal separation of climate change (SSP1-2.6/2-4.5/5-8.5 at 2050) and microclimate (LCZ 2/5/6) effects. Three compound climate–microclimate scenarios additionally test the orthogonal design's superposition assumption, and post-hoc sensitivity analyses examine the cost, energy, and discomfort objective formulations. The proof-of-concept reveals that weather scenario selection fundamentally alters which configurations are optimal: present-day and future climate scenario groups share only 22.7% of their Pareto-optimal solutions. Despite this, 35 configurations are universally Pareto-optimal across all scenarios. Opaque insulation choices are highly robust across scenarios (cross-scenario correlation r > 0.85), while glazing selection is substantially more sensitive ( r = 0.41). Retrofit improvement potential diminishes under warming (20% to 17% energy savings), as reduced heating demand narrows the gap between the unretrofitted baseline and the envelope-limited optimum. These findings demonstrate that single-weather-file optimisation — the prevailing approach — may produce recommendations that are non-robust under plausible future conditions, and that a systematic multi-scenario framework is essential for climate-resilient retrofit decision-making.

title: Parametric simulation-based environmental performance assessment of enclosed recessed balconies in mid-level residential buildings
Fabrication of BS/FEVE-g-PDMS composite radiative cooling coatings and the synergistic mechanism of optical-mechanical properties

Energy performance certificates, care quality ratings, and the regulatory information gap: A national linked analysis of english care homes
abstract: England's care homes serve approximately 400,000 residents, yet the two regulatory systems overseeing them, the Care Quality Commission (CQC) for care quality and the non-domestic Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) regime for building energy, operate independently, with no formal connection. This study presents the first comprehensive national dataset linking CQC and EPC records, matching 11,768 care homes (79.4% of the registered stock). The matched homes had an average EPC score of 55.6 (Band C), with 83.8% heated by natural gas and an estimated annual total CO₂ emissions of 1.44 million tonnes. Importantly, care quality ratings and building energy performance are decisively independent, indicating that care oversight does not reflect building energy efficiency. Regression analysis shows that heating fuel type is the primary factor influencing EPC scores. Cluster analysis identified three distinct building archetypes—gas-heated mainstream homes (86.7%), electric-heated homes (9.0%), and oil-heated rural residences (4.3%), each requiring different decarbonisation strategies: fuel switching, deep fabric retrofit, and off-grid renewable heat solutions. Spatial analysis reveals significant geographic clustering of poor performance, underscoring the need for targeted, place-based interventions. Implementing a worst-first approach could reduce the sector’s CO₂ emissions by 17.1% by focusing on only 15% of homes. Overall, the findings highlight that England's care home estate presents three distinct decarbonisation challenges, shaped by a regulatory framework that currently obscures building energy risks.

title: Quantifying the impact of improved heat pumps in Germany's residential sector: A simulation-based scenario analysis
abstract: The electrification of residential heating through heat pumps is a central pillar of energy transition strategies. While numerous studies assess the system-level implications of large-scale heat pump deployment, heat pump performance is typically represented using static or averaged current efficiency assumptions. At the same time, ongoing developments in power electronics and compressor control are expected to yield component-level efficiency improvements. However, the system-level impact of such efficiency improvements has not yet been systematically quantified from component level to building and national energy systems. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a bottom-up framework that links component-level efficiency gains derived from experimental observations to building-level performance and national electricity demand impacts. The approach is grounded in laboratory measurements of a frequency converter–compressor system representative of mass-market air-source heat pumps. The measurements reveal that frequency converter efficiency depends on compressor rotational speed, with efficiencies in the range of 88–91% at the most relevant operating conditions, indicating improvement potential. An operating-condition-dependent efficiency improvement is assumed to calculate improved heat pump performance maps. These are used in dynamic building simulations. Results are aggregated nationally using a representative German residential building stock model and projected to 2045 under scenario-based decarbonization pathways. This shows that the considered efficiency improvements, with a mean increase of ~2%, lead to terawatt-hour-scale reductions in national electricity demand, reaching over 3 TWh annually by 2045. The study demonstrates the system-level relevance of experimentally grounded component improvements and provides a transparent framework for technology assessment.

title: Radiative and thermal characteristics of building envelope materials governing outdoor heat stress in compact low-rise urban canyons
Cool cities, local contexts: A typology of cooling interventions across the disciplines to address extreme heat and decarbonization in urban areas
abstract: Interventions to mitigate and adapt to extreme heat are becoming increasingly necessary at the local scale to contend with the negative health and energy security implications of rising temperatures caused by climate change, the urban heat island effect and urbanization. Interventions across fields have yet to be harmonized, nor have interstitial risks, benefits and implementation challenges been consistently investigated. This study develops a typology of cooling interventions to address extreme heat: lowering temperature, altering buildings, changing behavior, and decarbonizing energy and material systems. The typology is based on a review of relevant literature covering microclimatology, sustainable buildings, behavioral science and energy systems decarbonization. We develop a categorization of interventions which address increasing temperatures through a mix of climate mitigation, infrastructural resilience, climate adaptation and geoengineering approaches. Increasing temperatures has complex and multi-disciplinary impacts, and the cooling interventions must be intentionally chosen to match this problem with equal nuance, rigor, and efficacy.

Incorporating heritage value assessment and economic analysis into the energy-efficient retrofitting framework: A case study of an industrial heritage building in Qingdao, China
Building integrated performance simulation of an innovative dynamic BIPV shading device
abstract: This study presents a method for the assessment of the building integrated performances of a novel BIPV shading system, which consists of dynamic and extensible blinds integrating PV. A typical office module, located in Milan (Italy), with a South oriented façade, was chosen as case study. Different Window to Wall Ratios (WWR) and different type of controls – fix shading or lamellas tilted and extended on the basis of indoor temperature and/or solar irradiance - of the BIPV system were considered. The shading control strategy was implemented in Building Controls Virtual Test Bed software (BCVTB). In fact, BCVTB enables to dynamically combine EnergyPlus for the thermal calculation and Radiance for daylighting evaluation. The overall energy performance was assessed taking into account heating, cooling and lighting needs as well as PV generation. The results show that the innovative dynamic system, even without PV, reduces the overall energy needs, and with PV generation allows to achieve the nearly zero energy target.

title: A hybrid physics-machine learning framework for improving simulations of urban air-conditioning electricity consumption
Techno-economic comparison of low-carbon heating solutions and building retrofit using CATHeaPS-FatCat: a case study for two urban neighbourhoods in Glasgow
abstract: Heating buildings accounts for half of Scotland's energy consumption and over 20% of the country's greenhouse gas emissions. A transformation in the way buildings are heated is required to reach net zero targets. Literature reveals an absence of techno-economic-environmental models that can compare alternative heat decarbonisation solutions for a given area without extensive user input. This study investigates how open-access Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) and Unique Property Reference Number (UPRN) datasets can be used to support early-stage heat and retrofit planning though a user-friendly tool suitable for communities, local authorities, and government. The existing Centralised Analysis Tool for Heat Pump Systems (CATHeaPS-Kitten) is enhanced, integrating EPC and UPRN data, non-linear network routing, and modelling of pre- and post-retrofit scenarios, giving rise to CATHeaPS-FatCat. This third iteration of the model provides more accurate estimates of network costs and pipework requirements than conventional density-based averages as well as expanding heating-and-retrofit-system modelling capabilities. CATHeaPS-FatCat is applied to two contrasting case study areas in the city of Glasgow, UK to demonstrate its use and provide a replicable framework for similar studies elsewhere. Findings show that the most appropriate low-carbon heating and retrofit strategy depends on local area characteristics. While retrofit reduces overall energy demand and carbon emissions, it is not always cost-effective. Assessing retrofit impacts before selecting a heating solution helps avoid oversizing and unnecessary capital expenditure. Overall, the study provides stakeholders with a transparent, practical framework for using open access data in early-stage heat decarbonisation planning in line with UK policy objectives.

title: Ventilation performance of standalone ERV retrofit strategies for existing buildings under VRP and IAQP design approaches
Climate-responsive atrium geometry in large public buildings: meta-sample modelling and robust energy-saving ranges across five climates
An AI-augmented urban building energy Modeling framework integrating physics-based simulation, machine learning, and computer vision: The CityEnerTwin UBEM module
Why are heat pump installation costs so much higher in Germany? Evidence from a European comparison
abstract: Heat pumps are central to residential heating decarbonisation across Europe, yet installation costs vary dramatically between countries. In Germany, gross installation costs for air-to-water heat pumps in existing single-family homes range from €23,000 to €40,000 or more, compared with €9000 to €20,000 in comparable European countries. This paper analyses the drivers of this cost differential using market data, consumer organisation analyses, engineering cost studies, and field research covering the period 2022–2025. Drawing on a specification-matched bilateral comparison with the United Kingdom, we decompose the gap into identifiable cost components. Underlying cost-structure drivers (equipment pricing, foundation and electrical-connection requirements, and labour) account for roughly half of the differential; value-added tax, levied at 19% in Germany against a zero rate in the United Kingdom, amplifies this already-high base and accounts for a further third; and the remaining fifth reflects amplifying factors, chiefly the incentive effects of proportional subsidy design, alongside market dynamics and early refrigerant technology transitions. A key finding is a subsidy paradox: despite Germany operating one of Europe's most generous percentage-based heat pump support programmes, German households still pay more in absolute net costs than households in the United Kingdom under a modest fixed-grant scheme. We conclude that reducing Germany's installation cost premium requires action on technical standardisation, subsidy design reform, and market structure, and that the German experience carries important lessons for European heat pump deployment policy.

title: Preventing parasitic learning in online identification of building RC thermal models: A stochastic-volatility Rao–Blackwellized particle filter
abstract: Accurate online identification of building thermal models is central to energy-efficient operation; however, intermittent unmeasured heat gains can bias online estimators by being absorbed into resistance–capacitance (RC) parameters (“parasitic learning”), degrading both dynamics and uncertainty calibration. We propose a Rao–Blackwellized Particle Filter (RBPF) that introduces a stochastic-volatility state to scale the process covariance and suppress parameter adaptation during disturbance-dominated periods. We validate the approach on a semi-synthetic testbed with known ground truth and on the Ecolar Home real-building testbed. In the semi-synthetic testbed, the RBPF reduces transfer-function distortion relative to Extended and Unscented Kalman filter baselines. Its 95% prediction intervals stay close to nominal coverage in low-disturbance periods and remain far better calibrated than these baselines when the model is structurally mismatched. In two real-building measurement periods, the one-step prediction intervals of the RBPF stay close to their nominal coverage. During low-disturbance night-time windows, its open-loop simulations are more accurate than those of an offline least-squares baseline. These results support the proposed use of stochastic volatility as an inverse model-trust indicator for online RC parameter learning, not as a method for identifying individual heat-gain sources.

title: Beyond U-values: A monitored-data-driven energy and convective exergy workflow for comparing envelope material solutions
abstract: Innovative envelope materials are commonly evaluated using steady-state indicators such as thermal transmittance ( U -value), although these metrics do not capture the time-dependent response of building envelopes under real operating conditions. This study presents a monitored-data-driven comparative workflow for assessing predefined envelope material substitution scenarios using a calibrated reference Building Energy Model (BEM). The workflow combines steady-state ( U SS ) and simulation-derived equivalent transmittance ( U SD,eq ) references, surface-temperature and temperature-factor indicators, transient conduction and heat storage indicators, reference-conditioned demand shifts, and indoor-side convective exergy and irreversibility diagnostics. The BEM was derived from a BIM-based geometric and material representation, with material properties structured for consistent BIM-to-BEM transfer and transient simulation requirements. The approach is demonstrated on a renovated office building in Lavrion, Greece, using monitored outdoor and indoor temperature data to impose common boundary conditions across all scenarios. Results show deviations of up to 47% between U SS and U SD,eq for opaque assemblies, and 69% for the baseline glazing system. Layer placement can modify conductive losses and storage/release indicators by more than 40% in selected configurations, while the screening-derived composite scenario produces reference-conditioned cooling- and heating-demand reductions of 3.98–4.70% and 2.80–2.93%, respectively. Radiative and solar-related effects are represented in the BEM heat balance but are not included in the exergy post-processing. The workflow is therefore positioned as an operational-energy and convective-thermodynamic screening tool for envelope solutions.

title: Adapting ISO 9869-1 for post-retrofit low U-value walls: Evidence from 130 days of continuous in-situ monitoring
abstract: Large scale retrofit programmes require a practical means of verifying that newly insulated walls perform as designed. ISO 9869-1, the international heat flow meter method, permits test durations as short as 72 hours, a threshold established when uninsulated walls lost heat far more rapidly than today’s high performance retrofits. This study evaluates the suitability of the standard for modern post retrofit construction and proposes evidence based adaptations. A recently insulated cavity brick wall in Liverpool, UK (design U-value 0.18 W/(m 2 K)), was monitored at two adjacent points over 130 days. Heat flux and indoor and outdoor temperatures were logged at 10-minute intervals alongside on site weather data. The Average Method was applied to all 13,687 candidate time windows to examine the influence of test duration, starting hour, rainfall, and other environmental factors. The 72-hour minimum performed poorly: only 5–10% of windows satisfied the convergence criteria, and among these the mean absolute error against long duration references was approximately 32%. A minimum of 14 days was required for indicative results, and 28 days for accuracy within ± 5%. Starting hour was statistically irrelevant once windows exceeded three days. Moisture proved decisive: wet periods inflated measured U-values by 13–16%, with recovery of 4–6 mW/(m 2 K) per consecutive dry day. Measured values of 0.206 and 0.188 W/(m 2 K) exceeded the design value by only 0.026 and 0.008 W/(m 2 K) in absolute terms. Three adaptations to ISO 9869-1 are proposed: a wall-type-dependent minimum duration, mandatory dry-spell pre-conditioning, and a combined absolute and relative tolerance for design measurement agreement. Together these provide a measurement based quality assurance route for large scale retrofit delivery.

title: An adaptive building energy anomaly detection and load prediction framework with factorized sequential neural networks
Decentralized energy control in IoT-enabled smart buildings with the edge-efficient learning network and ALOCO optimizer
R290 leakage in a commercial VRF enclosed ceiling plenum: dispersion, flammability hazard and zoned emergency ventilation
Compute-cooling Coordination in Data Centers: Mechanism and Matching Strategy
A review of the application of machine learning in the field of fire public safety: From risk assessment to emergency decision-making
Editorial Board
Comparing residential peak demand response under dynamic pricing and direct load control: impacts of program design and smart thermostat ownership
abstract: Residential demand response (DR) is an important flexibility resource for supporting power system reliability and deferring costly infrastructure investments, yet observed peak reductions remain highly heterogeneous across households and events due to differences in program design, automation, and household context, limiting predictability for utility planning and program design. This study evaluates residential DR performance across two dynamic pricing designs and a direct load control (DLC) program in Quebec, using linked survey data and 15 min smart meter data from 492 households during the 2024–2025 winter season. Peak curtailment was quantified to compare reduction magnitude and consistency across programs and smart thermostat ownership groups and to identify key drivers of event-level peak reductions. Mean event-level peak reductions were 0.5 kW (standard deviation [SD] = 0.3 kW) and 1.3 kW (SD = 0.5 kW) for the two dynamic pricing programs, compared with 3.4 kW (SD = 0.6 kW) for the DLC program, where SD reflects event-to-event variability. Within the dynamic pricing programs, smart thermostat ownership was associated with substantially higher mean event-level peak reductions than non-smart thermostat ownership under the penalty-based pricing design (1.7 vs 0.3 kW) and the reward-based pricing design (3.7 vs 0.5 kW). Feature screening and interpretable decision-tree analysis indicated that program design and smart thermostat ownership were the dominant predictors of event-level peak reductions, with timing effects emerging conditionally within specific program–technology contexts. Overall, the results suggest that residential DR is stronger and more consistent when automation and enabling technology reduce reliance on real-time manual response.

title: Policy advisers for the widespread implementation of green roofs based on socioeconomic feasibility
abstract: The rapid urbanisation and population growth have led urban areas to face challenges related to the adverse effects of climate change, such as increased urban heat island effects, flooding, and biodiversity loss. The European Union have been addressing these challenges by proposing the integration of green roofs into urban infrastructures. This study aims to identify key factors and policy instruments that may incentivise the widespread adoption of green roofs in Portugal. Acknowledging that the population preferences, perception and willingness to pay for green roofs should be taken into account, this study tests three hypotheses. The first hypothesis addresses the relationship between individuals' experience of the effects of climate change and their willingness to construct a green roof. The second hypothesis is that greater knowledge of green roofs is associated with a greater willingness to adopt them. The third hypothesis explores the relationship between willingness to pay and the population's perception of green roof benefits, aiming to assess whether people's willingness to spend money on constructing a green roof matches its actual market value. With this aim, a survey considering sociodemographic, population's perception and preferences questions was made available, resulting in 456 responses. The majority of the respondents were female and specialists in intellectual and scientific activities. The data analyses were performed by testing statistical assumptions, considering composite indices for climate experience and knowledge, and examining correlations. The findings showed that experience with climate events, the population's knowledge level, and government incentives play a key role in promoting the adoption of green roofs. However, sociodemographic variables, such as age and level of education, do not appear to influence the population's willingness to adopt or pay for a green roof. Therefore, this study may provide an evidence-based foundation for designing governmental policy instruments to promote the large-scale implementation of green roofs.

title: Implementing occupant-centric control in educational buildings: Energy impact, ventilation, and AI considerations
Indoor microclimate assessment for cultural heritage buildings: Statistical analysis and machine learning-based prediction
Surrogate-assisted rolling-horizon multi-objective HVAC setpoint optimization for office buildings with BIPV systems
Hospital energy systems under transition: global consumption patterns, technology integration, and pathways toward fully renewable healthcare facilities
abstract: Hospitals and healthcare facilities are among the most energy-intensive and operationally demanding building types in the built environment. Their continuous 24/7 operation, coupled with the stringent requirements for a high-quality, uninterrupted power supply to power critical medical equipment, heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems, lighting, and other essential infrastructure, presents a significant challenge for decarbonization and the integration of renewable energy systems. This article presents a comprehensive analysis of hospital energy consumption patterns worldwide and the specific nature of the healthcare sector's energy demands. A key contribution of this work is the structured analysis of the scientific literature in a field where research remains limited, particularly regarding renewable energy systems and emerging technologies in healthcare settings. The study examines the technological, operational, economic, and environmental factors influencing the adoption of renewable energy solutions in hospitals, integrating them with sector demand, energy storage, and resilience. Furthermore, it explores the concept of the “100% Renewable Hospital”: a fully sustainable healthcare facility designed to maximize the use of renewable energy sources and capable of maintaining critical operations during grid disturbances or outages through resilient and partially autonomous energy system configurations, thereby reducing dependence on the external power grid. The document analyzes the main engineering and economic challenges associated with achieving this level of autonomy and identifies key considerations, such as implementation constraints and system-level trade-offs, to support the development of technically feasible and economically viable solutions. It also proposes a structured, multi-layered framework for 100% renewable hospitals.

title: Dynamic moisture content and an integrated climatic-factor model for a porous facing brick after wind-driven rain in hot-humid regions
Closed-loop semantic digital twin for real-time thermal comfort management during heatwaves
Diagnosing and assessing the synergistic cooling and carbon reduction potential of university campus green spaces: a tool for climate-adaptive campus design
Corrigendum to “Building portfolio retrofit pathways: A generic process development and case study application” [Energy Build. 369 (2026) 117938]
Map-based supervisory control strategies of a single-pipe CO2 thermal network connected to local heat pumps
abstract: This paper investigates supervisory control for a single-pipe CO 2 thermal network (CO 2 TN) that supplies the source side of multiple local heat pumps (LHPs) in a multi-zone building. The network comprises a reversible CO 2 vapor compression circulation unit coupled to a ground loop heat exchanger, with all LHPs connected in series on a single CO 2 loop. Two supervisory strategies are formulated and compared. The minimum-mass-flow strategy enforces two phase operation along the loop and selects the smallest CO 2 mass flow that satisfies the aggregate zone demand. The temperature-bounded strategy constrains loop temperatures within a narrow band around saturation, permitting limited single-phase operation to shift the cycle toward thermodynamically favorable states. Both strategies are implemented using an offline map, and executed online via lookup of the optimized decision variables. Annual co-simulation (TRNSYS + MATLAB tables) for a five-zone office building in Montréal shows that the temperature-bounded strategy improves performance relative to minimum mass flow: the mean time-step coefficient of performance, COP sys , increases from 3.08 to 3.75 (+22.1%), the median from 2.95 to 4.27 (+44.7%), and the seasonal performance factor (SPF sys,ann ) increases from 2.98 to 3.65 (+22.3%).

title: Experimental evaluation of heat–moisture regulation and energy performance under different ventilation modes in an underground granary
Towards sustainable multi-bed hospital wards: numerical evaluation of infection control, thermal comfort, and energy savings under real-world ventilation strategies
abstract: Hospital wards are high-risk environments where ventilation strategies directly influence infection risk, thermal comfort, and energy savings. This paper systematically evaluated real-world ventilation in Singapore's B2-class multi-bed cubicles using a validated CFD–dose–response framework to investigate patient-to-patient interactions over prolonged exposure periods. Multiple ventilation strategies and passive intervention were analysed. Natural ventilation through open room configurations (e.g., open windows and doors) does not necessarily guarantee lower infection risks, as effectiveness depends critically on return air (RA) placement. In the studied ward, cross-ventilation from backside windows was drawn toward the front RA, carrying particles downstream and increasing infection risk by ≥ 35% above baseline. Fomite deposition analysis further identified side walls, RA, and bathrooms as hotspot regions that should be prioritized for cleaning to reduce secondary transmission. Passive interventions demonstrated clear benefits: purifiers actively removed particles, and curtains reduced cross-bed exposure, with both measures lowering infection risks by ≥ 48%. Beyond infection risk, thermal comfort analysis showed lying patients were more vulnerable to cold discomfort under the baseline air-conditioning (AC) diffuser setpoint of 20 °C. When room openings were introduced, airflow shifted the Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) toward neutrality, reducing discomfort to below 20%. While no single configuration fully resolves the competing demands of infection risk, comfort, and energy use, the findings highlight three practical pathways: (1) closed rooms with AC and raised setpoints (~24.4 °C), (2) open rooms with fans supplemented by purifiers or curtains, and (3) hybrid AC–fan rooms as short-term options at higher energy demand.

title: Drivers and multi-scale heterogeneity in operational energy consumption of China's buildings: A STIRPAT-based analysis of multidimensional urbanization across climatic zones
abstract: Against the backdrop of global climate governance and carbon neutrality goals, identifying the driving factors of operational energy consumption in residential and commercial buildings is critical to advancing building decarbonization and energy transition. Nevertheless, existing studies have paid limited attention to climate-zone-specific energy consumption attribution at the provincial scale in China, and the regional heterogeneous impacts of multidimensional urbanization on building energy consumption remain under-explored.. This study constructs a three-tier analytical framework covering the national, climate-zone, and provincial levels, based on an extended STIRPAT model and provincial data from 2010 to 2022. The findings show that over the study period, China's total operational energy consumption of residential and commercial buildings has continued to rise, accompanied by widening regional gaps in energy efficiency. At the national level, population agglomeration and income growth are the primary drivers of energy consumption growth, while the impacts of multidimensional urbanization on building energy consumption exhibit significant differences across climate zones. By examining the differentiated effects of multidimensional urbanization under climate constraints, this study provides a more systematic interpretation of the evolutionary characteristics and regional differentiation of building energy consumption, and offers scientific reference for formulating zone-specific energy conservation and carbon reduction policies.

title: A frequency domain-based approach to building energy flexibility quantification
abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources poses a challenge to the control of power grids. Buildings can provide energy flexibility by modulating their consumption profile while guaranteeing comfort conditions. This work proposes a method for quantification of the energy flexibility of buildings that is independent of boundary conditions, duration of the flexibility event, and applied control strategy, and that does not require comparing the flexibility scenario to a baseline scenario. The method leverages the frequency domain analysis to correlate the fluctuation of the thermal power provided to the building to that of the zone temperature. The method was validated against a high fidelity building performance simulation tool, and was then applied to quantify the available storage capacity of a simulative case study building, comparing three different heat emission systems. For example, a zone temperature square wave like variation of 1 ∘ C for 2 hours was quantified to store 13.9, 21.7, and 237.3 Wh/ m 2 for the convective, radiator-based and floor heating system respectively.

title: Renewable energy communities in Canada: an integrated techno-economic risk assessment framework for behavioral, regulatory, and investor uncertainties
Examining future resilience of passive house design for a warming climate: a systematic review of challenges and knowledge gaps
abstract: This systematic review identifies challenges and research gaps in Passive House design regarding thermal comfort, indoor air quality, occupant behaviour and the performance gap in the context of a warming climate. Besides the climate change challenges, energy efficiency plays a crucial role in building a resilient future. The Passive House Standard in the construction industry offers promising benefits for these concerns; however, we report in this review that there is consistent evidence that indoor environmental quality remains a challenge for high-performance Passive House buildings. This review follows the PRISMA methodology. A total of 84 relevant studies were selected from 2293 initial results across four well-known databases. Findings reveal that challenges related to indoor environmental quality, which include both thermal comfort and indoor air quality, account for 89% of issues mentioned in the literature reviewed by this research. The remaining 11%, which represents only 9 of the 84 articles, is attributed to occupant behaviour, adaptability to climate change, cost, embodied carbon, and affordable housing. Furthermore, the study identifies critical knowledge gaps: 73% of the reviewed articles (61 sources) highlight the need for research on indoor environmental quality in Passive House buildings. However, the overheating problem dominates, drawing attention away from indoor air quality, which also plays a crucial role in indoor comfort. The review concludes by presenting alternative future research scenarios that take indoor air quality into account, highlighting the knowledge gaps identified in this review. It is essential to investigate further indoor environmental quality, design adaptations and user-centred approaches in Passive House buildings to ensure resilience in a warming climate. Future research should prioritise enhancing overheating performance, optimising user acceptance and interaction, and improving design flexibility to provide a more comfortable indoor environmental quality.

title: AutoControl-MPC: An automated model predictive control development framework based on large language models for HVAC systems
Gender-based differences in temperature and humidity experience in naturally ventilated classrooms: a case study from Central Poland
abstract: The paper presents the results of research on thermal comfort in a classroom, with particular emphasis on air temperature and relative humidity in relation to the students' gender. The research was carried out during real academic classes, combining measurements of internal environment parameters with the assessment of students' subjective feelings obtained using a survey method. The measurements were carried out in the winter-spring-summer period, recording the temperature and air humidity at 5-min intervals. The range of temperature variability was from 19.6 °C to 28.7 °C, and the relative humidity ranged from 30.1% to 52.3%. In parallel, surveys were conducted among students, including the assessment of thermal sensations, level of satisfaction with environmental conditions and preferences regarding their changes. The analysis of the results showed significant relationships between air parameters and the perception of thermal comfort. Studies have shown that the highest level of thermal comfort in the analyzed naturally ventilated classroom occurred at temperatures not exceeding 24 °C and a relative humidity of 30–50%. Men and women perceived thermal conditions similarly; however, women reported dissatisfaction with the prevailing environment significantly more often. The AMV (Actual Mean Vote) values were virtually identical for women and men, standing at 0.61. At the same time, the APD (Actual Percentage of Dissatisfied) index revealed a significantly higher level of dissatisfaction among women (35.85%) than among men (20.28%). The results suggest that thermal comfort analysis should not be limited solely to the assessment of thermal sensations but should also take into account the level of user satisfaction.

title: Deciphering morphology-dependent response intervals in exposure-weighted thermal hazard networks: an explainable machine learning approach for targeted mitigation
Economic model predictive control for building multi-energy systems under evolving feed-in regulations: A comparative study with rule-based strategies
abstract: Advanced control strategies for building multi-energy systems are essential to manage renewable generation variability while maintaining grid stability and minimizing costs. This paper presents a comprehensive comparison between conventional rule-based control and economic model predictive control (EMPC) strategies for a residential building system comprising photovoltaic (PV) generation, battery storage, and an air-source heat pump with thermal storage, thereby combining detailed component modeling, multi-energy system optimization, and evaluation under recently introduced dynamic feed-in regulations. A mixed-integer linear programming framework is developed that incorporates part-load and temperature-dependent heat pump performance, battery charge acceptance, and equipment degradation costs. The control strategies are evaluated through time-resolved and annual analyses using real weather data and consistent demand profiles, considering two distinct regulatory scenarios for PV feed-in limitations: static power caps and dynamic zero-compensation periods during negative electricity prices. Results demonstrate that while an enhanced rule-based control strategy with forecast-based battery management and surplus-driven heat pump operation improves performance over the reference approach, EMPC achieves superior outcomes across all metrics. Compared to the reference rule-based control, EMPC reduces net annual costs by 37.5%, grid imports by 13.1%, battery throughput by up to 15.2%, heat pump cycling by 25.5%, and PV curtailment by 41.3%. EMPC’s advantages stem from adaptively optimizing energy flows across multiple domains, strategically utilizing thermal energy storage to extend effective battery capacity, and minimizing conversion losses through intelligent power routing. These findings indicate that advanced predictive control becomes particularly advantageous under increasingly dynamic market and regulatory conditions.

title: From theory to practice: A collective voting-based multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for real-world HVAC control
Experimental study of a solar-driven humidity pump using capillary fibers for long-term indoor humidity control
Thermal and exergy performance of the imogura in traditional Japanese wooden houses: field measurements and Bayesian RC modeling
AI-based analytics and energy modeling framework for characterizing urban energy systems
abstract: Developing location-specific district energy models is essential for understanding energy patterns and providing communities with vital information to make decisions about their future energy use. However, accurately characterizing these models is challenging due to gaps in building characteristics and energy-use behavior data, as well as the labor-intensive nature of traditional modeling processes. To address this, we developed a framework that integrates top-down and bottom-up building energy data. Using these data, the framework trains and deploys neural network models to predict missing characteristics and generate inputs for urban energy models. The framework then generates scenarios based on user-selected efficiency targets across multiple variables. Our framework integrates with URBANoptTM, a bottom-up district energy modeling platform for co-located buildings. Because data such as insulation, occupancy, and energy usage are often unavailable at the building level, we leverage census-tract-level ResStockTM data and develop methods to disaggregate it for URBANopt integration. The neural network model architecture is customized based on user-defined known and missing inputs, as well as the data modalities of these inputs. The models learn relationships between known and unknown characteristics, predicting data gaps and targeted scenarios for URBANopt models. These capabilities enable efficient urban energy characterization by generating missing inputs and creating ``What-If'' scenarios for upgrades, supporting efficiency targets. We demonstrate this methodology on a residential neighborhood in Baltimore, MD, validating it against Baltimore data in ResStock and physics-based simulations in URBANopt. Results show high predictive accuracy in data completion and scenario generation, ensuring reliability and alignment with energy dynamics. Our automated framework streamlines energy modeling and provides a reliable tool for building energy characterization.

title: A method for calculating hourly incident solar radiation on building envelopes using a single fisheye image
Estimating occupant counts using deep neural networks and CO2 sensors in a mechanically ventilated environment
abstract: Improving the energy efficiency of buildings is critical for reducing energy consumption and mitigating environmental impacts. Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems are significant contributors to building energy use, and optimising these systems can lead to substantial energy savings. One promising approach is to control ventilation rates based on real-time occupancy, reducing unnecessary energy use while maintaining indoor air quality. However, real-world testing remains limited, especially with machine learning methods. Therefore, this paper tests occupant count estimation with a Convolutional Deep Long Short-Term Memory (CDLSTM) model in a room with variable mechanical ventilation. Transfer learning is utilised in combination with simulated data to reduce the required data requirements. During testing, we achieved an accuracy of 79% using CO 2 and airflow measurements. Occupancy-based ventilation control did not result in a significant decrease in accuracy, achieving around 75%. This study demonstrates the potential of machine learning-based occupancy estimation to support occupancy-centric demand-driven ventilation, enabling reduced ventilation rates during low occupancy while maintaining indoor air quality, and thereby offering a pathway to lower HVAC energy consumption.

title: Impact of carbon policies on housing affordability: a system dynamics model
Seasonal performance analysis of a flexible heat-recovery VRF system in high-humidity regions
From climate-zone migration to retrofit prioritisation in Spain: A multiscale climate-envelope-affordability framework for adaptive residential renovation
abstract: Climate change is weakening the assumption that regulatory climate zones remain stable over the service life of residential buildings. This article evaluates future CTE-equivalent climate-zone migration in Spain and translates that territorial signal into construction-period vulnerability, envelope sensitivity, cooling-affordability exposure and socio-energy retrofit prioritisation. The climate-change signal is framed within the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR6) and operationalised for Spain through AEMET/AdapteCCa regionalised RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 projections for 2055 and 2085. The analysis uses a municipal reassignment database covering 7,966 municipalities and explicitly separates the official legal CTE zone from a present recalculated analytical baseline. Winter and summer severity components are decomposed to quantify complete-zone change, winter relaxation, summer intensification, Heat-Shift Index and absolute future summer exposure. The territorial layer is connected to a documented HULC/CTE-HE residential case in Málaga and to two certified existing-building cases in Alpujarra de la Sierra and Rincón de la Victoria. Results show that 84.17-93.18% of municipalities change CTE-equivalent zone depending on scenario, while the share of municipalities in maximum summer severity rises from 29.35% to 85.35% under RCP8.5-2085. In the Málaga case, cooling demand increases from 12.81 to 24.70 kWh/m²·year in the high-end future sensitivity. The certified cases confirm that retrofit measures are not thermally symmetric: roof and opening interventions reduce cooling demand more consistently in warm climates than undifferentiated façade upgrades. The main contribution is a decision-oriented climate-envelope-affordability framework that combines climate migration, construction cohort, envelope weakness, cooling burden, social sensitivity and photovoltaic opportunity to support climate-adaptive residential renovation in Spain.

title: Experimental investigation and numerical modeling of the thermodynamic behavior of a workplace
In-situ deployment of model-predictive controls with sequential model parameter estimation
abstract: The growing interest to improve HVAC energy efficiency has motivated development of advanced supervisory control strategies, including data-driven and machine learning-based approaches. Model predictive control (MPC) is a well-established framework that predicts thermal dynamics and proactively adjusts system and zone operations to reduce energy use while maintaining comfort. Despite strong results in simulations and testbeds, relatively few studies report on MPC performance and deployment challenges in operational buildings. This paper presents a field deployment of an inverse-model-based MPC in a multi-zone VAV AHU commercial office building in Ottawa, Canada, developed using historical sensor data to model zone-level thermal behaviour and forecast disturbances. Compared to baseline rule-based control, the MPC reduced cooling energy by 4.6% and cut early-morning start-up cooling loads by 15.8%, while decreasing total discharge airflow by 52.5%. Heating energy was reduced by 28.7%, with a 54.3% reduction during the later-afternoon period preceding end-of-occupancy. In-situ deployment revealed several challenges, including semantic data integration, unexpected equipment behaviour, and unresolved system faults, which increased deployment lead times and constrained achievable energy savings. The results highlight the importance of robust data infrastructure and practical integration over model complexity.

title: Multi-objective assessment of BIPV yield, complementarity, and economic feasibility
abstract: Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) are essential for the transition towards net-zero energy buildings, yet a comprehensive multi-regional understanding of how energy yield, temporal complementarity, and economic feasibility interact across diverse configurations remains limited. Task 15 of the International Energy Agency Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme conducted a cross-regional, multi-objective assessment of 357 BIPV design options across eight application types in 44 cities, using a standardized 1 m 2 module with efficiencies between 5% and 25%. Energy yields were simulated using climate-specific irradiance datasets, and economic viability was assessed under three price tiers. A multi-objective Genetic Algorithm optimized the azimuths of vertical BIPV based on temporal complementarity and smoothness of the aggregated generation profile with optimal-yield rooftop BIPV system and conventional PV system (BIPV-PV). The combination of rooftop and vertical BIPV demonstrates strong daily and seasonal complementarity, enhancing the stability and continuity of solar energy conversion across time scales. Complementary area-ratio analysis indicates that vertical BIPV surfaces require approximately 1.7–2.5 times more area to match the yield of optimally tilted rooftop BIPV-PV systems. At low BIPV prices, over 90% of configurations become economically viable for efficiencies starting at around 18%, and in some cases even lower. Even at high price ranges, more than half remain viable, highlighting BIPV's increasing competitiveness and cost-reduction potential through improved installation practices and knowledge sharing. Overall, BIPV economic performance depends on complex, interdependent factors, indicating that single measures such as product cost-reduction are insufficient without holistic financial and market integration.

title: Bridging financial and environmental payback gaps: a life cycle-based retrofit framework for net-positive university campus buildings
Identifying residential building energy retrofit priorities across climate zones and end uses using machine learning and explainable AI
abstract: Energy retrofits of existing residential buildings are essential for reducing energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. However, limited resources require effective prioritization of retrofit measures. As retrofit effectiveness varies by climate zones, end uses, building characteristics, and future climate conditions, uniform retrofit strategies are often inefficient at national scales. Unlike previous studies that typically focus on a single climate condition or energy end use, this study develops a data-driven framework systematically comparing climate-zone and end-use-specific retrofit priorities under both historical and future climate scenarios, enabling climate-responsive retrofit planning and policy development. A synthetic database of over 72,000 parametric simulations of residential building archetypes is used to train climate-zone-specific machine learning (ML) models for predicting heating and cooling energy use intensity (EUI). Explainable artificial intelligence, based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), is applied to interpret model predictions and quantify parameter importance and directional influence. Results show substantial climate-zone-dependent differences in retrofit priorities. For cooling EUI, window SHGC and south-facing façade window-to-wall ratio (FDWR) are the two most influential features across all climate zones, exhibiting SHAP distributions approximately 1.5–2 times wider than those of other features. Cooling system efficiency and foundation type are additional key retrofit priorities in warmer and transitional climates (CZ 4–6), whereas ventilation rate plays a larger role in colder zones (CZ 7 A–8). For heating EUI, window U-value dominates in CZ 4–5, with SHAP ranges approximately 2–3 times wider than other variables, while foundation type becomes the primary driver in CZ 6–8. Under future climate scenarios, mechanical cooling efficiency gains importance in CZ 4-7 A, while heating performance in colder zones remains dominated by envelope, foundation, and ventilation system with heat recovery. Overall, the proposed ML-XAI framework provides transparent insights to support regionally differentiated climate-responsive retrofit strategies and evidence-based energy policy development.

title: A systematic review of machine learning based methods for applications in urban building energy modelling
Enhancing thermal performance of energy piles: a numerical investigation of a novel pipe network
Scenario framework for diversified upgrading of green building: Threshold expansion, technology upgrade and standard update
Research on the classification and spatial characteristics of rural settlement spatial morphology based on convolutional neural network——A case study of the Chengdu Plain
Thermal performance of borehole thermal energy storage for building energy systems in stratified ground with groundwater advection
Beyond the surface: a comprehensive hybrid life cycle assessment of embodied greenhouse gas emissions in green and conventional roofs in Melbourne
abstract: Green roofs are increasingly recognised as multifunctional solutions to urban environmental challenges; however, the embodied greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with their construction remain an underexplored component of their environmental performance, particularly in the Australian context. This study applies a hybrid life cycle assessment (LCA) approach to quantify and compare the life cycle embodied GHG emissions of conventional and green roof assemblies commonly used in Melbourne, Australia. Extensive and intensive green roofs were assessed over a 50-year lifespan and compared with conventional concrete, flat timber and pitched timber roof assemblies. Embodied emission calculations were performed using material quantities and hybrid life cycle inventory data from the Environmental Performance in Construction (EPiC) database, which combines process-based and environmentally extended input–output data to capture upstream supply chain emissions. Results show that conventional roofs in Melbourne have average annual life cycle embodied emissions of approximately 2.54 kgCO₂-eq/m 2 for concrete roofs and 1.64–1.66 kgCO₂-eq/m 2 for timber roofs. Extensive green roofs increased embodied emissions by approximately 0.97 kgCO₂-eq/m 2 /year, while intensive green roofs increased emissions by approximately 1.99 kgCO₂-eq/m 2 /year, primarily due to substrate and additional system layers. Substrate depth and composition and structural system selection were identified as the main drivers of embodied emissions. The results also show that hybrid LCA produces higher embodied emission estimates than many process-based studies due to more comprehensive system boundary coverage, highlighting the importance of methodological choice in life cycle assessment. This study provides region-specific hybrid LCA data for green roof systems in Australia and identifies key design parameters that can reduce embodied emissions, supporting more informed material selection and low-carbon roof design.

title: Structure of the energy performance gap in an education nearly zero-energy building (nZEB)
abstract: The energy performance gap (EPG), defined as the difference between predicted and measured energy use, remains a major challenge in the post-occupancy evaluation of nearly zero-energy buildings (nZEBs). Evidence on public educational nZEBs in cold-temperate climates remains limited, particularly with respect to monthly and end-use disaggregated analyses. To address this gap, this study investigates the EPG of a public educational nZEB in western Poland equipped with an earth-to-air heat exchanger, thermally activated building slabs, and a photovoltaic system. This analysis is based on three consecutive years of monthly operational data combined with weather observation data to minimise the effects of interannual climate variability. The EPG was evaluated for both total final energy use and individual building systems, including heating and cooling, domestic hot water, lighting, and auxiliary electricity. The measured total final energy use was 17–31% lower than the design prediction. However, this favourable overall result concealed substantially larger discrepancies at the system level. System-level EPG values ranged from −89% to −80% for domestic hot water, −50% to −32% for lighting, −33% to −14% for auxiliary electricity, −21% to −8% for PV generation, and 104% to 116% for heating and cooling. These findings demonstrate that an apparently satisfactory overall energy balance may conceal major errors in the predicted performance of individual building systems. Consequently, monthly, end-use-disaggregated analyses are necessary to improve operational diagnosis, building energy modelling, and design decision-making for educational nZEBs.

title: Deployable representative seasonal monitoring windows for residential energy consumption using genetic algorithm search and dynamic time warping
Temporal graph convolutional networks with morphological adjacency matrix: microclimate prediction for building energy modeling
abstract: Urban microclimates exhibit substantial spatial variability, yet conventional city-scale weather files often fail to capture these differences, leading to notable errors in building energy modeling. Data-driven microclimate prediction offers a promising alternative but is typically constrained by data scarcity at individual sites. This study proposes temporal graph convolutional networks (TGCNs) built on a morphological adjacency matrix (MAM) that incorporates spatial coordinates and urban morphological features to represent cross-zone microclimate relationships. This design allows external data to be selectively leveraged while maintaining site-specific microclimate characteristics and limiting noise from unrelated monitoring points. A campus-scale case study is conducted to examine prediction performance and its influence on building energy modeling. The TGCN model using morphological adjacency matrices (TGCN-MAM) demonstrates superior accuracy in predicting air temperature and relative humidity compared with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) model trained on single-site data (GRU-single) and a GRU model trained on multi-site data (GRU-multi). Relative to these two baselines, it reduces air temperature root mean squared error (RMSE) by 15.1% and 6.9%, and reduces relative humidity RMSE by 15.0% and 17.1%, respectively. When applied to energy modeling for three buildings, the generated weather data from the TGCN-MAM model keeps cooling energy deviations below 4%. These results demonstrate the model's effectiveness in providing more accurate urban microclimate prediction and improving the reliability of building energy modeling in heterogeneous urban environments.

title: Large language model-driven context-aware eco-feedback generation and evaluation
abstract: The objective of this study is to demonstrate the potential of generating context-aware eco-feedback - eco-feedback that reflects a household's contextual characteristics alongside its energy use patterns - through a large language model-integrated framework. Previous studies have introduced personalized eco-feedback, mostly relying on household energy use patterns; however, they frequently did not reflect distinct household characteristics, including their persona or non-negotiable routines, leaving eco-feedback ineffective and sometimes superficial. To address these limitations, we introduce a contextual engineering framework that generates eco-feedback using a self-consistency with chain-of-thought prompt, leveraging household energy analysis data, utility rate structures, and household characteristic information. We conducted a rigorous empirical validation and a combinatorial evaluation analysis to assess this framework systematically. The former tested the framework's ability to generate accurate and contextually grounded eco-feedback for three households by comparing its output against reference interventions independently derived from the same household data. The latter examined the framework's adaptability across 400 scenarios spanning 50 households, two utility rate structures, and four behavioral personas. Our framework generated eco-feedback that aligned with reference interventions at a mean rate of 92.0% and grounded its recommendations in the provided household data with 95.7% citation accuracy. It also proved highly adaptive, shifting both the appliances targeted and the energy-saving strategies recommended in response to rate structure and household context. Ultimately, this study contributes to realizing the next level of context-aware interactions between occupants and buildings which paves the way for higher occupant living quality and sustainability.

title: Thermo-mechanical characterization and building energy simulation of eco-friendly sandwich and lightweight concrete materials using natural pozzolan for sustainable construction applications
Thermal imaging with instance segmentation for quantifying sleep thermally adaptive quilt coverage behavior
Can climate finance support low-carbon transitions in the built environment? Evidence from developing countries
Data-driven control of split heat-pump system based on thermal preference prediction
abstract: In this work, an experimental investigation was conducted in an office building involving a total of 16 participants. Subjective thermal sensation and thermal preference were assessed through periodic surveys. Several machine learning classification models were developed and evaluated, including Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machines, Logistic Regression, and Decision Trees. The Random Forest algorithm achieved the highest predictive performance, reaching an accuracy of 96.36% under random data splitting and 65.6% when chronological splitting was applied. The developed model was further evaluated under real operating conditions using a developed dynamic control framework for a split heat-pump system. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating thermal preference prediction into the control of split heat-pump systems under real office operating conditions.

title: Seasonal–diurnal nonlinear and interactive associations between built–natural–topographic indicators and land surface temperature in a coastal urban agglomeration
An AHP experiment with the smart readiness indicator applied in a local reality
abstract: This paper describes an experiment intended to evaluate the appropriateness of the weighting scheme used to compute the Smart Readiness Indicator (SRI), an index introduced by the European Commission and Parliament with the double aim to measure the “intelligence” of a building and to encourage the adoption of smart technologies in both new buildings and existing constructions to be retrofitted. This index is based on a hierarchical scheme including criteria related to energy savings and flexibility as well as to the comfort, convenience and wellbeing of the building occupants. In particular, the weights to assign to the criteria related to the needs of the occupants are largely subjective, and the technical support group established by the European Commission to draw up the SRI scheme did not find any scientific evidence to differentiate them, so all of them received equal weights. Exploiting Saaty’s Analysis of the Hierarchical Process (AHP), we involved a local group of engineers, architects, technicians and administrators to obtain cardinal rankings for these criteria. The results are likely to depend on the local context where our inquiry has been conducted, central Italy, but also show that the opinions of our experts are diverse, even within professionally homogeneous subgroups, and do not justify the equal-weight choice made by the technical support group. Our results can also constitute one of the many expected local contributions to the revision of the present SRI scheme.

title: Development of a statistical model for long-term electricity forecasting in residential buildings
abstract: Buildings account for 36–40% of global energy consumption and CO₂ emissions, with electricity representing nearly 55% of global electricity use. Accurate long-term forecasting is critical for grid stability and net-zero targets, yet most predictive models require extensive multi-year datasets or complex machine learning architectures. To our knowledge, no prior study has employed Fourier series methods integrating climate variables and weekday residual corrections to predict full annual electricity consumption using only a single year of training data, representing a methodological gap for long-term, one-year-ahead prediction in data-scarce environments. This study develops a simple modeling framework using Fourier series enhanced by multivariate regression incorporating climate variables (air temperature, humidity, sunshine hours) and seasonal residual correction. The developed models were tested on 322 apartments in a residential building in Japan, using hierarchical clustering to identify distinct consumption clusters (low, medium and high). The model achieved high accuracy across all clusters in this case study (RMSE = 0.472–1.20 kWh, MAPE = 7.1–8.9%) when forecasting one year ahead. Autoregressive residual correction further improved day-ahead forecasting accuracy (RMSE = 0.49–0.83 kWh, MAPE = 4.8–5.5%). Residual analysis revealed systematic weekday–weekend patterns and strong correlations with temperature. High-consumption clusters exhibited two to three times greater temperature sensitivity than low-consumption groups. The proposed Fourier approach provides an interpretable, data-efficient alternative to complex machine learning models, enabling accurate one-year-ahead electricity forecasting using only a single year of historical data. It offers a practical tool for building energy managers and policymakers operating in data-constrained contexts.

title: Electrification and renovation in the EU building sector decarbonization: a multi-model comparison
abstract: Policymakers rely on building sector energy models to design decarbonization strategies, yet different models can produce divergent projections even under similar assumptions. We address this through a systematic comparison of five building sector energy models (FORECAST-Buildings, Invert/EE-Lab, Invert/Opt, PRIMES-Buildings, EDGE/REMIND-Buildings) applied to shared scenario narratives for EU27. The scenarios vary along two dimensions: supply-side technology focus (electrification, district heating, hydrogen, and synthetic fuels) and demand reduction ambition (moderate efficiency, high efficiency, lifestyle change). High-efficiency scenarios achieve final energy demand reductions of 31% to 53% by 2050, while moderate-efficiency scenarios achieve 20% to 44%, depending on model structure and renovation dynamics. Electrification via heat pumps emerges as the dominant strategy across all scenarios, with projected capacity reaching 800 to 1600 GW by 2050 and electricity's share of final energy demand rising to 60% to 86%, even in scenarios not explicitly focused on electrification. In district heating-focused scenarios, shares reach 14% to 28% of final demand, while in other scenarios shares remain at 8% to 17%, reflecting sensitivity to spatial planning assumptions and infrastructure development. Hydrogen and synthetic fuels play only a marginal role, with shares below 10% by 2050. This comparison identifies heat pump electrification and deep renovation as robust, no-regret strategies, while clarifying conditions under which district heating becomes viable at scale. By comparing structurally diverse models under harmonized assumptions, this study provides policymakers with evidence on which strategies are robust regardless of the modeling approach.

title: Rebound effects of residential PV adoption under progressive electricity tariffs in South Korea
abstract: Residential photovoltaic (PV) systems have emerged as a key instrument in household-level decarbonization strategies worldwide, as self-consumed generation directly reduces grid electricity consumption and associated costs. However, this cost reduction may induce a rebound effect whereby households increase electricity consumption relative to the expected post-PV level, partially offsetting the intended energy and emissions savings. This study estimates the rebound effect in Korean residential PV adoption under a progressive electricity tariff, decomposing it into substitution and income components using a simulation framework based on hourly PV generation and household load data. The substitution component arises from marginal-price changes induced by tariff-tier transitions, and the income component is scaled to household disposable income. A factorial analysis varies consumption level and system capacity independently across both seasons, and a net-metering scenario is additionally examined. Rebound is reported as the conventional share of expected savings offset, enabling comparison with prior studies. The results indicate that rebound is governed primarily by whether the post-PV net load crosses a tariff-tier boundary: households undergoing a tier transition exhibit a rebound of approximately 11.1–21.9% (0–6.7% under the consumption-based formulation), whereas households without a transition exhibit near-zero rebound. Under net metering, more households cross tier boundaries and the substitution rebound increases. These scenario-based estimates suggest that rebound adjustment factors differentiated by tariff-tier transition, system capacity, and net-metering eligibility should be considered for more accurate assessment of residential PV decarbonization outcomes.

title: Geometric activation of spectrally selective coatings for passive solar control in transparent systems
Analysing EN16883:2017 guidelines on energy retrofit and its use outside of Europe:A proposal for New Zealand tailored guidelines
abstract: As nations set more ambitious carbon dioxide reduction targets as result of international climate agreements, the energy retrofit of historic and heritage buildings has emerged as a key strategy for reducing energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. This approach not only helps mitigate climate change but also preserves the cultural and historical significance of these buildings. With growing concerns about climate change, there is an increasing recognition that addressing environmental impacts in the built heritage sector can yield both environmental and social benefits, aligning with global efforts to achieve sustainability and resilience. Internationally, many countries have adopted energy retrofit policies, and there has been an increasing number of projects and published material on the energy retrofit of historic buildings. However, New Zealand, unlike Europe, has no country-specific guidelines for historic retrofit considering social, cultural, environmental and economic aspects. This article explores whether other countries outside Europe, such as New Zealand, would benefit from adopting guidelines similar to the European Standard EN 16883:2017 by its application onto three hypothetical energy retrofits of heritage buildings in the country. It investigates the benefits and limits on the application of this specific procedure, multiple criteria assessments, some recommended methods and risk analysis for the renovation process. This paper discusses the environmental, economic and social benefits of such guidelines, the country-specific requirements for adopting energy retrofit guidelines for historic buildings, and the recommended adaptations to enable a better usability of energy retrofit guidelines both locally and internationally aiming to reduce historic buildings environmental impact.

title: Lightweight WaveNet-enhanced deformable attention model for appliance-level building energy monitoring and disaggregation
Life cycle assessment of building envelope for social housing: Balancing embodied impacts and operational energy
abstract: Improving operational energy efficiency in buildings often leads to an increase in the embodied environmental impacts of the materials used. In Brazil, mass-produced social housing programmes often overlook this life-cycle trade-off and regional climate variations. This study aims to evaluate the environmental impacts of different envelope construction systems applied to a standard social housing unit through a comparative Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). Eight configurations were analysed for a 41.16 m² single-family house over a 40-year lifespan, using São Paulo (Bioclimatic Zone 2M) as the baseline. The variations included four wall systems (ceramic block, concrete block, cast-in-place concrete, and light steel framing) and two roofing options (timber ceiling and solid concrete slab). Operational energy demand was estimated via EnergyPlus simulation, while environmental impacts were calculated in SimaPro using the Ecoinvent 3.5 database and the ReCiPe method. The results reveal a critical balance between operational efficiency and material-intensive construction. Although using a solid concrete slab reduces cooling energy demand, it significantly increases the building’s overall environmental footprint due to the high embodied impacts of cement and steel. The combination of cast-in-place concrete walls and a timber ceiling demonstrated the lowest overall environmental impact. Conversely, uninsulated light steel framing yielded the highest energy consumption and the poorest life-cycle performance. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that local climate and occupant behaviour are determining factors, reinforcing the necessity for holistic material selection in social housing design to balance thermal comfort and embodied environmental costs.

title: Life cycle assessment of disassemblable partition components in housing refurbishment: A discrete event simulation approach
DeMuNet: adaptive decomposition and multi-source learning neural network for electric household load forecasting
Cooling load forecasting for multi-user scenarios: A unified iTransformer framework with personalized knowledge fine-tuning
Measured heating impacts of window retrofits in cold, dry-winter housing: Changepoint diagnostics with AI-assisted interpretation
abstract: Window retrofits are widely implemented in existing residential buildings, yet their measured heating impacts under real operating conditions remain insufficiently verified, particularly in cold-climate regions with high seasonal heating demand. This study evaluates the measured heating impacts of a government-supported window retrofit program in cold, dry-winter housing using pre- and post-retrofit utility data from 39 dwellings in Goyang City, South Korea.
