A three-parameter heating changepoint model (3PH-CPM) was used to derive temperature-adjusted heating diagnostics, including heating slope, heating-zone intercept, base load, and heating energy above base. Retrofit effects were then assessed through parametric and nonparametric pre-post statistical tests. The results showed statistically significant post-retrofit improvements in key heating diagnostics, indicating reduced temperature sensitivity and lower heating demand. To examine heterogeneity in retrofit response, dwellings were grouped using CPM-derived heating metrics reflecting improvement magnitude, heating sensitivity, and pre-retrofit energy use. AI-assisted interpretation based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was then applied to identify the household and building characteristics associated with stronger or weaker measured benefits. The analysis revealed both the magnitude and direction of variable influence, highlighting the physical and occupancy-related factors linked to heterogeneous retrofit outcomes. The proposed dual-level evaluation framework provides a transparent and practical approach for assessing measured window retrofit performance under weather-varying conditions and may support more informed screening and follow-up evaluation of retrofit programs in heating-dominated regions.

title: A missing data imputation method for chillers based on denoising diffusion probabilistic model
Mapping the evolution of outdoor summer thermal comfort in a Mediterranean country in the context of climate change
A Bayesian-optimized deep learning framework for interpretable smart window energy performance prediction and multi-climate design evaluation
Pathways and dilemmas of near-zero carbon transitions in existing communities: evidence from pilot communities in Chengdu, China
Comparative performance analysis of ejector-enhanced graded coupled solar-air dual-source heat pumps for cold and low-irradiance applications
Unraveling the differentiated effects of spatial morphology on urban heat island intensity under distinct functional constraints
Performance analysis and experimental investigation of various configurations of air-cycle heat pump systems with turbine power recovery
Life cycle assessment of biocomposite material substitutions in window frames to implement circular design approach
abstract: The construction industry is a major contributor to environmental impacts due to its reliance on resource-intensive and fossil-based materials. Window frames, which significantly influence both the embodied and operational performance of buildings, are predominantly manufactured from aluminum, PVC, and hybrid wood-aluminum structures. While these materials provide durability and thermal efficiency, they also impose considerable environmental burdens, particularly in terms of embodied carbon, fossil resource depletion, and end-of-life management. This study evaluates the environmental implications of substituting conventional materials in wood-aluminum window frames with biocomposites, using a life cycle assessment (LCA) framework in accordance with ISO 14040/44. Five scenarios were modelled: the baseline (conventional materials), replacement of aluminum cladding with biocomposite, substitution of PVC glass holders, replacement of handles, and a combined substitution of all components. The selected biocomposite, consisting of recycled polypropylene (rPP) reinforced with 30% bleached softwood kraft pulp (BSKP), was assessed across the impact categories of global warming potential, acidification, fossil resource depletion, and human toxicity. Results indicate that aluminum substitution provides the most substantial environmental improvements, with reductions of up to 39% in global warming potential and 43% in fossil depletion compared to the baseline. The combined scenario achieved the strongest benefits overall, with a 40% reduction in global warming potential. Substitution of PVC and Zamak components yielded limited individual benefits but enhanced overall performance when combined, while sensitivity analyses underscored the importance of recycled polymers and low-carbon aluminum pathways. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of targeted biocomposite substitution to support circular design and reduce the environmental impacts of window manufacturing.

title: Governance mechanisms for collective energy decisions in homeowner associations: a two-stage delegation-consensus model
abstract: Collective energy-retrofit decisions in multi-owner housing often stall because quorum and supermajority rules interact with low attendance and heterogeneous preferences over cost, carbon performance, and comfort. This study develops an exploratory two-stage agent-based model for Dutch homeowner associations (VvEs). In Stage I, absent owners delegate to the attending member with the highest modeled trust score; in Stage II, weighted representatives enter a fuzzy consensus-reaching routine over retrofit options. Exploratory interviews inform the plausibility of selected assumptions, and Dutch housing-survey variables provide stylized household profiles. Across Monte Carlo experiments and a controlled paired comparison, Stage I delegation procedurally represents all ownership shares when only 50–65% of owners attend, while the Stage II consensus routine yields high mean support (93.2% versus 87.4% without delegation, and 67.7–80.9% for direct-vote and Condorcet benchmarks). Crucially, when attendee sets are held constant, delegation alone produces only a small change (+4.0 pp.; d = 0.43) in final support, indicating that its governance value lies primarily in input-side representation rather than in improving the quality of agreement. High consensus is structurally induced by the positive averaging routine and is not empirical evidence of VvE convergence or legitimacy. The framework is positioned as an exploratory governance foresight sandbox for small-N residential collectives.

title: Pathway to carbon emission reduction of green buildings in China based on LDA topic model and fsQCA configuration analysis
Do feasibility-stage decarbonisation conclusions survive tariff and carbon-factor drift? A controlled current-data rebasing audit of four calibrated UK primary-school retrofit cases
abstract: Feasibility studies can remain in public-estate investment pipelines after the tariffs, emission factors and cost levels used to produce them have changed. This study develops a controlled current-data rebasing audit that first reconciles a completed feasibility dataset, then freezes its physical energy quantities and retrofit configuration while updating only explicitly identified exogenous accounting variables. The audit is applied to four anonymised 2022 primary-school retrofit cases from one UK local-authority estate. Their baseline OpenStudio/EnergyPlus models were calibrated to 12 monthly utility observations and met the ASHRAE Guideline 14 monthly NMBE and CV(RMSE) criteria, although the retained evidence package does not recover the exact calibration dates or several model-input assumptions. Under the 2022 source-report basis, the combined packages reduce reported operational CO₂ by 56.7–67.8% (case mean 62.6%), leaving a 32.2–43.3 percentage-point residual within the stated location-based accounting boundary. Rebasing the same physical quantities to the 2026 UK Government conversion factors raises the case reductions to 72.5–78.8% (mean 76.3%) and narrows the residual to 21.2–27.5%. Whole-package utility-cost comparisons are tariff-contingent: the three gas-fired cases change from 13.3 to 16.4% cost increases under the 2022 tariffs to 5.1–13.1% savings under Q1 2026 average electricity and gas tariffs, while the oil-fired case saves 33.0% when Q1 2026 electricity is paired with the retained source-case oil price of £0.085/kWh. A small-consumer-band gas test remains mixed (−0.6% to +5.4%). A separate output-level heat-system counterfactual shows why these package results must not be labelled as ASHP-only effects: at η = 0.85 and SCOP = 3.0, the current-price incremental ASHP cost remains positive for the gas cases (£4.3–10.5 thousand/yr) while the oil case saves about £1.6 thousand/yr. Recasting sequencing as cumulative emissions gives 1283 tCO₂ avoided over eight years for the carbon-led sequence, compared with 1106 tCO₂ for fabric-first and 912 tCO₂ for cost-led sequencing. The contribution is therefore a reproducible, bounded method for distinguishing durable physical conclusions from tariff-, factor- and accounting-vintage effects; it is not a statistically representative assessment of the UK school stock.

title: Optimized design and thermal performance study of latent heat thermal energy storage device with integrated PLC control
abstract: Latent heat thermal energy storage (LHTES) technology, with its high energy storage density and isothermal heat release characteristics, has demonstrated broad application prospects in the field of heating. However, current LHTES heating systems predominantly employ a centralised control model for operating multiple LHTES units, and there remains a lack of development in integrated, self-controlled LHTES unit suitable for distributed heating. This study addresses issues such as the poor heat exchange performance and low level of automation in traditional LHTES devices. By optimizing the spacing between the heat exchange tubes and integrating a Programmable Logic Controller (PLC), a PLC-integrated LHTES unit was developed, enabling real-time monitoring and dynamic strategy adjustment of the heat storage and release processes. This study investigated the effects of different inlet water temperatures, flow rates, and operational strategies on the thermal performance and economic efficiency of the system under a peak-valley electricity pricing mechanism through experiments under various conditions. The results show that compared with conventional serpentine coils, the variable-pitch coil device reduces the heat exchange time by 4% and improves the problem of uneven heat exchange in the direction of gravity. The PID control strategy enables precise adjustment of the heat output of the device. When the heat release power was kept constant at 1.5, 2.0, and 2.5 kW, the heat release time of the PLC-integrated control device was extended by 45.5%, 46.1%, and 100%, respectively. Compared to central heating systems, heat storage heating that takes advantage of time-of-use electricity pricing reduces costs by 52.0%. Compared with coal-fired heating, the costs are similar, but heat storage heating utilizing time-of-use electricity rates can significantly reduce carbon emissions. This study provides technical support for the application of single LHTES device in distributed heating systems.

title: Absorptive energy scheduling architectures for PEMFC-based building poly-generation: Parametric analysis and performance evaluation
Material use and embodied GHG in refurbishment and adaptive reuse of existing buildings
Enhanced interlaboratory reproducibility of emulator-type load-based tests
abstract: The feed-forward compensation (FFC) method for the emulator-type load-based testing was developed to ensure adequate trackability of the return air condition in test facilities, thereby improving the reproducibility and standardization of dynamic test results. A linearized model of thermal and transport delays within the testing facility forms the basis for the recalibration of temperature and humidity control signals from the room emulator to the reconditioning unit of the psychrometric chamber. To achieve reproducibility levels comparable to current steady-state tests this study develops a model formulation that minimize chances of unstable control of the testing environment, practically deploys the FFC technique in interlaboratory tests, and demonstrates its effectiveness. Consequently, its implementation on a 10 kW ceiling-cassette-type unit demonstrated improved trackability, leading to delays and deviations from the emulator signal limited to 60 s and 0.1 K, respectively. It is demonstrated that delay compensation generally reduced sources of results variability on repeated measurements in the same testing environment. Interlaboratory results show deviations in the recorded coefficient of performance within 2% for all investigated testing conditions during both cooling and heating operation. The proposed method does not require additional equipment and is therefore proposed to enhance the reliability of current testing equipment in conducting precise and reproducible dynamic tests.

title: Laboratory and season-long field evaluation of AI-based predictive control for residential heat pumps in DHW and space-heating operation
abstract: Residential heat pumps are commonly controlled using static rule-based controllers such as fixed heating curves and hysteresis-based DHW control, which can lead to unnecessary temperature lifts and avoidable storage losses as building and occupancy conditions change. This paper presents two AI-enabled predictive control strategies for (i) DHW production and (ii) space-heating supply-temperature control. In both cases, forecasting/modeling and optimization are separated to facilitate implementation. For DHW, a learned demand forecast is combined with Modelica-based simulation-in-the-loop scheduling that minimizes electrical energy while enforcing service constraints. Laboratory experiments show reductions in electrical energy use of 5-8% for an individual-housing configuration and 38-43% for a collective-housing configuration, together with a substantial increase in the heat-pump coefficient of performance (COP). For space heating, an attention-augmented encoder-decoder LSTM temperature predictor is embedded in a fast surrogate-assisted receding-horizon controller. A field trial in one residential building during the 2024-2025 heating season showed an 8% reduction in daily electricity use, an increase in mean COP from 3.95 to 4.15, and a reduction in mean absolute comfort deviation from 0.3 to 0.1 K. The results demonstrate that forecast-informed optimization can improve heat-pump efficiency while maintaining comfort, although broader field validation across building types and climates remains necessary.

title: Improving indoor occupancy prediction using graph neural networks and positional encodings
abstract: Managing residential energy efficiently without compromising comfort is challenging. The key difficulty lies in predicting occupancy in real time. Intelligent control strategies are widely used for residential energy management. As sensors become increasingly common in homes, occupancy prediction has gained significant attention as one such approach. Traditional occupancy prediction methods analyze temporal patterns within individual rooms but overlook spatial connectivity. This lack limits the accuracy of occupancy-forecasting methods. Incorporating spatial information could improve prediction accuracy and enhance the effectiveness of occupancy-based energy management. One promising approach to represent such spatial information is through the use of embeddings, which encode spatial connectivity in a data-driven vector space. Another complementary method is to represent the building layout as a graph, where nodes correspond to rooms and edges capture spatial connectivity. In this study, we evaluate multiple occupancy prediction architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTM). These models are further enhanced by positional encoding (PE) and Graph Neural Networks (GNN) that explicitly encode spatial connectivity among rooms. Results indicate that spatial embeddings improve predictive performance, with graph-based methods providing the highest performance. Among all models, the hybrid GNN + PE + CNN yielded the best overall performance. However, considering practical heating control scenarios, balancing comfort, energy savings, and computational complexity, we found that LSTM + PE emerges as the most suitable choice.

title: When the sun is in occupants' field of view: assessing discomfort glare, thermal comfort, and overall comfort
abstract: This study investigates the cross-effects between thermal comfort and discomfort glare in office environments where the sun is in the field of view (FOV). While thermal and visual comfort have been extensively studied independently, their combined effects under real sunlit conditions remain unclear. A 2 × 2 within-subject experiment was conducted in a controlled test facility located in Germany, exposing 36 participants to two thermal conditions (lower temperature: -1 < PMV < 0 and higher temperature: 0 < PMV < +1) and two perceived glare levels (imperceptible and noticeable) under clear and stable sky conditions. Subjective comfort responses and physiological parameters (skin temperature and heart rate variability) were collected alongside environmental data. Results under these stimulus conditions showed no significant effect of temperature on glare discomfort, nor of glare discomfort on thermal perception, suggesting that thermal and visual sensations may not strongly interact under the tested conditions. However, glare discomfort showed a negative effect on overall comfort, while thermal variables (acceptability and sensation) showed weaker but still significant positive associations with overall comfort. Physiological analyses revealed that neither skin temperature nor its spatial variability were significantly associated with glare discomfort or thermal acceptability. However, glare discomfort showed a significant yet non-intuitive negative association with cardiovascular activation. Taken together, these findings suggest that discomfort glare due to the sun in the field of view may play a more prominent role in overall comfort perception than the thermal variations investigated in this study, while emphasizing the value of effective shading to improve occupants' well-being in office spaces.

title: Towards environmental optimization for achieving indoor thermal comfort using windcatchers
abstract: The effectiveness of conventional windcatchers as passive environmental design components in enhancing thermal comfort in the interior in hot arid climate conditions is tested in this study. The research has tried to investigate the impact of windcatchers on four different building designs, thus adding to the development of the green building paradigms through the recognition of the best design parameters, including the ratio of windows to the wall (WWR) and the building orientation, in order to boost indoor thermal performance. DesignBuilder (DB) simulation tool is used to develop the accurate climatic conditions through meteorological data of Egypt. Moreover, the use of the Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) makes it possible to conduct a strict analysis of how the factors used in the design of a building can affect the interior conditions including air velocity. In summer, when the weather is at its best, the Hollow Square design is the most efficient in Cairo, as it has the least CO2 emissions (251.8 kg) and hours of thermal discomfort (156.8 h), due to its small size, low (20%) percent of window to wall ratio, and ideal orientation. The results highlight the importance of the windcatcher performance, the structure of the building, the velocity of the wind, and the direction of the wind to the improvement of the thermal comfort in the building environment.

title: Long-term field performance of an innovative dew point evaporative cooling system as a low-energy cooling solution for a live edge data Centre
abstract: Small-scale edge data centres and server rooms are expanding with digitalisation, AI deployment and distributed computing, but their cooling systems are often less efficient than those in large data centres. This paper presents, to the authors’ knowledge, the first full-year real-life monitoring study of an innovative dew-point evaporative cooling (DPC) system installed in a live edge data centre in the UK. The study moves DPC evaluation beyond laboratory testing and short-term prototype trials towards higher technology readiness under practical operating conditions. The system was assessed using performance mapping, full-year monitoring data, seasonal temperature profiles, hourly summer-event analysis and microbiological monitoring. During annual operation, the DPC system provided effective indoor temperature management, with monthly average COP values generally between 27 and 36 during normal operating periods. However, the COP reduced to approximately 18 during the constrained summer operation in July. The analysis shows that DPC performance depends not only on the heat and mass exchanger, but also on system-level factors such as installation arrangement, outdoor conditions, ductwork, airflow management and interaction with existing split units. Microbiological monitoring showed that no dip-slide sample exceeded the unacceptable threshold when a bespoke risk management protocol was applied. The results demonstrate that DPC can provide high-COP, low-electricity base cooling for small edge data centres. However, successful deployment requires appropriate system-level design, hybrid control with auxiliary split units, and low-burden water-side maintenance strategies. These findings provide first-hand long-term field evidence for the practical application of innovative DPC technology in edge data centre cooling.

title: A BIM-based adaptive surrogate framework for efficient uncertainty quantification in building energy simulation
abstract: Uncertainty quantification in building energy modelling is essential for reliable retrofit decision-making, yet conventional Monte Carlo approaches require numerous simulations that are prohibitive for high-fidelity models. This study presents a novel BIM-based adaptive surrogate framework that combines sparse Polynomial Chaos Expansion (PCE) with sequential sampling to efficiently propagate input uncertainties and compute variance-based sensitivity indices for multiple building energy outputs at varying temporal resolutions. The framework was applied to four representative Irish residential archetypes, including bungalow, semi-detached, detached, and terraced. Uncertain parameters were introduced progressively across three physically distinct domains: envelope fabric (6 variables), operational and behavioural factors (7 additional variables), and geometric form (1 additional variable), yielding a 14-dimensional uncertainty space at the fullest stage. The sparse PCE surrogates achieved holdout R 2 ≥ 0.99 and R 2 ≥ 0.93 for energy use intensity (EUI) and annual heating demand for all archetypes and stages, respectively, using only 480–560 training simulations per stage. Independent Monte Carlo benchmarking confirmed that the surrogate-predicted mean EUI falls within the MC 95% confidence interval at all three stages. Global sensitivity analysis revealed that the dominant EUI driver is archetype-dependent: wall U-value for the bungalow, domestic hot water demand for the semi-detached, and window U-value for the detached and terraced houses. In contrast, HVAC system efficiency dominates heating demand uncertainty across all archetypes. These findings demonstrate that archetype-specific sensitivity analysis is essential for informed retrofit decisions, and that the proposed framework provides a computationally tractable pathway to achieve this within BIM-based building energy workflows.

title: Conservative valuation and fair allocation of pipeline thermal inertia in multi-park district heating systems

A systematic review of building decision-support tools utilizing simplified models
abstract: Simplified models use computationally efficient methods and reduced input requirements to approximate complex building performance behaviours. These capabilities have led to their increased integration as the underlying engines of decision-support tools used in early-stage building design and analysis. This study presents the first systematic review of scientific articles that integrated simplified models into decision-support tools for building applications, including thermal (energy and comfort), structural, and resilience analysis. Following a screening of over 1400 publications, 22 studies were selected for in-depth analysis focusing on engine choice, interface design, and engine-interface integration. The findings highlight several critical gaps in the literature, particularly the need for open data sharing, the lack of participatory design, and the absence of guidelines for balancing trade-offs between computational cost, data storage, and input flexibility. The review also introduces a classification of engine-tool integration into four types (model-in-the-loop, database-in-the-loop, user-defined integration, and static integration), providing guidance on selecting among them according to tool hosting, model complexity, and database size. This study provides unique and timely insights that can guide researchers and practitioners in developing more accessible and effective decision-support tools for the built environment.

title: Simulation investigation on the thermal regulation performance of eutectic hydrated salt capsule gypsum wall
Development of an indoor adaptive thermal comfort model using the causal diagram method
abstract: The application of adaptive thermal comfort models is currently limited to naturally ventilated and/or mixed-mode buildings, based on the correlational relationships between prevailing outdoor temperature and indoor neutral temperature observed in those buildings. However, correlation does not indicate causation, and building scientists are often primarily interested in understanding the causal mechanisms by which the outdoor climate affects indoor thermal comfort. We hypothesize that thermal adaptation is mainly driven by the indoor conditions to which occupants are most exposed, regardless of the outdoor climate or the building's cooling systems. Because the adaptive thermal comfort field studies are non-experimental, meaning they are observational, we used the causal diagram method and developed a comprehensive diagram using the ASHRAE Thermal Comfort Database II. From there, we showed how to create a more focused, simplified causal diagram to test the hypothesis. We found that the indoor thermal conditions drive adaptation independently of outdoor climate or the building's cooling type. The resulting causation-based adaptive model quantifies the causal effects of indoor thermal conditions on occupants' thermal sensation votes. The new indoor adaptive thermal comfort zone is between 19 °C and 28 °C (using the Standard Effective Temperature metric, or SET). The causation-based model can inform the design of new buildings and the operation of existing ones, regardless of their cooling strategies. This approach could reduce the trend of over-cooling in air-conditioned buildings and have significant implications for sustainable building practices.

title: Editorial Board

Integrated methodological framework for in situ evaluation of the heat loss coefficient, improvement of energy modelling and evaluation of its adaptation to climate change in heterogeneous architectural solutions
abstract: This paper describes an integrated methodology for characterising the energy performance of an educational building with heterogeneous construction characteristics under real operating conditions. To this end, it (1) combines multivariable monitoring, (2) calculates the heat loss coefficient (HLC) empirically, and (3) calibrates and validates the building model to (4) incorporate projected climate files for various scenarios. The novelty relates to the analysis of a heterogeneous envelope with mixed renovation solutions, which justifies the validation based on experimental data. The monitored data are systematically processed using cleaning, integration and transformation techniques to ensure their applicability. Data from equivalent winter periods over three academic years are compared, demonstrating that the increase in heating consumption is due to alterations in natural ventilation regimes, forced by sanitary conditions. The experimental HLC value reflects intensive ventilation related to the academic year conditioned by the Covid-19 pandemic (1.88 kW/K), and a homogeneous HLC is calculated for subsequent winters related to an airtight building (1.30 kW/K). This analysis demonstrates the sensitivity and reproducibility of the experimental HLC method. The calibrated BES model, according to the NMBE and Cv(RMSE) indicators, includes meteorological files with future projections that consider various SSP climate scenarios generated according to the EC-Earth3 and CNRM-CM6–1-HR models. Although with different results, the trends in all scenarios suggest a reduction in the building's heating demand of between 27 and 43% in response to rising outdoor temperatures. The discrepancies between models, of up to 10–15%, highlight the need to choose the specific climate model for the energy analysis. This work develops a framework for validated energy analysis of buildings, based on experimental data and addressing a forward-looking analysis. This approach serves to design buildings and implement strategies in public buildings using complex architecture.

title: Extension-layer fine-tuning for transfer learning in multi-agent reinforcement learning-based HVAC control
abstract: Reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) control, but its practical application is limited by high training costs and insufficient cross-environment generalization. Although existing transfer learning methods can partly alleviate this issue, their transfer stability and adaptability remain limited in complex HVAC systems involving multi-agent interactions. To address this challenge, this study develops an extension-layer fine-tuning strategy within the multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) framework for transferring multifunctional HVAC control policies, where separate agents regulate indoor temperature setpoints and fresh-air ventilation. During transfer, the pretrained actor and critic networks are retained as transferable knowledge backbones, and newly added adaptation layers are trained to capture target-environment-specific policy and value-function representations. The proposed strategy is compared with partial fine-tuning, full-model fine-tuning, MADDPG trained from scratch, and a rule-based controller under cross-climate and cross-building-type transfer scenarios. The results show that, across all test scenarios, the proposed strategy maintains indoor temperature and CO2 concentration within prescribed ranges while achieving energy-saving performance comparable to fully trained MADDPG. In addition, compared with training from scratch, transfer learning reduces retraining time by more than 90%, and the additional computational burden introduced by the newly added adaptation layers is limited. These results indicate that extension-layer fine-tuning provides an effective pathway for efficiently and reliably deploying multi-agent reinforcement learning controllers in heterogeneous building environments.

title: Energy resilience in the built environment under disruptive events: hazard-, climate- and equity-informed systematic scoping review
abstract: Buildings are primary sites where climate hazards translate into human crises, yet research on their ability to withstand and recover from energy disruptions remains conceptually fragmented and rarely integrates building physics with social science perspectives. Energy resilience is increasingly critical as climate extremes, grid instabilities, geopolitical shocks, and widening socioeconomic inequalities increasingly disrupt energy services. This systematic scoping review synthesises evidence across the built environment to examine how energy resilience is defined, conceptualised, and measured across technical, climatic, and equity dimensions. Following PRISMA-ScR procedures, Web of Science and Scopus were searched for studies between 2000 and 2025, yielding 167 studies supplemented by 9 foundational resilience frameworks ( n = 176). The analysis reveals three structural challenges. Only 25% of studies (44 of 176) provide operational definitions, with most using resilience as a rhetorical construct. The field utilises twenty-nine distinct building-scale indicators, including several mathematically equivalent formulations that remain unrecognised across disciplines. Most studies rely on single-building, short-term, event-based metrics, with limited attention to multi-hazard trajectories, district-scale dynamics, or equity weighting. Empirical evidence is geographically skewed toward heat-related hazards in high-income regions, with fewer than 10% of studies addressing the Global South and limited coverage of cold-climate events. Passive envelope performance emerges as the most consistent determinant of resilience across climate contexts, while efficiency-resilience trade-offs remain underexplored. This review identifies an inverse relationship between research density and climate exposure and highlights the absence of a cold-climate passive survivability standard as a critical gap. A six-step assessment framework is proposed, integrating hazard, climate, and equity dimensions to support harmonised metrics and policy development.

title: Numerical and experimental study on the thick desiccant wheel phenomenon: mechanism and occurrence conditions
Thermal captives on campus: a mixed-methods assessment of maintenance workers' heat exposure and building climate resilience during a severe heatwave
abstract: The adaptive comfort model assumes occupants can act on discomfort. We examined a population for whom it fails: campus maintenance workers without HVAC control, unable to relocate, in mandated uniforms, and working at 2.0–4.5 met, beyond the model's validated range. During a July 2025 heatwave in Daegu, South Korea (outdoor maximum 37.4 °C), we monitored thermal conditions in 23 buildings with a 52-sensor IoT network (740,804 data points) and surveyed and interviewed the 30 workers assigned to them. K-means clustering identified three building thermal types (pairwise Adjusted Rand Index 0.86–1.00). Indoor temperatures ranged from 25.5 to 31.9 °C, and 74% of buildings exceeded the CIBSE TM52 overheating threshold. Hourly indoor–outdoor regression yielded mean R 2 = 0.020: indoor temperature was largely decoupled from concurrent outdoor temperature, consistent with thermal mass retention rather than contemporaneous transmission. Minimum indoor temperatures remained above 28 °C in 8 of 13 hottest-cluster buildings, leaving no period of thermal relief in the monitored zones. The Griffiths neutral temperature (27.2 °C) was only 0.7 °C above the ASHRAE prediction, yet 22 of 30 workers (73%) claimed habituation while describing symptoms. Heat-stress symptoms followed the building thermal gradient (fatigue: 69% in the hottest cluster, 25% in the coolest), while humidity-related symptoms showed the reverse pattern. We term this structural denial of adaptive opportunity thermal captivity. For such populations, sensation-scale neutrality may not indicate physiological wellbeing, and standards relying on it alone may underestimate occupational heat risk. A vulnerability matrix identifies priority buildings where retrofit addressing heat retention may reduce this risk.

title: HISRO: an IoT-enabled occupant-centric tool for building operational performance assessment

Deep sequence learning models for hotel room air conditioner runtime estimation via ambient sensing
abstract: Hotels are among the buildings with the highest energy consumption. In most hotels, air conditioners are controlled by guests, making their operation unpredictable and largely invisible to building managers. Direct measurement of room-level air conditioner runtime requires additional infrastructure that most hotels do not have or cannot afford. This study presents a non-intrusive method to estimate air conditioner operational status using ambient temperature and humidity data collected from in-room sensors, without requiring any modification to existing building infrastructure. Unlike conventional non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) approaches that rely mainly on aggregate electrical load signatures and have been evaluated primarily in residential or office settings, this work targets hotel rooms, where AC use is guest-controlled and direct instrumentation is often limited by cost, privacy, and operational constraints. We evaluate three deep learning models (GTN, BiLSTM, and 1D CNN) across 405 configurations on a dataset of 3.3 million labelled one-minute samples collected over approximately 2300 room-days across 17 rooms within a single hotel in Melbourne, Australia. The dataset is publicly available to support future research. The best configuration, BiLSTM with combined temperature–humidity input, achieved an F1-score of 97.5% and a median daily runtime error of four minutes on the held-out evaluation room. Temperature was more informative than humidity alone, while temperature-only BiLSTM achieved a slightly lower median daily runtime error of three minutes. These findings indicate that ambient sensing combined with deep sequence learning provides a practical, low-cost approach for estimating room-level AC operation in hotels.

Calibration as Diagnosis (CaD): A proof of concept for a physics-based framework for fault detection and diagnosis in building systems
abstract: • Calibration as Diagnosis reframes model calibration as a fault detection tool. • Calibrated parameters act as physically interpretable fault indicators. • Severe outdoor airflow deficits are revealed despite compliant indoor CO 2 levels. • Method provides numerical reference for quantifying fault magnitude. Conventional fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) methods in buildings primarily rely on sensor alarms or data-driven pattern recognition, which often lack physical interpretability and although they may identify a fault, they often struggle to determine its location or underlying cause. Existing FDD and commissioning approaches typically employ calibrated white-box models as comparative references or dynamic baselines for residual monitoring. However, model calibration is treated as a preparatory step aimed at improving predictive accuracy, rather than as part of the diagnostic framework. This paper introduces Calibration as Diagnosis (CaD), a proof-of-concept framework that reframes the calibration process as an integral component of FDD. Rather than using calibration solely to improve model fidelity, CaD interprets systematic deviations in physically meaningful calibrated parameters as indicators of operational faults and building performance deficiencies. This CaD framework is demonstrated in a non-residential building conditioned by an air-based Heating, Ventilation and Air-Conditioning (HVAC) system. Four calibration formulations are tested, ranging from a single-step simplified HVAC, single-objective temperature-focused approach (Model A), to single-step simplified HVAC multi-objective thermo–energetic (Model B) and hygrothermal–energetic (Model C) approaches, and finally a two-step detailed HVAC hygrothermal–energetic formulation (Model D). Despite differences in objective functions, HVAC representation, calibration period, and predictive capability, all formulations converged towards a consistent diagnostic interpretation. The inferred ventilation shortfall exceeded 75% relative to the design requirements. Furthermore, the subsequent on-site inspection identified an architectural configuration consistent with the inferred diagnosis and representing the most plausible explanation for the inferred ventilation deficiency, revealing a building design flaw that would have been difficult to identify through conventional sensor-based diagnostics alone because the building’s low occupancy kept indoor CO 2 concentrations within recommended limits. By elevating calibration from a preprocessing task to a diagnostic observable, the proposed CaD approach offers a physics-based pathway for fault detection, commissioning and building auditing under realistic monitoring conditions. Although further validation is required, these results suggest that calibration-derived parameters can act as physically interpretable fault indicators, enabling quantitative auditing without additional airflow instrumentation.

title: Early adopters: An examination of solar PV electrified homes in Ireland
abstract: Residential solar photovoltaic (PV) is a significant contributor to sustainable energy systems. Early adopters can provide insights into its effectiveness and lessons for policymakers and grid operators. This study investigates electricity use in 59 early-adopter PV homes in Ireland, integrating household survey data with high-resolution smart meter and PV system data. The dataset enables analysis of technology adoption, load profiles and self-usage. Data standardisation was challenging due to 12 different PV data sources, 25 file formats, and seven temporal resolutions. This underscores the need for harmonised data protocols. Early adopter electrified homes differ markedly from national averages: mean annual electricity use was 9279 kWh, 2.2 times the Irish mean, and baseloads were well below the ~250 W expected from national load profiles. Fewer than 10% of households peaked in the evening (5–7 p.m.), while 53% peaked overnight, reflecting EV charging, battery operation, and tariff-driven load shifting. Average self-consumption rate (SCR, 57%) was above the 30% assumed in fuel savings calculations but below the 100% used in building energy rating assessments. In bivariate tests, battery ownership was associated with ~ + 16 pp. higher SCR while smart tariffs were associated with lower SCR and Self-Sufficiency Rate (SSR) (~ − 16 pp. and ~ 12 pp. respectively). EV ownership was linked to materially higher annual use and higher peak import, but not to higher SCR, implying sub-optimal charging alignment with PV output. The findings highlight to policymakers opportunities and risks in scaling PV adoption, particularly the importance of aligning flexible loads with renewables to maximise SCR/SSR and reduce peaks.

title: GAT-LSTM hybrid model for dynamic carbon footprint accounting in prefabricated steel structure buildings: a spatio-temporal integration perspective
Techno-economic assessment of retrofitting in-apartment propane heat pump systems in existing German multi-family buildings
abstract: Space heating (SH) and domestic hot water (DHW) in millions of existing apartments in Central Europe are still supplied by apartment-wise wall-mounted gas boilers, typically installed in kitchens, bathrooms, or small storage cabinets. Replacing these boilers with heat pumps (HPs) is essential for decarbonizing residential heat supply. However, strict spatial constraints, heterogeneous boundary conditions in existing multi-family buildings (MFBs), and the regulatory shift towards natural refrigerants mean that no one-size-fits-all solution currently exists. This study presents an integrated techno-economic assessment of retrofitting in-apartment propane HP systems in existing German MFBs. It examines how system design choices and use-case characteristics interact to determine thermal comfort, energy performance, infrastructure requirements, and economic outcomes. Multiple system variants were designed around a low-charge brine-to-water propane HP prototype and differed in heat source, hydraulic configuration, storage technology and size, and backup-heater location. Their operation was simulated using high-resolution SH and DHW load profiles for representative MFB archetypes. The results show that well-configured in-apartment propane HP systems can maintain thermal comfort across diverse use cases, but no single variant dominates all performance indicators. Direct-to-SH variants with a DHW-dedicated storage improve DHW stability and seasonal performance factors, while buffer-tank variants improve SH comfort under peak loads. Ground-source variants, where borehole installation is feasible, reduce electrical peak loads and can achieve lower life-cycle costs than air-source variants. Counterintuitively, lower SH demand, resulting from smaller apartments, envelope renovation, or more compact building geometry, reduces absolute energy costs but also lowers seasonal performance factors and increases the levelized cost of heat. The findings provide design guidance and policy-relevant evidence for scaling in-apartment propane HP retrofits across existing MFB stocks.

title: EcoCube: An IoT-driven cube for environmental awareness and human-building interaction
Passive cooling retrofits for mitigating indoor overheating in Canadian single-family housing under future extreme climates
abstract: Overheating has become an increasing concern in Canadian housing, as the current housing stock was designed for climates in which summertime overheating was not historically considered a critical design constraint. This study develops three representative single-family housing archetypes reflecting major energy-performance tiers of the Canadian housing stock, informed by national energy codes and the EnerGuide for Houses database. Using dynamic building energy simulations, a suite of scalable low-cost passive cooling retrofit strategies was evaluated under both historical and projected future climates. The analysis considered alternative natural ventilation behaviours representing both ideal conditions and constrained scenarios associated with climate change impacts or limited occupant adaptability. Results show that under free-running conditions with windows closed, operative-temperature exceedance can reach 12-15% of annual hours by the end of the century, while adaptive ventilation substantially mitigates overheating. The proposed passive strategies further reduce overheating risk by roughly 15-21%, and cooling demand by 20-40%. However, future climate warming still leads to significant risks, particularly in older housing archetypes. A mismatch of 5-13% in overheating assessment is observed between dry-bulb temperature and operative temperature metrics. These findings suggest that passive retrofits and adaptive ventilation improve thermal resilience but do not fully offset future overheating risks, highlighting the need for improved operational controls and, in some cases, mechanical cooling.

title: A novel approach to rapidly identifying, quantifying and ranking air leakage
abstract: Infiltration can account for a significant proportion of domestic space heating demand. Therefore, identifying, quantifying and reducing air leakage is crucial if the energy and carbon performance of dwellings is to be improved. Although methods are available that can be used to identify areas of air leakage, such as anemometers, infrared thermography and smoke pencils, they often require the building envelope to be complete, require sufficient air movement, pressure and/or a temperature differential to be deployed and they are often only capable of providing a qualitative measure of air leakage. In recent years, acoustic methods have emerged as a possible alternative to the conventional methods. Acoustic methods are unaffected by environmental conditions, do not require the building envelope to be complete and can provide a quantitative measure of air leakage. This paper comparatively evaluates the performance of a novel hand-held ultrasonic device that has the potential to rapidly identify, quantify and rank specific areas of air leakage. Comparative tests were undertaken with existing technologies on a range of direct and indirect leakage holes of known size and area within a controlled environment. Given the specific conditions associated with the test environment, the tests found the novel ultrasonic device can be used in parallel with the existing technologies to provide an important complementary role; that is detecting and quantifying specific leaks within an area that is suspected to contribute significantly to the air permeability of the envelope. For direct air leakage holes, the results obtained from the novel ultrasonic device closely matched the true air leakage area. For the indirect air leakage areas, the novel ultrasonic device was able to rank the relative severity of the leaks. These measurements were achieved independent of air movement, pressure or a temperature differential.

title: Thermoelectric brick with carbon nanotube-enhanced mortar and encapsulated phase-change material for bidirectional façade energy harvesting

A simulation-based operational thermal resilience framework for intermittently occupied high-density spaces: development and application to Gulf mosque prayer halls
abstract: Rapid congregation surges in Gulf mosque prayer halls create transient sensible and latent loads that fixed-setpoint, steady-state assessments do not express as an operational thermal capacity. This study develops a simulation-based thermal-resilience framework that combines congregation-weighted Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) comfort zones with a reduced-order heat-and-moisture model and introduces the normalized Comfort Capacity Index (CCI*). CCI* quantifies, within the model, the maximum additional congregation that can be accommodated during a specified interval before the warm-side PMV or humidity-ratio limit is exceeded. Two comfort criteria were considered: a Standard zone, defined by |PMV| ≤ 0.5, and a Relaxed zone, defined by |PMV| ≤ 0.7. The model was evaluated under four operating cases: zero load removal, instantaneous design-balanced air delivery, first-order HVAC response, and first-order response with occupied-period infiltration. At 55% relative humidity, the Standard-zone upper boundary was approximately 23.5 °C, indicating that an initial condition of 24 °C provides essentially no thermal reserve. Pre-cooling to 22 °C substantially increased the number of worshippers that could be accommodated before comfort failure. Active HVAC response increased this capacity further, whereas delayed response and outdoor-air infiltration reduced it markedly. A prescribed fan-assisted air-speed scenario also improved comfort under warm, humid peak-occupancy conditions. Clothing composition and short periods of elevated activity produced additional reductions in thermal reserve. Published mosque measurements supported the adopted parameter ranges and transient timescale, although they did not permit calibration of absolute CCI* values. The resulting capacities therefore represent conditional thermal-simulation outputs rather than field-validated or code-compliant occupancy limits. The framework supports prayer-schedule-linked pre-cooling, timely HVAC ramp-up, and controlled air movement in spaces with short and predictable occupancy surges.

Optimizing multi-layer/multi-physics passive adaptive thermal enclosures for climate-responsive energy regulation: a numerical study
abstract: Adaptive facades regulate heat transfer by adjusting their thermal behavior in response to environmental conditions. Passive adaptive systems, including stimuli-responsive thermal storage materials, tunable radiative coatings, and variable-conductivity layers, offer significant potential for material-based thermal regulation. However, their combined potential remains unexplored, as most studies examine individual mechanisms in isolation. As a result, trade-offs among energy savings, material usage, design complexity, and climate responsiveness are often underrepresented, overlooking coupled interactions in multilayer assemblies limiting their effectiveness. This study develops a transient three-dimensional numerical framework coupling heat transfer with multi-objective optimization to evaluate trade-offs between minimizing annual energy consumption and enclosure thickness. Three configurations, semi-static, passive adaptive with realistic limits, and passive adaptive with ideal limits, were evaluated using two heat-storage materials across three climates (Phoenix, Baltimore, Fairbanks) and two applications, benchmarked against a static enclosure. Relative to the static enclosure, passive adaptive configurations reduced annual heat gain and heat loss by: 44.4–81.4% and 47.9–80.1%, under ideal limits, and 19.1–49.1% and 30–70%, under realistic limits. Optimal wall thickness decreased from 16.6 cm to 4–7.1 cm (ideal) and 9.5–10.8 cm (realistic). Near-optimal performance is attained within semi-static and realistic ranges, while ideal-limit configurations define upper bounds for theoretical future development. Results reveal climate-dependent roles: thermal storage is most effective in cold and moderate climates, radiative modulation dominates in hot climates, and tunable conductivity benefits all conditions. The proposed-framework establishes quantitative design guidelines for climate-responsive multilayer material-enabled enclosures, supporting material selection and system design for thermal management.

title: Passive cooling strategies for improving indoor thermal comfort of tropical school buildings
Data driven appliance identification for residential demand response
abstract: Residential smart meter data can provide insights into appliance usage patterns, peak demand, time of use (ToU) behavior for demand response (DR),demand side management (DSM), and load forecasting applications. However, appliance identification from low frequency smart meter data remainschallenging due to overlapping appliance operations, sparse ON/OFF events,and poor generalization across heterogeneous households. This paper proposes a two step appliance identification framework for high power flexibleapplainces such as air conditioners (AC), electric vehicles (EV), and dryers(DY) using aggregate smart meter data, appliance ownership information,and ambient temperature. Step I introduces a household adaptive eventdetection method based on k means clustering to derive appliance specificthresholds from limited historical measurements. Step II presents a temperature dependent synthetic dataset generation methodology for AC, EV, andDYtomodel appliance operating behavior under varying ambient conditions.Statistical and temporal features are extracted to train ownership awaresupport vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), XGBoost, LSTM andCaTBoost models. Evaluation on 24 households from the PECAN datasetachieves average F1 scores of 0.71, 0.58, and 0.76 for AC, DY, and EV appliances, respectively, with corresponding NMSE values of 0.40, 0.67, and 0.35.The proposed framework achieves disaggregation accuracy ranging from 0.65to 0.86 and demonstrates effective generalization across diverse householdconditions, particularly for temperature dependent AC loads.

Towards a pathway for residential sector decarbonization in Brazil
abstract: Energy use in the residential sector is a major issue in energy transition worldwide. The decarbonization of this sector is an important challenge to be addressed in terms of achieving sustainability today and in the future. This study presents a conceptual model to decarbonize the energy consumption in the residential sector in Brazil. Prior to the proposition, a comprehensive analysis of energy consumption dynamics in the Brazilian residential sector was presented. Using national datasets, the research maps energy consumption trends across states and income classes. Social energy indicators, such as per capita electricity consumption and Energy Gini Index, are used to monitor disparities across country territory and over time. Building on these insights, we proposed a conceptual decarbonization pathway based on theory of change and structured in four interrelated action pillars: Socially Oriented Energy Efficiency education, Performance Compliance with Minimum Energy Performance Standards (MEPS), Equitable Electrification, expansion of renewable energy. These strategies are supported by a governance and data infrastructure framework. The pathway aims to reduce carbon emissions, promote energy justice, and enhance resilience in the context of increasing climate extremes, especially in the Global South.

Air bypass in air source heat pump outdoor units: characterization and quantification
abstract: Air source heat pumps (ASHPs) are increasingly adopted for building heating and cooling due to their low carbon emissions. However, their delivered energy use is often higher than expected. This study investigated air bypass around the outdoor heat exchanger as a previously unexamined factor affecting ASHP outdoor unit performance. Field experiments were conducted on four heat pump models from different manufacturers to identify, characterize, and quantify air bypass pathways. Six additional units from other manufacturers were examined to measure the size of their air bypass locations. All ten units exhibited substantial air bypass, indicating that this issue is widespread across manufacturers. Air bypass on the four primary tested heat pumps was measured using two approaches: direct airflow measurements and an indirect area–pressure (orifice flow) method based on fluid dynamics. Directly measured bypass airflow ranged from 4.5% to 7.1% of rated airflow across the four primary tested units, while the orifice-based estimates ranged from 5.7% to 10.9%. Sequential air sealing experiments demonstrated that targeted sealing interventions could reduce measured bypass airflow by 43%–87%. Units with large, unsealed gaps at coil perimeters showed the greatest improvements. The reproducibility of results was evaluated by performing air bypass quantification using direct air bypass measurements on two pairs of identical heat pump outdoor units; within-pair agreement was 0.4 percentage points for one pair and 1.8 percentage points for the other pair. Project findings indicate that air bypass is a measurable and reproducible phenomenon, but that modest design improvements can significantly reduce the problem as a way to enhance capacity and efficiency.

CFD-RSM-based multi-objective optimization of supply-air conditions in a hospital oncology pharmaceutical cleanroom
authors: Manoel Antonio da Fonseca Costa Filho
abstract: This study presents a multiobjective optimization framework for thermal–energy performance and indoor air quality in an ISO 7 hospital pharmaceutical cleanroom used for chemotherapy drug preparation through the integration of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), Box–Behnken Design (BBD), Response Surface Methodology (RSM), and hybrid AHP–Entropy weighting. The validated CFD model was used to evaluate four performance indicators: thermal comfort at the workstation, breathing-zone contaminant exposure, contaminant removal efficiency, and ventilation energy utilization. A baseline operational domain, representative of the actual operating condition of the facility, and an initial target domain, based on recommended hygrothermal control ranges, were first analyzed to identify the main performance trends. The initial target domain indicated a boundary-seeking improvement direction, motivating the definition of a shifted target domain centered on the most promising operating region. In this shifted domain, a Box–Behnken design with 15 CFD simulations was employed to fit a quadratic response surface model for the global multicriteria score. The fitted model was statistically significant (p = 0.0023), with R2 = 0.9721 and adjusted R2 = 0.9219, indicating strong explanatory capability. The response surfaces of the global score revealed a robust compromise region within the shifted domain, with a representative operational optimum around vin = 0.33 m/s, Tin = 290.9 K, and w = 0.0050 kg/kg. This region was consistent with the best-performing Box–Behnken cases and was confirmed through additional CFD simulations, supporting its interpretation as a stable high-performance operating range rather than as a single extrapolated optimum. The results demonstrate that shifting the operational domain can transform an initially boundary-driven optimization problem into a robust multicriteria design region, providing quantitative support for retrofit-oriented hygrothermal control strategies in critical hospital cleanrooms.

title: Experimental characterization of the energy performance of an heat harvesting window integrating an air to PCM latent heat exchanger
abstract: Adaptive building envelopes can enhance building energy performance by dynamically managing ventilation, solar control, and thermal storage. This paper presents the experimental evaluation of a Heat Harvesting Window (HHW), that combines a ventilated triple glazing unit with an Air to Phase Change Material Heat Exchanger (a-PCM HEX) positioned at the cavity outlet. Unlike conventional windows or Double Skin Facades, which restrict fresh air supply in Outdoor Air Curtain (OAC) or Thermal Buffer (TB) modes, or cause overheating in Supply Air mode, the HHW continuously delivers fresh air at temperature closer to thermal comfort range, by exploiting the latent heat storage. In winter Supply Air mode, median pre-heating efficiency reached 0.7–0.8 and daily heat losses were reduced by up to 90% compared with the references, mainly by lowering ventilation heat losses. In mid-season Thermal Buffer mode, the cavity efficiency exceeded unity for nearly 40% of daytime hours, indicating frequent net heat gains from passive solar buffering. In summer Outdoor Air Curtain mode, dynamic insulation efficiency was positive for over 90% of the monitored period, with an average value of 0.75, and the HHW reduced daily heat gains by more than 40%. The a-PCM HEX provided additional air-temperature moderation, including early daytime pre-cooling of about 4 °C under peak summer conditions. The study demonstrates the potential of integrating ventilated façades with latent heat storage to develop climate-responsive envelope systems capable of ensuring continuous fresh air supply and improved thermal performance.

title: Multi-objective optimization of sinusoidal impinging jet ventilation under medium-to-high cooling loads using a hybrid CFD-machine learning approach
Agentic building energy management systems: adoption and design insights from surveys and interviews with building operators
Neural network-assisted unscented Kalman filtering with unknown inputs for joint parameter identification and temperature prediction in RC thermal models
Physics-informed RC–MLP modelling for building thermal prediction
abstract: Reliable multi-horizon building thermal prediction is essential for energy-efficient HVAC operation, model predictive control, and demand response, yet existing models often face trade-offs among physical interpretability, data efficiency, and predictive accuracy. This study develops a physics-informed RC–MLP modelling framework for single-zone indoor temperature prediction using a publicly available high-resolution operational dataset from real office spaces. A 4R3C resistance–capacitance model was first selected as the grey-box thermal baseline by comparing candidate RC structures using both prediction accuracy and physical parameter plausibility. A residual multi-layer perceptron was then trained to correct systematic RC prediction errors using horizon-specific features derived from thermal history, solar forcing, time-of-day variables, and operational indicators. The framework was evaluated at prediction horizons of 5, 30, 60, 180, and 360 min under standard, seasonal shift, and limited-data conditions. Results show that prediction accuracy alone was insufficient for RC structure selection, as candidate models produced similar RMSE values while only the 4R3C structure satisfied all plausibility checks. Residual analysis revealed autocorrelated, diurnal, and solar-driven error structures. On the standard split, the RC–MLP model reduced RMSE by 4.4% at 30 min and 21.3% at 360 min relative to the RC baseline. Under seasonal shift, it retained a 16.8% improvement at 360 min, whereas limited-data experiments showed that mismatched residual calibration could degrade performance. These findings demonstrate that physically plausible RC models provide robust baseline predictions, while residual MLP correction is most effective when calibration data are representative of deployment conditions.

title: From local suitability to global applicability: An integrated experimental-numerical investigation of climate-responsive hygrothermal performance of a novel straw bale wall
abstract: Achieving balance between thermal performance and moisture resistance remains a major challenge in building envelope design. Prior study on a novel straw bale wall, composed exclusively of bio-based and geo-sourced materials, demonstrated its long-term durability in temperate oceanic climate. However, a comprehensive evaluation of its hygrothermal performance remains mandatory to ensure its applicability beyond specific climatic conditions. In this study, an extensive investigation on the hygrothermal performance of this novel assembly is conducted using an integrated experimental and numerical approach. The wall assembly composition was introduced along with the in-situ experimental conditions and monitoring framework. The results of this campaign enabled the calibration and validation of a WUFI 2D® model, thus virtually reproducing the wall's behavior under identical environmental conditions. To further extend the analysis, the validated numerical model was adopted to perform simulations under a wider range of global representative climates. Subsequently, several assessment criteria were selected to quantify the wall's thermal efficiency, moisture levels and guaranteeing the absence of any risk of mold growth using WUFI®Bio bio-hygrothermal model. The results demonstrate that the wall meets the requirements in the majority of environmental scenarios, exhibiting high hygrothermal performance while ensuring occupant's comfort. Nevertheless, in critical climates where the wall did not meet the criteria, design modifications incorporating ecological materials were implemented to improve its behavior and mitigates risks. Overall, the findings highlight the reliable applicability of the novel straw bale wall in 17 climates and its modified version in 6 harsh climatic contexts.

title: Modeling buildings load flexibility potential in the United States
abstract: Electricity demand is expected to grow at an unprecedented rate in the United States, possibly resulting in significant increases in system costs to serve the load. The buildings sector, consisting of residential and commercial buildings, consumes nearly three-quarters of the total U.S. electricity and thus flexible building demand could potentially be a large resource for a growing electricity system. Several regional and national-level analyses that have demonstrated the capabilities of buildings to provide flexible resources are mostly influenced by the average performance parameters from existing demand response programs; therefore, they likely do not account for the full capabilities of buildings. Further, these studies do not incorporate variations in the need and availability of flexible resources across different demand futures. In this study, we demonstrate a methodology to model load shed and shift technical potential of a subset of flexibility measures whose performance is characterized purely based on the response capabilities of buildings. We assess and compare the flexibility resource potential across four demand scenarios and three snapshot years - 2030, 2040, and 2050, across the contiguous US. The results from this study indicate that the building flexibility measures could provide significant grid benefits by reducing seasonal peaks by over 30% in some scenarios. They also show that the relative importance of these resources to power systems could vary over time and by demand future. These findings could encourage greater consideration and utilization of demand-side building flexibility in power systems planning and operations.

title: Multi-objective optimization of aluminium and plastic rotary heat exchangers for energy-efficient ventilation systems
Adaptive window opening optimization of multi-scenario classrooms using CFD and FNN surrogate model
Assessing building-integrated bioremediation infrastructure within the context of unsustainable rising atmospheric CO2
abstract: Atmospheric CO 2 concentrations are projected to increase from current concentrations (420 ppm) to 670–936 ppm within the next 50 years. While not acutely toxic, emerging evidence raises concern that continuous, chronic exposure within this range may contribute to significant negative health outcomes, including systemic inflammation, bone demineralization, and oxidative stress. This trend is particularly concerning for urban residents, who spend 90% of their time indoors where CO 2 regularly exceeds 700–1000 ppm and pollutant levels are 2 to 10 times higher than outdoors. Most contemporary heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems reduce indoor CO 2 concentrations by increasing exchange with outdoor air, leaving indoor occupants increasingly exposed as atmospheric conditions deteriorate. This study investigates the potential for biogenic systems to decouple indoor CO 2 levels from outdoor conditions through the incorporation of bioremediative metabolisms into building infrastructure. Quantification of performance across design parameters produced scalable remediation models, shown to be viable for a range of real building conditions. We calculated a 43-fold improvement in module-scale CO 2 remediation capacity across common operational parameters, such as airflow orientation and light intensity, that could be modulated to meet the customized requirements of building occupancy, patterns of use, and building systems integration. Architectural, HVAC, and CFD modeling demonstrated that a range of scales and spatial configurations of bioremediation systems within the evaluated conditions may reduce indoor CO 2 levels below outdoor baselines, while delivering psychological and biophysical co-benefits, including biophilia and microbiome diversification. These findings provide a quantitative framework for integrating living systems into building-scale air quality management, illustrating a pathway toward adaptive, multifunctional infrastructure capable of improving human exposures as climate change reshapes atmospheric conditions.

title: A hybrid of genetic algorithm and differential evolution for the chiller plant operation planning
An integrated performance assessment of modular residential buildings: Systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Modular residential buildings (MRBs) are gaining attention as a solution to the housing shortfall crisis. While MRB research is growing rapidly, its environmental performance has not yet been systematically synthesised with recent empirical data. To address this gap, this study conducted a semi-automated systematic literature review and meta-analysis to synthesise state-of-the-art research findings. The review identified three main themes within MRB's environmental performance: GHG emissions reduction, energy efficiency and Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ). Qualitative analysis indicates that research primarily focuses on the upfront emissions, with material embodied emissions, factory-based emissions, and transportation distances as highly sensitive parameters. The meta-analysis shows that reported upfront GHG emissions for MRBs range from 73 to 900 kgCO₂e/m 2 , with timber-based systems having lower emissions than steel- or container systems. Modular houses are more likely to meet the 2030 Science-Based Targets initiative (SBTi) benchmarks than modular apartments; however, substantial reductions in both typologies are necessary to reach the 2050 SBTi targets. Synthesised evidence indicates that construction quality, envelope materials, and climate conditions influence both energy efficiency and IEQ. The review identifies three gaps: limited data on in-use, operational, and end-of-life GHG emissions; insufficient evidence to distinguish energy-efficiency and IEQ performance from that of conventional housing; and limited integrated performance assessments despite their necessity. Finally, this study proposes an integrated performance assessment framework to evaluate outcomes across low-carbon, energy-efficient, comfortable, affordable, and climate-resilient dimensions. Findings show that MRBs are a high-performance housing option, but real-world performance assessments at the building and stock levels are vital for justification.

title: ASHRAE 169 climate zone mapping of Türkiye: a provincial-level classification and comparative validation against the Köppen-Geiger system
Long-term comparative analysis and experimental validation of bifacial gain in rooftop PV systems under real operating conditions in Southern Brazil
abstract: The advancement of photovoltaic (PV) technologies has intensified efforts to improve efficiency and optimize energy utilization. This study presents a long-term comparative assessment of bifacial (bPV) and monofacial (mPV) monocrystalline silicon PV systems based on real operational data collected over 24 months. Both systems were installed parallel to a metallic rooftop in southern Brazil, allowing the evaluation of energy generation, final yield, bifacial gain (BG), and implications for electrical design. The average energy yield was 116.88 kWh/kWp for the bPV system and 109.76 kWh/kWp for the mPV system, with the bPV configuration achieving a 7.46% higher monthly average energy yield. The monthly median BG ranged from 6.53% to 7.64%, with greater dispersion observed between May and July. Analysis based on the clearness index (Kt) indicated an average BG of 7.77% on sunny days, 7.22% on intermediate days, and 6.35% on cloudy days. The bifacial PV system exhibited a substantially higher frequency of overpower events than the monofacial PV system, particularly during the summer, emphasizing the need to account for bifacial gain in inverter sizing. A low correlation between daily irradiance and BG suggests that rear-side contribution is not directly proportional to global irradiance. Low standard error values (<1%), similar RMSE across classifications, and coefficients of variation between 12.69% and 16.03% confirm the robustness of the experimental dataset. The consistent energy gains observed in rooftop-parallel bifacial systems influence peak power behavior and DC energy production, with direct implications for inverter sizing and DC/AC ratio definition. These results provide long-term real-world evidence to support safer operation and more accurate electrical design of rooftop-integrated bifacial PV systems.

title: Energy poverty, health and social well-being: empirical evidence from Greece
Building energy forecast routing for grid-responsive BEMS: Selective conformal screening under operational uncertainty
abstract: Grid-responsive building energy management systems (BEMS) use short-horizon load forecasts for schedule confirmation, anomaly screening, demand-response preparation, and peak-alert triage, yet forecast reports rarely indicate whether a building-hour prediction is reliable enough for automation. We evaluate selective conformal forecasting as a reliability-routing layer, not a new point-forecast model. A residual LightGBM backbone supplies forecast centers and residual scales; split conformal intervals and a calibration-fixed score from residual scale, lag disagreement, and historical group risk route low-risk forecasts to automation and high-risk forecasts to wider intervals, fallback, review, or logging. On 1,104 Building Data Genome Project 2 (BDG2) buildings from 16 sites, routing about 30% of the highest-risk 1-step forecasts away from automation gives 89.81% retained coverage; retained interval width, mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean squared error (RMSE) decrease by 57.64%, 60.72%, and 79.13% versus no abstention. The same setting gives 89.92% retained day-ahead coverage and 91.75% on the related ASHRAE Great Energy Predictor III (GEPIII) labeled-year benchmark with 1,230 buildings. Random review, held-site transfer, building-normalized metrics, weather-noise checks, event attribution, fallback diagnostics, and backbone screens indicate that the retained region is not arbitrary sample deletion. In shadow-mode peak-alert triage, high-error automated alerts fall from 11.02% to 1.96%, while random review leaves 11.01%. The result is bounded, retrospective evidence that calibrated uncertainty can support auditable BEMS routing while separating all-test conformal coverage from retained-sample operating reliability.

title: HeatShift-HP: A Techno-Economic framework for assessing heat pump load shifting under dynamic tariffs and grid fees
abstract: Rapid growth of electric demand combined with increased penetration of intermittent power sources increases the value of flexible electric heating, but the techno-economic role of central hot-water storage under realistic tariffs remains unclear. This paper introduces HeatShift-HP , an open-source Python/Modelica co-simulation workflow. The framework couples a generic air-to-water heat pump and a stratified storage tank Functional Mock-up Unit with a supervisory rule-based controller and time series of weather, heating load, and end-user electricity prices. The framework targets plant-side flexibility and varies specific tank volume, nominal supply and return temperatures, heat-pump sizing, controller settings, and tariff variants, including a price-responsive boosting strategy constrained by a cost-neutral coefficient of performance approximation. The workflow is applied to a single-family reference building in Berlin and Chicago using 2025 weather and hourly retail prices with and without dynamic grid-fee components. A theoretical pre-analysis shows that typical hot-water buffers provide only limited stand-alone autonomy compared with building thermal mass. Annual simulations show that nominal system temperature is the dominant driver of both seasonal performance and paid heat costs. Lowering the nominal supply temperature from 40 ∘ C to 35 ∘ C reduces the median paid specific heat cost by about 3.7 % in Berlin and 4.4 % in Chicago for the standard controller, with similarly strong reductions under price-based control. By contrast, additional storage mainly improves operational flexibility by reducing cycling and increasing low-price heat generation. The pooled effect of price-based control remains below 1 % in both cities, but matched Berlin dynamic-grid cases show savings of up to 4.0 %. Dynamic grid fees in Berlin reduce median paid heat costs by about 7.0 % to 7.6 % relative to the fixed-grid tariff. The results show that low-temperature system design minimises absolute heat costs, whereas the incremental value of price-based control depends primarily on sufficient storage, moderate control actions, and retail tariffs with sufficiently strong temporal price variation.

title: Component-wise similarity analysis and component-level transfer learning for building energy consumption prediction
Impacts of residential block morphology and microclimate on operational carbon emissions: evidence from Xi'an, China
