A closed-loop integration framework for grid-interactive residential buildings: Automated modeling, EMS-based control, and flexible regulation optimization
Experimental and numerical investigation of the thermal performance of a cascaded latent heat thermal energy storage unit for solar fresh air preheating in severe cold regions
Computationally efficient and accurate stratified electric water heater model for aggregated demand response
A predictive rule-based control strategy for integrated building energy systems with photovoltaic, heat pump, thermal tank and electric vehicles
Reinforcement learning for data center cooling performance optimization: A systematic review and gap analysis for deployment in tropical wet climates
Hierarchical physics-guided graph attention network for interpretable fault diagnosis of variable refrigerant flow systems
Bridging the digitalization gap in nZEB renovation: a systemic barrier assessment framework for smart deep energy retrofits
abstract: The integration of smart technologies in deep nZEB renovation projects is often hindered by systemic barriers that limit the achievement of expected operational performance. While buildings may comply with energy requirements at the design stage, they frequently underperform in terms of adaptive control, data-driven optimization, and interoperability. This discrepancy is conceptualized as a digitalization gap—a lifecycle-accumulated divergence between intended smart readiness and realized digital capability. This study addresses the identified research gap by proposing a Systemic Digitalization Gap Propagation Model (SDGPM) combined with a Digitalization Gap Index (DGI). The objective is to develop a framework that captures how digitalization barriers emerge, propagate across lifecycle phases, and accumulate into measurable performance constraints, and to assess its applicability through exploratory validation. The methodology integrates lifecycle-based barrier mapping, root-barrier identification, and expert-based multi-criteria assessment. The framework was applied to a typical public building, identifying 64 barriers, including 7 root barriers that generate 57 derived and emergent constraints. Results show that derived barriers dominate the system (70%), suggesting strong cross-phase propagation effects. Root barriers—particularly those related to data governance, digital architecture planning, and organizational competence—exhibit the highest systemic influence. Exploratory validation through two public buildings renovation case studies demonstrated a 27–32% reduction in the digitalization gap and provided preliminary evidence that early-stage digital planning and organizational capacity significantly decrease the number of root barriers and mitigate barrier propagation. A sensitivity analysis further demonstrated that the principal conclusions of the proposed framework remain robust under alternative Barrier Severity Score (BSS) weighting schemes. The proposed framework provides a replicable approach for assessing digitalization gaps and supports the transition from nZEB compliance toward digitally enabled, high-performance, and environmentally optimized buildings.

title: A nonparametric least squares method for flexible modeling and benchmarking of energy performance in school buildings
Phase change materials for passive thermal regulation in energy-efficient buildings: A comprehensive review of building envelope applications
Spatially heterogeneous impacts of 2D/3D urban form on thermal comfort: insights from urban functional zones
Toward heat mitigation II: Effect of rooftop photovoltaics on summertime near-surface air temperature and building cooling energy demand across local climate zones
Uncertainty of retrofitting scenarios in France based on building ages due to energy performance gap
abstract: France has progressively updated its building energy regulations (RT1974, RT1982, RT2005) to improve residential energy efficiency, targeting cumulative reductions of 25%, 20%, and 15% over previous standards. However, it remains unclear whether these norms have effectively delivered thermal performance improvements, particularly in the context of large-scale renovation. In this study, we develop a data-driven temperature sensitivity model to estimate heating consumption across construction periods and regions, using aggregated actual electricity data. These empirical estimates are compared to theoretical heating demand derived from Energy Performance Certificates (EPC), enabling the identification of energy performance gaps (EPG) and the projection of retrofit benefits. Our results show that in most regions, the implementation of thermal norms has not led to the expected reductions in temperature sensitivity. EPCs tend to overestimate energy demand, especially for newer buildings. While EPC-based retrofit scenarios suggest up to 60% savings, our model indicates that more than 30% of buildings could experience increased consumption after retrofit. These discrepancies are particularly pronounced for post-2006 buildings and low-income housing segments. The findings highlight the limitations of EPC-based retrofit projections and emphasize the need to incorporate behavioral and socio-economic factors into energy policy assessments. Accurate, behavior-sensitive models are essential to realistically estimate retrofit potential and support France’s progress toward its net-zero target.

title: Decoupling natural ventilation and traffic noise in railway-adjacent dwellings: Field measurements and passive design strategies
UAV-informed envelope diagnosis and proof-of-concept case study for existing cold-region residential buildings
Tariff-resilient campus energy transition in Nigeria: Standards-based auditing, retrofit optimisation, and PV–battery techno-economic analysis
Towards smart HVAC systems in airport terminals: LSTM-based predictive control for improved control performance
Comparative life cycle assessment of aggregates produced from industrial by-products and construction and demolition waste
Time-series reconstruction of faulty measurements for one-dimensional hygrothermal transfer in building envelopes
Scalable HVAC flexibility aggregation with DRL and linear programming
abstract: Large-scale HVAC demand response can provide grid flexibility, but market participation requires fast aggregate allocation, device-level feasibility and protection of occupant comfort. Although recent research has advanced building-flexibility assessment, learning-based control and distributed service provision, evidence is still limited for allocating a post-clearing dispatch request across many lower-level HVAC aggregators while accounting for accumulated thermal comfort burden. Here we develop a hierarchical aggregation framework in which a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) allocator assigns market-requested flexibility among resource aggregators using both current conditions and accumulated comfort impact. Local linear programming (LP) controllers then schedule HVAC operation under comfort and power constraints. The framework is evaluated for supply-demand adjustment requests defined by flexibility magnitude, direction, response-time tolerance and continuous delivery period. Compared with a centralised LP benchmark and a rule-based Greedy+LP baseline, the proposed DRL+LP framework reduces computation from more than 1,000 to a few seconds at large scale. At the 3,600-room scale, it assigns requests up to 0.792 MW for three hours and keeps aggregate assigned requests within a ± 10% tolerance in nearly all reported extraction intervals. Its comfort-violation metrics remain close to the centralised LP reference, with absolute differences no larger than 0.052 ∘ C in mean absolute error (MAE) and 0.045 ∘ C 2 in mean squared error (MSE) in the reported cases. It also avoids the uneven comfort burden observed in greedy allocation under low-flexibility requests. In an unseen two-request daily scenario, the learned policy maintains request allocation within tolerance and median comfort deviations of approximately 0.04–0.05 ∘ C. These results establish a scalable and comfort-aware allocation approach within the simulated market-dispatch and continuously modulatable HVAC setting considered here. Evidence remains limited to a single calibrated room model, cooling operation and one climatic region; performance under heating, heterogeneous buildings, diverse occupancy and field communication or model uncertainty has not yet been established.

title: Retraction notice to “Region-specific climate change projections: Forecasting energy needs in Finland's residential building stock” [Energy Build. 329 (2025) 115181]
Grounding agentic AI in building semantics: From information retrieval to automated simulation
abstract: Building intelligence remains limited by fragmented data, labor-intensive semantic modeling, and AI interfaces that lack grounding in verifiable building facts. This study presents an Agentic AI framework that combines a simplified semantic modeling approach, termed KebGraph, with large language model (LLM)-based AI agents. The framework enables end-to-end workflows from natural language instructions to engineering services. KebGraph organizes heterogeneous building context into a queryable semantic layer, while a multi-agent architecture maps user requests to concrete engineering actions through tool execution. Evaluated on a real office building, the framework is tested across four large language models on a 213-question benchmark. Grounding on KebGraph attains the highest factual question-answering accuracy of the compared representations, ahead of a conventional Brick model and a raw-document baseline, while using the fewest input tokens among the grounded representations. In an agentic function-calling evaluation, it also achieves the highest average argument-formation score across the evaluated models. On invalid or adversarial requests, the capable models largely decline or ask for clarification rather than retrieving fabricated data. An indoor thermal modeling workflow further demonstrates agent-driven construction, calibration, and evaluation of thermal models end to end over a one-month winter period. These results indicate that grounding LLM agents in a lightweight building semantic layer improves the accuracy, efficiency, and reliability of information retrieval and tool use on this building, while broader generalization across buildings and seasons remains future work.

title: A triple-mode VO2/hydrogel multilayer smart window for balancing daylighting and building energy performance
A multi-criteria life-cycle analysis for sustainable residential construction in India: Sustainability map and sustainability index development
Modelling cognitive decline under sustained mental workload in thermoneutral indoor environments using heart rate variability indices
Development of a mixing box-based ERV structure and an intelligent multi-objective control algorithm for indoor thermal load reduction
A novel methodology to generate stochastic and heterogeneous urban occupancy profiles from time use survey data
abstract: Energy modelling of the built environment plays a central role in supporting decarbonisation strategies and sustainable urban planning. However, in this context, the representation of occupancy remains a major source of uncertainty, as deterministic and standardised schedules are still widely adopted despite their limited ability to capture behavioural heterogeneity and temporal variability. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a novel, reproducible methodological framework for generating stochastic, heterogeneous urban occupancy profiles from open-access Time Use Survey (TUS) data. The framework operates at the individual level and integrates three components: (i) unsupervised clustering of daily activity-location diaries to identify population-representative occupancy patterns; (ii) a time-inhomogeneous first-order Markov Chain model to generate synthetic, time-resolved occupancy profiles consistent with observed transition dynamics; and (iii) a systematic allocation and normalisation procedure to convert person-based profiles into space-based schedules compatible with existing building and urban energy simulation tools. The approach explicitly incorporates socio-demographic differentiation and reconstructs daily presence across residential, non-residential, transport, and outdoor domains, enabling a context-sensitive representation of population dynamics. The methodology is demonstrated using the last available Italian TUS. Compared with normative deterministic schedules, the generated stochastic schedules introduce variability across both days and buildings of the same typology, capturing non-zero weekend occupancy in offices and building-specific peak densities driven by synthetic population allocation. By relying exclusively on publicly available survey and demographic data, the proposed framework offers a transparent, transferable, and scalable solution for improving occupancy representation in building and urban energy simulations, thereby supporting statistically grounded and context-aware energy analyses. Moreover, it has strong potential for replicability and scalability.

title: Editorial Board
Review of energy systems components for exploring model predictive control in energy management systems for multiple community levels
abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) is increasingly applied in energy management systems (EMS), where performance depends on the models and forecasts of the system components. Previous reviews address microgrid definitions, topologies, and control structures rather than these component models. This review paper compares 97 EMS-based MPC works on models, uncertainty, costs, and operational modes of consumption, production, and storage at building, district, and community levels. Distinguishing levels by internal energy exchange rather than by the number of buildings shows that aggregated communities of up to 7045 houses reduce to a single balance, so reported level and modeling structure frequently differ. The component models are level-invariant, and only the time resolution, the aggregation, and the exchange variables change with the level. In most works the forecast uncertainty is emulated by imposing an unjustified deviation of 2 to 30 %, several of these values exceeding the reported accuracy of 6 to 25 % MAPE. The share of demand treated as flexible ranges from 7.7 to 40 % and is expressed against the total, base, original, or critical demand, making it not directly comparable. Storage and generator operating ranges and tariff ratios are consistent, with utility grid flat and valley prices 39 and 61 % below the peak price. Within the MPC problem, states originate from the storage, thermal, and controllable component models, while critical demand and RES generation enter only as disturbances, so component modeling sets the state dimension and the number of binary variables. Comparison criteria and open requirements are derived to guide the selection of component models in EMS-based MPC design. The results are addressed to system engineers and developers of EMS-based MPC for buildings, districts, and communities, and indicate which modeling detail is required at a given level, which parameters can be adopted from the literature, and which assumptions have to be justified.

title: Cross-device small-sample one-class fault detection for ground-source heat pump systems via manifold-constrained sample augmentation
Sleep-state-aware model predictive control for cooling-dominated residential bedrooms: closed-loop energy–IEQ–low-disturbance trade-offs
Energy and environmental implications of thermal bridge reduction in the knee wall area
abstract: In order to reduce energy demand in buildings, it is necessary to improve the thermal performance of building envelopes, with particular attention to their junctions, which may affect both heat losses and internal surface conditions. At the same time, thermal bridge mitigation reduces operational energy use and the associated operational CO₂ emissions, while the additional insulation introduces an embodied carbon burden that should also be considered when assessing the carbon performance of the retrofit.. This study assessed the effect of applying a thermal insulation strip in the knee wall area of an unheated attic on heating-energy demand and operational CO₂ emissions, while also comparing the embodied carbon of the analysed insulation variants.. The steady-state thermal bridge calculations were combined with an assessment of the embodied carbon footprint based on the EPDs within the A1–A3 range. A 2D model of the junction was used in order to compare the energy impact and calculate carbon payback, while a 3D model was used to assess local surface temperature minima. The impact of Ψ parameter was converted into annual energy savings, operational CO 2 emissions and carbon payback time, with adopted operational and emission assumptions. Under the adopted climatic and operational scenarios, the estimated annual energy savings ranged from 176 to 236 kWh for the analysed building. Despite a similar thermal effect, the carbon payback time differed significantly and ranged from 7.31 to 11.02 years for the wood fibre strips and from 9.60 to 14.94 years for the rock wool strips. Moreover, the 3D calculations demonstrated lower local surface temperature minima than in the case of 2D model. The results show that a similar thermal bridge reduction does not necessarily mean a similar environmental effect, while taking into account the 3D geometry may be significant for the assessment of local surface temperature minima of the analysed junction.

title: EEG-based investigation of indoor occupant tolerance under “three elements of stimuli”: Taking glare perception as an example
Physiological dynamics of fan-assisted cooling during transient heat-stress recovery: Evidence from skin temperature, core body temperature, and heat storage
Multi-objective optimization of kindergarten activity unit layouts for thermal comfort in Kunming, China
Transient physiological and perceptual thermal responses to environmental and metabolic step-changes in summer
Annual operational dynamic transmittance of adaptive façades with PCMs: A climate-dependent characterization methodology
abstract: PCM-enhanced adaptive envelopes can improve thermal inertia and reduce heat transfer, but their performance is still assessed through heterogeneous indicators. Current regulations remain mainly based on steady-state transmittance, U , which cannot represent phase change dynamics, while the harmonic dynamic characterization defined by ISO 13786 depends on the specific boundary conditions applied, which do not represent the annual response of the envelope. Whole-building metrics, in turn, are case-specific and cannot characterize the envelope component independently. This work proposes a component-level methodology for the operational dynamic characterization of PCM-envelopes. Keeping ISO 13786 as the conceptual basis, the annual operational dynamic transmittance Y was defined as a transferable annual comparison metric that remains physically interpretable under realistic operation. The transient envelope's response is determined by numerical simulation, analyzing monthly typical days, used to then calculate annual indicators. The methodology is demonstrated for a macroencapsulated PCM façade under three Spanish climates, four orientations, two PCM positions, and eleven peak phase change temperatures. Results show that Y provides a meaningful metric to compare PCM façades under realistic operation, distinguishing between favorable, near-optimal, and unsuitable PCM configurations. Y captures the climate and configuration-dependent response of the envelope, with maximum reductions of 37.10% in Gijón and minimum reductions of 3.52% in Madrid, where lower Y values are associated with higher phase change efficiency. A local uncertainty analysis supported the robustness of the proposed calculation procedure after design screening, since the predicted Y values showed limited dispersion under realistic perturbations, with coefficients of variation below 12% for exterior PCM configurations and a maximum of 21% only in the most sensitive case. This creates a common methodological basis for component-level screening, more consistent design assessment, and for future standardization of adaptive envelopes.

title: Thermal synchronization of residential cooling demand limits diversity benefits: Evidence from year-long smart-meter data in a hot-arid climate
Editorial Board
Thermal performance of shipping container housing in hot climates: a trade-off between passive comfort and energy efficiency
How green is your house? Mandatory energy performance certificates and energy consumption
A hierarchical energy management strategy for PV–BESS retrofit in a zero-energy building: Capacity sensitivity and performance evaluation
abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) systems are widely adopted to achieve zero-energy performance in buildings, but the temporal mismatch between PV generation and electricity demand limits operational self-sufficiency. Retrofitting existing PV-equipped buildings with battery energy storage systems (BESSs) can increase on-site PV utilization, reduce grid dependence, and manage peak demand. However, measured-data-based evidence on the capacity-dependent performance of PV–BESS retrofits remains limited. This study proposes a hierarchical energy management strategy for a PV–BESS retrofit in an existing zero-energy building (ZEB). The strategy coordinates PV self-consumption, BESS charging and discharging, and peak shaving under state-of-charge (SOC) and power conversion system (PCS) constraints. Five BESS capacities (100–500 kWh) were evaluated using a measured-data-driven simulation based on one year of 15-min PV generation and building load data. A 300 kWh BESS (1.10 kWh/kWp) increased the annual self-sufficiency rate (SSR) from 65.6% to 88.5% and the self-consumption rate (SCR) from 38.4% to 52.5%, while reducing maximum grid-import demand from approximately 128 kW to the 100 kW control target (about 22%). Performance gains diminished markedly as capacity increased beyond 300 kWh because of constraints imposed by PV surplus, load profiles, SOC limits, PCS capacity, and the peak-control target. Accordingly, 300–400 kWh (1.10–1.47 kWh/kWp) was identified as an operationally favorable capacity range for the investigated building. The proposed strategy provides a practical basis for BESS retrofit sizing and coordinated energy management in existing PV-equipped ZEBs.

title: Balancing collective thermal preference sensitivity and energy cost for occupant-centric demand response
Multi-domain environmental interventions for restoration and human well-being in windowless environments: A systematic review
Balancing cost and carbon: prioritising office retrofit pathways in Manchester
abstract: City-scale office retrofit planning requires evidence on which buildings to prioritise, how deeply to intervene and when upgrades should occur. This study develops an expert-informed and policy-aware framework for Manchester, United Kingdom (UK), combining 4236 Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) records, 31,403 linked recommendations, 19 semi-structured interviews and two expert workshops. Three representative office types are assessed over 30 years through Life-Cycle Cost (LCC) and planning-level Whole-Life Carbon (WLC) accounting. Exact enumeration establishes reference pathways. A Deep Q-Network (DQN) evaluates learning-based approximation and a bounded Large Language Model (LLM) structures approved evidence and explains verified results. Offices below 1000 m 2 comprise 70.5% of records but 12.3% of recorded floor area, while larger offices account for 87.7% of floor area. Staged choices improve the preferred solution in 71 of 153 comparisons, with static Year-0 choices remaining sufficient in 82. Small and medium offices show preference- and timing-sensitive pathways. Large low-performing offices consistently favour immediate deep retrofit, reducing LCC by 13.0% and WLC by 22.3%. Single-human review classifies 275 of 612 LLM completion records as accepted, 240 as accepted after evidence-based editing and 97 as rejected. The study contributes an audited link from city-stock diagnosis to timed retrofit pathways and separates exact optimisation, learning approximation and governed explanation. Its current scope covers one city, three planning anchors and a partial WLC boundary. Future work will extend the office-type library, calibrate assumptions with audited projects, compare pathways with realised performance and use independent human reviewers.

title: Simulation-assisted evaluation and improvement of Guideline 36 for district cooling systems
Applicability analysis of zeotropic refrigerant mixtures with different temperature glides in cascade high temperature heat pumps
Non-Intrusive Building Load Energy Monitoring Method Based on Multi-Feature Images and Dual-branch CNN-SENet
Simplified operational strategy for CO₂ thermal networks in building applications
Regenerative twins as catalysts for circular, net-zero readiness in built environments: A systematic review of enablers, applications and challenges
abstract: The construction sector contributes 34% of global energy-related CO2 emissions and approximately 50% of global material extraction, yet material circularity has declined from 9.1% in 2018 to 6.9% in 2025. This review examines regenerative digital twins, defined as digital twins that encode material flow, embodied carbon, and end-of-life reuse potential, as enabling infrastructure for circular, net-zero-ready built environments. A PRISMA 2020 systematic review of Scopus and Google Scholar (2015 to 2026) yielded 88 studies after deduplication and two-stage screening, synthesised using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis. Publication growth is exponential, with a relative growth rate of 0.41 per year and a doubling time of 1.69 years. Enabler concentration is moderate (Herfindahl-Hirschman Index of 0.179), with application technologies dominant. A Jaccard Index (JI) of 0.455 indicates moderate integration between the regenerative-twin and broader circularity literatures. Enablers cluster into perception, network, storage, application, and design-process categories. Applications concentrate in the design and operational stages, and end-of-life regenerative feedback loops represent a critical research void, covering only 9% of studies. Challenges divide into technical barriers such as interoperability and standardisation, and socio-economic obstacles such as absent secondary-material markets, regulatory lag, and trust deficits. Policymakers should mandate standardised material passport schemas and incentivise secondary-material markets, while practitioners require interoperable BIM, LCA, and digital twin platforms and upskilling in circular design. The review distinguishes regenerative twins from generic digital twins, introduces four bibliometric indicators of field maturity, exposes the end-of-life research void, and proposes a testable framework linking enablers, applications, and challenges.

title: National energy and material flows along the building supply chain in the EU
abstract: Construction activity is responsible for substantial greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, but most of these reflect only a single stage of the building construction supply chain. Closing the gap, this work presents a cross-supply-chain perspective on annual material and energy consumption and GHG emissions for the sector on the European scale. These are estimated at the country level, disaggregated for raw material extraction, material manufacturing, demolition, and several intermediary transport stages. The study underscores cement, steel, flat glass, and ceramic bricks as manufactured materials; and sand, limestone, clay, iron ore, and coal as raw materials. Estimates consider both new construction and renovation, across varied typologies of residential and non-residential buildings. The results show that new construction & renovation of the building stock emits 212.44 Mt of CO2 annually, excluding energy consumption for building operations. These are associated with the consumption of circa 2 252.8 Mt raw and construction materials, and circa 1 617.76 PJ of final energy per year. These figures correspond to 3.5% of the total EU values (45 923 PJ). New building construction and renovation account for 63% of the materials used, while the material manufacturing stage accounts for 68% of the final energy consumption. By adopting a full supply chain perspective at the European level, we can support the development of holistic and more targeted public policies to decarbonize the sector.

title: Load-bearing hydrated porous inorganic frameworks for low-grade heat harvesting and intermittent wireless sensing
Reassessing air conditioning as a climate change adaptation measure: benefits, constraints, and feedback effects
abstract: Rising global temperatures and the increasing frequency and intensity of heatwaves have significantly amplified the need for effective thermal adaptation strategies. Air conditioning (AC) has emerged as the dominant technological solution to mitigate heat exposure, offering substantial benefits in terms of thermal comfort, health protection, and productivity. This paper provides a comprehensive and integrated assessment of the multifaceted impacts of air conditioning, encompassing energy, environmental, health, economic, social, and cultural dimensions. The analysis highlights that AC plays a critical role in reducing heat-related mortality and morbidity, improving cognitive performance, and sustaining economic productivity under high-temperature conditions. However, these benefits are accompanied by considerable challenges. The rapid growth of AC deployment drives substantial increases in electricity demand, particularly during peak periods, placing significant strain on power systems and contributing to grid instability and blackouts. Additionally, AC use exacerbates climate change through increased greenhouse gas emissions, waste heat release that intensifies urban heat islands, and environmental impacts associated with refrigerants, material extraction, and lifecycle processes. The paper also emphasizes profound inequalities in access to cooling, with low-income and vulnerable populations facing limited availability or affordability of air conditioning, leading to heightened exposure to thermal risks. Even where AC is available, economic constraints often restrict its use, resulting in insufficient protection during extreme heat events. Beyond technical and economic considerations, the widespread adoption of air conditioning has reshaped cultural norms, architectural practices, and human adaptive behaviour, fostering increased dependence on mechanically controlled indoor environments. The findings demonstrate that while air conditioning is an essential component of climate adaptation, it is insufficient as a standalone solution and may create reinforcing feedbacks that intensify energy demand and environmental stress. The study concludes that a transition toward integrated and sustainable cooling strategies is necessary, combining energy-efficient technologies, passive design measures, urban climate mitigation, and equitable policy frameworks. Such an approach is crucial to ensure resilient, low-carbon, and socially inclusive responses to rising thermal risks in a warming climate.

title: Global insights from mandatory building energy benchmarking and disclosure: Policy design, impacts, and implementation lessons
abstract: Building Energy Benchmarking and Disclosure (BEBD) policies have emerged as an important policy instrument for improving building energy performance and supporting climate mitigation goals, yet global evidence on their design, implementation, and effectiveness remains fragmented. This study addresses this gap through a systematic review of 31 peer-reviewed articles on global mandatory BEBD policies, combining policy-based coding of regulatory design with thematic coding of reported impacts, benchmarking metrics, and implementation challenges. The findings indicate that mandatory public disclosure, more than benchmarking alone, is the primary driver of improvement. By reducing information asymmetry, benchmarking has been associated with approximately 5–14% reductions in energy intensity in major city-level programs, including those in New York City and Chicago. Persistent challenges remain, including inconsistent data quality, the limited predictive value of static annual metrics that can obscure inefficiencies such as unoccupied base loads, weak links to broader climate policies, and operational performance gaps related to occupant behavior and building management. The study proposes strategies to strengthen BEBD implementation, including phased and locally calibrated policy frameworks, multi-metric benchmarking approaches, transparent public disclosure, technical and financial support for building operators, and stronger integration with building performance standards and retrofit policies. These findings provide a global evidence base for more effective and scalable BEBD policy design.

title: Decarbonising office buildings: balancing building fabric insulation and geothermal energy for optimal efficiency
abstract: The decarbonisation of office buildings requires a careful balance between reducing energy demand through fabric efficiency and integrating renewable heating and cooling technologies. This study investigates the combined influence of building fabric insulation and closed-loop geothermal energy systems using the University of Cambridge Civil Engineering Building as a case study. A calibrated building energy model was coupled with subsurface simulations to evaluate energy performance, system viability, and economic implications under three levels of building fabric insulation scenarios (BFI–BFIII). Results show that improved insulation significantly reduces heating demand (from 785 to 271 GWh for lowest and highest levels of insulation), enabling geothermal systems to operate more efficiently and within design constraints, while poorly insulated buildings impose unsustainable loads that require auxiliary systems. Shallow borehole heat exchanger (BHE) arrays provided reliable performance for moderately insulated buildings but were limited under high loads, whereas 1 km deep borehole heat exchangers (DBHEs) offered higher stability and efficiency with minimal surface footprint. For instance, in the base case scenario the lowest temperature encountered in the shallow array was 0.6 °C, whilst for the DBHE it was 6.1 °C. Economic analysis indicated that moderate fabric upgrades (BFII) combined with geothermal systems deliver the most favourable balance of cost, operational savings, and carbon reduction, with diminishing returns observed for deep retrofits (BFIII) when embodied emissions are considered. Over a 50-year period, the combination of building fabric improvements and geothermal technologies can reduce carbon emissions associated to operational conditions by up to 9.5 kt CO₂e. The findings highlight the necessity of a fabric-first approach, integrated with appropriately scaled renewable solutions, in this case closed-loop geothermal systems, to provide a robust and cost-effective pathway for office building decarbonisation.

title: Energy-harvesting one-part geopolymer composites for thermoelectric building applications: balancing mechanical performance and waste-heat-to-power response
abstract: Thermoelectric building materials offer a potential route to harvest low-grade thermal gradients from building envelopes, pavements and other infrastructure surfaces for low-power sensing and auxiliary energy supply. However, most cement-based thermoelectric composites still suffer from limited thermoelectric response, carbon-intensive binders, and insufficient mechanical compatibility with construction applications. This study develops a construction-compatible one-part geopolymer composite using fly ash, ground granulated blast-furnace slag, steel slag aggregate and graphite as functional components. Steel slag was used to replace quartz sand, while graphite was incorporated to tailor the thermoelectric response. The results show that the full replacement of quartz sand with steel slag produced an all-solid-waste geopolymer mortar with a 28-day compressive strength of 51.2 ± 1.5 MPa and a Seebeck coefficient of 651.5 ± 4.6 μV/K. The incorporation of graphite further modified the electrical transport behaviour, with the best overall thermoelectric response obtained at 4 wt.% graphite. The enhanced response is mainly associated with composition-dependent interfacial polarization, conductive pathway formation and energy-filtering effects within the heterogeneous geopolymer matrix. Excessive graphite or larger graphite particles introduced defects and weakened both mechanical and thermoelectric performance. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using one-part geopolymer composites as low-carbon, mechanically robust thermoelectric building materials for harvesting distributed thermal gradients in buildings and infrastructure.

title: How can green value recapture support EPBD implementation? Private activation, redistributive leverage and assisted compliance in Italy
abstract: The recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) raises a major implementation challenge in countries with ageing residential stock, fragmented ownership, and limited owner capacity to finance retrofit. This study investigates whether Green Value Recapture can support EPBD implementation by capturing part of the real estate value increase generated by energy upgrading and reallocating it to collective purposes without undermining private activation. An exploratory multi-objective framework is developed and applied to a pilot sample of ten inefficient residential units in Rome. Four policy scenarios are compared: no minimum energy performance standards, EPBD compliance without financial support, assisted compliance through a zero-interest loan, and assisted compliance through a concessional loan. The model evaluates total energy benefit, private economic benefit, and social benefit, while comparing upfront owner-side costs with the discounted present value of repayment streams in financed scenarios. Solutions are selected through a balanced feasible rule that retains only configurations with non-negative aggregate private benefit. The results indicate that recapture remains compatible with private activation only within a narrow range in non-assisted scenarios. Financial support substantially enlarges this feasible range. Zero-interest lending provides the greatest stability across the tested recapture levels, while concessional lending also improves feasibility but with lower resilience under stronger redistributive pressure. The findings suggest that Green Value Recapture is unlikely to function as a stand-alone implementation tool. Its potential appears greater when embedded in broader assisted-compliance arrangements that combine redistributive goals with private feasibility and financial support.

title: Soft state-of-charge estimation for adsorption energy storage: Black-box and physics-informed approaches
abstract: Adsorption-based thermochemical energy storage is an emerging technology with strong potential for waste-heat recovery and integration into sector-coupled energy systems. However, operating such complex systems remains challenging and requires in-depth data analysis. One of the key challenges is the real-time, precise tracking of State-of-Charge (SOC) instead of relying on temperature difference in the external adsorption and desorption loops. In this context, this work develops and validates machine learning models as soft sensors of the key states in adsorption-based thermal energy storage systems, overcoming the real-time limitations of conventional physics-based approaches. Using experimental data collected through an edge computing platform, we evaluate both black-box Neural Networks (NNs) and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). The goal of using instantaneous sensor data is to reconstruct (estimate) the unmeasurable current states, mainly the refrigerant update and the adsorption-desorption temperatures in real-time. The proposed PINN introduces a specialized physical loss coupling thermochemical energy balances with adsorption kinetics, driven by instantaneous edge inputs for direct SoC tracking. The comparative evaluation demonstrates that PINN consistently achieves higher predictive accuracy than the conventional NN across all key outputs, relative to a high-fidelity white-box dynamic model. For the adsorption and desorption mass fractions, the PINN attains R 2 values of 0.939 and 0.938, respectively, improving upon the NN's 0.922 and 0.905. Similarly, for adsorption and desorption temperature estimations, the PINN achieves R 2 values of 0.994 and 0.992 compared to the NN's 0.989 and 0.985. These improvements correspond to 15–25% reductions in MSE, MAE, and RMSE, confirming a more precise reconstruction of key thermodynamic states. When applied to SOC estimation, the PINN further demonstrates enhanced fidelity with R 2 value of 0.939 versus 0.922 for the NN, highlighting its ability to generalize the coupled adsorption-desorption behavior by integrating the system's thermochemical energy balance and driving force relationships into the learning process. A robustness test with noisy measurements, reflecting real-world industrial conditions, confirmed that the PINN outperforms the standard NN due to its embedded physical constraints.

title: Calculated versus measured energy in ten municipal buildings: Data resolution and the diagnostic limits of energy performance certificates
abstract: Energy performance certificates (EPCs) are the principal instrument for assessing and communicating building energy performance in Europe, yet studies testing EPCs against measured energy compare, almost without exception, whole-building totals. This study examines what that practice conceals. In a census of ten recently completed municipal buildings in Sandnes, Norway, every floor area, meter scope, and calculation basis was verified against primary sources, and EPC-calculated and measured delivered energy were compared at three levels of data resolution: whole-building for all ten buildings, energy-carrier for one, and end-use for one. Measured energy exceeded the calculation in eight of ten buildings; the portfolio-mean deviation is +28% (range − 8% to +102%). At end-use level, a building with an unremarkable aggregate deviation of +17% (net energy) deviated by −38% to +110% on its individual end uses, opposing errors cancelling at the meter. A cancellation index, C = 1 − |Δ|/D, quantifies the effect: C = 0.66, two-thirds of the deviation magnitude invisible in the whole-building total. A verified floor-area error alone would otherwise have made the same building appear compliant. Whole-building agreement is therefore not evidence that a building performs as calculated. Certificate validation needs the end-use resolution that building performance evaluation has long applied to diagnosis, and the study shows the cost of proceeding without it.

title: Progressive filtering and cluster-localized calibration for customized UBEM
abstract: Urban building energy modeling (UBEM) has become increasingly important in recent years for understanding energy use in urban buildings. Traditional models often rely on a ‘one-size-fits-all’ approach based on a limited set of archetypes, which oversimplifies building diversity and undermines confidence in the results, while generating one archetype per house is computationally prohibitive. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a “Three-Layer Filtering” approach with dual model that progressively reduces structural mismatch and enables scalable house-level refinement. It first constrains candidate archetypes using taxonomy-based classification, then derives representative archetypes via multi-parameter clustering and enables reusable assignment through a supervised classifier, and finally localizes each assigned archetype to individual houses using sensitivity-guided, surrogate-assisted Bayesian calibration under annual electricity EUI constraints. As a proof of concept, this work is demonstrated on 100 all-electric single-detached houses in Montreal using annual electricity EUI as the sole calibration target. The proposed approach progressively reduces building-level mean absolute percentage error from 80.7% to 23.3% after clustering and further to 4.3% after localized calibration. Aggregate bias is minimized to near zero, with a 95% posterior predictive interval of [−1.7%, 0.2%]. This proposed approach is methodologically general and can be replicated in similar data settings, providing a practical pathway to scalable, building-specific archetype refinement for urban energy analysis.

title: Performance-based assessment of thermal resilience in hot-humid affordable housing using standard effective temperature
Airflow organization evaluation and multi-level energy-saving optimization for cleanroom systems: A review
Graph learning for multi-zone CO2 forecasting
Investigations of energy management strategies for AHU in indoor swimming pools based on an experimental study
abstract: Indoor swimming pools (ISPs) are highly energy-intensive facilities, consuming up to three times more energy than outdoor swimming pools or buildings of comparable size. This high demand stems from the need to heat large volumes of water and dehumidify and heat an indoor environment characterized by high evaporation rates. The present paper proposes first a dynamic model of the air and water circuits in an ISP which is satisfactorily validated against experimental measurements conducted on a real building. It is then used to evaluate simple energy management strategies applied during vacancy and their combination for the air loop, particularly the use of water surface cover, reduced air renewal duration, and reduced temperature and moisture content setpoints. It is found that limiting air renewal duration during vacancy is a key strategy for reducing energy demand in both the air and water circuits. This enables achieving around 24% overall energy savings compared to a baseline case, while preventing trichloramine accumulation and condensation on walls. Applying night setback setpoints for temperature and humidity yields the same results. Although the use of cover individually also achieves significant energy savings (14%), its combination with other strategies does not significantly improve the results. The combination of all strategies results in 27% energy savings.

title: Multi-agent storage dispatch in building communities: Information availability, inter-building dynamics, and the distribution of benefits
abstract: Building energy communities are expected to provide grid flexibility through coordinated storage dispatch, and multi-agent reinforcement learning is increasingly proposed to deliver it. This study evaluates, on one CityLearn benchmark instance, the relative value of temporal representation under a pre-specified removal of weather and solar lead variables, and asks how the benefits of dispatch are distributed across a community. A five-building community from the CityLearn 2020 Climate Zone 1 benchmark is used to evaluate multi-agent proximal policy optimisation under centralised training with decentralised execution. A pre-registered 2 × 3 factorial crosses temporal representation against the availability of forecast information over five paired seeds and full-year episodes, alongside three reference controllers this literature rarely reports together: a rule-based schedule, a zero-action null controller, and a rolling-horizon model predictive controller with stated information assumptions. Withholding weather and solar leads did not differentially advantage the temporal controller over a capacity-matched feed-forward one: the paired difference-in-differences interval lies inside a pre-specified ± 2% equivalence bound. Under perfect foresight, model predictive control is cheaper than every learned controller, and the null controller records the lowest ramping cost of any controller evaluated, so ramping improvements measured only against a rule-based baseline may reflect that baseline’s own storage activity. Contribution to district peaks does not follow energy share: one building’s share of peak-hour load is 2.18 times its share of annual energy, an ordering unchanged by a controller that dispatches nothing. Two limits of the benchmark are reported as results. Comfort is exactly invariant across all controllers, because storage cannot actuate indoor temperature; and same-building warming cannot be simulated, because demand and indoor series are precomputed.

title: Acute cardiovascular responses to indoor-outdoor step-change cold exposure among older adults: A field study during the heating season
Digital-driven thermal and energy performance assessment of heritage buildings using HBIM, environmental monitoring and energy simulation
abstract: Conservation and management of built cultural heritage require a multidisciplinary approach. To enhance building energy efficiency and support informed decision-making, projects should include a digital transformation strategy that incorporates digitisation, simulation and monitoring. In this work, an integrated digital framework to improve the energy performance assessment and conservation of heritage buildings. The approach combines HBIM (Heritage Building Information Modelling), environmental monitoring through low-cost wireless sensors, as-built data collection, dynamic Building Energy Modelling (BEM), and data visualisation within a digital shadow framework. Applied to the Monserrate Palace in Portugal, the methodology included model calibration using in-situ temperature measurements and simplification of complex heritage geometries for energy simulation. Experimental and simulated data showed a reasonable agreement between, demonstrating the capability of this methodology to support reliable energy analysis. The integration of monitoring and simulation data within the HBIM digital shadow enables a proactive, data-driven approach to heritage conservation and management.

title: Thermal perception and heat adaptation of residents toward climate warming in cold regions: Evidence from the 2025 Nordic heatwave
Thermal and EEG responses of Chinese urban and rural older women to different lower-body heating modes in winter
Urban block spatial form indicators in relation to summer daytime land surface temperature in China: a review
Measured thermal performance and the stability of Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) classifications: evidence from 30 UK dwellings
abstract: Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs) guide retrofit policy, standards and housing market decisions, but their reliability depends partly on how accurately survey-based assessment represents dwelling heat loss. Prior studies show that EPC outputs can diverge from measured energy use, and separate measurement studies show that dwelling heat loss can be measured or inferred. This paper directly tests how measured whole-dwelling Heat Transfer Coefficient (HTC) evidence changes EPC score movement, distance-to-threshold effects and band-switching risk. Using 30 UK dwellings, RdSAP-calculated HTC showed weak agreement with measured HTC (R2 = 0.359; CVRMSE = 16.49%). Mean bias was small, with RdSAP underestimating measured HTC by 2.8%, but dwelling-level deviations ranged from −21% to +58%. Substituting measured HTC changed the EPC score in 83% of dwellings and the EPC band in 30%. EPC score sensitivity was approximately linear: a 1% increase in HTC reduced the EPC score by 0.22 points on average, equivalent to an HTC change of 4.61% per EPC point. For dwellings close to the C/D threshold, band changes occurred with HTC corrections as small as −3.28% and +5.42%. More detailed survey evidence for geometry, infiltration and exposure changed calculated HTC but rarely changed EPC bands. Average model agreement can therefore mask material dwelling-level error. EPC classifications should be treated as less robust near policy or market thresholds, and measured thermal-performance evidence, including SMETER-type methods, could provide targeted validation for high-consequence cases. The classification-margin problem is internationally relevant wherever model-based energy certificates are converted into banded regulatory, financial or market thresholds.

title: Spatiotemporal deep learning for multimodal thermal comfort assessment and prediction in community elderly day-care centers
From comparison to deployment: Operationalizing deep learning energy forecasting for smart campuses
abstract: Accurate short-term energy forecasting is essential for improving sustainability and operational efficiency in smart infrastructures. University campuses, as sensor-rich and data-intensive environments, offer an ideal setting for deploying predictive intelligence under real-world constraints. This study presents an end-to-end forecasting pipeline based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, a soft computing approach well suited to modeling sequential energy data. Three model configurations were evaluated, incorporating full temporal context, minimal inputs, and PCA-reduced features, to explore the trade-offs between prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. The most lightweight configuration was deployed on a low-power edge device and delivered consistent day-ahead forecasts with an average error below 8 percent over a three-month operational period. The system was integrated into the Kunna Smart Campus platform through a distributed multi-agent architecture that supports modular deployment and real-time inference. Communication with platform services is managed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling secure and standardized interactions. Results demonstrate that accurate and efficient energy forecasting is achievable on embedded hardware, bridging the gap between algorithmic design and real-world deployment. This work outlines a scalable and practical approach for embedding intelligent forecasting capabilities into next-generation smart campus infrastructures.

title: Energy retrofit decision-making for functionally diverse rural buildings: A unified–adaptive multi-objective optimization framework
Measured vs. simulated post-retrofit energy-use in 149 public buildings using dynamic simulation
Understanding preferences for low-carbon technologies, retrofit and ownership models for domestic heating in the UK
abstract: Despite advancements in renewable energy technology adoption, the uptake of low-carbon heating technologies in the UK and many other countries remains insufficient to align with governmental objectives and targets. This has been attributed mainly to high capital costs, limited consumer awareness, and unclear economic and environmental benefits. This study aims to understand these challenges and analyse ways to overcome them by exploring consumer willingness to support the transition to low-carbon heating, using data from a two-wave survey of over 1,000 UK households conducted in 2023 – 2024. The first wave assesses current household contexts, which inform three stated-preference scenarios in the second wave: (1) choosing between gas boilers, hydrogen-ready boilers, and air-source electric heat pumps, with varying costs, emissions, and support schemes; (2) deciding on retrofit levels (none, minor, major) characterised by costs, savings, and support; and (3) selecting between ownership and operation models (full ownership, shared ownership, service-based heating), each with different costs, contract lengths, and flexibility features. By using discrete choice modelling, the analysis provides insights into how different consumer segments, defined by sociodemographic and attitudinal factors, respond to attributes such as capital and operational costs, as well as the impact of support schemes. The study estimates willingness to pay for reduced nuisance or emissions, and the compensations required for participation in flexible pricing or demand-side response, offering guidance for policies that encourage low-carbon heating adoption across diverse user groups.

title: From database uncertainty to procedural errors in building LCA: Evidence from G-SEED-certified buildings in South Korea
Climate-adaptive thermal performance assessment of naturally ventilated offices using surrogate modeling under present and future climates
abstract: Building performance assessment under climate change requires surrogate models capable of representing diverse climatic conditions while remaining computationally efficient. However, representing weather information in surrogate models is challenging because climate variables consist of long, highly variable time series that cannot be directly used as model inputs. This study develops and evaluates a surrogate-modeling framework for rapid overheating assessment in naturally ventilated cellular office buildings using compact climatic descriptors. More than 155,000 EnergyPlus simulations were performed using historical and future weather files, and twelve alternative approaches for representing wind speed and direction were systematically evaluated. Artificial neural networks were trained to predict the fraction of occupied hours with operative temperatures above 26~°C (FHOT26). The selected surrogate model achieved high predictive accuracy (R² = 0.949, MAE = 0.037, AE95 = 0.157). The results show that predictive performance depends not only on the climatic variables adopted but also on how they are represented. The highest accuracy was obtained by combining occupancy-hour descriptors for wind direction with full-day descriptors for wind speed, indicating that climatic variables should be represented according to the physical mechanisms through which they influence building performance. Training exclusively with historical weather data did not compromise predictive performance under future climate scenarios, and the model also generalized well to geographically distinct climates. The proposed framework provides an efficient and transferable methodology for incorporating climatic information into surrogate models, supporting rapid climate-adaptive overheating assessment during early-stage building design.

title: Prototype building energy modeling method with customized geometry and hierarchical parameter configuration
Downscaling bias-corrected climate projections for future heat and cold stress assessment across local climate zones
Orienting PV panels to maximise self-sufficiency in residential communities
abstract: Solar panels on residential dwellings are typically installed facing the equator to maximise the energy collected. However, the power generated by an equator-facing panel peaks around midday, whereas residential loads typically peak in the morning and afternoon. By orienting panels in different directions it is possible to minimise the shortfall between load and generation, which benefits the end user by decreasing the energy imported from the grid. We demonstrate this benefit for residential communities of separate dwellings and an apartment building in Adelaide, South Australia, using a simple linear program to determine panel orientations that maximise annual self-sufficiency. If the total panel area is small enough that generation does not exceed load at any time then panels facing the equator will generate more energy and minimise shortfall. For larger panel areas, where midday generation exceeds load, it is better to orient panels more east and west.

title: Automated BIM-to-BEM reconstruction for EnergyPlus thermal load simulation using BIM-derived room boundary data
Building energy prediction under future climate scenarios: A Hybrid multi-scale graph–temporal framework with physics-based corrections
abstract: Global warming is causing future climate conditions to gradually deviate from historical distributions. This shift introduces considerable uncertainty into power distribution planning, energy efficiency retrofits, and load management in buildings. Existing studies have not fully considered the input features related to multi-scale fluctuations in building load series. In addition, many previous methods remain tied to the historical distribution of building energy consumption, which limits their direct applicability to non-stationary load responses under future climate conditions. Therefore, predicting building energy consumption under such scenarios remains insufficiently addressed. To reduce the instability caused by directly training graph–temporal neural networks on limited samples and strongly non-stationary load series, this study proposes a multi-scale graph–temporal framework for building energy consumption prediction under future climate scenarios. This study builds on conventional data-driven building energy prediction models by introducing multi-scale signal decomposition to process raw building load series. A hybrid model combining a feature-level graph neural network and a bidirectional long short-term memory network is then used to model load components at different frequency scales. This design allows the framework to support future climate scenario analysis, rather than being limited to historical short-term prediction or simulation-derived proxy samples. Based on this hybrid model, an empirical energy–weather relationship is constructed for scenario-based projection. Correction terms are then formulated from simplified thermodynamic mechanisms and operation-strategy settings, and are added to project hourly building electricity loads under future climate scenarios. Building data from different functional types were used together with weather data under different climate scenarios to demonstrate the proposed workflow. The results show that the proposed framework can represent complex fluctuations and non-stationary features in building load series. Historical-stage evaluation across aggregate, transition, ramp, and peak-oriented measures showed comparable overall accuracy to the strongest decomposition-enhanced baseline, with clearer gains during morning and evening load transitions and daily peak prediction. Under the given future meteorological scenarios, the framework can further characterize building-specific changes in typical daily load profiles, annual and seasonal energy consumption, and peak load indicators. Therefore, the proposed method provides an implementable workflow for building energy scenario analysis under future climate conditions.

title: A multi-site experimental database for machine learning and SHAP interpretability in ventilated façade performance
Probabilistic lookahead HVAC control for thermal comfort
Retraction notice to “Unpacking the energy performance gap: Household variation in actual vs. theoretical heat demand in energy-efficient homes” [Energy Build. 365 (2026) 117677]
Analysis of the work of a high-temperature concrete-ground thermal energy storage unit integrated with RES
abstract: Alongside the increase in the share of renewable energy sources, considering their significant dependency on atmospheric conditions, and therefore an equally large wavering in energy generation, both within daily and annual timespans, the development and integration of energy storage solutions is of the utmost importance. Depending on the season and the geographical location considered, where a significant amount of energy is utilized for heating, a sensible solution is the direct storage of said energy within thermal energy storage (TES) systems.This article presents the concept of a high-temperature concrete-ground heat storage integrated with a heating network and an electric boiler.The presented system is powered with energy generated by a small wind farm and is also capable of operating in an off-grid system. The heating network is characterized by an annual energy consumption of 17 GWh/year. The heat storage, depending on the variant, consists of 120 or 150 identical modules with dimensions of 4.5 m × 6 m and a depth of 23 m.A proprietary calculation algorithm based on solving the unsteady equation of thermal conductivity using the finite difference method was used to analyze the operation of the thermal energy storage. This algorithm was subjected to a validation process and effectively enabled the analysis of the heat storage operation under variable boundary conditions during the calculation year.The analyses also showed that the heat storage itself provides 35.5% of the total energy consumption in the heating network. The remaining part is obtained directly using the energy produced by the wind farm. Heat losses in the TES, depending on the variant considered, amount to 20.5% - 23.5% of the energy introduced into the system.

title: AI-driven optimization of timber-based indoor environments for energy performance and cognitive comfort
A hybrid model for predicting the operation status and power of residential air conditioning based on coupled indoor-outdoor hygrothermal variations
Zero-shot facade parsing for generating building energy modeling inputs using vision-language models and generative image editing
abstract: Building energy modeling (BEM) is a key instrument for assessing energy demand and CO 2 emissions of the building stock and for planning decarbonization strategies. Its reliability, however, critically depends on accurate geometric and material input data, including facade-related parameters such as window areas and window-to-wall ratios that strongly affect solar gains and transmission losses. These facade components can be extracted from images, but current approaches are dominated by supervised deep learning models, which require large annotated datasets, generalize poorly across cities and architectural styles, and struggle with real-world occlusions from vegetation and street furniture. To address these limitations, we propose a zero-shot semantic segmentation workflow with integrated occlusion compensation. The segmentation stage is based on a vision-language model (VLM), and the occlusion compensation stage uses a generative image editing model. Both stages are controlled purely via text prompts and do not require any task-specific fine-tuning. We systematically analyze prompt designs and evaluate the workflow across six facade datasets, including a newly introduced Lemgo Musicians’ Quarter (LMQ) dataset of 92 detached and multi-family residential buildings with pixel-accurate annotations. The experiments show that a unified vision-language-mask model (SAM 3) combined with a flow-matching generative model (FLUX.1 Kontext) achieves the best overall performance: generative occlusion compensation improves Mean IoU on LMQ from 0.760 to 0.801. The downstream analysis shows that occlusion compensation is particularly beneficial for building-area estimation, while its effect on WWR is smaller but removes a systematic overestimation; minor window hallucinations remain a relevant limitation. In cross-dataset evaluation SAM 3 achieves the highest Mean IoU of 0.602, outperforming the strongest per-dataset-trained supervised baseline by approximately 8.6 percentage points, and remaining competitive even against supervised baselines trained on the combined data of all six datasets, while performing on par in intra-dataset settings. By enabling accurate, scalable extraction of facade components with minimal reliance on human-annotated training data, the proposed approach helps mitigate a key data bottleneck in BEM and supports more transferable, up-to-date assessments of building energy performance.

title: Rethinking thermal comfort in a changing climate: a review of indoor thermal discomfort
Navigating zero carbon building definitions and approaches: A multi-dimensional comparative review of global standards and frameworks
Assessing aggregated building thermal mass energy flexibility for the design and operation of local energy communities
abstract: Local energy communities (LECs) can enhance renewable energy integration, mitigate grid congestion, and enable coordinated use of distributed energy resources. Existing community-level studies focus on electrical batteries and photovoltaic systems as energy flexibility assets, while the inherent flexibility potential of aggregated building thermal mass remains underexplored. This study presents a simulation-based optimization approach to quantify and evaluate aggregated building thermal mass energy flexibility at the community scale. The approach couples building energy simulations in OpenModelica with a mixed-integer linear programming aggregator model implemented in Python, enabling coordinated day-ahead scheduling of heat pumps, battery storage, and photovoltaic curtailment under multi-criteria objectives. The approach is applied to a case study LEC consisting of seven office buildings in the Netherlands, evaluating economic, environmental, and technical performance indicators. The results show that coordinated aggregator-level control significantly improves LEC performance compared to building-level optimization. Aggregated building thermal mass provided flexibility comparable to a 700 kWh community battery and, during certain periods, exceeded the flexibility contribution of conventional distributed energy resources. Across the design space, a stakeholder-driven and controller-robust design configuration was identified, consisting of a 700 kWh battery and photovoltaic systems covering 70% of the total roof area. This configuration achieved a net present value of up to 1.25 M€, reduced the CO₂ footprint by up to 9.1%, and lowered the one-percent peak by 65 kW across different control strategies. These findings demonstrate that aggregated building thermal mass represents a cost-free flexibility resource that can significantly enhance the economic, environmental, and technical performance of LECs.

title: Experimental characterization of aerosol and bioaerosol transfer in an energy recovery ventilator for airborne pathogen transport assessment in HVAC systems
Quantifying combined performance of stormwater mitigation and cooling energy savings for green roof deployment
abstract: Urban environments increasingly face compounding warm season stresses from intense rainfall and high building cooling demands. While green roofs provide a multifunctional retrofit solution, their stormwater and energy benefits are rarely evaluated jointly across diverse weather events and building stocks. This study integrates parsimonious roof-scale hydrological modelling with urban building energy modelling (UBEM) to quantify combined stormwater and cooling performance for green roof deployment in Shanghai during the warm season (May to September). Three green roof typologies are evaluated across 113 representative buildings and distinct extreme rainfall event sets. The results demonstrate that green roofs deliver robust multi-hour stormwater mitigation, achieving median six-hour runoff reduction ratios of 0.35 to 0.39 and peak flow reductions of 0.33 to 0.35 m 3 s −1 km −2 . In parallel, building cooling energy use intensity is reduced by an average of 2.3% to 2.4%, though savings are highly heterogeneous depending on building geometry and operational characteristics. The combined performance analysis, constructed from the Cartesian product of independently simulated building-level cooling outcomes and event-level stormwater outcomes, shows that the greatest concentration of synthetic combinations occurs in a moderate regime. This pattern reflects the shapes of the two marginal outcome distributions and does not represent an observed probability of simultaneous building-storm outcomes. City-scale extrapolations are heavily constrained by deployable roof area. This integrated approach provides a decision-relevant perspective for urban planners, emphasising that evaluating the combined performance space across building and event heterogeneity is essential for robust green roof deployment.

title: Corrigendum to “An observation-based quantile delta mapping method for generating future weather data in building performance simulations” [Energy Build. 369 (2026) 117955]
Full-spectrum solar and methane complementary CCHP system for flexible cooling, heating, and power supply in positive energy buildings
Leakage-safe cross-domain AHU fault detection for building operation: adaptation reliability under limited target information
Cement-based phase change material composites for building energy efficiency: a critical review of integration strategies, performance trade-offs, and pathways to practical application
Optimized model horizon and updating interval for day-ahead prediction-based control of building energy storage systems
Multi-objective optimization for building envelope retrofits: Balancing energy efficiency, economics, and climate adaptability
Editorial Board
Daytime radiative cooling-coated air-conditioning in hot and humid climates: Effect of film material and coverage area
Re-sizing energy retrofits for low-temperature district heating: Integrating residents' heating practices and a multi-criteria selection
abstract: To connect dwellings to sustainable low-temperature district heating (LTDH), it is typically recommended that dwellings with low or moderately insulated envelopes undergo deep renovation. These recommendations are grounded in standardized assumptions about thermal comfort, which do not reflect the diversity of residents' heating practices. As a result, deep retrofit interventions often prove costly, highly disruptive, and may fail to achieve the projected energy savings. This study addresses this gap by integrating residents' heating practices into retrofit decision-making to reassess the scale of renovations necessary for LTDH readiness. Using a Dutch terraced house as a reference case, we apply a multi-criteria framework combined with parametric simulations to evaluate renovation strategies in terms of thermal comfort, heating savings, environmental impacts, costs, and resident nuisance. The results indicate that although deep retrofits with full radiator upgrades emerge as the most technically robust solution, their benefits are not distributed equally across resident profiles. For households with economical heating behaviour, deep renovation yields significantly lower-than-expected savings and carbon reductions, and considerably longer payback times. Conversely, less intensive strategies, such as radiator upgrades alone or combined with single or moderate retrofit packages, are technically sufficient to enable connection to LTDH, often at lower cost and reduced disruption. Rather than converging to one standardized solution, the analysis identifies up to 28 viable retrofit pathways depending on the resident profile. These findings challenge the prevailing one-size-fits-all deep renovations and demonstrate how integrating residents' practices can resize renovation, supporting flexible, resource-efficient, and socially just pathways toward low-carbon heating transitions.

title: Validation of fault monitoring method for chiller condenser fouling guided by temporal pseudo-labels
Who pays the bills, Who bears the burden? A mixed-methods examination of utility bill-paying responsibility and energy insecurity among New York City residents
Thermodynamics-aware pre-training for few-shot chiller performance prediction
Unlocking renewable energy community benefits through retrofit and energy sharing in mixed-use districts
abstract: In the process of urban decarbonisation, building-level energy retrofits alone are often insufficient to meet policy targets, particularly in dense urban areas where renewable potential is spatially constrained. District-scale strategies can overcome part of this limitation by exploiting inter-building synergies and improving the local use of renewable energy within Renewable Energy Communities (RECs). However, building-retrofit pathways and REC operation are still assessed separately. Limited evidence shows the way retrofit depths reshape collective self-consumption, self-sufficiency, and operational energy costs in mixed-use districts. To address this gap, this study couples an occupant behaviour-aware Urban Building Energy Modelling (UBEM) workflow with a REC energy-sharing and economic assessment. The approach is applied to a mixed-use district in Bari, Italy, under three scenarios: a baseline characterized by low-performance envelopes and gas-based systems; an envelope-focused retrofit; and a deep retrofit combining envelope upgrades with full electrification through air-source heat pumps. Full electrification maximises local renewable energy use at the community level, reaching a self-consumption index of 0.93 and increasing locally exploited PV generation by 14% compared with a non-REC configuration, while reducing natural gas consumption by up to 94%. However, this scenario also increases electricity demand and operational costs, especially when renewable generation is insufficient to cover electrified loads. Findings demonstrate that retrofit interventions within community-level energy management can amplify retrofit benefits while revealing energy-related trade-offs. Maximising collective self-consumption does not necessarily minimise operational costs. These results support a shift from building-centric renovation decisions toward district-level planning for REC and, further, Positive Energy District pathways in dense urban contexts.

title: Explainable machine learning for thermal comfort modelling in warm-humid mixed-mode buildings
Multi-objective optimization of expanded metal meshes for office buildings in humid continental climates
Integrating passive design, renewable energy, thermal flexibility, and intelligent control in net-zero energy buildings: A system-level review
Airflow distribution and pollutant removal limitations of ACH-based ventilation in multi-zone restaurant kitchens
Energy savings using occupancy light sensors in unowned office spaces
Comparative characterization of energy flexibility across functional building types: A systematic review toward grid-interactive buildings
CFD-based assessment of natural ventilation strategies for occupant thermal comfort in a heritage building under hot-dry climatic conditions: Bayt al-Sitt Wasila, Historic Cairo
Office plug-load dataset for non-intrusive load monitoring in buildings using an open metering platform
abstract: Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) can support building energy management by estimating appliance-level consumption from aggregate electrical measurements. Yet, most public benchmarks are residential and provide limited evidence for office plug-load monitoring. This paper presents an office plug-load dataset acquired with Open Multi Power Meter v2, an open, low-cost, multi-channel metering platform for time-aligned aggregate and appliance-level monitoring in office and institutional buildings.
