The dataset was collected under natural operating conditions, without programmed switching sequences or artificial load automation, thereby preserving realistic standby periods, sparse events, low-power operation, and interactions among office devices. The dataset comprises 346,252 time-stamped records from six meters over approximately 10 days of continuous office operation. Active power and complementary electrical and environmental variables were recorded at a 15 s sampling interval and converted to a NILMTK-compatible format. Baseline results show that office plug-load disaggregation is governed by load observability. A Factorial Hidden Markov Model achieved the best overall balance between accuracy and execution time, whereas the two lowest-power devices yielded zero F1-scores despite low absolute power errors. This indicates that some office loads can be measured accurately at the submeter level but remain weakly disaggregable from aggregate active power alone. The results highlight practical limits for device-level NILM in offices and support monitoring strategies based on device grouping, selective submetering, or complementary features.

title: Global energy-saving potential of asymmetric emitters revealed by building energy modeling with transient ground surface temperature
Reassessing mixed-mode ventilation in tropical climates with elevated air movement
Identifying dominant performance degradation mechanisms in seawater-driven indirect evaporative cooling systems
FMCW millimeter-wave radar gesture recognition for smart buildings
Field-derived pareto-informed adaptive thermal comfort thresholds for summer overheating assessment in eastern mediterranean social housing
abstract: Eastern Mediterranean social housing lacks field-validated neutral-temperature benchmarks that account for clustered household data and constrained adaptive opportunities. This study developed and evaluated a Pareto-informed neutral adaptive thermal comfort threshold for summer overheating in a Famagusta social-housing estate. Fanger's PMV/PPD heat-balance model was integrated with adaptive comfort theory, Griffiths neutral-temperature estimation, and multiobjective Pareto optimisation. Of 200 approached households, 100 participated (50%), providing paired surveys and environmental monitoring across 32 observed tower-block clusters and 500 room thermal sensation votes. Household and occupied room levels were analysed using AICc-guided regression, HC3 and block-CR1 inference, random-intercept models, block-bootstrap/fixed-effects sensitivities, and Pareto triangulation. Griffiths neutral temperatures were regressed on concurrent outdoor air temperature. The population-average relationship was Tₙ = 18.023 + 0.374 OUT_TA (block-CR1 slope 95% CI 0.125–0.624, p = 0.005; R 2 = 0.086). Thirty-one near-neutral records had a median indoor operative-temperature proxy of 31.40 °C (IQR 29.85–31.85 °C). The temperature-by-humidity interaction was significant before contextual adjustment but attenuated afterward; current room condition remained jointly associated with thermal sensation (F(2,31) = 7.92, p = 0.002). Prediction was weak. The study provides an evidence-graded, cluster-aware Eastern Mediterranean benchmarking framework and demonstrates that near-neutral votes can occur at comparatively high indoor temperatures without claiming universal or causal thresholds. Multi-season, multi-city longitudinal validation should include nighttime bedrooms, co-located microclimate, ventilation/infiltration, pre-vote exposure, air speed, radiant temperature, clothing, metabolic rate, cooling operation, and nonresponse tracking.

title: A viable solution? Feasibility of applying thermochromic coatings to enhance building energy efficiency in urban built environments: Cases in Hangzhou, China
A multilevel subjective perception relevance evaluation method for BIPV/T architectural aesthetic features and its application
Energy performance and modular design potential of hexagonal and rectangular prefabricated building modules: A BIM-based comparative study
abstract: Building geometry influences energy demand and the environmental performance of buildings; however, the impact of alternative modular geometries remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates the effects of square and regular hexagonal module geometries on energy performance, operational CO₂ emissions, and modular design potential using small railway station buildings as a case study. BIM models were developed in Archicad and analysed using the EcoDesigner STAR energy simulation tool. Two single-storey buildings with identical floor area, internal volume, envelope thermal properties, occupancy schedules, and HVAC systems were compared. The investigated variables included building geometry, orientation, and glazing configuration. In addition, the modular potential of both geometries was assessed by analysing spatial configuration possibilities, prefabricated component requirements, external wall length, and the envelope-to-volume ratio (A/V).The results demonstrated that the single-module hexagonal building achieved, on average, a 21.1% lower total net energy demand than the square reference building due to its more favourable compactness and lower A/V ratio. The most energy-efficient hexagonal configuration was obtained when the external walls were oriented towards NW, N, NE, SE, S, and SW, with one of the principal façades facing south. South-facing windows consistently produced the lowest energy demand, confirming the dominant role of solar exposure and glazing orientation. Increased solar gains reduced heating demand but simultaneously increased cooling requirements, largely independently of building geometry. For compact multi-module configurations (A/V ≈ 1.1), the influence of module shape became negligible, indicating that overall building compactness is more important than individual module geometry. The hexagonal module also reduced operational CO₂ emissions by approximately 1 kgCO₂/(m²·year), provided substantially greater configuration flexibility, and required fewer prefabricated component types than the square alternative. The findings indicate that regular hexagonal modules represent a promising alternative to conventional rectangular modular systems, combining lower operational energy demand and CO₂ emissions with enhanced design flexibility. The proposed approach may support the development of energy-efficient modular buildings and transport infrastructure facilities.

title: Optimal capacity configuration of a solar–air source heat pump system coupled with dual thermal storage under different heating scenarios in northern rural China
Ultra-short-term air-conditioning load forecasting using a spatio-temporal graph network based on multi-scale frequency-band reconstruction
From policy contexts to compliance pathways: a review of practical definitions of net-zero carbon buildings
abstract: The Paris Agreement has accelerated global climate action, prompting countries to formulate policies that steer buildings toward net-zero carbon emissions. This review critically examines the practical definitions of “net zero” in the building sector by comparing core NZCB standards with selected jurisdictional implementation instruments. Three key features of current Net Zero Carbon Buildings (NZCBs) are identified: the elimination of direct fossil fuel use, alignment of building operational performance with explicit efficiency targets, and adoption of carbon reduction credits with defined constraints. A dynamic NZCB framework is proposed, incorporating these features and embedding large-scale building decarbonization into a pathway for regulatory compliance. The study emphasizes the importance of NZCB frameworks that link national and local conditions to clearly articulated decarbonization responsibilities. The findings not only provide actionable guidance for policymakers but also offer researchers an in-depth perspective on current industry transformation trends and the evolving landscape of net-zero carbon building strategies.

title: System boundaries in positive energy district assessment: a systematic review
abstract: Positive Energy Districts (PEDs) are prominent in European district-energy policy, but published assessments use heterogeneous spatial, energy-domain, temporal, carbon-accounting, and grid-interaction boundaries. Previous reviews have focused on definitions, tools, and implementation challenges, while the boundary–model–outcome relationship has received less systematic attention. Following PRISMA 2020, this review included 104 peer-reviewed studies published between 2012 and 2026. Of these, 80 studies focused directly on PEDs, PENs, PEBs, or related positive/net-zero district and community concepts and formed the Tier-1 analytical corpus; 21 boundary-sensitivity cells from 13 studies formed the graded outcome-evidence synthesis. In the Tier-1 corpus, electricity-only and electricity-plus-heat scopes accounted for 32/80 studies (40.0%), 45/80 (56.3%) used hourly or sub-hourly simulation within an annual criterion, and 2/80 (2.5%) imposed an explicit physical exchange constraint. Across all 21 evidence cells, six (28.6%) crossed a technical, economic, carbon-accounting, or classification threshold, but only one was a direct controlled crossing; the other five involved re-optimisation, coupled assumptions, or design changes. Quantitative and same-case quantitative subsets yielded 6/12 and 6/11 threshold crossings, respectively, with one direct controlled crossing in each set. Boundary choices therefore influence admitted loads, resources, credits, and exchanges, while these cell-level shares characterise the evidence map rather than the prevalence of reversals across the wider PED literature. We propose a six-element reporting framework and routine boundary-sensitivity testing to improve comparability and decision relevance.

title: A hybrid DTW-KMeans and transformer model for predicting occupants' window-AC co-regulation behavior in mixed-cooling bedrooms of hot-humid climates
SCAle-BEM: self- and cross-consistent agentic LLM/VLM framework for geometry identification and automated building energy modeling
Comparative life cycle assessment (LCA) of glued laminated bamboo structure versus conventional structural systems: A case study of three-storey frame structure
The dual impact of solar green façades on indoor energy performance and outdoor microclimate in a hot-Humid Desert campus residential building
Delivered-energy and operative-temperature trade-offs for learned-probability-informed HVAC supervision in a weather stress grid
Architectural style as a rapid proxy for city-scale energy retrofit prioritization
Green façades and climate resilience: A comparative analysis across retrofit scenarios for an Italian building archetype in two representative climatic contexts
abstract: Accounting for 32% of global energy consumption, buildings not only impact climate change but are also affected by it. To address these challenges, in addition to decarbonising the building stock, there is a need to implement climate-resilient solutions that enhance climate adaptation. The proposed study explores the energy efficiency and climate resilience of non-traditional solutions like green façades for a representative Italian residential building archetype in two distinct climate zones, Rome and Turin, under current (2020s) and projected (2050s and 2090s) climate scenarios. The green façade is analysed using a detailed calculation tool implemented within the EnergyPlus (version 23.2) energy simulation software. The analysis covers both existing buildings without insulation and buildings retrofitted with insulation, solar shading, and ventilative cooling. Results indicate that green façades—particularly when applied to multi-orientations of the building—can significantly reduce cooling need and overheating in pre-retrofit buildings, with reductions of up to 59% and 85%, respectively. In retrofitted buildings, green façades offer additional benefits beyond standard retrofit packages, with further cooling need reductions of up to 24.7% and decreasing overheating by up to 54.8%. Although their relative effectiveness generally declines with climate change due to rising temperatures and reduced plant evapotranspiration, green façades continue to provide relevant benefits even under the 2090s scenario. A comparison between the two climate zones reveals greater cooling reductions in Rome due to higher summer heat loads and lower winter heating penalties. These findings underscore the green façade potential as a passive design strategy to support the transition towards more sustainable and climate-resilient residential buildings.

title: Natural language processing and shapes constraint language-based method for green building compliance validation
Energy consumption as a census proxy: Occupancy dynamics and residential energy benchmarks in collective housing in Algiers
Energy implications of reducing COVID-19 risk with different clean-air delivery solutions. A simulation study in a school
abstract: Present simulations examined the energy performance of different solutions for delivering clean air at a rate that keeps the secondary infections arising from one infected student in a school, entering a classroom over a week, ≤0.9. Only airborne transmission with SARS-CoV-2 was considered, and the infection occurring in the far field. Simulations were made in the school building in a temperate climate during the heating season. Infection risk was modelled using the Wells-Riley equation, and energy use using IDA ICE. The tested solutions comprised natural ventilation by window opening with and without portable HEPA air cleaners, extract ventilation with exhaust fans with and without portable HEPA air cleaners, mechanical ventilation with heat recovery with and without recirculation combined with improved filtering. Ventilation scenarios meeting ASHRAE Standard 62.1 and Standard 241 requirements and the Center for Disease Control’s recommendations were also simulated. The calculated risk levels and energy use reflect the assumptions made, and simulations must be repeated in other climates. Nevertheless, the results can be used to draw general conclusions regarding the direction that should be taken to develop sustainable technical solutions for reducing the risk of infection by clean air delivery with the least possible energy use. The results showed that the most energy-efficient solution was adding portable air cleaners in classrooms, and the least energy-efficient one was the extract ventilation using an exhaust fan, also comparable to open windows providing the same outdoor air rate. Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery was more energy efficient than extract ventilation. Recirculating the air through an efficient filter in the ventilation system was less energy efficient than using portable air cleaners.

title: Evaluating thermal and condensation performance of detachable secondary glazing for single-glazed window retrofits
Smoothly clipped absolute deviation penalized low-rank imputation for univariate building energy consumption: from statistical method to statistics-informed deep learning
Indoor temperature forecasting and control in hydronic systems using grey-box models and model predictive control: A field experiment
abstract: Accurate indoor temperature forecasting is critical for effective indoor climate control and energy-efficient building operation. In radiator-heated buildings, a key modelling challenge is the dynamic discrepancy between the indoor air temperature experienced in the room and the local temperature measured at thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs). This discrepancy is often simplified as a constant offset, although it can vary during operation due to radiator activity, weather conditions, and local room dynamics. This paper presents a field implementation of a non-linear grey-box room model integrated in a model predictive control (MPC) framework for hydronic space heating in a school building. The model explicitly distinguishes between the indoor air temperature and the TRV sensor temperature and was deployed for rolling temperature forecasting and control in three classrooms during an experimental period from 28 February to 11 March 2025. The MPC maintained the measured indoor temperature within the comfort bounds for 90.3 % to 95.5 % of the evaluated period across the classrooms. Rolling forecast errors for indoor temperature were moderate, with room-level RMSE values between 0.47 ∘ C and 0.56 ∘ C. In the independent recursive multi-step validation, the indoor temperature RMSE at the 24-hour horizon remained between 0.50 ∘ C and 0.73 ∘ C, while TRV sensor temperature forecasts showed slightly larger errors. Benchmark reruns further indicated that the non-linear MPC formulation was computationally feasible for a 30-minute control interval under typical operating conditions (median 17.5 s, 95th percentile 37.6 s wall-clock time). The results demonstrate the practical feasibility of using a dynamic non-linear grey-box model with TRV dynamics in an operational MPC setting and highlight implementation challenges that remain important barriers to large-scale deployment of MPC-based room-level MPC in buildings.

title: Occupant-centric control of automated solar shading devices in office buildings: A systematic review of input variables, control strategies, and system integration
Identifying the influence area of point thermal bridges in walls through numerical heat flux vector analysis
Energy assistant for buildings: A knowledge-augmented multi-agent framework for market-integrated and occupant-centric energy management
abstract: The growing complexity of modern buildings integrating distributed energy resources such as photovoltaic systems (PV), battery energy storage systems (BESS), electric vehicle (EV) charging stations, heat pumps (HPs) and smart appliances require more intelligent and coordinated energy management strategies. In this context, building-level assistants capable of jointly managing energy assets, occupant comfort and electricity market participation remain largely underexplored. This paper proposes an Energy Assistant for Buildings (EAB) acting as a micro-aggregator based on a hierarchical edge-to-fog architecture that coordinates room-level control, building-level optimization and electricity market interaction. Unlike conventional building energy management systems that typically optimize assets in isolation, rely on fixed supervisory rules or require computationally intensive reinforcement-learning training, the proposed EAB integrates deterministic optimization with knowledge-augmented multi-agent reasoning to coordinate building flexibility, occupant comfort and market participation within a single feasible and safety-constrained decision framework. The Optimizer computes feasible operational schedules and baseline trading strategies, while the Trader and Controller refine these decisions using contextual knowledge and feedback-informed reasoning. Simulation results for an office building equipped with PV, BESS, EV charging and flexible loads demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework. Over a 90-day interval, the framework achieves a Grid Dependence Index (GDI) of 27%, Self-Sufficiency Index (SSI) of 73%, Self-Consumption Index (SCI) of 89%, reducing electricity costs by 84%. Thus, combining hierarchical optimization with knowledge-guided agentic reasoning improves energy autonomy, market responsiveness and economic performance of smart buildings.

title: Experimental and simulation of multilayer phase change material-aerogel roof tiles: a novel passive cooling solution
Re-imagining risk evaluation of building energy retrofit: A BRIDGE framework
Beyond RMSE: Do the most accurate building load forecasts deliver the most operational value?
Thermography-based method to estimate radiative heat fluxes on whole body for local thermal comfort evaluation
abstract: Radiative heat exchange is a key determinant of human thermal comfort, because it accounts for approximately half the heat exchange between the human body and its surroundings in indoor environments. In residential environments, insufficient thermal performance often results in the surfaces of windows and exterior walls having excessively low or high temperatures, causing local thermal discomfort due to radiative heat exchange even when the mean radiant temperature remains within a thermally acceptable range. Therefore, this study develops a novel method for estimating incident radiative heat flux (RHF) distribution on whole body for evaluating the effects of the non-uniform radiant environments on human thermal comfort. The method integrates spherical thermography with a digital manikin model and was validated using one seated nude thermal manikin in a climate chamber under four radiant conditions. The estimated RHF showed consistent agreement with pyrgeometer measurements at 19 validation locations. Furthermore, application of the method to a representative residential environment with lower insulation performance showed that the conventional evaluation index based on radiant-temperature asymmetry satisfied the ISO 7730 criterion, with a maximum value of 2.7 °C for plane radiant temperature (PRT) in the vertical direction. In contrast, the proposed method revealed a maximum equivalent radiant-temperature difference of 5.3 °C between body parts. These results demonstrate that the proposed method can characterize body-part-specific variations in radiant exposure that are not directly represented by conventional PRT asymmetry.

title: What should be automated in offices? Occupants' preferences for automation levels from a large survey in Spain and the Netherlands
abstract: Occupant-centered building control requires defining not only which building services should be automated but also the role occupants prefer to retain in the control loop. However, empirical evidence remains fragmented across single services, leaving a gap in understanding how preferred automation levels varies across building services and daily routines. This study establishes an evidence-based typology for occupant-centered building automation, mapping preferences across ten services and three workday phases through a large-scale questionnaire of 3,504 office workers in the Netherlands and Spain. Using a consistent five-level automation scale, we map preferences across ten building services and three distinct workday phases (arrival, active work, and leaving). Results show that automation preferences are context-dependent, varying according to the specific building service and the current workday phase. HVAC systems, particularly mechanical ventilation, show the strongest acceptance of automated control, whereas directly reachable elements, such as openable windows and personal devices, are predominantly preferred under manual control. A primary finding of this study is the prevalence of 'mixed-control' profiles (61.5% of respondents), showing that occupants' desire for personal control is service-dependent. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence of the interaction strategy gap, demonstrating that higher automation acceptance is statistically contingent upon digital, desk-reachable, and information-rich control interfaces. Prior experience with automated systems emerged as the most consistent predictor of acceptance of automation, suggesting that trust in the control loop is experience-based. These findings argue against one-size-fits-all automation and provide empirical basis for designing adaptive, service-specific control strategies that balance building energy goals with occupant agency.

title: Occupant's thermal responses in non-uniform radiation environment: efficient radiation vs conventional radiation
Techno-economic optimization of waste heat recovery in actual supermarket refrigeration systems using Genetic Algorithm
abstract: This study evaluates the performance of integrated transcritical R744 supermarket refrigeration systems implementing waste heat recovery in two real case studies in Stockholm (Sweden) and Nordborg (Denmark). The integration of geothermal false load (FL) and an R600a heat pump with R744 booster supermarket refrigeration systems was analyzed and compared for heat export to the district heating network (DHN). In addition, the integration of geothermal FL with advanced R744 configurations incorporating parallel compression (PC) and ejectors (EJ) was also analyzed. The analysis incorporated real thermal loads, DHN characteristics, electricity prices, ambient temperature, and the costs associated with buying and selling heat. A genetic algorithm was employed to minimize the total operating cost of the integrated systems over the winter period from October 1, 2024, to April 30, 2025. The performance was benchmarked against a baseline configuration in which an R744 booster refrigeration system meets the cooling demand while space heating is supplied entirely by the DHN. Additionally, the initial investment cost, operating cost savings, and simple payback period (SPP) were evaluated for all integrated configurations. The results indicated that integrated systems could achieve annual cost savings of €12,463–€14,442 for the Stockholm supermarket and €3,089–€4,099 for the Nordborg supermarket. Among the integrated configurations, the R600a heat pump integrated system was found to have the most favorable economic performance, with SPP of 3 years in Nordborg and 4.4 years in Stockholm.

title: DELFT-UBEM: An automated database-driven pipeline for district-scale building energy modeling, demonstrated on Dutch district retrofit
abstract: District-scale energy transition planning requires building-level energy profiles, yet current Urban Building Energy Modeling (UBEM) workflows require substantial manual data preparation with no integrated path from building registries to scenario comparison. This paper presents DELFT-UBEM, an automated tool that generates dynamic simulation models from building registries and national performance standards through a lookup-table architecture that maps building age, function, and energy label to physical parameters, translating regulatory documents into simulation-ready parameters within a unified, database-driven pipeline. The pipeline shifts repeated project-level preparation into reusable database, lookup-table, and configuration components: once these components and a geographic boundary are available, data ingestion, geometric processing, archetype assignment, Input Data File (IDF) generation, parallel simulation, and post-processing execute as a connected automated workflow, producing analysis-ready results for downstream policy evaluation. Against national benchmarks, the model reproduces structural variation in Dutch residential heating demand across 35 archetypes without building-specific calibration. Comparison with measured postcode-level gas consumption across 63 postcodes (~3,000 buildings) corroborates this at aggregate scale, with residual errors systematically traceable to known data barriers and modeling limitations. To demonstrate downstream analytical capability, two contrasting Dutch districts were used to define custom retrofit and electrification applications, producing path-dependent marginal abatement cost curves with building-level sequencing across 3,404 upgrade steps. The paper discusses open challenges in UBEM validation standards and cross-tool comparability, highlighting how the pipeline’s modular architecture supports continuous refinement. The complete pipeline, archetype library, and parameter mappings are published as open-source resources, and DELFT-UBEM is accessible as a web-based digital twin platform.

title: From shallow data to deep insights: A dual-layer information augmentation framework for urban building energy management
Study on the performance of a composite phase change material roof with diurnal/nocturnal radiative sky cooling in the hot season
Vision-physics fusion unlocks ventilation flexibility for occupancy-centric control in large airport terminals
A change-point model-based inverse surrogate framework for building and operational parameter inference
abstract: Building parameter characterization is essential for energy performance assessment and retrofit planning, but detailed audits and calibrated simulations are difficult to scale across large building portfolios. This study proposes an inverse surrogate modelling framework to infer unknown building and operational parameters, including internal gains, after-hours plug-load operation, ventilation rate, after-hours ventilation, heating and cooling setback temperature offset, solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) and effective envelope performance (U eff ), from the change-point model (CPM) features extracted from heating and cooling loads. Physics-based simulations were used to generate datasets for four building archetypes across four Canadian weather files, with three weather files used for model development and one reserved as an entirely unseen climate for generalization testing. For each simulation case, occupied and unoccupied heating and cooling CPMs were fitted, and their balance temperatures, slopes, intercepts, and fit-quality metrics were used as inputs to archetype-specific machine learning models. The trained models achieved strong predictive accuracy on the test set, with R 2 values generally ranging from 0.82 to 0.98 across the seven targets and four archetypes. Internal gains, U eff and temperature offset were among the most accurately predicted parameters, with R 2 values of 0.89–0.98 and CV(RMSE) values mostly below 0.18. When evaluated on the entirely unseen weather file, the models maintained promising generalization performance, with most outputs achieving R 2 values above 0.85. Overall, the proposed framework offers a scalable pathway for rapid virtual audits and portfolio-level building characterization.

title: Non-intrusive HVAC scheduling for PV and comfort optimization: A cross-climate predict-then-optimize pipeline
abstract: As solar generation scales across the grid, the bottleneck for decarbonization shifts from production to consumption and the ability of buildings to adapt their largest loads to match renewable availability. Thermal conditioning accounts for a dominant share of building energy demand, and balancing HVAC load shifting with comfort constraints is further complicated by the absence of dense sensor infrastructure in legacy buildings. This paper presents a climate-agnostic, data-driven predict-then-optimise pipeline for HVAC load shifting that maximizes photovoltaic self-consumption while preserving thermal comfort as quantified by the PMV-PPD index. The framework operates in three stages. First, an unsupervised disaggregation algorithm extracts heating and cooling operational states directly from aggregated smart meter readings, eliminating the need for sub-metering. Second, a regime-aware hybrid forecasting architecture combining Temporal Convolutional Networks, LightGBM, and CNN-LSTM models, predicts indoor temperature and relative humidity at the horizon required for comfort-aware scheduling. Third, a predict-then-optimize scheduling loop couples a MILP-based dispatcher which aligns HVAC operation with photovoltaic generation under soft comfort bounds, with the trained forecasting models, repurposed here as comfort simulators that iteratively detect and repair constraint violations, forming a closed-loop control scheme. The framework is validated on two heterogeneous real-world datasets: a residential energy community in Greece (Mediterranean climate,dual heating-cooling regime) and a commercial office complex in Thailand (tropical climate, cooling-only regime). The hybrid forecaster achieves a Mean Absolute Error below 1°C across both test environments. In the first case, the scheduler improves PV self-consumption by an average of 67% while raising occupant comfort by 13%. In the second case, the framework identifies and corrects thermally aggressive AC profiles, yielding a 10.7% comfort improvement and a 16% reduction in overall HVAC activity.

title: Safe mean-field reinforcement learning for cooperative control of large-scale multi-zone HVAC systems
abstract: Efficient control of HVAC systems is essential for reducing building energy consumption while maintaining indoor environmental quality. However, in multi-zone scenarios, strong thermal coupling among zones, together with interactions among temperature, CO 2 concentration, and humidity, results in highly nonlinear and strongly coupled dynamics, thereby significantly increasing the complexity of control decisions. Furthermore, as the number of zones grows, the joint state–action space expands rapidly, leading to the curse of dimensionality and difficulties in coordinated optimization. Consequently, traditional methods struggle to achieve both scalability and satisfactory control performance. To address these challenges, we develop a dynamic optimization model for multi-zone HVAC systems, where multi-variable coupled control is formulated as a multi-agent decision-making problem, capturing both inter-zone and inter-variable interactions. Building upon this, we propose a Safe Mean-Field TD3 (SMF-TD3) algorithm to enable efficient and scalable cooperative control. Specifically, mean-field theory is introduced to approximate individual interactions via aggregated behaviors, thereby reducing system complexity and enabling scalable decision-making. Meanwhile, to satisfy thermal comfort, air quality, and equipment safety constraints, a Lagrangian-based safe reinforcement learning mechanism is adopted, where constraints are embedded into policy optimization and Lagrange multipliers are adaptively updated to balance performance and constraint satisfaction. Finally, in the seven-day, 12-zone simulation, SMF-TD3 reduces electricity cost by 3.37% relative to CPO and 17.11% relative to MADDPG, and cumulative constraint violations by 75.05% relative to MF-TD3. Across the 12-, 20-, and 30-zone systems, training time is reduced by 52.48%–58.44% relative to MASAC, supporting improved economic performance, constraint satisfaction, and scalability under the tested conditions.

title: Modeling global vertical solar illuminance on building façades using adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems under all-sky conditions
abstract: Global vertical illuminance on building façades is used in daylighting analysis, façade performance assessment, and energy-efficient building design. However, direct measurements are rarely available at conventional meteorological stations, limiting assessments involving different orientations, sky conditions, and interannual variability. This study develops an ANFIS-based methodology to estimate global vertical illuminance for the four cardinal orientations (north, east, south, and west) using only commonly available radiometric and geometric variables: direct normal irradiance (DNI), diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI), and the cosine of the incidence angle on each façade. Models were trained using 115,250 records from 2024 and evaluated using 750,294 records across six independent years (2019–2023 and 2025) to assess temporal robustness. Results show that the models adequately reproduce global vertical illuminance for all façades under all-sky conditions. Over the six independent years, normalized root mean square error (nRMSE) ranged from 9.91% to 22.60%, and normalized mean absolute error (nMAE) ranged from 6.44% to 15.83%. The largest errors occurred for the north-facing façade, whereas the east-, south-, and west-facing façades maintained nRMSE values of 16.50% or lower. The methodological contribution lies in directly estimating LGV from commonly available radiometric variables and façade incidence geometry, without requiring vertical irradiance measurements, explicit sky classification, or intermediate luminous-efficacy calculations. These results support the use of the proposed approach to estimate LGV at the study site when direct vertical measurements are unavailable. Transferability to other locations should be assessed through independent validation.

title: Data-driven assessment of north–south differences in urban thermal stress perception in Chinese Cities
Thermal resilience and passive survivability of residential buildings during extreme temperature events and power outages: Implications for household energy security
Virtual smart metering in district heating networks via heterogeneous spatial-temporal graph neural networks
abstract: Intelligent operation of thermal energy networks aims to improve energy efficiency, reliability, and operational flexibility through data-driven control, predictive optimization, and early fault detection. Achieving these goals relies on sufficient observability, requiring continuous and well-distributed monitoring of thermal and hydraulic states. However, district heating systems are typically sparsely instrumented and frequently affected by sensor faults, limiting monitoring. Virtual sensing offers a cost-effective means to enhance observability, yet its development and validation remain limited in practice. Existing data-driven methods generally assume dense synchronized data, while analytical models rely on simplified hydraulic and thermal assumptions that may not adequately capture the behavior of heterogeneous network topologies. Consequently, modeling the coupled nonlinear dependencies between pressure, flow, and temperature under realistic operating conditions remains challenging. In addition, the lack of publicly available benchmark datasets hinders systematic comparison of virtual sensing approaches. To address these challenges, we propose a heterogeneous spatial-temporal graph neural network (HSTGNN) for constructing virtual smart heat meters. The model incorporates the functional relationships inherent in district heating networks and employs dedicated branches to learn graph structures and temporal dynamics for flow, temperature, and pressure measurements, thereby enabling the joint modeling of cross-variable and spatial correlations. To support further research, we introduce a controlled laboratory dataset collected at the Aalborg Smart Water Infrastructure Laboratory, providing synchronized high-resolution measurements representative of real operating conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating the potential of graph-based learning to support efficient, reliable, and flexible operation of modern district heating systems.

title: A load-based dynamic testing method for residential air conditioners: from linear load profiles to multi-node virtual building loads
Online model-based reinforcement learning for building energy systems
abstract: Reducing the energy cost while maintaining comfort in buildings is a heavily researched area.Using more sophisticated control algorithms like model predictive control (MPC) or reinforcement learning (RL) are promising approaches.Unfortunately MPC and RL are rarely adopted in real applications since their initial configuration is cumbersome and complex.Especially model free RL architectures need long interaction times to learn a sufficiently accurate control policy.Model-based RL (MBRL) architectures instead combine MPC and RL to tremendously speed up the learning process while also inheriting the robustness of MPC.The model consists of Gaussian Processes (GP), which are capable to quantify the uncertainty of the model.This work combines MBRL with online learning of the GPs with a maximum datapoint budget, alleviating the need for episodic learning while also incorporating new unseen datapoints into the controller.We show that our online learned agents need only one day worth of initial training data to outperform a rule-based PI-controller.

title: Data-driven thermal comfort control in UK schools using evolutionary surrogate inversion: An offline prescriptive analytics study
abstract: Existing thermal comfort control strategies primarily optimise temperature settings, with limited integration of occupant behaviour or prescriptive optimisation. We present an inverse optimisation framework pairing machine learning surrogate models with Differential Evolution (DE) for prescriptive thermal comfort control in UK schools. The framework is evaluated on a fixed optimisation subset of 330 test instances from the ASHRAE Korsavi dataset. The best-performing surrogate configuration (Gradient Boosting with DE) achieved surrogate-predicted successful outcomes in 99.1% of cases (67.3% under independent PMV verification) with a mean heating adjustment of 1.31 ∘ C, representing a 39% reduction compared with temperature-only control. Post-hoc PMV verification confirmed 222/330 analytically comfortable outcomes for the recommended configuration. Clothing adjustment alone resolved 38% of cold classrooms without requiring HVAC intervention. The reproducible framework is available here , providing school managers with a practical, low-cost toolkit to maintain thermal comfort while reducing the temperature-adjustment energy proxy. This is an offline surrogate-inversion analysis; results represent analytical recommendations rather than a deployed real-time control system.

title: Configuration-aware selection of PV-battery home energy management strategies under day-ahead demand forecast uncertainty
An innovative applied holistic analytical tool for prescriptive maintenance in the residential sector
abstract: This paper presents a novel holIstic ANalytical Tool FOr PRescriptive Maintenance (INFORM), designed to enhance the reliability and efficiency of home appliances by integrating AI-driven anomaly detection, and automated prescriptive recommendations. Unlike conventional predictive maintenance approaches that require extensive historical, household-specific data before they can be deployed, INFORM combines an offline, cross-device meta-trained model with real-time power consumption analysis, enabling fault detection from the moment of deployment without requiring pre-collected historical data from the specific household or appliance instance, and is subsequently refined through local retraining as real-time data accumulates. Using Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) combined with an Autoencoder-Convolutional Neural Network (AE-CNN), the proposed framework adapts to various household appliances, ensuring accurate fault diagnosis and targeted intervention strategies. The experiments, conducted on washing machines, dishwashers, and clothes dryers, demonstrate improvements in anomaly detection performance and proactive maintenance support, while an illustrative assumption-based analysis indicates the potential of INFORM to support energy-efficiency improvements and Demand-Side Management. The results highlight the potential of INFORM to transform home appliance maintenance into an adaptive, real-time, and prescriptive approach, with the potential to contribute to sustainability and cost reduction in residential energy management.

title: Residential load archetype extraction under low-carbon technology adoption using two-stage DTW meta-clustering
abstract: Understanding household electricity consumption patterns is essential for accurate residential demand modelling, flexibility services, and customer-centric energy interventions. This paper introduces a two-stage clustering framework for half-hourly residential electricity profiles from 495 households in Great Britain, with a sample enriched in low-carbon technology (LCT) adopters. In Stage 1, each household’s 48-point daily net-balance profiles are clustered using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) with a constrained Sakoe–Chiba window. In Stage 2, the resulting 2,511 household-level centroids are re-clustered using DTW to derive 50 cross-household meta-clusters. The proposed approach is benchmarked against Euclidean and unconstrained DTW alternatives. Constrained DTW selected 5.07 clusters per household on average and produced partitions that were distinct from Euclidean clustering (ARI = 0.24 ) while retaining moderate agreement with unconstrained DTW (ARI = 0.71 ). Reconstruction of the clustered profiles achieved range-normalised MAE of 4.0 ± 1.4% at household-centroid level; applying the global meta-clusters to individual households increased this to 5.0 ± 1.8%. At the aggregate level, the constrained-DTW representation produced a range-normalised MAE of 4.7%, with high-demand tiers retaining peaks within the adopted ± 3 h window for 95.5–96.7% of assigned household-days. The constrained DTW implementation required 6.6 times the Euclidean runtime on average, slightly below unconstrained DTW at 6.8 times, while preserving behaviourally interpretable timing features. The resulting archetype library supports demand modelling, flexibility characterisation, and tariff or scheduling studies for LCT-enriched samples.

title: Low-carbon technological innovation diffusion among prefabricated component enterprises: Evolutionary dynamics in weighted networks
An adaptive time-step model integrating empirical mode decomposition and long short-term memory with dynamic updates for building heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning load prediction
Design parameters for the construction of energy-efficient living modules in military bases and barracks
GTNet-CI: A thermal prediction surrogate model using graph-transformer networks with channel-independent for hybrid cooling data centers
A knowledge-based fault diagnosis library for air handling units with diagnostic Bayesian networks in commercial buildings
abstract: Diagnostic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) offer a practical trade-off for Air Handling Unit (AHU) fault diagnosis, but existing studies rely on limited expert input or single building experiments and rarely publish their model parameters. This study developed a framework for building a Knowledge-Based AHU Fault Diagnosis Library through semi-structured interviews with 17 Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning professionals from three companies. The library provides the structure and parameters to develop a DBN for AHU fault diagnosis in commercial buildings. In a case study, a Knowledge-Based DBN (KDBN) derived from the library was compared against a Literature-Based DBN (LDBN), parameterized from published literature, and a Data-Driven DBN (DDBN) serving as an internal benchmark, parameterized from Building Management System data. The KDBN identified reference faults within the top two ranked faults for six of seven symptoms without prior calibration, demonstrating acceptable diagnostic performance. The LDBN identified reference faults for only three of seven symptoms, suggesting that direct parameter adoption from published literature is insufficient. The DDBN achieved top two identification for all seven symptoms, though its parameters were derived from the same dataset used to define the Experimental Benchmark. Sensitivity analysis confirmed that uniform prior probability scaling has a limited influence on diagnostic rankings, while variable prior probabilities have a greater influence. These findings suggest that a KDBN derived from the library shows promising agreement with the Experimental Benchmark, and that the library may provide a useful starting point for DBN-based AHU fault diagnosis when labeled, building-specific fault data are unavailable.

title: Modeling heat and moisture transfer in photovoltaic greenery canopies under subtropical hot humid conditions
Towards zero-carbon housing: a tri-layered, systematic review of market failures, institutional voids and financing gaps in Sub-Saharan Africa

A staged assessment framework for demand-response flexibility under operational constraints in central chiller–storage cooling systems serving batch-process cooling loads: A field-measured large-facility case
Thermal performance of EPS-Core reinforced concrete Sandwich panels with EPS-modified concrete wythes: An experimentally validated numerical parametric study
Thermal comfort assessment in extreme heat conditions: a multi-method study of building performance and occupant response in hot semi-arid climate
Toward sustainable cooling in hot–arid climates: techno-economic evaluation of a four-stage indirect evaporative cooling system
Multi-model methodology for urban development scenarios and evaluation of future city-scale building energy efficiency
abstract: Built structures in cities affect urban surface energy balances and local microclimates. To understand and quantify effects of urban form on local micrometeorology, high-resolution urban parameter inputs to numerical simulation models are needed. Furthermore, with changes in large-scale climate conditions and increasing urban population density, the capability to assess the impact of new buildings and their collective morphology (shape and layout) on building energy demand under future weather conditions is important but understudied. This is because new built infrastructure is difficult to project at decadal scales. To address this challenge, we have developed a chain of models that generates ensembles of plausible future neighborhoods for a given city and evaluates their building energy use under current and future weather conditions. Energy use is reported as total and per-building annual energy consumption (kBtu and kBtu) and, where floor-area normalization is available, as energy use intensity (EUI; kBtu/ft 2 /year). This model chain integrates population predictions, high-resolution city-scale land-use and land-cover change projections, Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-generated building footprints, heights, and locations for new neighborhoods based on historical training examples and urban scaling theory, and future building archetypes with and without energy-saving technologies that are evaluated using a building energy model. Here, we describe the components of this modeling chain and demonstrate, using an example morphological projection under a population-intensification scenario, how projected neighborhood morphology, future weather, and energy-saving technologies is evaluated alongside building energy use in Los Angeles County. Our example shows that, for the current residential building stock simulated under end-of-century SSP5-8.5 weather, EUI increases by 5.72%, indicating higher energy demand under warmer and more humid future conditions. EUI for large office buildings increases by only 0.51%, indicating a lower sensitivity to the change in weather conditions. For the projected 2100 morphology, future weather EUI use by 6.9% for residential buildings and 8.4% for large office buildings relative to simulations using current typical meteorological conditions. Overall, these results show that future weather increases building energy demand, although the magnitude of the increase varies by building type and projected urban morphology. Because this initial experiment does not couple the projected morphology to a numerical weather simulation, it does not capture local microclimate feedbacks caused by changes in urban form. However, retrofit measures reduce annual per-building energy use by up to 19.6% for residential buildings and 17.4% for commercial buildings, suggesting a potential path forward for energy-efficient urban planning.

title: Energy vulnerability from a building perspective: An EPC-based assessment and retrofitting analysis in the Basque country
abstract: Energy vulnerability is increasingly recognised as a structural issue linked to the energy performance of the residential building stock. Conventional expenditure-based indicators may underestimate its extent because financially constrained households can reduce consumption below adequate comfort levels. This study proposes an alternative approach based on estimated energy requirements derived from Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs). Using administrative data representing 11,902 dwellings in the Debabarrena region of the Basque Country, Spain, energy vulnerability is measured through Foster–Greer–Thorbecke indices. The analysis also evaluates the potential effect of simulated energy-efficiency improvements. It shows that the incidence of energy vulnerability falls from 12.08% initially to 7.37% after potential G-to-F improvements and to 4.23% when eligible G-rated dwellings reach an E-equivalent consumption level. These results indicate that targeted renovation of the least efficient dwellings could substantially reduce structural energy vulnerability and provide policymakers with a practical basis for prioritising buildings and areas for further rehabilitation assessment and support.

title: A high-temporal-resolution interpolation framework for time-series downscaling based on time-domain decomposition and deep learning: A case study of building occupancy data
Neutral temperature, cool preference and the limits of adaptive-slope estimation in naturally ventilated social housing under low outdoor variability, Mexico
abstract: This study reports a field investigation of adaptive thermal comfort in the A(C)w1 Köppen-García climate (semi-warm subhumid, moderate altitude) of Mexico, based on 614 cross-sectional surveys collected on 125 field dates between July 2024 and December 2025 in naturally ventilated social housing in Chilpancingo de los Bravo, Guerrero (1264 m a.s.l.). Outdoor temperature was reconstructed from ERA5-Land reanalysis with a local bias correction ( R 2 = 0.884 ), and neutral temperature was derived with the Griffiths method using an empirically calibrated constant of 0.225 K − 1 . Seasonal mean neutral temperatures ranged from 25.5 to 26.2 °C (overall mean 25.8 °C) with overlapping confidence intervals. The adaptive slope could not be reliably estimated over the observed range of the prevailing mean outdoor temperature ( T rm ; R 2 < 0.001 for four running-mean formulations): with the observed SD ( T rm ) of 0.65 °C, the power to detect the ASHRAE 55 reference slope was 18.8%, and about 1.7 °C would be required for 80% power under the present assumptions. The winter–summer difference in mean clothing insulation was 0.02 clo. The Predicted Mean Vote (PMV), computed with a validated ISO 7730 implementation, reproduced the mean observed sensation (bias + 0.10 ) but compressed its range (slope 0.47 against the thermal sensation vote, TSV). Although the sensation distribution was near-symmetric, 43% of occupants preferred cooler conditions versus 4% warmer, 33% still preferred cooler when reporting neutrality, and thermal satisfaction was highest for cool sensations, a pattern consistent with thermal alliesthesia. These sample-specific findings provide preliminary local evidence for future multi-site evaluation of comfort criteria and are not proposed as provisions for building standards.

title: From single optima to near-optimal insulation ranges: A life-cycle-based method for façade retrofit decisions under decarbonising heat supply
abstract: Building retrofits are often assessed through operational energy, while embodied impacts of façade insulation are overlooked. This becomes critical when fossil heating systems are replaced by heat pumps, as lower operational impacts heighten the significance of embodied impacts from insulation. This study considers both contributions. It determines optimal insulation thicknesses based on their combined life-cycle impacts. Life-cycle impact curves over insulation thickness often show shallow minima. The analysis therefore identifies the thinnest insulation thickness within 1% and 5% of the minimum. These bounds indicate material savings while maintaining near-minimum impacts. Dynamic building energy simulation was combined with life-cycle assessment for a reference German single-family house from 1958 to 1968. The façade retrofit was evaluated for GWP, ADPF, and PE under current and 2040 climate scenarios. Heat-supply included a natural-gas boiler and a heat pump. The heat pump was tested with current and future electricity mixes. Four materials were assessed: EPS, mineral wool, wood fibre, and straw. Thicknesses ranged from 0 to 40 cm, with multiple product-specific datasets. Lower-bound near-optimal thicknesses are substantially below exact optima. With heat pumps, future electricity, and 2040 climate, median GWP optima are 12 cm for EPS and 17 cm for wood fibre. The 5% lower bounds are 5 and 6 cm, respectively. For PE, median optima are 16 cm for EPS and 9 cm for wood fibre. The lower bounds are 6 and 3 cm. At stock level, lower-bound solutions reduce insulation volume by 70–85% versus a uniform 20 cm retrofit.

title: Short-term cooling-load forecasting and chiller capacity recommendation with physics-enhanced residual-change LSTM
Uncertainty-aware explainable multi-horizon building load forecasting with reservoir computing
abstract: The European Union (EU) is at a pivotal juncture in its energy policy, driven by global energy transitions and the pressing need to combat climate change. Buildings, which account for approximately 40% of total energy consumption and 36% of carbon dioxide emissions in the EU, represent a critical area for optimization. This study proposes an advanced explainable multi-horizon building demand forecasting framework based on Reservoir Computing (RC), enhanced with Monte Carlo dropout(MCd) to quantify predictive uncertainty and an out-of-distribution (OOD) detection mechanism for robust interval forecast validation. The framework leverages the computational efficiency of RC, combined with probabilistic forecasting techniques, to deliver accurate multi-step energy load predictions across diverse operational conditions. Experimental results demonstrate improved forecast measured by multiple metrics, stable prediction intervals that increase under OOD scenarios, and enhanced reliability compared to baseline models. The integration of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), provides detailed insights into the temporal and contextual drivers of energy demand. Key benefits include improved decision-making for energy managers, enhanced occupant comfort, optimized HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning) operations, and seamless integration of renewable energy sources. This framework aligns with the EU's European Green Deal target of carbon neutrality by 2050, offering a scalable solution for smart building energy management. The methodology also supports regulatory compliance, reduces operational costs, and mitigates risks associated with unpredictable energy demand fluctuations.

title: A machine learning-driven framework for mapping urban heat Island governance zoning
Passive design strategies in Indian green building rating systems: A comprehensive review on GRIHA, IGBC, ASSOCHAM GEM, and BEE frameworks
Evaluating the performance of seasonal borehole thermal storage in 5th generation district heating and cooling networks
abstract: The operating temperature range of borehole fields includes low-temperature levels that may be suitable for fifth-generation district heating and cooling (5GDHC) networks, while also enabling bidirectional heat exchange and seasonal thermal storage. However, their performance depends on network temperature management, the balance between annual heat extraction and injection, and local ground conditions. This study investigates how supply- and return-temperature set-points affect short-term heat-pump coefficient of performance (COP) through their influence on the borehole entering-fluid temperature; whether cooling-season charging improves winter COP and seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) while mitigating long-term thermal drift; and whether year-round bidirectional operation or explicit summer recharge better supports multi-year thermal stability. An integrated TRNSYS model combining a low-temperature network, building-level water-to-water heat pumps, and a composite borehole-field model was used to simulate hourly and multi-year operation under three ground configurations, including an idealised representation of groundwater-induced temperature stabilisation. The results show that the heat pumps meet building thermal demands within the 5GDHC operating range, achieving SCOP values between 3.41 and 3.88. Maintaining a higher borehole entering-fluid temperature through appropriate temperature and mass-flow control improves heat-pump COP. Cooling-season charging improves winter performance and mitigates thermal drift when sufficient injected heat is retained in the ground. Balanced thermal-demand operation therefore provides greater multi-year thermal stability than heating-dominated operation with limited recharge.

title: Editorial Board
Lagged and cumulative associations between thermo-hygrometric exposure and video-derived behavioral engagement in naturally ventilated university classrooms
HVAC demand-management strategies in a simulated Bangkok medium office: Effects on peak demand, energy, comfort, and cost
One-year demonstration of remote-controlled residential heat pump water heaters toward coordinated demand response in Japan
abstract: Increasing photovoltaic penetration in Japan has intensified periods of very low daytime day-ahead electricity prices. Specifically, from April 2024 to March 2025, prices hit 0.01 JPY/kWh for a total of 97.5 h. This situation highlights the need for practical demand-side flexibility. Residential heat pump water heaters (HPWHs) represent a promising flexible load, however, evidence on the long-term and frequent remote control of commercially available HPWHs under Japanese operating conditions remains limited. This study developed a demonstration system in which hot-water demand measured in a collaborator's home occupied by a family of three was reproduced in a dedicated test house, referred to as the COMMA House. The system scheduled daily water heating in the COMMA House using day-ahead market prices downloaded once per day around noon, and HPWH status and hot-water demand at both homes were monitored hourly via a smartphone application throughout an approximately one-year demonstration from April 2024 to March 2025. The monitoring success rate reached 98.6% (excluding periods with intentional router shutdown), supported by retry and fallback handling. The required water-heating duration varied seasonally by a factor of 2.87 and showed a strong correlation with outdoor temperature (R 2 > 0.95). Under a day-ahead price-linked tariff in the Tokyo area (FY2024), daily price-based scheduling reduced annual water-heating electricity charges from 71,963 JPY (midnight heating) to 65,177 JPY, achieving savings of 6786 JPY (9.4%). In addition, retrospective alternative strategies showed additional savings potential, increasing the annual reduction rate to 11.2% by considering observed seasonal variation of water-heating time, and to 12.4% by utilizing non-consecutive lowest-price time slots.

title: Energy-efficient window coatings for sustainable buildings
Household allocation to professional heat-resilient renovation guidance: Cooling-cost value and professional evaluation in Singapore
abstract: Residential renovation is an important implementation point for design choices that can shape indoor thermal comfort and cooling-related energy use over many years. Yet technically relevant measures can influence dwelling performance only if they enter household renovation decisions. Using original survey data from 570 respondents in Singapore, this study examines the maximum share of a renovation budget that households state they would allocate to the same specified package of professional heat-resilient renovation guidance covering ventilation, shading, airflow, materials, layout, and cooling-related choices. Respondents selected among seven allocation ranges from zero to more than 5% of the renovation budget. Positive stated allocation is widespread (92.5%), but only 14.9% allocate at least 3% and 6.3% more than 5%. The perceived value of an anticipated 10% reduction in cooling-related electricity costs is strongly and consistently associated with higher stated allocation. For allocation of at least 3% of the renovation budget, each one-category increase in perceived cooling-cost value is associated with an approximately 9-percentage-point increase in predicted probability. Two distinct dimensions of professional evaluation—confidence that expert renovation and design advice can improve indoor thermal comfort and perceived professional attention to thermal comfort—are jointly associated with stated allocation, although their individual associations vary across different levels of stated allocation. By contrast, reported thermal conditions, cooling use, and renovation priorities provide less consistent evidence once other factors are considered. The findings identify an upstream household decision that precedes the implementation and subsequent performance of heat-resilient renovation measures. The results are associational and concern hypothetical stated allocation rather than realised renovation decisions, market demand, or measured thermal and energy outcomes.

title: A multi-agent actor-critic framework for smart home energy scheduling under uncertainty and user-centric constraints
A clustering-based framework to analyse intra-building variability in residential energy performance using geometric descriptors
abstract: Understanding variability in residential energy performance at dwelling level remains challenging due to the combined influence of physical characteristics, occupant-related factors and data privacy constraints. This study uses a demonstrator building to propose clustering-based methodological framework to analyse intra-building variability while preserving data anonymity. Dwelling typologies are defined exclusively using geometric and solar exposure descriptors, avoiding the inclusion of energy variables and preventing feedback between classification and evaluation. Energy performance is subsequently assessed using Weather-Normalised Heating Energy Intensity and Degree-Hours of Discomfort analysed at daily resolution and aggregated at monthly and interannual scales. The methodology is demonstrated through its application to a social housing building over three consecutive winter seasons. Results reveal differentiated patterns of energy use across typologies, which remain consistent in their relative behaviour over time despite seasonal variations in magnitude. However, a substantial level of variability is observed within clusters, indicating that similar geometric configurations can be associated with markedly different energy performance outcomes. In contrast, thermal deficit remains generally low and appears as intermittent events, with no consistent relationship to the geometric descriptors considered. The combined analysis highlights a partial decoupling between energy use and indoor thermal conditions, indicating that energy consumption alone does not fully represent indoor performance. From a methodological perspective, the proposed framework enables the identification of useful typological patterns for several stakeholders while supporting privacy-aware analysis through cluster-based aggregation. The approach provides a methodological basis for analysing residential energy performance in privacy-sensitive contexts and supports the detection of atypical behaviour at building scale.

title: Hydration-state-dependent multi-mode passive cooling in bio-based alginate–cellulose semi-IPN hydrogels with confined erythritol and titanium dioxide
Comparative evaluation of borehole heat exchanger efficiency in different climatic zones of European capital cities
abstract: Borehole heat exchanger (BHE) systems are key components of ground-source heat pump systems for renewable building heating and cooling; however, their design and long-term performance are strongly governed by climate-driven thermal loads, subsurface thermal properties, and borefield configuration. This study presents a standardized, design-oriented comparison of BHE performance across 11 European capital cities spanning ASHRAE climate zones from hot/dry to cold/humid conditions, using the same 1600 m 2 university-building archetype. Building thermal loads were evaluated using CitySim Pro with Meteonorm climatic data and subsequently coupled with city-specific ground thermal conductivity, volumetric heat capacity, and undisturbed ground temperature in GLHEPro. Two 40-borehole configurations, compact rectangular and open-rectangular, were evaluated at identical 10 m borehole spacing over a 30-year operating horizon while maintaining heat-pump entering-fluid temperature within 0–40 °C. The GLHEPro framework was independently benchmarked against a first-principles Excel–VBA model based on ASHRAE and EED formulations, and ground thermal conductivity and volumetric heat capacity were additionally subjected to ±30% sensitivity variations. The required 30-year borehole depth ranged from approximately 98.3 m in Vienna to 253.9 m in Helsinki, corresponding to about 158% regional variation under otherwise standardized system conditions. The open-rectangular configuration reduced long-term borehole thermal interference and produced approximately 15–20% lower depth requirements in several cases, while cumulative heat-pump electricity consumption was also reduced. A ± 30% variation in ground thermal conductivity produced approximately ±8–19% variation in required depth, compared with ±4–9% for volumetric heat capacity, confirming the stronger design sensitivity to thermal conductivity. The results demonstrate that BHE sizing cannot be reliably transferred between climatic regions without simultaneous consideration of building-load imbalance, ground thermal characteristics, and borefield geometry. The proposed framework provides a climate-responsive basis for early-stage BHE design and comparative shallow-geothermal assessment across Europe.

Vernacular local energy factors (VLEF): A barrier to generalizable local-level building energy estimation for Decarbonization planning
abstract: Urban Building Energy Modelling (UBEM) accessibility challenges for a growing diversity of stakeholders hampers effective translation of the approach to energy efficiency and decarbonization policy evaluation for buildings. Vernacular Local Energy Factors (VLEFs) manifest as spatial variability in model performance stemming from the tradeoff between the generalizability and localizability of parameterizations in the absence of data. A high spatial and temporal resolution validation of a bottom-up UBEM framework was carried out at a prefectural scale in Japan to gauge the spatial variability of model performance using hourly gridded smart meter data to understand the prevalence and impact of VLEFs. The model demonstrated generalizability despite the lack of high-resolution building data with validation standards being met for 62% of electricity consumption at the municipal-monthly level and 84% of households at the municipal-annual level. However, localized poor model performance revealed potential VLEFs caused by water heating parameterization. Calibrating the model to account for this VLEF led to quadrupling the decarbonization potential of water heating electrification, highlighting an example of the material impact of VLEFs. Localized data pipelines through cross-jurisdictional cooperation should be established to ensure communities are not disadvantaged due to data infrastructure gaps striving for equitable modelling and policy evaluation towards national climate goals.

A Hierarchical Energy Management Strategy for Real-Time Control of Residential PV–Battery Systems Under Forecast Uncertainty
abstract: The increasing adoption of PV–BESS systems by residential prosumers requires effective energy management. However, combining long horizon economic scheduling and battery aging with uncertainty aware real time operation on limited local hardware remains challenging. To address this issue, this paper proposes a hierarchical EMS with three levels that accounts for degradation and is coordinated through an Energy Router. L1 solves a 24h LP problem that considers calendar and cyclic battery aging and provides terminal SoC limits to L2. L2 formulates a short moving horizon Multiparametric Linear Programming (MPLP) problem in which the load, PV power, and initial SoC are treated as parameters. Its offline solution generates critical regions and their associated affine control laws. Based on local measurements, L3 performs Real Time Decision Making (RTDM) by identifying the active critical region and applying the corresponding power references. Results show that, after analytically removing the constraints that prevent simultaneous grid exchange and battery operation, the LP produces the same dispatch as the MILP model and solves in 0.0358 s, compared with 495.62 s for the NLP model. For the selected day, calendar and cyclic aging account for 28.39% and 71.61% of the total degradation, respectively. Over the selected 4h interval, the daytime MPLP generates 1064–1285 regions in less than 155 s for the different uncertainty ranges tested, while the case without PV generates 302–326 regions in less than 70 s. A 2h closed-loop validation under forecast deviations of up to 30% demonstrates the adaptability of RTDM, while comparison with implicit LP-MPC confirms identical operating results with approximately 17.8 times faster online computation. Accordingly, the proposed EMS concept is aligned with a cloud and edge architecture, where the cloud would perform heavy computations, while the edge would perform lightweight and fast local RTDM.
